1.1.1:
*Concerning the nine guides of scholars*
Whoever enters upon that rough, arduous, and long journey, which with constant labor finally leads to the high temple of the nine Muses, seems to require nine guides for this journey. Of these, the first three lead us in heaven, the next three in the mind, and the last three on earth. In the beginning, Mercury, in heaven, either compels or encourages us to undertake the investigation of the Muses’ path. For the duty of all investigation is attributed to Mercury. Then, Phoebus himself illuminates both the seeking minds and the objects sought with such abundant splendor that what was sought is clearly found by us. Then comes the most graceful Venus, mother of the Graces, and she arranges and adorns the whole matter in such a way, with her nourishing and joyful…
1.1.2: …gifts, that whatever was sought through the urging of Mercury and already found through the guidance of Phoebus is suffused with a certain marvelous and healthy charm by Venus, so that it might always delight and benefit. The three guides of this journey who follow in the mind are, namely, an ardent and stable will, sharpness of wit, and a tenacious memory. The last three, on earth, are the most prudent head of the household, the most approved teacher, and the most skillful physician. Without these nine guides, no one ever could or ever will be able to arrive at the temple of the nine Muses itself. God Almighty and nature have primarily bestowed the other guides upon us from the beginning, but our own diligence must provide the last three. Many wise men of antiquity have treated the precepts and duties that pertain to the head of the household and the teacher regarding literary studies, especially our Plato, both often elsewhere and most diligently in his books on the Republic and the Laws. Then Aristotle in his Politics, and Plutarch and Quintilian also did so admirably. However, there has been no physician thus far for students of letters to reach out a hand to those traveling, and to assist those whom neither heaven, nor mind, nor head of household, nor teacher has abandoned, with healthy advice and medicines. Therefore, I, having pitied the most laborious lot of those who pursue the difficult journey that drains the nerves of Minerva, am the first to come forward as a physician to the weak… and the infirm, but would that I had the ability as complete as my intention is favorable. Rise now, adolescents, led by God, cheerfully. Rise, young men and mature men, whom the overly ardent study of Minerva exhausts. Come willingly to the physician, who, with God showing the way and favoring, bestows upon you healthy advice and remedies for the perfection of your undertaking.

1.2.1:
*How much care must be taken of the brain, the heart, the stomach, and the spirit*
In the beginning, just as athletes are accustomed to take care of their legs and arms, and musicians of their voice, so too should students of letters take care of the brain, the heart, the liver, and the stomach. Indeed, they should take even greater care, insofar as these members are more excellent than those, and they use these members more frequently and for more important tasks than athletes use theirs. Furthermore, every skillful craftsman takes the most diligent care of his tools: the painter his brushes, the smith his hammers and anvils, the soldier his horses and weapons, the hunter his dogs and birds, the lute-player his lute, and everyone else similarly. But the priests of the Muses alone, the hunters of the highest good and truth, are so negligent (alas, the shame) and so unfortunate that they seem to neglect entirely that instrument by which they can, in a certain way, measure and comprehend the whole world. An instrument of this kind is the spirit… itself, which physicians define as a certain vapor of the blood, pure, subtle, warm, and bright. And from the heat of the heart itself, created from the most subtle blood, it flies to the brain, and there the mind uses it assiduously to exercise both internal and external senses.
1.2.2: Wherefore the blood serves the spirit, the spirit the senses, and the senses finally the reason. The blood, however, is made by the natural virtue that thrives in the liver and stomach. The thinnest part of the blood flows into the source of the heart, where the vital virtue thrives. From there, spirits created ascend to the citadels of the brain and (if I may say so) of Pallas, in which the animal force, that is, the power of sensing and moving, dominates. And so, contemplation is almost as much like the compliance of the sense itself. Moreover, the sense is such as the spirit is: the spirit is such as the blood is: and those three powers which we have mentioned, namely the natural, the vital, and the animal, are such as they are from those by whom, through whom, and in whom the spirit itself is conceived, born, and fostered.

1.3.1:
*That those devoted to literature are prone to phlegm and black bile*
Not only must those devoted to literature take the most diligent care of those members, forces, and spirits, but they are also commanded to avoid phlegm and black bile no differently than sailors avoid Scylla and Charybdis with the utmost caution. For as much as they are idle in the rest of their body… they are busy in their brain and mind. From this, they are compelled to generate phlegm, which the Greeks call phlegma phlegm, and from this, black bile, which the same people call melancholia melancholy. The former often dulls and suffocates the wit; the latter, if it should abound or flare up too much, vexes the mind with constant care and frequent delusions and disturbs judgment. So it could not undeservedly be said that the learned would be perfectly healthy if phlegm were not a nuisance, and they would be the happiest and wisest of all if, due to the defect of black bile, they were not often forced to grieve or sometimes to lose their reason.

1.4.1:
*How many causes there are by which the learned are, or become, melancholic*
That the learned are melancholic is caused by three primary types of causes. The first is celestial, the second natural, the third is human. The celestial [cause exists] because Mercury, who invites us to investigate doctrines, and Saturn, who brings it about that we persevere in investigating doctrines and keep what has been found, are said by the astronomers to be in a certain way cold and dry. Or if by chance Mercury is not cold, he is nevertheless often, by his proximity to the Sun, very dry, which is the nature that physicians call melancholic. Mercury himself and Saturn impart this same nature to students of letters and their followers from the beginning, and they preserve and increase it… daily. Moreover, the natural cause appears to be that, in order to pursue sciences, especially difficult ones, it is necessary for the soul to withdraw from external things to internal ones, just as if from a certain circumference to the center, and while it contemplates, to remain most stably in that very center (so to speak) of the human being. Indeed, to gather oneself from the circumference to the center, and to be fixed in the center, is most characteristic of the earth itself, to which black bile is very similar. Therefore, black bile continually provokes the soul to collect itself into one, to stand in one place, and to contemplate. And, being similar to the center of the world, it forces one to investigate toward the center of individual things and raises the mind to comprehend the highest things: since it corresponds most closely with Saturn, the highest of the planets. Contemplation itself also, in turn, by a certain continuous collection and as it were compression, contracts a nature very similar to black bile.
1.4.2: Truly, the human cause arises from us. Since frequent agitation of the mind dries out the brain vehemently, therefore, with the humor largely consumed (which is the fuel for natural heat), the heat also is usually extinguished in large part, whence the nature of the brain turns dry and cold, which is indeed named a terrestrial and melancholic quality. Furthermore, because of the most frequent motion of inquiry, the spirits also are continually resolved by the motion. But it is necessary that the resolved spirits be restored from the more subtle blood. Wherefore, with the more subtle and clearer parts of the blood often consumed, the remaining blood is necessarily rendered dense, dry, and black.
1.4.3: The remaining blood is necessarily rendered dense, dry, and black. Added to this is the fact that nature, in contemplation, being intent entirely on the brain and heart, abandons the stomach and liver. Therefore, because the nourishment, especially if it is richer or harder, is poorly digested, the blood becomes cold, thick, and black from this. Finally, due to the excessive idleness of the limbs, neither are the superfluities excreted, nor do the glutinous, tenacious, and dark vapors exhale. All these things usually make the spirit melancholic, and the mind sad and fearful. Since interior shadows, much more than exterior ones, occupy the mind with sorrow and terrify it.
1.4.4: Truly, those of all learned men who are most oppressed by black bile are those who, devoted to the diligent study of philosophy, withdraw the mind from the body and bodily things, and join it to incorporeal things: both because the work is quite difficult and requires a greater intention of the mind, and because insofar as they join the mind to the incorporeal truth, to that extent they are compelled to disjoin it from the body. Hence their body is sometimes rendered as if half-alive and melancholic. This, indeed, our Plato signifies in the Timaeus a Socratic dialogue by Plato concerning the nature of the physical world, saying that the soul, contemplating divine things most often and most intensely, grows and becomes so powerful through such nourishment that it surpasses its own body more than the nature of the body can suffer, and sometimes, by its own more vehement agitations, it either escapes it in some way, or sometimes seems as if to dissolve it.

1.5.1:
*Why the learned are ingenious, and who among them are of this kind, or otherwise*
Thus far, it should be enough to have shown, by reasons first celestial, second natural, and third human, for what cause the priests of the Muses are melancholic, whether they are so from the beginning or become so by study. This, indeed, Aristotle confirms in his book of Problems a collection of Aristotelian inquiries: “For he says that all men who are excellent in any faculty have been melancholic.” In which matter, he confirmed that Platonic saying written in the book on science: namely, that ingenious men are accustomed to be very agitated and furious. Democritus also says that no men who are great in genius can ever exist except those who are stirred by a certain frenzy. This, indeed, our Plato seems to prove in the Phaedrus a dialogue by Plato concerning the soul and love, saying that the gates of poetry are knocked upon in vain without frenzy. Even if he perhaps wishes for divine frenzy to be understood here, yet no such frenzy is ever stirred up among natural philosophers in any others, except the melancholic. Next, however, the reasons must be assigned by us why Democritus, Plato, and Aristotle assert that some melancholics occasionally excel all others in genius to such a degree that they seem not human, but rather divine.
1.5.2: Democritus, Plato, and Aristotle assert this without a doubt, yet they do not seem to explain the reason for such a great matter sufficiently. Nevertheless, we must dare (with God as our guide) to investigate the causes.
1.5.3: Melancholy (that is, black bile) is twofold: the one is called natural by physicians, the other occurs through combustion. Natural melancholy is nothing other than a denser and drier part of the blood. But that which is combusted is distributed into four species. For it is conceived by the burning of either natural melancholy, or purer blood, or bile, or salty phlegm. Whatever is born from combustion harms judgment and wisdom: for when that humor is ignited and burns, it is accustomed to make men agitated and furious; which the Greeks call mania frenzy, but we call fury. But when it is already being extinguished, with the more subtle and clearer parts resolved, and only the dark soot remaining, it renders them dull and stupid, which state they properly call melancholy, amentia, and madness. Therefore, only that black bile which we called natural leads us to judgment and wisdom. Yet not always. Indeed, if it is alone, by its excessively dense mass it darkens the spirits, terrifies the soul, and blunts the genius.
1.5.4: But if it is mixed with simple phlegm, when cold blood has obstructed the region around the heart, it brings on sluggishness and torpor through a certain thick coldness, and as is the nature of every very dense material, when such melancholy grows cold… it is intensified to the summit of coldness. In which state nothing is hoped for, all things are feared, and one grows weary of beholding the vaults of heaven. If black bile, either simple or mixed, putrefies, it generates a quartan fever, tumors of the spleen, and many things of the same kind. When it exuberates too much, whether it is alone or joined with phlegm, it makes the spirits thicker and colder. It continually affects the soul with tedium, blunts the sharpness of the mind, and the blood does not leap around the region of the heart.
1.5.5: However, it is necessary that the black bile be neither so sparse that the blood, bile, and spirits lack a bridle, whence it happens that the genius is unstable and the memory labile; nor so abundant that we appear to doze off, weighed down by excessive burden, and in need of spurs. Therefore, it is necessary that it be, as much as its nature allows, most subtle. For if it has been thinned as much as its nature allows, it will perhaps be able to exist in great quantity without harm; and even so much that it seems to equal the salty bile in weight.
1.5.6: Therefore, let black bile abound, but let it be very thin; let it not lack the humor of more subtle phlegm infused around it, lest it dry out completely and turn very hard. Yet let it not be mixed entirely with phlegm, especially if it be colder or in great quantity, lest it grow cold. But let it be mixed with bile and blood in such a way that one body is fashioned from the three, composed in a double proportion of blood to the other two. Where there exist eight parts of blood, two of bile, and two again of portions of black bile. Let it be ignited somewhat… from those two other humors, and once ignited, it shines; yet it is not consumed, lest it should burn and agitate too vehemently, as the harder material is wont to do while it boils. Truly, while it cools, it likewise chills to the summit. For black bile, like iron, when it is strongly directed toward cold, chills to the summit; when, on the contrary, it declines toward hot, it heats to the summit. Nor should it seem a wonder that black bile can be easily ignited and, once ignited, burn with great intensity. For we see lime, which is similar to it, begin to boil immediately when sprinkled with water and then burn. Melancholy possesses such great power toward both extremes, stable in the unity of a fixed nature. Indeed, this extremity does not occur in the other humors. When heated to the highest degree, it provides the greatest boldness, even ferocity; when chilled to the extreme, it produces fear and extreme cowardice. When affected by degrees midway between cold and heat, it produces various emotions, not unlike unmixed wine, which, being especially potent, is wont to induce various emotional states in those who drink to the point of drunkenness or even a little more freely. Therefore, it is necessary that the black bile be opportunely tempered. When it is thus moderated, as we have said, and mixed with bile and blood, because its nature is both dry and, by its condition, as thin as its own nature allows, it is easily ignited by them. Because it is solid and very tenacious, once ignited, it blazes for a very long time, for it is most potent in the unity of its tenacious dryness, and it heats up with great intensity.
1.5.7: Just as if wood and straw are both ignited, they heat and glow more intensely and for a longer time. Moreover, from prolonged and intense heat, a great radiance and a vehement and lasting motion proceed. Heraclitus points to this: A dry light is the wisest soul.

1.6.1:
*How black bile renders men ingenious*
Someone might perhaps ask: what is the nature of that body, composed of those three humors in the proportion we have mentioned? In color, it is nearly like the gold we see, but it inclines somewhat toward purple. And when it is ignited, as much by natural heat as by the motion of the body or the soul, it heats and glows almost like ignited and reddening gold mixed with purple, and, like the rainbow, it draws forth various colors while the heart burns. Someone might ask again: in what way does a humor of this kind contribute to genius? Indeed, the spirits created from this humor are, in the first place, subtle, not unlike that water which they call the water of Life or the Vine, and Burning, whenever it is expressed from thicker wine by a certain distillation toward fire, as is wont to be done. For the spirits, compressed within the narrower channels of this black bile, are attenuated to the maximum by a more intense heat due to its unity, and being forced through tighter passages, they burst forth more subtly. Then, they are warmer likewise and for the same reason, they are clearer; third, they are agile in motion and most vehement in action; fourth, flowing steadily from a solid and stable humor, they serve action for a very long time. Our soul, relying on such service, investigates vehemently and persists in investigating for a longer time. It easily finds whatever it has investigated, perceives it clearly, judges it sincerely, and retains its judgments for a long time. Add that, as we have indicated in the preceding pages, the soul, through an instrument or incitement of this kind, which in a certain way corresponds to the center of the world and (if I may say so) gathers the soul into its own center, always seeks the centers of all things and penetrates their innermost parts. Moreover, it corresponds with Mercury and Saturn; the latter, being the highest of all the planets, raises the investigator to the highest things. Hence, singular philosophers emerge, especially when the soul is thus recalled from external motions and its own body, and, being as close as possible to the divine, becomes an instrument of divine things. Whence, filled from on high with divine influxes and oracles, it always conceives of new and unusual things and predicts the future. This is affirmed not only by Democritus and Plato, but also confessed by Aristotle in his book of Problems and Avicenna in his book on Divine Things and his book on the Soul. Why so much about the humor of black bile? So that we may remember how much this black bile—or rather, this white bile—is to be sought and nurtured as something excellent, just as that which stands against it, as we have said, is to be avoided as something most evil. For it is such a dire thing that Serapio said its impulses are instigated by an evil demon, and the wise Avicenna did not deny it.

1.7.1:
*The five chief enemies of the studious: namely Phlegm, Black Bile, Sexual Intercourse, Satiety, and Morning Sleep*
BUT to return to that from which we have now digressed quite far, the road that leads to truth and wisdom is very long, full of heavy labors of land and sea. Whoever, therefore, undertakes this journey, as some poet might say, is often endangered on land and sea. For whether they navigate the sea, they are tossed continually among the waves—that is, the two humors, namely phlegm and that harmful melancholy—as if between Scylla and Charybdis. Or if they travel by land (if I may say so), three monsters immediately confront them. The first is earthly Venus, the second is Bacchus and Ceres, the third is nocturnal Hecate, whom they frequently oppose. Therefore, Apollo from the ether, Neptune from the sea, and Hercules from the earth must often be called upon so that Apollo may pierce these monsters —enemies of Pallas—with his arrows, Neptune may subdue them with his trident, and Hercules may crush and lacerate them with his club. The first monster is indeed sexual intercourse, especially if it exceeds one’s strength even a little. For suddenly it exhausts the spirits, especially the more subtle ones, weakens the brain, and undermines the stomach and the heart’s region there can be no greater enemy to genius than this evil. Why did Hippocrates judge sexual intercourse to be similar to the falling sickness? Except because it strikes the mind, which is sacred, and is so harmful that Avicenna said in his book on Animals: if any sperm flows out in intercourse beyond what nature can tolerate, it does more harm than if forty times that much blood had been lost. Thus, not without reason did the ancients wish the Muses and Minerva to be virgins. That Platonic remark points here: when Venus threatened the Muses that she would arm her son against them unless they worshipped the rites of Venus, the Muses replied: “O Venus, threaten Mars with such things. For your Cupid does not fly among us.” Finally, nature has separated no sense further from intelligence than touch. The second monster is satiety of wine and food. For if wine is either too much or too hot and vehement, it will fill the head itself with the worst humors and fumes. I pass over the fact that drunkenness makes men insane. Excessive food, indeed, first calls back all the power of nature to the stomach to digest it. Whence it happens that it cannot attend to the head and to speculation at the same time. Then, being improperly digested, it blunts the edge of the mind with many thick vapors and humors. Furthermore, even if it is digested sufficiently, as Galen says, the soul, suffocated by fat and blood, can barely perceive anything celestial. cannot believe it. Finally, the third monster is to stay awake frequently until late at night, especially after supper, which forces you to sleep after the sun has risen. Since many students err and are deceived in this matter, I shall explain at length how much it harms their genius and provide seven primary reasons for this. I draw the first from the heavens themselves, the second from the elements, the third from the humors, the fourth from the order of things, the fifth from the nature of the stomach, the sixth from the spirits, and the seventh from the imagination.
1.7.2: In the beginning, three planets, as we stated above, favor contemplation and eloquence most of all: the Sun, Venus, and Mercury. These, moving almost in equal steps, flee from us as night approaches; yet they rise again and revisit us when the day approaches or has already dawned. But after sunrise, they are suddenly thrust into the twelfth region of the sky, which astronomers assign to prison and darkness. Therefore, those who do not study at night when the planets flee from us, nor after sunrise when they enter the house of prison and darkness, but rather when they are either nearly approaching the dawn or are already rising—those who rise themselves to contemplate and write—are the only ones who speculate most acutely and who write and compose their findings most eloquently. The second reason, which is drawn from the elements, is as follows: when the sun rises, the air is moved, thinned, and brightened; but when it sets, the opposite occurs. Furthermore, blood and spirits… are necessarily compelled to follow the quality of the surrounding air and a similar nature. The third reason, which is derived from the humors, is of this kind. At dawn, the blood is moved and reigns supreme, and by its movement, it is thinned, warmed, and clarified; the spirits, indeed, are accustomed to follow and imitate the blood. But as night approaches, that heavier and colder melancholia black bile and pituita phlegm dominate, which undoubtedly render the spirits very inept for speculation. The fourth reason, which is drawn from the order of things, shall be this: the day is given to wakefulness, the night to sleep. For when the sun either approaches our hemisphere or travels over it, it opens the pores of the body with its rays and dilates the humors and spirits from the center to the circumference, which indeed excites and conduces to wakefulness and action. Conversely, however, when it withdraws, everything is contracted, which by a certain natural order invites sleep, especially after the third or fourth part of the night. Therefore, whoever is drowsy in the morning when the sun and the world are stirring, but stays awake until late at night when nature commands us to sleep and rest from our labors, this person without a doubt resists the order of the universe and also himself, while he is troubled and distracted by contrary movements at the same time. Indeed, while he is moved by the universe toward the exterior, he moves himself toward the interior; and conversely, while he is drawn by the universe toward the interior, he meanwhile withdraws himself toward the external. Therefore, by a perverse order and contrary movements, both the whole body and the spirit and the genius are utterly undermined.
1.7.3: In the fifth place, we argue from the nature of the stomach in this manner. The stomach is dilated significantly as the pores open during the long activity of the daytime air, and the spirits eventually become quite weakened as they fly out. Therefore, as night comes on, it demands a new supply of spirits by which it may be comforted. Wherefore, whoever begins long and difficult contemplations at that time strives to pull those very spirits toward the head. But these, being distracted, suffice neither for the stomach nor for the head. It is especially harmful if, after supper, we sit up late and apply ourselves too attentively to such studies. For at that time, the stomach requires more spirits and much heat to digest the food. These two things are diverted toward the head by such late-night study. The result is that they are sufficient for neither the brain nor the stomach. Add to this that the head, because of such movement, is filled with thicker vapors from the food, and the food in the stomach, deprived of heat and spirit, becomes raw and putrid, whence it again clogs and harms the head. Finally, in the morning hours, when one must rise so that each member may be purged of all the excrements retained during sleep, the very worst thing happens: one who had completely interrupted digestion by staying up at night is forced to hinder the expulsion of excrements for longer by sleeping in the morning. All physicians consider this to be most harmful to both genius and body. rightly, therefore, those who use the night instead of the day against nature, and conversely the day instead of the night, like owls, also imitate owls in this—even if unwillingly—that just as their eyes grow dim under the light of the sun, so also does the edge of their mind grow dim under the splendor of truth. In the sixth place, the same is proven from the spirits. By daily fatigue, the spirits—especially the most subtle ones—are eventually resolved. Therefore, at night, only a few thick spirits remain, which are most inept for the study of letters, so that the genius can fly upon the maimed wings of these spirits no differently than bats and owls. Conversely, however, in the morning after sleep, when the spirits are refreshed and the members so corroborated that they require very little aid from the spirits, many subtle spirits are present, which may serve the brain and obey more readily, being little occupied in comforting and directing the members. Finally, the seventh reason is derived from the nature of the phantasia imagination in this way: the phantasia, or imagination, or thought, or by whatever other name it should be called, is distracted and troubled by staying awake with many long and contrary images, thoughts, and cares. This very distraction and perturbation is extremely contrary to subsequent contemplation, which generally requires a mind that is thoroughly tranquil. Only by nocturnal rest is that agitation finally calmed and pacified. Therefore, when night approaches, we set ourselves to studies with a mind that is always troubled; but when it departs, as is usually the case… we set ourselves to our studies with a tranquil mind. However, whoever attempts to judge things while the mind is too agitated, they are no different from those who suffer from vertigo, who think everything is spinning (as Plato says) when they themselves are spinning. Wherefore, Aristotle wisely commands in his Oeconomica Economics that one should rise before light, and he asserts that this benefits the health of the body and the study of philosophy as much as possible. But this must be understood in such a way that by a light and moderate supper we very diligently avoid morning indigestion. Finally, that holy poet David, the trumpet of the omnipotent God, never says that he rises in the evening, but always in the morning and at dawn to sing to his God with the lyre and with psalms. We ought to rise in mind at that hour entirely, and soon also in body, if only it can be done conveniently.

1.8.1:
*Which hour is more opportune for beginning studies, or what is the method of continuing*
From those things which have been discussed above, it is now almost sufficiently clear that we initiate our studies most opportunely either at sunrise or at most an hour or two before the sun rises. But before you rise from bed, rub the whole body a little and gently with your palms, then the head with your nails, but that a little more lightly. Let Hippocrates advise you in this matter. For, he says, if friction is vehement, the body is hardened… if it is light, it should be softened; if there is much, it should be diminished; if it is moderate, it should be replenished. When you have risen from bed, do not immediately devote yourself to reading or meditation. Grant at least half an hour to some form of evacuation, then diligently prepare for meditation, which you will prolong for about an hour, as your strength allows. Afterward, relax the tension of your mind for a little while, and in the meantime, comb your hair diligently and moderately with an ivory comb, drawing the comb from the forehead toward the nape of the neck forty times. Then, rub your neck with a somewhat coarse cloth. Finally, having returned to meditation, dedicate two additional hours, or at least one hour, to study. Indeed, studies can sometimes be prolonged until the noon hour, provided that some intervals of rest are taken. Furthermore, even during the day, though rarely, unless we are compelled to take food, we should do so around two hours after midday. For the sun is powerful around its rising, and it is also powerful in the middle of the sky. In that region of the sky which immediately follows the meridian, which the astronomers call the ninth house and the house of wisdom, the Sun takes the greatest delight. Since all poets wish Phoebus to be the leader of the Muses and the sciences, it is fitting that if anything deeper needs to be thought out, it should be considered during these hours. If the Muses are to be sought, let them be sought in these same hours with Phoebus as guide. For the remaining hours seem better adapted to reading the works of the ancients and others, rather than devising new things of one’s own. However, we must always remember that we should relax the tension of our minds at least once every hour for a short while. For when the spirits are dissipated due to such tension, you will rightly become sluggish if you never cease to strain. While you work with your mind, meanwhile let your body rest. Fatigue of the body is bad, fatigue of the mind is worse, and both together are the worst of all, tearing a man apart with opposing movements and destroying his life. Finally, let meditation proceed no further than is pleasurable, and indeed, keep it on this side of that limit.

1.9.1:
*Rules for Avoiding Phlegm*
It seems worthwhile to repeat briefly those things which we have said are harmful to the learned, and to apply remedies to each. Therefore, so that phlegm is not increased too much, one should use exercise daily while the stomach is nearly empty, yet never so laborious that the subtle spirits are dissolved. Excrements must be purged most diligently from all bodily passages. Impurities from the skin of the entire body, and especially of the head, should be wiped away thoroughly through both washing and friction. Cold foods should be avoided, and—unless black bile hinders—so should moist foods, and altogether any foods that are fatty, poisonous, viscous, oily, and glutinous, or those that easily putrefy. If the stomach is cold either by nature or by age, the drinking of water must either be abandoned entirely or at least diminished. Food should be moderate, but drink should be more moderate still. The dwelling place should be high, far removed from heavy and cloudy air, and humidity should be expelled through the use of fire and warm scents. Cold must be kept from the head, and especially from the neck and feet, for this is very harmful to the intellect. The moderate use of spices in colder meals is beneficial, especially nutmeg, cinnamon, saffron, and also ginger preserved in sugar, taken in the morning on an empty stomach, which is also very beneficial for the senses and memory. and far removed from heavy and cloudy air. Humidity should be expelled through the use of fire and warm scents. Cold must be kept from the head, especially from the neck and the feet, for this is very harmful to the intellect. A moderate use of spices is beneficial in colder meals, especially nutmeg, cinnamon, saffron, and also ginger taken in the morning on an empty stomach, which is also very beneficial for the senses and memory.

1.10.1:
*By What Method Black Bile is to be Avoided*
That worst black bile, which we abhorred in the preceding chapters, is increased by the following: thick and cloudy wine, especially black wine; hard, dry, salty, sharp, pungent, old, burnt, roasted, and fried foods; beef and hare; old cheese; salt-fish; legumes, especially fava beans, lentils, eggplant, arugula, cabbage, mustard, radishes, garlic, onions, and leeks; mulberries, dates, and whatever heats or cools while simultaneously drying; and all black things. It is also increased by anger, fear, pity, sorrow, leisure, solitude, and whatever offends sight, smell, and hearing—and, above all, darkness. Furthermore, excessive drying of the body, whether it arises from long vigils, much mental agitation or worry, frequent intercourse, excessive use of hot and dry things, or from some immoderate evacuation, purging, laborious exercise, or fast- ing, thirst, heat, or by a drier wind or cold. Since black bile is always very dry, and also cold, though perhaps not equally so, it must certainly be resisted by things that are moderately warm and, indeed, as moist as possible. Use boiled foods frequently, which are easily digested and generate a subtle and very clear blood. But in the meantime, so that the condition of the stomach and of phlegm is also taken into account, as well as that of black bile, let meals be seasoned with cinnamon, saffron, and sandalwood. Seeds of pumpkin and cucumber, and washed pine nuts are helpful. All dairy products are suitable: milk, fresh cheese, and sweet almonds. Suitable also are the meats of birds and chickens, or of suckling quadrupeds, especially soft-boiled eggs, and of animal parts, the brain. Sweet apples, pears, peaches, melons, Damask plums, and similar fruits are good. Well-cooked pumpkin and moist, non-viscous herbs are beneficial. However, I do not at all recommend cherries, figs, or grapes. I strongly detest nausea and overeating. But nothing is more powerful against this plague than light, clear, sweet, and fragrant wine, which is most suitable for generating spirits that are clearer than all others. For, as pleases Plato and Aristotle, this humor is softened, sweetened, and cleared by this wine in the same way as lupines soaked in water, or iron heated by flames. Truly, as much as its use benefits the spirits and the intellect, so much does its abuse harm them. Furthermore, it is consistent that pouring gold or silver, especially when heated, or their foils, into cups or in the broth itself is beneficial, and it is helpful to drink from a golden or silver vessel and to consume food from them. It is also very useful if licorice juice is swallowed often on an empty stomach, as is the juice of sweet pomegranates and sweet oranges. Sweet scents, especially those that are temperate, are of no small benefit; but if cold reigns, they should incline toward the warm, and if heat dominates, they should lean toward the cold. Therefore, they should be tempered from roses, violets, myrtle, camphor, and sandalwood, which are cold. Again, they should be made from cinnamon, citron, orange, cloves, mint, lemon balm, saffron, aloe wood, amber, and musk, which are warm. Spring flowers are especially beneficial, as are the leaves of the citron or orange and fragrant apples, but most of all, wine. Such scents, as is appropriate for each person, should be drawn into the nostrils and applied to the chest and stomach. We do not approve of scents that are very warm and dry if they are used alone and continuously. One should hold hyacinth in the mouth, which vehemently exhilarates the mind. Hierobotana sacred herb, that is, wild clary, is beneficial both in food and in scent. Again, bugloss, borage, and lemon balm, and the water of these three, are useful. Furthermore, lettuce, endive, raisins, and almond milk should be very familiar to the table. One must flee from air that is either scorching, or too icy, or cloudy, but temperate and serene air should be admitted most freely. Mercury, Pythagoras, and Plato command that a discordant or grieving mind should be soothed with the lyre and song. to compose as well as to stir up the mind, with a style that is as constant as it is harmonious. Furthermore, David, the sacred poet, liberated Saul from insanity with the psaltery and psalms. I also frequently experience at home—if it is permitted to compare small things with great—how much the sweetness of the lyre and song avails against the bitterness of black bile. We praise the frequent view of bright water, of green or red color, the use of gardens and groves, walking along rivers and through pleasant meadows; we also strongly approve of horseback riding, carriage travel, and gentle sailing; and above all, variety, easy occupations, diverse tasks that are not burdensome, and the constant company of graceful people.

1.11.1:
*On the treatment of the Stomach*
It follows that we must take care of the stomach as diligently as possible, so that overeating never brings on nausea or indigestion, nor offends the head. Food should be taken twice daily, and it should be moderate and light, seasoned moderately with cinnamon, mace, and nutmeg. Nevertheless, dry food should always exceed soft nourishment and drink in weight, unless perhaps we greatly fear the dryness of black bile. Hunger should await the food, and thirst should await the drink, if it can be conveniently done. Greed for both should be left at the table. Loathing and satiety should remain far away. One must abstain from those things which, because of excessive humidity or virulent, greasy, and viscous matter, weaken the stomach by relaxing it, or which are even cold or very hot, or which are difficult to digest because of their hardness. One must also avoid those things that leave a troublesome taste on the palate long after the meal, or that cause bloating, or fill the head with many vapors; and above all, one must avoid anything that easily rots, either outside or inside the gut. We do not approve of sweet or sharp flavors if they are taken alone; rather, we want sweet things to be tempered with something sharp, pungent, or dry. Mastic and dried mint, fresh sage, raisins, quince apples cooked and preserved in sugar, chicory, rose, coral, and lotus capers seasoned with vinegar are most friendly to the stomach. Furthermore, pomegranates, with a flavor halfway between acid and sweet, and in general anything that is moderately acid and slightly austere— which physicians call styptic—or things that are somewhat pungent, salty, or aromatic, are beneficial. However, myrobalans dried medicinal fruits surpass all else. Red wine is also better than white, with a slightly sub-bitter taste, and unless heat or destillatio a catarrh or downward flow of humors demands otherwise, the best method is to drink it little by little. In any case, more liquid foods should be taken before harder ones. After food has been taken, it is fitting to consume coriander, quince preserved in sugar, pomegranates, austere pears, medlars, dried peaches, and similar things. One must chew each individual item most thoroughly before swallowing. If necessary, the stomach should be warmed from the outside with mastic, rose, mint, and coral. One must take care not to— after a meal, during the next two or three hours, engage deeply in difficult thinking or reading. Four hours of leisure will perhaps be necessary if the food or drink was more abundant, or the food harder to digest. It is bad to distend the belly with food or drink, and worst of all for the stomach, when so distended, to engage in difficult thinking. Therefore, either take the lightest nourishment, or, having taken it, rest until you have almost digested it. One should not sleep at midday after a meal unless the greatest necessity compels it, and even then, not until two hours have passed. However, if supper is taken at night, one hour of waking is sufficient, as it seems. Sexual intercourse is pestilent to the stomach, especially if you engage in it immediately while full or while hungry. The stomach mourns in idleness, but it rejoices in exercise, except when it is full of food. Once food is taken, one should walk moderately, but soon after, sit.

1.12.1:
*On those things which foster the primary members and the powers of the spirit*
But now, since I am about to make it worth the reader’s while, let us bring into the open some things from the pharmacy of physicians which either keep the powers of the stomach, heart, brain, and the spirits of the intellect intact, or restore them, and if either phlegm or black bile grows, or nausea threatens, drive it far away. All physicians have agreed without controversy that nothing is more wholesome than Theriaca a medicinal treacle or antidote for fostering and strengthening both the individual members and powers, as well as the spirits and the intellect.
1.12.2: Therefore, we shall use this first in the amount of half a drachma, or at least a third of a drachma, twice every week in winter and autumn. But in summer and spring, use it once, either alone or, if you like, in cold and humid seasons with a little clear, sweet wine. In hot and dry seasons, however, especially if your nature or age is warmer, take it with two or three ounces of rose water, with the stomach empty, six or seven hours before food. If Theriaca treacle is unavailable, we shall give Mithridatum a compound antidote. But when we take Theriaca or Mithridatum, one must abstain completely from all hot things on that day, and if it is summer or spring, cold things should be used. In the second place, Aloë aloes, properly selected and washed, is approved by everyone for the same purpose. Take two drachmas of yellow myrobalans, and one drachma each of purple roses, red sandalwood, emblic myrobalans, cinnamon, saffron, citron peel, behen an herb used in cordials, and lemon balm; take twelve drachmas of Aloë properly selected and washed. From these, make pills with the best wine, which you should use once every week at daybreak, in the weight that suits your nature: in summer with rose water, but at other times with wine. On days when you do not take Theriaca or the pills, use a confection of this kind morning and evening, two or three hours before food. Take four drachmas of the finest cinnamon, two of yellow myrobalans, and the same amount of emblics, half a drachma of saffron and roses, two drachmas of red sandalwood, one drachma of similar coral, and as much of the whitest sugar as is sufficient. Dissolve the sugar in rose water and the juice of citron or lemons, in equal portions, and cook gently. Then add a third of a drachma of musk, and as much amber. Finally, make solid boluses which are commonly called morsels, and wrap them in gold. We have tested these three things ourselves in the usage we prescribed: Theriaca and Aloë tempered as we have said, and that confection, all contribute to the members, powers, and spirits, sharpen the senses and the intellect, and confirm the memory. Furthermore, phlegm, bile, and black bile are easily either drawn out or corrected by those pills. Moreover, these three things are considered most familiar to every age and nature.

1.13.1:
*Pharmaca, or remedies, that repress and draw out phlegm*
If we must fight more sharply against overflowing phlegm, we shall give at dawn pills made from the Hierapicra a sacred bitter purgative of Galen, or those which Mesue calls Elephanginae purgative pills named for their strength, specifically in the number and frequency required, or even in a more robust constitution, pills composed of equal parts of hiera and agaric troches, always with liquid rose honey, oxymel a mixture of vinegar and honey, and water of fennel. of the stomach. This syrup is certainly most useful for digesting phlegm, both before and after the pills. If other humors are also disturbed along with the phlegm, we shall purge them opportunely with the pills of Reu barbaro rhubarb by Mesue, or the pills which later authors call “Without Which.” We completely condemn any violent and sudden evacuation or purgation. For it weakens the stomach and the heart, exhausts many spirits, confuses the humors, and darkens the spirits with the murky fumes of the humors.

1.14.1:
*Remedies for Catarrh and Distillation, the common plague of students*
Where the head fluctuates with distillations due to phlegm, we shall sometimes give some of the pills we just described at the hour of sleep. Furthermore, we shall command them at that hour, and at other times, to chew Thus frankincense; for it wonderfully assists distillations, all the senses, and memory. Again, nutmeg and theriaca a medicinal treacle or antidote held in the mouth are approved; also maiorana marjoram, which they call amaracum marjoram, either its water applied to the nostrils or infused. After food, however, we shall restrain the fumes of the nourishment with coriander and quinces.

1.15.1:
*On headache*
IF the head should ache often, burdened by a cold humor, besides those things we have recounted, we shall command that the confection they call Diambra an aromatic powder, or diacori a heartstrengthening confection of sweet flag, or Plirisar a compound medicine for the head be kept in the mouth. Furthermore, chew mastic a resinous gum often. In addition, smear the forehead, temples, and neck with the leaves of maiorana marjoram, fennel, and ruta rue bruised together with rose oil, and similarly with aloë aloe, vinegar, oil, and rose water perfectly diluted.

1.16.1:
*The remedy for dimness of sight*
WHEN the eyes are dim, yet neither red nor showing any other sign of heat, then a collyrium made from the water of fennel, maiorana marjoram, chelidonia celandine, and ruta rue, with the addition of saffron and antimonium antimony, is beneficial. But water of this kind must first be squeezed through a thick cloth. However, do not apply anything to the eyes unless you have first purged them often with pills of Light. But if the dim eyes are red, purge them immediately with pills composed of fumus terrae fumitory. Soon, a collyrium made from rose water and sugar is beneficial. Sometimes, indeed, egg white, tutia zinc oxide/tutty, and milk added together helps as soon as possible. Overall, however, the daily use of maratrum fennel preserves and sharpens the sight. It is necessary to hold its seed in the mouth frequently, and to eat the leaves. The “Lesser Triphera,” described by Mesue, is best. It is best to take myrobalanum a dried fruit used as a purgative, specifically the preserved chebulam chebulic myrobalan, daily on an empty stomach, and with it some bread made from sugar and maratrum fennel reduced to a powder: which, moreover, wonderfully benefits the intellect and prolongs life. The use of Eufrasia eyebright is also a singular protection for the eyes.
1.16.2: In all cases of either headache or dimness of the eyes, vapors must be diverted backwards by friction and cupping. And if heat is the cause, and blood abounds, we shall apply leeches to the neck and shoulders.

1.17.1:
*On restoring the sense of Taste*
The stomach of those who study literature often loses almost all taste if this occurs due to the vice of phlegm, which a sour taste in the mouth or much sticky saliva indicates. After you have cleared the bowels with the medicines we described above, use “Aromatic Rose,” namely rose sugar mixed with honey, or rose honey with cinnamon, or even ginger alone, whether preserved or in a syrup of mint; but above all, use Theriaca a medicinal treacle.
1.17.2: But if an abundance of bile happens to occur, which the mouth usually shows by being bitter, similarly take it after a purgation prepared from Aloë aloe, as we have said, or reubarbaro rhubarb, or triasandalum a mixture of three sandalwoods, or Oxysacchara a syrup of vinegar and sugar, composed of sugar, white vinegar, and the wine of a sharper pomegranate. Or peaches or pears, whether preserved or made into a syrup, as Mesue teaches, or our own confection of this kind, which is most healthy for the taste. Take four ounces of rose sugar, two ounces of diamarenati an electuary of cherries, the same amount of diacytonites an electuary of quinces, namely two ounces, half an ounce of chebula myrobalans, the same amount of emblic myrobalans, and half a drachm each of red sandalwood and red coral.
1.17.3: Pour in addition a julep a sweetened medicinal drink of three or two ounces of citron or lemon juice. But if the stomach is weak and cold, add two drachms of cinnamon. These are to be used two hours before food. Diacytonites an electuary of quinces and the use of capers with vinegar always remove nausea born from either humor. Also, a moderate drink of white rose vinegar on an empty stomach, if mixed with double the weight of sugar. Again, syrup of mint and wormwood. Also, mint either preserved in vinegar or diluted and moistened with the acidic juice of a pomegranate.

1.18.1:
*Most exquisite remedies for black bile*
But let us now leave these as lighter things, and return to that which is most dangerous, namely black bile, which, as often as it abounds and rages, weakens the whole body, and most especially the spirit, as a certain instrument of the intellect, and the intellect and judgment itself. Let the first precept in curing it be, as Galen taught, that we should not strive to draw it out suddenly, lest perhaps, with its more liquid and subtle part removed, the remaining part resides very dense and dry; but it should be softened and digested little by little, and at the same time drawn out. Second, that meanwhile, both by moister foods and by gentle and moderate baths and similar ointments, the head and the whole body should be moistened as much as possible, with this caution however: that neither distillation be irritated, nor the stomach or liver be destroyed, nor the passages of the body be obstructed. The third, and this is indeed most necessary, is that the heart should be continuously cherished and strengthened by appropriate things, partly taken internally, and partly applied externally to the chest or nostrils. Also, those things which delight should be constantly seen, heard, smelled, and thought about. Conversely, contrary things should be kept far away.

1.19.1:
*Syrups for the greatest benefit of the melancholic*
Many things have indeed been composed by many against this humor. I, however, shall bring forward in the present three kinds of remedies chosen from many, the most excellent of all and the safest, accepted first from the ancients, then confirmed by the moderns, and sometimes even adapted by us for our own use. In the first is the composition of the best syrup. In the second, the most approved pills. In the third, the most healthy electuaries. When these three are opportunely applied, the melancholic humor is softened, digested, and dissolved; the spirits are sharpened and brightened; the intellect is cherished; and the memory is confirmed. The syrup is of this kind: Take borage, bugloss, the flowers of both, balm, maidenhair fern, endive, violets, dodder, polypody, senna, and epithyme, as much of each as can be grasped by the hand, twenty Damascus plums, fragrant apples, [?nu] ten raisins, one ounce, half an ounce of licorice, three drams each of cinnamon, red sandalwood, and citrus peel, and half a dram of saffron. Boil all of these, except the dodder and the aromatics, in water until one third has evaporated. Afterward, the strained decoction should be boiled again moderately with sugar and dodder. Finally, infuse the aromatics, namely the cinnamon and saffron. Three ounces of this syrup should be drunk in the morning while warmed, together with two or three ounces of bugloss water, and along with these, at least two or more of the following pills should be taken, as is suitable for each person, in such a way that the bowels are moved a little every day.

1.20.1:
*Pills for softening and purging vicious humors*
As regards the matter of pills, there are two kinds: some are suitable for delicate people, others for the more robust. The first can be named golden or magical enchanted/wonder-working pills, composed partly in imitation of the Magi Persian wise men/astrologers and partly by our own invention, under the very flow of Jupiter and Venus, which draw out phlegm, bile, and black bile without discomfort, strengthen individual limbs, and sharpen and illuminate the spirits. It dilates them so that, being constricted, they do not bring about sadness, but rather rejoice in dilation and light. In this way, they stabilize them again, so that they do not vanish through excessive extension.
1.20.2: Take therefore twelve grains of gold, preferably of its leaves if they are pure, half a dram each of frankincense, myrrh, saffron, aloe wood, cinnamon, citrus peel, balm, raw crimson silk, mint, white been centaury root, and red been; one dram each of purple roses, red sandalwood, red coral, and the three myrobalans, namely Emblic, Chebulic, and Indian; and an amount of aloe, duly washed, equal to the weight of all the others. Make pills with the most exquisite pure wine. There follow pills for dissolving melancholy, which are somewhat stronger, yet not at all violent.
1.20.3: Take one dram each of peony, myrrh, Arabian stichados French lavender, balm, frankincense, saffron, the three myrobalans (namely Emblic, Chebulic, and Indian), and roses; three drams each of troches of agaric, polypody, dodder, senna, lapis lazuli blue mineral stone duly washed and prepared, and similarly prepared Armenian stone; and two ounces of washed aloe. Fashion the pills with perfect wine. If a manifest heat dominates along with the melancholy, the cold ingredients in this composition must be increased by one third of their weight. I have composed these pills for the convenience of scholars, in imitation of the Greeks, Latins, and Arabs; however, I did not wish to mix in stronger substances, such as hellebore, which the fanatic Carneades Greek philosopher used. For I advise this only to learned men, or those who are slightly stronger, who find nothing more pestilential than violence. Therefore, I have omitted the Indian pills, the preparations of lapis lazuli or Armenian stone, and the composition they call Ieralogodion sacred medicine. If, finally, it is appropriate to include a simpler composition that I use more familiarly: Take one ounce of washed aloe, two drams each of Emblic and Chebulic myrobalans, and two drams of mastic, as well as two drams of roses, especially purple ones, and make pills with wine. Furthermore, no one should ever use these pills —or any others we have approved—alone, lest they be dried out too much; for this is the worst thing in melancholy. Rather, take them either with the syrup that we described above, following partly Mesue and partly Gentile da Foligno, or with one, two, or three ounces of light, fragrant wine, as suits the individual. Or take them with honey water, raisins, and licorice. Or, if heat dominates anywhere, take them with violet julep and violet water. In any case, I advise scholars who are more prone to black bile to use this purging method twice every year—namely in spring and autumn—for fifteen or twenty continuous days, using the pills with the syrup and similar remedies. However, for those who are somewhat less prone to this illness, it will be enough to take the first or last pills throughout the year, once every week, in the summer with a julep, as we said, but otherwise with wine.

1.21.1:
*On the use of liquid medicines Remedy*
One must remember that where the greatest danger threatens from desiccation, yet necessity compels purging, it is worth the effort to omit the pills and, in the syrup itself or a similar decoction made in bugloss water, to infuse at times one ounce, or at least half an ounce, of diafena date-based purgative, diacatholicon universal purge, or Triphera Persica Persian electuary. But if the body is more robust or the bowels are tighter and harder, add one or two drams of electuary Hamech compound purgative. Prepared cassia is also useful here, and manna is more useful. These do not suit every type of melancholy, but especially that which is created by burning. If, however, the melancholy is natural, they are suitable, but especially if a double or triple portion of polypody, licorice, saffron, and raisins is added to the syrup. Likewise, two ounces of liquid rose honey should be added to the medicines. We have said above how often the syrup should be taken. But the medicine itself must be taken with it for sixty days. However, if no melancholic humor appears, but only a melancholic complexion bodily constitution—namely a cold and dry quality of the limbs—remember that purging the bowels or drawing blood is not at all expedient; instead, only do the other things that we have already stated, or that we will state. Especially whatever pertains to the body, to warm it moderately and to moisten it greatly, and to illuminate the spirits as much as possible, and to nourish the limbs. Where the humor of black bile itself overflows, we do not only moisten the body and the humor, but we also loosen the bowels with the caution that we have stated. But never vehemently. For Plato Greek philosopher warns us in the Timaeus Platonic dialogue that a long- standing disease, such as the melancholic one, should not be irritated with overly strong remedies and troublesome drugs.

1.22.1:
*Canons for bloodletting*
There are some who are more bold in bloodletting, whom wise doctors entirely detest. For blood is the tempering of black bile, the nourishment of the spirit, and the treasure of life. Only when there is an indication of an abundance of blood, or excessive laughter, much boldness and confidence, or a reddening color and swelling of the veins, should we, when the situation demands it, let blood from the scholars from the vein of the spleen of the left arm, with a wide incision, four ounces in the morning and the same in the evening. Then, after a few days—at least seven, at most fourteen—irritate the hemorrhoids with a somewhat harsh friction and by applying leeches, which they call bloodsuckers, so that three or four ounces of blood drain from there. Both of these procedures seem to be done only for the more robust. For the weaker ones, if necessity demands it, to, to irritate the hemorrhoids only as we have taught. But it is not permitted to loosen the bowels with medicines, nor to let blood, unless you have first softened them with rich and mild clysters enemas. And let this be a general rule for the melancholic nature: that care must be taken so that, if necessary, the lower belly is always kept lubricated and purged by such frequent clysters.

1.23.1:
*On Electuaries and Confections*
Electuaries follow, of which I certainly praise the one that Rafis Rhazes, a medieval Persian physician called Exhilarating. Furthermore, those which Avicenna medieval polymath and physician composes in the book On the Powers of the Heart, but much more the one that Mesue medieval pharmacologist writes down as follows: Take one pound of raw silk recently dyed a crimson color. Immerse it in the juice of sweet and sweetly-smelling apples, and in the juice of bugloss borage/ox-tongue herb, and rose water, one pound of each. After twenty-four hours, cook all of that gently until the water becomes red. Then extract the silk and squeeze it out diligently. Pour in immediately one hundred and fifty drachmas units of weight of the whitest sugar, and cook again until it thickens like honey. Remove then from the fire, and pour in while it is warm six drachmas of raw amber ambergris, finely cut, and allow the amber to melt. Finally, add to these a powder of this kind. Take of raw wood of aloes agarwood and cinnamon, six drachmas of each equally, lapis lazuli a deep-blue metamorphic rock used in traditional medicine duly washed, thirteen drachmas; pearls, that is, white pearls, two drachmas; of true gold, one drachma; of selected musk, half a drachma. Two drachmas or one of this are given with wine, in the morning and evening, three or four hours before food. This pleases me greatly above the others. However, I also approve of Mesue’s sweet diamuscum a medicinal compound containing musk and the composition of gems, provided they are taken with rose water. I would also marvelously praise that which was concocted by Petrus Abanensis Peter of Abano, a famous philosopher and physician, a most excellent philosopher, were it not that he himself feared excessive dilation and exhalation of the spirits from its immoderate use. For this reason, I have additionally devised two most safe [confections], and because of their temperament, they are most convenient for any time, age, and nature, in which the useful is mixed with the sweet. These nourish as much as they comfort and strengthen. Furthermore, they are suited to stabilizing the spirit and intellect as much as to sharpening and illuminating them. Take four ounces of rose sugar, two ounces of sugar boiled together with bugloss flowers, one ounce of citron peel preserved in sugar, two ounces of preserved chebulic myrobalan a medicinal fruit, one drachma of selected cinnamon, and of sandalwood and coral—namely the red of both—likewise half a drachma each of raw and shredded crimson silk, saffron, and pearls; one-third of a drachma each of gold and silver; and grains of amber and musk two. Pour all together with the juice of citron or lemon, boiled with sugar. Another confection follows, somewhat healthier, certainly much sweeter. Take four ounces of sweet almonds, of pine kernels—namely those washed for the space of one day—two ounces of each of cucumber seeds, four ounces of hard sugar which they call “Candum,” that is, white, and one and a half pounds of other, most white sugar. Pour all of these with rose water and the juice of lemon and citron, in which heated gold and silver have been quenched, and cook them together gently. Finally, add one drachma each of cinnamon, red been a medicinal root, red sandalwood, and coral; half a drachma each of the most bright pearls, saffron, and raw crimson silk finely ground; twelve grains each of gold and silver; and one-third of a drachma each of hyacinth, emerald, sapphire, and carbuncle. Truly, if gold, silver, amber, musk, or precious stones are lacking for someone, those confections will still be able to profit much without these. Of these, I choose three above all: namely, the one by Mesue which I reviewed, and indeed our two, which we have just described. How, indeed, these are to be used, we have explained sufficiently above. But if anyone desires something simpler, yet accommodated to everyone, let him crush a perfectly ripe citron fruit, whole, and with much sugar and much rose juice to, let him cook it. When cooked, let him season it with a little cinnamon and saffron, or let him use aromatic rose-sugar tempered in this way. Take one ounce of aromatic rose-sugar, two ounces each of rosesugar and sugar of bugloss, or similarly, let him mix diamuscum musk-based medicine. Although these two are not simple, they are nevertheless easily enough obtained. But if heat is feared, let diaprunum a medicinal electuary made from plums and violet sugar be added.

1.24.1:
*Remedies for Emaciating Sleeplessness*
It often happens to the melancholic, especially those devoted to letters, that they are worn out by long wakefulness as the brain is excessively dried. Since, however, nothing increases the evils of black bile more than long wakefulness, such a great evil must be relieved with all effort. Therefore, let them eat lettuce after other food together with a little bread and a little saffron, and let them sip pure wine after the lettuce, and let them not study beyond an hour. And when they betake themselves to sleep, let them take a confection of this kind. In which there should be two ounces of white poppy seed, one ounce of lettuce seed, half a drachma each of amomum a spice-plant and saffron, and six ounces of sugar. Dilute and cook everything together with poppy syrup. Let them eat two drachmas of this, and at the same time taste some poppy syrup or wine. You should smear their forehead and temples with oil of violets and of water lily, with camphor added. Likewise with milk and oil of almonds and violets. the scent of saffron and camphor, and the shells of sweet apples, you will bring to their nostrils. Furthermore, [use] a little vinegar, but a great deal of rose water. You will also strew the bed with the leaves of cold plants. You will soothe the ears with sweet songs and sounds. You will frequently moisten the head with such baths: namely, water in which have been boiled pieces of poppy, lettuce, purslane, mallow, roses, and the leaves of vine, willow, and reeds, with chamomile added. With gentle baths of such things, the legs and arms, and often the whole body, should be moistened. Furthermore, drinking milk mixed with sugar on an empty stomach, if only the stomach tolerates it very well, is most beneficial. These moist things marvelously help the melancholic even if they sleep enough. Remember that almond milk should be the most familiar thing at the table.

1.25.1:
*Remedies for Dull Memory and Forgetfulness*
It happens sometimes to students, either because they read or write diligently with their head inclined, or because they are sluggish from too much idleness, that a more viscous phlegm the cold and moist humor, together with excessively cold melancholy, occupies the head, weighs it down, and makes them dull and forgetful. For these people, therefore, the head must be relieved by those remedies which we have said elsewhere are suitable for phlegm. If those are not sufficient, have recourse to Indian pills a strong purgative medicine and cocchiae pills made of colocynth, and hieralogodion a medicinal electuary. Furthermore, to hiera diacoloquintidos a purgative containing colocynth, or that of Archigenes an ancient Greek physician, or
1.25.2: [prescribed by] Andromachus or Theodotion, or to the pills of the Jew, which Mesues describes in the chapter On Pain of the Head. But if your nature or age is colder, and summer does not prevent it, use that anacardine a confection made from the fruit of the cashew tree, thought to sharpen the intellect confection after purging, which Mesues calls the “Confection of the Wise” in his Antidotarium a book of antidotes and medicinal preparations. Use again that anacardine which he recounts in the chapter On Forgetfulness according to the opinion of the son of Zacharias. Give one dram early in the morning, but whoever takes it must strictly abstain from anger, coitus, drunkenness, labor, and warm things on that day. These are indeed most powerful against dullness and forgetfulness.
1.25.3: But if you prefer more familiar things, give candied ginger mixed with a little frankincense, which greatly benefits the senses and the memory, especially with these additions: namely, honey of anacardium, honey of myrobalans, sweet flag, cyperus, amber, and musk. Diambra a warming aromatic powder, pliris sarcoticon a digestive and strengthening medicinal paste, and diacori a medicinal preparation of sweet flag are also beneficial. These should be held in the mouth for a long time, and also infused into the nostrils and ears. The scent of frankincense, marjoram, fennel, nutmeg, rue, and cloves is also not unhelpful. Remember, however, that in these and similar cases, as we said at the beginning, Theriac a complex herbal antidote should never be postponed in favor of any other remedy. Furthermore, for the dull and forgetful, rub the temples and the neck with an ointment of this kind. Take one ounce of elder oil, two ounces of oil of ben, half an ounce of euphorbium, and the same amount of castoreum; you will rub the arms, legs, and neck vigorously. And if there is need, you will apply cupping glasses to the neck. Furthermore, you will cover and warm the crown of the head with marjoram, frankincense, and pounded nutmeg.
1.25.4: And if there is need, you will apply cupping glasses to the neck. Furthermore, you will cover and warm the crown of the head with marjoram, frankincense, and pounded nutmeg.

1.26.1:
*We ought to be intent on the custody of the spirits*
If men who are desirous of truth ought to care for the corporeal spirit with such diligence of physicians, lest perhaps, being altogether neglected, it be an impediment or serve unsuitably those who seek the truth, then without doubt it is fitting to cultivate the incorporeal spirit, that is, the intellect itself, much more diligently with the institutions of moral discipline. By this alone is truth itself grasped, since it is incorporeal. For it is not right to cultivate only the servant of the soul, that is, the body, and neglect the soul, which is the lord and king of the body: especially since it is the opinion of the Magi and Plato that the whole body depends on the soul in such a way that unless the soul is in good health, the body cannot be in good health. For this reason, Apollo, the author of medicine, judged not Hippocrates, even though he was born of his own lineage, but Socrates to be the wisest. Indeed, since Hippocrates studied as much as he could to heal the body, Socrates studied to heal the soul: although what they attempted, Christ alone accomplished. Therefore, we are commanded by Socrates to cultivate our mind with the best morals, so that we may more easily attain, with a serene mind, the light and truth sought by us through natural instinct, the more so because truth itself… is divine truth, is it not right to venerate it first and foremost with holy religion? The mind was created for seeking and grasping this in no other way than the eye was created for perceiving the light of the sun. And, as our Plato says, just as the sight perceives nothing visible anywhere except in the splendor of the highest visible thing, that is, the sun itself, so the human intellect grasps nothing intelligible except in the light of the highest intelligible, that is, God, who is always and everywhere present to us. In the light, I say, which illuminates every man coming into this world. In the light of which David sings: “In your light we shall see light.” Indeed, just as when eyes are purified and look into the light itself, its splendor is suddenly poured out, shining abundantly with the colors and shapes of things, so when the mind is first purified from all the perturbations of the body through moral discipline, and directed toward divine truth, that is, God himself, with a certain religious and most ardent love, suddenly, as the divine Plato says, divine truth flows into the mind, and it happily unfolds the true reasons which are contained within it, and by which all things stand: and by as much light as it sheds around the mind, by that much it simultaneously fills the will with blessed joy.

2.0.1: MARSILIO FICINO OF FLORENCE, in the Second Book on Protracting Life, to Filippo Valori, an epistolary preface.
2.0.2: Although our Plato lives by his own Genius, and will live, as I think, as long as the world itself lives, my own Genius nonetheless always drives me here: that after divine worship, I should look to the life of Plato above all things. The House of Medici has long aspired to this same end, more than others. You also, my Valori, a most dear friend of the Medici and very studious of Platonic glory and discipline, conspire toward the same thing. Therefore, the life that I always wish for Plato, I wish the same for the Medici, and a similar one for Valori. For this reason, I urge and beseech you, my Valori, that with as much effort as you always favor Platonic glory, you should one day read and keep these precepts of ours on protracting life with equal diligence. By keeping them, you may be able to live long, and for a longer time, together with the magnanimous Lorenzo de’ Medici, support the recently resurging discipline of Plato.
2.0.4: MARSILIO FICINO OF FLORENCE, distinguished Physician and Philosopher, On Protracting Life, or Long Life. BOOK II.

2.1.1:
*A long life is necessary for the perfection of science, which diligence provides*
It is not so much the quickness of wit or the strength of memory that leads us to art and perfect science, but the perspicacity of prudent judgment. Indeed, judgment—because of the ambiguity conceived from the diversity of conjectures—is so difficult that it must necessarily be confirmed by experiment. Experiment, however, is also deceptive, both because of the difficulty of judgment itself and because of the fleeting shortness of the time available for capturing the experiment. For these reasons, we rightly conclude with Hippocrates that art is long, and that we cannot attain it except through the length of life. But a long life is not promised only once by the Fates from the beginning, but is also provided by our own diligence. This, as Astraea… logicians confirm, when they treat of Elections and images; and the diligent care and experience of physicians confirms it. By such providence, not only those who are naturally robust, but also the infirm very often attain a long life, so that it is no wonder that a certain Herodicus, a student of letters and the most infirm of all his time, as Plato and Aristotle testify, completed almost his hundredth year through such providence. Plutarch further narrates that many, whose bodies were otherwise not very strong, attained a long life through diligence alone. I pass over for the present how many invalids I myself have known to have outlived the most robust through the gift of prudence. Therefore, it will be neither useless nor vain, after the book we composed On Curing the Health of Literati, to hand down further certain precepts leading to a long life for minds eager for science. Indeed, we do not wish for these principles to be communicated to the lazy and the slothful. For why should we desire them to live long, they who do not even truly live, as if we were nourishing drones, not bees? Nor to be divulged to men dissolved by the loss of desire for pleasures, who foolishly prefer short, daily pleasure to a long life. Nor to be opened to the wicked and the unjust, whose life is the death of the good. But only to men who are prudent and temperate, and who, with the powers of a clever mind, will benefit the human race, whether privately or publicly.

2.2.1:
*That vital heat is nourished by moisture, through the excess or deficiency of which corruption and dissolution occur*
Life consists, as it were, like a light in natural heat. The fuel for this heat is airy moisture, and it is greasy, much like oil. Therefore, if such moisture happens to fail, or if it exceeds [its measure], or becomes tainted, the natural heat is immediately weakened, and, once weakened, is finally extinguished. If the heat is weakened and lost by the defect of moisture, death occurs by resolution. If it is instead smothered by the excess or vice of moisture, life perishes by suffocation. Indeed, suffocation happens from the overflow or putrefaction of any moisture, especially when phlegm pituita phlegm is either growing or putrefying in any way, so that it has not been unfairly called “Phlegm seeking life.” Therefore, the most necessary precepts for prolonging life avoid equally, on the one hand, resolution, and on the other, suffocation and putrefaction. Equally, I say, by a common reason. For if they happen to treat a person who is hotter or drier, and for whom the passages are indeed open, the humors and subtle spirits are more prone to resolution. If, however, they treat a body affected by the contrary, they assist more against suffocation. They strive most of all for one or the other, if the place or time inclines toward one or the other.
2.2.2: But when advice is given to clever and studious men, both precepts are almost equally necessary, and one labors similarly in both. For in them, a sharp and hot wit, and the constant movement of the imagination, seem to threaten resolution; while bodily idleness and indigestion cruditas raw/undigested state seem to threaten suffocation. Physicians, therefore, never labor more intensely than in the treatment of such men. Although the entire argument of the previous book contributes most to the prolonging of life, such a great matter seems to demand a certain specific care, which I shall hereafter comprehend in as few words as I can.

2.3.1:
*How heat and moisture are to be tempered by a certain counsel of Minerva*
Moreover, while we treat this greasy oil—necessary to our fiery vigor—with the wisdom of Minerva, the olive-bearing Minerva, born from the head of nourishing Jupiter, laughs meanwhile, because while we see clearly the quantity of her gift, we do not see its quality well enough. Laughing, therefore, she says, “I have given you oil not only in abundance, such as would be enough to nourish the flame, but I have also poured it into the lamp pure and without amurca the watery dregs of olives.” This she said. But we, wandering while speaking, stumble, since the word of the lamp is not yet heard by our feet. Therefore, from this lamp… let us learn that oil must be supplied continuously to the flame, with such diligence that we do not extinguish the light with a sudden flooding. Nor, again, should we delay the drink for the thirsty one. But we think these two things have been sufficiently treated in the previous pages.
