Two things remain for us, one of which we seem to have touched upon lightly, and the other we have barely touched. Meanwhile, we touch upon Pallas in such a way that, though she is never accustomed to laugh, she might laugh at us. What then? First, we will consider that a flame, even a small one, is utterly consuming, and therefore that lamp lasts longer in which the small flame is tempered to the wick, that is, the light, so that it does not drink the oil, but sips it. Therefore, we also will take care in every diet, lest the implanted fire, by its own nature voracious, ever become too strong, especially in youth. It will be enough, then, to ward off both the inundating moisture and the penetrating cold. Then we will consider that a lamp is frequently extinguished when one has not poured in pure oil, but (if I may say so) dregs amurca the watery dregs of olives. Hence, a little later, fungus-like growths form from the dregs and extinguish the light. Now, we have received from Pallas the nourishing oil, namely, that which is as airy as possible and pure, and tenacious and firm by a natural viscosity. What is therefore supplied to this, as it is gradually consumed, must not only be equal to it, but similar. And in order to be similar, it must not only be airy and greasy, but entirely separated from the dregs, that is, from the sediment.
2.3.2: …from a certain sediment collected from the earth and thicker water. To avoid this collection and sediment, we should flee from such foods, and from idleness, indigestion, and filth. Meanwhile, let us cultivate Minerva with such moderation that she may increase for us the head from which she herself was born, but not diminish the nerves and the stomach.

2.4.1:
*The causes of the drying of the natural moisture and the exuberance of the foreign. And how necessary perfect digestion is for life*
These things quickly dry out natural moisture: a more abundant flow of blood; violent loosening of the bowels; the bowels being loose for a long time; profuse sweat; passages that are opened too widely; intercourse performed to the point of weakness; panting thirst; gnawing hunger; long vigils; the use of things that are too hot and simultaneously dry; laborious movement of mind and body; anxiety; anger; pain; air that is drier and warmer, especially when heated by fire; and a wind that is dry, violent, and persistent. Things contrary to these increase moisture beyond measure. Frequent drunkenness does both. For it dries the drunken person with excessive heat and at the same time suffocates them with moisture. But nothing is more harmful to both than indigestion. For where the food is not digested, on one hand, there is a lack of what is needed to irrigate the natural moisture; and on the other, the putrefied food… is harmful, because it overflows and overwhelms natural heat. For this reason, Avicenna says that the blood is corrupted when digestion itself is corrupted, and following Galen, he calls digestion the root of life. This rule of Galen is therefore the best and almost the only one: to care for the digestion of food above all else. For what seems to be the greatest precept, namely to use healthy things, will be of no use if you do not digest them. Indeed, almost as if from their opposites, a harmful humor flows if raw materials enter the members. Yet, even from foods less praised by art, less harm is often received as nourishment if they are digested more vigorously. Therefore, let us most diligently avoid crudity as a grave cause of both resolution and suffocation, specifically by the quantity of food and drink accommodated to us: by quality, simplicity, preparation, mastication, by fasting to summon hunger, and if necessary, by the external application of heat to the stomach, and by certain astringent things taken internally after meals. And let us take diligent care that drink does not exceed the food, or that the food is not too liquid or too hard, or that this or that is not strongly cold in its activity, or that the nourishments are not vastly different, or that we do not add raw food to raw food. For these things greatly hinder digestion. Furthermore, let us take the most diligent care not to hinder digestion by intercourse immediately after a meal, or by midday sleep when it is not necessary, or by nocturnal vigil, or by any strenuous labor of mind or body, or in any other way. I speak, indeed, not only of the first digestion which happens in the stomach, but also of the second which happens in the liver: and furthermore, the third which occurs in the veins: and finally, the fourth which is effected in the members. These require a certain long interval, and if any of them is hindered, nourishment is not supplied to the humor. Therefore, just as with digestion, it is necessary above all for life to aid the evacuation of waste. It is necessary to cleanse filth from the skin as well. Continuous, temperate, and varied bodily motion is necessary, just as the motion of the heavens, the air, fire, and water: provided only that the necessity of digestion and sleep is observed, while avoiding exhaustion and dissolution. Moreover, we draw rot and decay upon ourselves under the shade. We live in the open air, in the light. This my father, Ficino, an outstanding physician, frequently had on his lips. But to carry these things out successfully, it would be worth the effort to have accustomed the body from an early age not so much to urban business as to certain rustic exercises, and in some way to similar things. Sometimes also, to have maintained a somewhat varied diet. My prudent father often warned me of this. For those who live in every age with a certain excessive curiosity often live less safely. Those, however, who did not accustom themselves to this as youths, should at least accustom themselves as adults, though attempting it with more cautious steps and little by little.

2.5.1:
*Blood and the humor accommodated to life ought to be airy, temperate in quality, and in substance, intermediate and tenacious*
All the Greeks, among the precepts most necessary for a long life, command that we use euchymia good juices. We call euchyma foods producing good juices those healthy nourishments which bring good nourishment, that is, good blood. We call blood good when it is not cold, not dry, and not turbulent, but warm, moist, and clear. Warm, indeed, with a heat that is not sharp. Moist with a moisture that is not watery. Clear, but also not, in the meantime, too thin. Now, a hotter blood both sharpens natural heat and dries out the humor, and the humor or heat it brings is rendered resolvable and fleeting. Furthermore, blood that is too moist and prone to water dulls natural heat, and it either weakens the natural humor, or impels it to liquefy under heat, or suffocates the heat with moisture. And in general, if any portion of natural humor is drawn from watery blood, it then rots easily, and it quickly flows away and is dissolved. Hence, it comes about that those who eat softer fruits and herbs, unless perhaps they take them rarely and then only as a medicine to loosen the bowels, soon fill their veins with raw juice that is prone to putrefaction. And so that this does not happen, it is safer for food to be either cooked or at least mixed with bread. Therefore, let the blood be neither fiery nor watery, but airy. Not similar to thicker air, so that it might not be more inclined toward water. Not like the most subtle air, so that it might not easily heat up into fire: but let it hold an intermediate substance, in which the intermediate air has the greatest dominion. Let the other elements be present, insofar as they are accommodated to the empire of the air. Let its substance not be most subtle, lest it generate an unstable humor and a volatile spirit subject to dissolution. Let it not be most thick, otherwise it will not serve the intellect at all, and it will scarcely be transformed into natural humor and spirit; it will obstruct the passages and provide an occasion for suffocation. And the spirit which is at length created thick from that source is itself, by its own density, poorly suited for life, and it suffocates natural heat just as thicker smoke immediately compresses and extinguishes a flame. I omit the fact that it is at least so dark that it makes life mournful and worse than death. But above all, as it seems to me, for a long life, it is expedient for the blood to have, along with an airy substance that is not excessively thick, some glutinous and tenacious humor in itself, such as olive oil possesses along with its subtlety, and the humor of a fat yet thin eel, and the oil drawn from turpentine by a certain sublimation. Therefore, you must diligently choose foods and all other things which, according to their power, make the blood and humor such as these. For such blood and humor, just as oil is to a flame, is fuel for vital heat, and along with subtlety, it also possesses firmness. For it is a precept of Rasis Rhazes, the Persian physician for preserving youth: to use things that lead the blood to the heart, condense it there, and cherish the heart. Avicenna proves this, commanding that watery and unstable blood be avoided. However, the reason must be held in this, according to the difference of bodies. For where the body is denser, one must incline toward the subtlety of the blood; where it is rarer, toward the thickness of the same; one must turn away from this with all remedies. Where there is an intermediate physical constitution, we proceed more safely by a similarly intermediate path. Yet, we shall never attempt to extirpate the natural constitution of the body, otherwise we would extirpate life itself. It is also expedient to remember that where we greatly fear the subtlety of the blood, and the stomach is not particularly strong by nature in the meantime, one must approach thickness by smaller degrees while we strive to nourish a thin man with thicker foods, while in the meantime the stomach is to be cherished and sleep is to be prolonged. Bodily exercise is to be increased according to one’s strength, and that of the mind is to be decreased, for it very often harms many people. But if one cannot bear nourishments that are too viscous and hard or excessively cold, one should at least make use of corals, sandalwood, roses, coriander, myrobalans, quinces, and quince preserves. or of opinion, and with rose sugar and astringent things, we shall finally achieve that firmness of blood and humor which we cannot safely achieve here with excessively glutinous things. Most conveniently, those who cannot digest the viscous limbs of larger animals will be nourished with pine nuts and pistachios, the juice of glycyrrhiza licorice, and starch with sweet almonds added, as well as their oil, the seed of quinces, and sesame oil, along with the whitest sugar and rose water. We will grant them, in addition, the extremities of hens or kids, as well as tortoises, snails, and testicles. We shall provide wines, not white, but red and astringent and somewhat sub-bitter. Temper the wine with water or mastic. We shall also lightly soften the skin with oil of mastic and quinces, and meanwhile, we shall forbid those things that make the blood thin or burning, unless perhaps we infuse a little saffron or cinnamon into the more tenacious meals, so that they may both be digested more easily and, once digested, be transferred to the limbs through the narrow passages. For it is difficult to lead viscous or slightly firmer foods from a stomach that is not very strong all the way to the third and fourth digestion, unless they are carried by vehicles of this kind and are further stimulated by gentle friction. When you perform these, make sure to use softer hands. And remember to moisten your hands with a certain aromatic wine in which you have boiled chamomile, myrtle, and roses.

2.6.1:
*On the common rule of eating and drinking, and the quality of meals*
But let the most obtuse or most thin bodies of men be set aside for the present, so that we may arrive at a common manner of living, entirely suited to a common and middle habit of body. Take care that by no means do the passages of the body either open beyond measure or become too obstructed. For in the former lies the danger of resolution and harm inflicted from without, while in the latter lies the danger of putrefaction and suffocation. And if I do not restrain you with the tightest rein of a rule, which Hippocrates condemns, I do not nevertheless loosen the reins for you to the point of license. Consume more humid herbs and fruits sparingly. Consume milk and fish more sparingly, and both with honey. Consume mushrooms most sparingly, and with aromatics and pear seeds. Similarly with the pure drinking of water, and along with spareness. What is more humid or fatty, season with aromatics and sharp things; otherwise, they introduce much alien and putrid humor into the limbs, and if they supply any humor necessary to nature, they subject it to very swift corruption. This is not otherwise than how watery wine is quickly disturbed and corrupted. Hence arise quick graying of the hair, and pallor, and the wrinkles of old age. Meats also, if they are eaten daily, and even if they approach the weight of bread, bring about quick putrefaction. Whence Porphyry, relying on the authority of the Pythagoreans and the ancients… detests the eating of animals. Did we not receive that men before the flood were long-lived, and spared animals? Although physicians do not forbid the use of meats so much as their abuse. Finally, flee humid things as being prone to putrefaction, keeping in mind that the humid and the fat grow old and die more quickly. Which Hippocrates also says, and the thing itself declares. Again, take the driest things moderately, or at least temper them with more liberal drink. Safely choose the intermediate things. Even though Avicenna prefers a slightly drier form of food over a soft one, to avoid graying. Be most cautious regarding things that are too cold or too hot. Pursue things that are both hot and humid. If the air is burning, let the moisture of the meals surpass the heat; if it is cold, let the heat surpass the moisture. In both cases, however, let the excess be moderate. Everywhere, let the heat and moisture have something somewhat glutinous and astringent, so that the humor, irrigated from there to the limbs, may adhere more firmly and endure for a long time under the heat. Select wheat and select bread have this above all. Secondly, red and astringent wine, and a little sweet. Thirdly, pine nuts and things very similar to them in temperament and viscosity. Fourthly, meats that are not humid and lax, such as pork and suckling lamb. Ancient physicians, especially Galen, greatly recommend their meats and blood because of a certain similarity to our body. They are, therefore, best for similar bodies, such as those of rustics and the robust, and those who exercise their body much, especially… if they are kept preserved for four days, seasoned with cloves and prepared coriander, and salt. And blood is perhaps useful if it is boiled with sugar, and if it has been clarified to the highest degree and is liquid. But to return to the number, the more humid meats—such as those we have mentioned—are not approved, nor are those hard and dry, such as those of an older hare or ox; rather, certain intermediate ones, such as those of hens, chickens, capons, peacocks, pheasants, partridges, and perhaps also squabs, especially domestic ones. Such also are young roe deer and calves, and year-old rams as well as boars. I do not spurn suckling kids and fresh cheese. Indeed, I have passed over small birds. For the frequent use of thinner foods is appropriate only for a stomach that does not tolerate thicker ones at all. But he who is stronger carries off from them a fleeting vapor or humor. However, I do not pass over hens’ eggs, if the yolk is eaten together with the white. For the yolk alone is the nourishment of delicate people: for Avicenna proves that no nourishment is more expedient in the diminution of blood and the dissolution of the cardiac spirit than the yolk of a hen’s egg, or that of a partridge or pheasant. Nor perhaps would it be beside the point to nourish geese with spelt or clear water, and after slaughter, to preserve the meats for seven days, seasoned with salt and coriander and prepared with vinegar, before you eat them. And similarly with deer, if the stomach has been very strong. For it is probable that certain long-lived animals contribute to a long life, provided, however, that such meats of the young are eaten. Likewise, let other meats be taken in turn, both roasted and boiled.
2.6.2: Let food be double the amount of drink. Let bread be one and a half times the amount of eggs, triple the amount of meat, and quadruple the amount of fish, herbs, and more humid fruits. Let the meal not begin with drink, nor let the drink be plentiful at one time. Let something astringent always follow the meal without drink, or with very little. Where the complexion, age, place, or time inclines toward hot or dry, you too should decline slightly toward the opposites. Where it inclines toward cold or humid, similarly incline toward the opposites. Where there is a temperate state, maintain that temperate state. To that extent, exercise of the body is to be increased and that of the mind decreased, insofar as we eat firmer meals, which are perhaps sometimes necessary for the longevity of life. Let your meals be two in the nine hours of the day, and in both cases spare. A sparser dinner, however. Bodily exercises should be nearly two, after the first digestion, brought almost to the point of sweating. Nighttime sleep, because it is always necessary, is always good; daytime sleep, however, is never good unless it is absolutely necessary.

2.7.1:
*That one should not use foods that quickly putrefy: Wine and wheat are to be chosen above others; putrefaction and resolution are to be avoided*
Whatever animals come into our care are to be nourished with clean and selected foods. must be taken before we eat. Furthermore, these and all other things should be chosen from higher and fragrant pastures. Among these, always keep in mind the rule approved by the philosopher Arnold above all others: one must select living creatures, herbs, fruits, grains, and wines from high and fragrant regions, as we have said, which temperate winds make serene and gentle rays of the sun nourish, where no waters stagnate, and where they are not fattened by manure, but by their native moisture, where whatever is born also remains uncorrupted for a long time. One must live precisely here, and eat of what is born here. One should not trust that we will acquire a long-lasting humor, removed from putrefaction, from foods that rot quickly. Nor should one hope to live long where the fruits of the earth are not preserved uncorrupted for a long time, and where men are very rarely long-lived.
2.7.2: How great a difference there is in place and diet, the Persian apple reveals: in Persia, indeed, it is a poison, but in Egypt, a friend to the heart. And hellebore, taken without harm in Anticyra, is elsewhere a poison. Aristotle chooses a dwelling that is high and looks toward the south and east, under a thin air that is neither humid nor cold. And Plato finds the long-lived in the highest and most temperate regions. It is truly the worst practice to manure fields or not to drain stagnant waters from the fields. For everything that is born there is subject to quick decay. Wherefore wherefore I cannot help but criticize those who criticize the wise Hesiod for omitting the dunghill in his work on farming. But that prudent man considered health rather than fertility. He believed that the field could be sufficiently enriched by the leaves of lupines and beans turned over at the right time. But if we are compelled to cultivate more humid and unclean regions and to consume foods that will not last, let us observe the diet that physicians have prescribed under pestilential air. We have said enough about this in the book Against the Plague. In summary, we shall use sweet and somewhat warm scents. We shall be purged often and lightly with properly prepared aloe. We say it is “properly prepared” if it has been washed in rose water or the juice of roses, or if it has been perfectly mixed with fresh, crushed roses. Then add to it myrobalan and mastic, and perhaps rose. This medicine is beyond controversy wonderful for preserving a healthy mind in a healthy body. Furthermore, we shall exercise the body and use a suitable hearth. We shall season our meals with this powder: let there be one quarter of an ounce of emblic myrobalan, one half of sandalwood, one full part of cinnamon, and one eighth of crocus. With this powder and substances that are sharp, we might perhaps inhibit the corruption impending from putrid foods and places. However, we should remember that where many more perish from putrefaction and suffocation than from resolution, there one must resist putrefaction and suffocation above all. Where the contrary is true, one should conversely use aromatic condiments and, as we have said, similar astringent scents at any time to prevent putrefaction; anoint with oil to prevent the injury of cold; use baths of water and oil to prevent the resolution impending from labor or hot weather. Likewise, often rinse the mouth with water, keep the juice of licorice or crystalline sugar in the mouth, wash the hands and face with plenty of rose water and a little rose vinegar, and use similar scents. Refresh oneself with moderate food every seventh hour; rest both body and mind, while avoiding heat. It matters a great deal what kind of wine and wheat we consume habitually. Therefore, let them be of such a nature that they remain whole for more than a year and preferably up to three, if we hope to receive incorruptible nourishment from them.
2.7.3: Wine, whether white or red, should be clear, sweet, styptic, fragrant, and such that it needs water. Unless perhaps you find a wine that is light and yet durable, which is very rare. As for what is stronger, the philosopher Isaac says that wine is a liquid “cooked” by the sun and purified by the winds; he orders it to be tempered with pure spring water some time before we drink it, so that it may be mixed more perfectly. He warns that watery, weak, or sour wine should be avoided, as it quickly becomes acidic within the veins and limbs, or otherwise putrefies. For watery wine is subject to putrefaction, if its substance has been preserved by cooking, it will at least be useful; otherwise, it is not praised, because it will not create a corruptible humor, but its sharpness must be tempered with select water. As for the wine we have approved, Isaac says, according to the opinion of the ancients, that it is very similar to great theriacs. As we have said, it warms the cold habit of the body, cools the heated, moistens the dry, dries the more humid, and (as Galen says) restores natural humor, fosters heat, and tempers both. Mixing such wine is more necessary for the young, less for the old, and least of all for cold old men. For cold and hard old age (as Plato says) is inflamed and softened by neat wine just as iron is by fire or lupine by water. You should also know that what we said is accomplished by wine—that opposites are reconciled and dissident things tempered—is also accomplished by licorice, but more weakly; it is also accomplished by rose oil, but externally. Let these things be familiar to you. Do not doubt that whatever is tempered in quality and potent in virtue can temper the rest, just as cold can cool other things; it possesses this primarily through the temperament of Jupiter, by which things are also most healthy. But these must be discussed elsewhere.

2.8.1:
*Diet, Living, and Medicine for the Aged*
Those who have already completed their seventh septenary, reaching their fiftieth year, should consider that Venus signifies the young, while Saturn signifies the old, and that among astronomers these stars are considered the greatest enemies of all. Therefore, those of the Saturnian temperament should flee from sexual matters, which even in the young draw much away from life. It does not provide for those who are born, but for those who are to be born, and it dries up the very herbs as soon as the seed is produced. Furthermore, they should consider the cold and the night air to be deadly to them, and they should maintain a diet from which they may hope for plenty of blood and spirit, namely from fresh egg yolks and wine that is somewhat sweet, but especially fragrant. For the yolk properly restores the blood of the heart, and wine especially restores the spirit. In summary, they should use only the most select and easily digested meats in their diet, increasing what is warm and moist. They should constantly refresh their spirit, especially with the scents of wine. They should avoid wakefulness, fasting, and thirst; they should also avoid the labor of the body and mind, as well as solitude and sadness. They should return to music if they have neglected it, for it should never be neglected. They should recall certain games and manners of their childhood as much as is appropriate. For it is very difficult (if I may say so) to be rejuvenated in body unless you first become a child again in spirit. Therefore, at every age, it is greatly conducive to life to retain something of childhood and to always seek out various amusements. However, do not engage in long and excessive laughter, for it dilates the spirit too much toward the exterior. But let us return to the aged. to the elderly. Furthermore, if they should feel cold, they should seek out aromatic and warm poultices fomenta warming applications/poultices, which are also moist. They should remember that the poultice of Avicenna—the one indeed made by David—is not exactly childish, though perhaps it was made too late. A wonderful poultice for an old man is: the marrow of fresh, still-warm bread with Malvasia Malmsey wine and powdered mint added, applied to the stomach and frequently used for inhalation. For even the marrow of this kind, by itself, retained the spirit of Democritus when he was at the point of death, as long as he wished the fugitive spirit to remain. Furthermore, they should use light friction, or sometimes baths that draw nourishment to the extremities. Above all, they should keep pine nuts nuclei pinei pine seeds—specifically washed ones—close at hand. For ancient physicians have proven this nourishment to be most suitable for the elderly. It is warm, moist, and oily; it alleviates all harshness and, what is remarkable, while it increases natural moisture, it simultaneously dries up superfluous moisture and purges putrid humor. There are those who provide one drachma of such nuts for the elderly to eat daily after meals. I would also provide another drachma to the elderly on an empty stomach, either fresh, warm, gilded, or with pine nuts. I would also compose an electuary in this manner: take four ounces of cleaned sweet almonds, the same amount of such nuts, two ounces of pistachios, one of cucumber seeds, and one of cleaned hazelnuts; crush them, and cook them together with the purest sugar sugar, to which you shall have added one drachma of fresh candied ginger, half a drachma of saffron, a third of musk, and an equal amount of ambergris; pour in sugar, water of melissa lemon balm (that is, bee balm), and roses; add many gold leaves to these. By the daily use of this, the elderly will obtain a stronger and longer life. They may take this at the table, and also several hours before the meal. It will be more useful, however, if they drink some white and fragrant wine together with this confection. In warmer times, however, rose sugar together with gold leaves and candied myrobalans dried fruits of tropical trees used in medicine will prolong the life of the elderly. No one doubts that theriac a medicinal treacle or antidote is suitable for the same humid people and times. Its use was discussed sufficiently in the previous book. No one will deny that the roots of enula elecampane and beenia sweetroot/bistort roots—both white and red, but especially fresh—are very beneficial to them. The former is used for nourishment, the latter also as an aromatic; indeed, all that are simply warm and moist, and simultaneously aromatic, astringent, and oily. It is certain that the elderly should habitually use the chosen juice of glycyrrhiza licorice. For they report that glycyrrhiza is very similar in heat and moisture to the human body; furthermore, it helps with various diseases of the elderly.
2.8.2: Almond milk and starchy food should be familiar, as well as sugar and raisins. Rasis Rhazes recom mends Triphera a specific medicinal paste made from Indian myrobalans—emblic and belliric. Likewise, Indian myrobalans candied with sugar, not only not only for retaining, but also for retarding old age, is highly approved. Avicenna praises the greater and lesser triphera of myrobalans. Again, a confection of iron scale, and especially of gold. He commands one to chew myrobalans—especially the chebulic variety—duly candied, every day, to defer the inconveniences of old age.

2.9.1:
*On the natures of aromatics and cordials, which are necessary: And again, what kind of diet is proper for the elderly*
Know that there are various virtues in myrobalans. One that wonderfully dries up superfluous humor, from which it prevents gray hair. A second that gathers natural humor and protects it from both corruption and inflammation, from which it prolongs life. A third that, through its astringent and aromatic power, gathers, fosters, and strengthens both natural and animal strength and spirit. Hence, some might think that the tree of life in paradise was perhaps the myrobalan. Gold and silver, coral, spodium zinc oxide/ashes of minerals, and precious stones do almost the same thing, although they bring the power of illumination through their aromatic virtue. But you must remember that aromatics are most beneficial to us for life (as we indicated above) when, along with a certain aromatic vigor, they are equally moist and warm, and possess an oily viscosity suitable for growth: such as, primarily, the roots of the beenia, both white and red. especially when they are fresh. Or at least when, with a certain subtle, fragrant, and sharp virtue, they possess a dense substance and a very astringent property—such a composition as appears to be present among the cold cordials first in myrobalans and amber. Next, in roses, and the juice and seed of the citron. Third, in sandalwood, coriander, myrtle, and other similar things. Among the warm cordials, however, are zedoary a ginger-like plant, wood of aloes, citron peel, cloves, nutmeg, mace, frankincense, mastic, and doronicum leopard’s bane: such as we also experience in sage. They report that ambergris and musk have an astringent virtue. Ginger, however, because of a certain humidity of its own, especially when fresh and candied, is often beneficial to the elderly. But this, and cloves, due to the intensity of their heat, seem to be taken with caution. Zedoary should also be used with caution, even though it is judged similar to theriac and has an astringent yet oily nature, which is most suitable for the elderly. Ambergris, because of its almost temperate heat, is taken quite safely; and because of its viscosity mixed with astringent subtlety, it has the prerogative for strengthening life in the members and spirits. Furthermore, if water is made from it and the skin is washed, it restores the fourth digestion and expels diseases arising from its deficiency. Those aromatics that have a very subtle substance, such as cinnamon and saffron, must be mixed with cold and harder cordials. For if aromatics are only warm warm and subtle and are taken alone, they excite the natural heat too much and dissolve the moisture. Yet they are necessary, both for digesting cooler and moister foods, and for transferring the hard cordials to the heart area. You must not be unaware that the very humor necessary for life has its primary seat in the heart, and in its arteries and veins. This is what Isaach Isaac Israeli ben Solomon clearly teaches; and, as Avicenna proves, this humor is frequently irrigated and fostered by the natural humor of the other members. Therefore, one must take care that the humor of any member does not dry up by some accident; and much more so, that the humor of the heart area præcordia the region about the heart is not diminished. And so that all nourishment, or poultices, and cordials may be most extensively carried through narrow passages to the heart area, add saffron to these. To ensure they are retained there, apply myrobalans. To achieve both, take musk and ambergris among the warm things; among the cold, roses and myrtle. Remember that sweet fennel will be beneficial to the elderly. For it diffuses nourishment through the members, and by the same faculty as milk, it increases natural humor. Whence Dioscorides says that by fennel, snakes shed their annual old age. We also approve of sage. For it temperately heats and strengthens the virtue of nature, and drives away paralysis. We also approve of the moderate use of candied ginger: for it possesses oiliness along with heat.

2.10.1:
*On Gold and Golden Foods, and the Refreshment of the Elderly*
Everyone approves of gold above all things, as it is the most temperate of all substances and the most secure from corruption. It is consecrated to the Sun on account of its splendor, and to Jupiter on account of its temperature; and thus it can miraculously temper natural heat with moisture, preserve humors from corruption, and confer solar and Jovian virtue upon the spirits and members. However, it is necessary to make the very hard substance of gold more subtle and very easy to penetrate. For those who prepare cordials know that they restore the hidden power of the heart most effectively when nature labors least to absorb them. So that it is not in the least fatigued, they must be administered either already made most subtle, or with the most subtle things. They believe it would be best if gold could be made potable without any alien mixture; if that is not possible, they desire it to be taken crushed and reduced to leaves. You will have nearly potable gold (so to speak): Collect the flowers of borage, bugloss, and melissa, which we call citraria lemon balm; and when the moon enters Leo, Aries, or Sagittarius, and looks upon the Sun or Jupiter, cook them with white sugar dissolved in rose water, and for every ounce, carefully add three leaves of gold. Take it while fasting with a certain golden wine. Also, take the water distilled from a capon, consumed by the fire or otherwise, together with rose julep, in which you have previously crushed the gold leaves.
2.10.2: Furthermore, extinguish ignited gold in the clearest spring water, and crush the same gold leaves with it. Temper golden wine with the same, and eat a fresh egg yolk together with such a drink. You will easily preserve the humor in the whole tree of the body if you preserve it in the roots. Therefore, take the heart, liver, stomach, testicles, and cerebellum of such hens, pullets, and capons; cook them in a little water with minimal salt. Once cooked, crush them with all the meat, all the broth, and sugar; add a fresh egg yolk, and make a cake seasoned with a little cinnamon and saffron, and gilded. Eat this once while hungry, at least every fourth day, and then eat it alone, although you may add clear wine for a drink.

2.11.1:
*On the Use of Milk and Human Blood for the Life of the Elderly*
Often, immediately after the tenth and sometimes after the ninth seven-year period, the human tree withers away as its moisture is gradually dried up. At that time, this human tree must first be irrigated with human and youthful liquid, so that it may grow green again. Therefore, choose a healthy, beautiful, cheerful, and temperate young girl, and while you are fasting, drink her milk while the moon is waxing, and immediately eat a little powder of sweet fennel prepared properly with sugar. Sugar indeed will not allow the milk to congeal or putrefy in the stomach; fennel, since it is both subtle and a friend to milk, will distribute it to the members. Those whom senile hectic fever consumes, diligent physicians strive to restore with the liquid of human blood, which has been distilled to the fire by sublime art. What, therefore, prevents us from sometimes restoring those who are almost finished by old age with this drink as well? There is a certain common and ancient opinion that certain old witch-women (who are called striges screech-owls/vampires in the common tongue) suck the blood of infants so that they might grow young again by their strength. Why should our elderly, who are clearly deprived of every other aid, not suck the blood of a youth? A youth, I say, who is willing, healthy, joyful, and temperate, whose blood is excellent but perhaps excessive. Therefore, let them suck one or two ounces like leeches from a vein of the left arm that has been barely opened. Soon, however, they will take as much sugar and wine, and they will do this while hungry and thirsty during the waxing of the moon. If it is digested with difficulty, let it first be cooked together with sugar, or distilled moderately to hot water mixed with sugar; then let it be drunk. It is also an immediate aid to warm the stomach then with pig’s blood: let a sponge soaked in hot wine absorb this blood as it flows from a pig’s vein, and let it be applied immediately while hot to the stomach. Galen and Serapio say that the bite of a rabid dog is cured by drinking dog’s blood. However, they did not see fit to assign the reason. I, therefore, having sought it for two days, believe at last that the poisonous saliva of a rabid dog, having been impressed and pressed into the injured foot of a man, ascends gradually through the veins to the heart, in the manner of poison, unless something diverts it in the meantime. If, therefore, he drinks the blood of another dog in the interval, that crude blood floats for many hours in the stomach, until at last it is to be expelled through the bowels as if it were a foreign object. In the meantime, this canine blood draws the canine saliva that is gripping the upper members—before it can reach the area about the heart— down to the stomach. For in canine blood there is a power to attract the saliva of the dog, and in the saliva, in turn, a power to pursue similar blood. The poison, therefore, is removed from the heart and, having been imbibed into the blood floating in the stomach, is carried down through the lower passages along with the blood, and thus it leaves the man unharmed. Why this? Firstly, so that I might uncover the cause of such an occult matter, which helps while one is waiting. Secondly, so that I may advise that blood can be drunk, and indeed healthfully; and that there is a power in human blood to attract human blood and mutually pursue it. Do not fear, perhaps, that youthful blood drunk by an old man can be drawn to the veins and members and be of the greatest benefit there.

2.12.1:
*On the Diet, Habitation, and Custom of the Elderly*
It is expedient for the decrepit to remember that a weak nature must not be fatigued by the weight of nourishment or even distracted by too great a diversity of feasts. For even youth is quickly made old by this vice. Therefore, let them divide their meals, and let them restore nature not so much with abundant food as with frequent, yet with an interval given in the meantime for digestion. For often, even after the stomach itself has digested the food, if the liver has not also, so to speak, digested it, taking further nourishment distracts and fatigues nature; and when this weariness is repeated too often, untimely old age flies in. In winter, let the elderly seek sunny spots like sheep; in summer, let them revisit pleasant places and streams like birds. Let them frequently be among green and sweetly smelling plants, for these living and breathing things conspire to increase the human spirit. Let them flee to places commonly friendly to bees, and taste honey in the winter. For honey is a food especially friendly to the elderly, unless a fire of bile is feared. Fresh cheese is friendly, as are dates, figs, raisins, capers, sweet pomegranates, jujubes, hyssop, scabious, betony, but pistachios are much more so. Pine nuts, however, are the greatest of all, as we have said. From these, they will derive the most help if they keep them in slightly warm water for twelve hours before they eat them. For thus they will not harm the stomach. And furthermore, if while they use these, they also move about among pine groves, olive orchards, and vineyards, or at least receive the vapor and scent of pine. Likewise, let them often anoint the body with the gum and tears of the pine mixed with oil or wine. For it is probable that trees trees naturally endowed with a long life, especially if they remain green even in winter, can benefit your long life through their shade, vapor, fresh fruit, wood, and any timely use. Regarding long-lived animals, we have spoken above. Furthermore, it will perhaps contribute to the same goal if you live mostly among those who are healthy, who are by nature similar to you while you are healthy, and who are your friends, and perhaps even more so if they are a little younger. As to whether and how frequent association with young people might be able to delay old age for a while, modest Socrates should be consulted.

2.13.1:
*What aids the elderly may receive from the Planets to nourish all the members*
But consult rather, you anxious elderly men, Apollo, who judged Socrates the wisest of the Greeks. Consult Jupiter, moreover, and Venus. Phoebus himself, the discoverer of the art of medicine, will give you nutmeg to nourish the stomach: Jupiter, with Phoebus, will give you mastic and mint: Venus, however, coral. Again, for nourishing the head, Phoebus gives peony, frankincense, marjoram, and with Saturn, myrrh: Jupiter gives spikenard and mace: Venus, finally, sweet fennel and myrtle. To nourish the heart, you will receive from Phoebus lemon balm, saffron, lignum aloes, frankincense, ambergris, musk, leopard’s bane, a small amount of cloves, lemon peel, and cinnamon: From Jupiter, lily and bugloss. basil and mint, and been a root used in ancient medicine roots, both white and red. From Venus alone, myrtle, sandalwood, and rose; together with Saturn, coriander. Pound these diligently: for those things belonging to the stomach, prepare them into the form of a cerate with quince oil: but for those belonging to the head, steep them in oil of spikenard and apply them to the neck, temples, and forehead. Finally, for those of the heart, sprinkle them with golden wine and rose water, and apply them externally to the area over the heart. But the liver, which is primarily necessary for creating blood, I have somehow overlooked. Phoebus will help this organ with Eupatorium agrimony/hemp-agrimony and opobalsam; Jupiter with pistachios and raisins; Venus, however, with liverwort, endive, spodium, and chicory. Finally, for nourishing the spleen, that Saturn of yours, together with Jupiter, will provide you with capers, spleenwort, and tamarisk. Just as Jupiter, with Venus, heals the bladder with pine, licorice, starch, cucumber seeds, mallow, althaea, manna, and cassia. However, do not flee from Saturn as much as the elderly are often warned to do, for he is as much a domestic companion to you as he is a stranger to the young. Therefore, so that he may also reinvigorate and strengthen your whole body according to his powers, you will sometimes receive from him while he is reigning, and likewise from Phoebus, mummy and the flesh of a roasted goose: soften these with a little goose fat, and pound them diligently. Cook them with honey of chebulic and Indian myrobalans, and season them with ambergris, musk, and saffron, believing that there is faith in the medicines that contribute to life. By which you should hope that God will also inspire you as you pray, and that the things created by him, especially those of the heavens, undoubtedly possess a marvelous power to increase or preserve life.

2.14.1:
*Regarding the conversation of the elderly under Venus through green meadows*
But from these more severe deities, I call you back, elderly men, for a little while to Venus, through the green gardens and meadows. I call you all to bountiful Venus, not playing with you, but joking. She pours out this joking oracle both to you, I say, and to me, now an old man, at the beginning. “I, my sons (if you do not know), gave you life through pleasure and movement. I, therefore, will preserve your life through a certain pleasure and movement, even if not the same. Liber, the sower of the vine and propagator of life, will also preserve the same with freedom. Liber himself always hates slaves, and the life he promises through wine, he fills with length only for the free. For my own life and mind, while Saturn was reigning, a reduced amount of mint was once beneficial, and it pleases me daily. For you, however, a greater amount of mint is beneficial to the mind and life, while a reduced amount is harmful. Gather laughter from my gardens, neglect the fig. But when you pick these violets, consider yourselves to be picking lilies, and in grasping the lily, you grasp the crocus. Jupiter himself, having obtained the crocus from Phoebus, propagated it into the lily.”
2.14.2: “I, receiving the lily from Jupiter, transformed it into these violets which you see here. Finally, let the rose be to you the Morning Star, and the myrtle the Evening Star.” After the oracle, we must think; he mandates that the nature of green things, insofar as they are green, is not only alive, but also youthful, and overflowing with a completely healthy moisture and a certain vivid spirit. For this reason, through smell, sight, use, and frequent dwelling, a youthful spirit flows into us from them. Meanwhile, walking among the green things, we shall investigate the cause for which the color green nourishes the sight more than others and delights it healthily. We will find, finally, that the nature of sight is luminous and a friend of light, yet volatile and easily dissipated. Therefore, while it dilates itself through the light as if it were a friend, it is sometimes completely seized by an excessive abundance of light and dissolved by violent dilation; yet it naturally flees from darkness as if it were an enemy, and for this reason draws its rays back into a narrow space. The sight desires to enjoy the light in such a way that it is indeed amplified through this friend of its, but is not dissipated in the meantime. Now, in any color where there is much more darkness or blackness than light, the ray of sight does not dilate, nor is it delighted according to its desire. Where, conversely, there is much more of a splendid color than black, it is spread more widely, distracted by a certain harmful pleasure. Wherefore, the color green, more than any other, tempering black with white, provides both, delighting and at the same time preserving… preserving it, and furthermore with a soft and still tender quality: just as water also resists the rays of the eyes without offense, lest they go too far away and be dispersed. For those things which are hard and at the same time rough, break the rays in a certain way. Those which are very rare, provide a path to dissolution. But those which have some solidity, and at the same time a smooth equality, like reflective bodies, do not themselves break the rays, nor do they permit them to be dispersed too far. Finally, those which, besides these benefits, are also tender and soft, like water and green things, soothe with their softness the liquid rays of the eyes. Finally, the ray of sight is something naturally kindled within us in a certain water of the eyes: and it requires a tempered light in a somehow resistant water. Therefore, it rejoices in water, is delighted by things similar to mirrors, and is charmed by green things. In these green things, indeed, the light of the sun, being still spring-like, has with it moisture and subtle water, full of a certain hidden light. From which it also happens that when the color green is thinned, it is resolved into yellow. Why all this? So that we may understand that the frequent use of green things, since it refreshes the spirit of sight, which is in some way principal among the animal spirits, also refreshes the animal spirit itself. And let us also remember, if the color green, because it is the middle and most tempered among the grades of colors, benefits the animal spirit so much, then those things which are most tempered through their qualities benefit the natural and vital spirit much more. and subsequently helpful, and very beneficial to us for life. Nothing in the world is more tempered than the heavens; nothing beneath the heavens is almost more tempered than the human body; nothing in this body is more tempered than the spiritus vital spirit. Therefore, through tempered things, life remaining in the spirit is refreshed. The spirit is conformed to celestial things through tempered things. Finally, let us learn from the temperance of the color green, which, by illuminating, equally gathers and dilates the animal spirit, and for that reason is most helpful: we too, in choosing, composing, and using cordials, should mix aromatic, subtle, and sharp things—which are accustomed to extend or even illuminate the spirit, as saffron and cinnamon do—with aromatic styptics and gathering agents, such as myrobalans dried medicinal fruits and similar things, and conversely. Nor should we overlook those things which, without sharp aromatic qualities, accomplish both: namely, they slightly dilate, yet they also significantly gather and greatly illuminate, which we have mentioned elsewhere. This is the effect of gold, silver, spodium zinc oxide/calcined material, coral, electrum, silk, and precious stones, among which the hyacinth—even when held in the mouth—is highly approved for its Jovial related to the planet Jupiter temperance. Since the most beautiful and almost celestial things cannot be produced beneath the earth without some supreme benefit of the heavens, it is probable that such things possess wonderful virtues from the heavens. Indeed, a composition of this kind, which equally gathers the spirit by dilating and illuminating it, so delights it internally and refreshes it, just as the green color refreshes the eyes externally, and preserves the body itself even in the elderly in a certain natural greenness, as if it were a laurel, an olive, or a pine that remains green even in winter. And it achieves this all the more effectively the more it does so internally, and especially if such a composition glows with aromatic scent and attracts with its flavor. Indeed, just as a body composed of the thicker parts of the humors is reduced to a fifth form, so the spirit, composed of the most subtle portions of the same, has a fifth form that is naturally most tempered and lucid, and therefore celestial. And it must be preserved in this very form so that it is indeed subtle, and yet firm, as we have said. Let it be entirely lucid, but also in some way solid. And furthermore, let it be assiduously fostered by odoriferous, firm, and lucid things, if we wish to preserve the life that thrives in the spirit and to claim for ourselves celestial gifts. Having reflected on these things thus far at the bidding of Venus, let us suppose that we have heard Venus herself.

2.15.1:
*A personification of Mercury advising the elderly regarding pleasure, scents, songs, and medicines*
Meanwhile, while Venus herself was conversing among the elderly, perhaps she had spoken well enough thus far, but she would have likely continued at greater length. Mercury, the author of speech, interrupts this discourse with these words.
2.15.2: What is it that you, elderly men, have to do with this Venus who is always a girl? And what, in turn, does Venus have to do with discourse? Are these not my words as well as yours? Is my reason not the same as yours? Listen to me, therefore, with the same attention now that you gave to her, and indeed with much greater attention than to Venus. You know that there are five senses: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. Learn again, so to speak, that there are five reasons. For while your mind is daily imbued through the five senses and conceives the reasons of things from them, meanwhile, notions and habits for judging things arise as five reasons. Furthermore, just as there are five senses on one hand and, in a certain way, reasons on the other, so the tenor of life is arranged in five grades regarding sense and reason.
2.15.3: Hence, five ages are counted. The first is drawn by sense alone. The second is enticed by sense more than it is led by reason. The third, after these, is conducted equally by the alternating persuasions of reason and sense. The fourth is led by reason rather than by sense. Finally, the fifth ought to be ruled by reason alone. Therefore, let the first and second ages, as if subject to Venus, hear Venus speaking if they wish; but let the rest hear Mercury. I, therefore, address all the rest of you, not only for myself, but also for this Diana here, whom you see at my left: indeed, since she is speechless and I am eloquent, I rightfully speak for her, whose tongue I possess. Venus has certainly implanted in you a harmful pleasure, which indeed harms you, but benefits those who are to come, exhausting you little by little through a certain hidden pipe, and filling and procreating something else with your liquids: finally leaving you on the ground like some old, exhausted shell of a cicada, meanwhile looking out for the more tender cicada. Do you not see that Venus generates from your matter something that is new, living, and endowed with sense? She steals your youth, life, and sense, from your whole body through the pleasure of the whole, to make a whole from it. I, meanwhile, warned by the quality of that matter which remains from the fourth digestion, remind you that foods likewise cooked by the fourth digestion assist your life significantly: namely, a fresh, whole, and softboiled egg together with sugar and a little saffron; human milk, or pig milk, or goat milk taken with a little honey. And these two are more healthful when they are still glowing with native heat: although the egg seems to desire another cooking soon, especially in a weaker stomach, but it is to be cooked lightly. But let us return to Venus for a little while. If you have ever seen Venus, you have seen her as very youthful, and polished as if with harlot’s cosmetics and ornaments. This one, who is always new, always craves what is new, hates what is old, and destroys what has been made, doing so in order to construct. it. She, in turn—if it is permissible to say so—is like a harlot who is not content with any one man. She loves the crowd. And, to speak dialectically, she favors the species everywhere rather than the individual. Now, she does not merely precipitate you through touch, but also deceives and ruins you daily through taste. For those flavors which you perceive in things as pleasant due to a certain moderate temperance, this Diana has handed down as a gift from Apollo and Jupiter. But Venus, the insidious one, fabricates the miraculous lures of flavors by which, caught as if by a hook, you wretchedly lose your lives in secret every day. Why, then, do you blame Mars? Why Saturn? Mars indeed harms you very rarely and openly. Saturn also more often shows himself to be an enemy through his countenance, harms more slowly, and denies time to no one for remedies. Venus alone comes openly as a friend, but comes secretly as an enemy. Therefore, blame her rather, if it is permitted to blame anyone among the gods. Against her multiple treacheries, instruct yourselves with the eyes of Argus, and arm yourselves with the shield of Pallas. Block your ears to her smooth promises, as if to the lethal songs of the Sirens. Finally, accept this flower of providence from me, by which you may avoid the poisons of this Circe. She promises—and barely grants, and these are lethal—two pleasures; I, however, by the benefit of my father and brother, promise you five, and offer you five: pure, perpetual, and healthful, of which the lowest is in smell, the superior in hearing, and the most sublime in sight. in appearance, more eminent in imagination, and more excellent and divine in reason. The greater the pleasure perceived in touching and tasting, the more gravely and frequently the detriment to life occurs. Conversely, the more you bring back daily greater pleasure in smell, hearing, and sight, as well as in imagination and often in reason, the longer you prolong the threads of life. But just as I warned you to be wary of the deceptive Venus in the enticements of touching and tasting, so also be wary of Saturnus Saturn in the secret and overly persistent pleasure of the contemplative mind. For there, he frequently devours his own children. For those whom he snatches with the lures of his more sublime contemplations, and whom he recognizes there as his own, he meanwhile (if only they stand their ground there too long) cuts down from the earth with a certain sickle, and often steals the earthly life from the unwary. He is at least more indulgent than Venus in this respect: Venus gives the life she takes from you to another, restoring nothing to you for the loss. Saturnus Saturn, however, in exchange for the earthly life—from which he himself is separated, and from which he finally separates you—returns a heavenly and eternal life. In this very thing, Venus and Saturn seem similar to each other; for just as he delights in Aquarius the Water Bearer, so he reigns in Libra the Scales, because both he and she vex men with the lust of generation and harm those who are vexed, so that posterity may benefit from it. But while she fertilizes the body and stimulates it to be fruitful, he urges the mind, pregnant with his own seed, to birth. birth. You, therefore, mindful of the proverb, “Nothing in excess”, restrain the lust of both the birthing mind and body with the constant reins of prudence. Although he harms those whom he oppresses with weariness, torpor, sorrow, cares, and superstition much more quickly and gravely than those whom he elevates to high places above the strength of the body and the customs of mortals. Truly, I advise you to preserve what the equitable Jupiter taught Pythagoras and Plato: that human life is preserved in a certain equal proportion of the soul itself with the body, so that each is nourished and similarly augmented by its own particular foods and exercises. If someone makes one significantly more robust than the other, especially through his own education, he causes no small loss to his life. Therefore, whoever chooses among the things praised by the art of medicine those which benefit the body and the intellect simultaneously claims for himself the greatest aid to life. Indeed, consider wine, mint, myrobalan an Indian fruit used in medicine, musk, ambergris, fresh ginger, frankincense, aloe, hyacinth, and similar small stones or herbs to be in that number, and those which are composed equally by physicians for the utility of both. But since these long circumlocutions are sometimes interrupted, I, too, a physician, have approached this matter. If the flavors accepted from things that are no longer living, as well as odors from aromatics already dry and devoid of life, are considered to contribute much to life, why do you doubt that odors from plants, still clinging to their roots and living, contribute to life in a wonderful way? while they are about to accumulate the powers of life? Finally, if vapors exhaling from merely vegetative life greatly benefit your life, how much do you think songs will benefit it—those that are aerial to an aerial spirit, harmonic to a harmonic one, still warm and living to a living one, endowed with sense to a sensual one, and conceived by reason to a rational one? Therefore, I hand over to you this lyre fabricated by me, and with it a song in the manner of Phoebus Apollo, a comfort for labors, a pledge of long life. For just as things that are most temperate in quality and simultaneously aromatic attune the humors among themselves and the natural spirit with itself, so do odors of this kind attune the vital spirit, and in turn, similar harmonies attune the animal spirit. Therefore, while you temper the sounds on the lyre and the tones in the voice, believe that your spirit within is being tempered similarly. And so that I myself may not be more stingy than Venus, who grows cold without Bacchus the god of wine, receive this nectar from me through this very Liber pater a name for Bacchus. Let those among you who are especially cold, at similar times every fourteenth day, take two ounces of sweet Vernaccia or Malmsey wine with one ounce of bread, three hours before the meal. Once, however, take one drachm of that sublime water distilled from wine with half an ounce of rose julep. With this liquid, they can also most conveniently anoint the skin and use it for scent. And so that after this nectar I may also bring you ambrosia, I grant this further medicine received from Jupiter: take four ounces of chebulic myrobalans a type of medicinal fruit, three of rose sugar, and—in winter—one ounce of candied ginger, but in summer, half an ounce.
2.15.4: Concoct these three things sweetly with the honey of emblic myrobalans, and decorate them with seven leaves of gold. Take a bolus fasting, four hours before lunch. Take this daily for at least a whole year, so that your youth may be renewed like that of an eagle. Thus far let us consider that Mercury has spoken.

2.16.1:
*Confirmation of the above. And precepts for avoiding sexual intercourse and constant deep thought*
Astrologers claim that Venus and Saturn are mutually inimical. However, since in the heavens, where all things are moved by love and where there is no defect, there cannot be hatred, we interpret “inimical” as “differing in effect.” Let us set aside other matters for the present. Behold, now Saturn has placed pleasure for us in the center, and Venus in the circumference. Pleasure, however, is a kind of bait for the spirits. Therefore, Venus and Saturn from opposite sides lie in wait for the flight of our spirit. She lures it to external things through her pleasure; he, meanwhile, recalls it to internal things through his. Thus, they distract the spirit if they move and dissipate it at almost the same time. For this reason, nothing is more pestilential to a contemplative or curious person than the venereal act; conversely, nothing can be more alien to one pursuing this act than care and contemplation. But a physical contemplativewe count the religious person in the same rank. And in a similar rank, anyone who is deeply thoughtful in his business affairs and subject to heavy cares. From this it follows, in turn, that if we wish to relieve and otherwise console someone who is either too occupied by Saturnian contemplation or pressed by care, we try to do so through venereal acts, games, and jests in vain and even with loss, as if through remedies that are far apart. And conversely, if we wish to moderate someone lost in a venereal act or relaxed in games and jests, we cannot easily improve him through Saturnian severity. The best discipline is to recall to the middle, through certain studies of Phoebus Apollo and Jupiter—who are intermediaries between Saturn and Venus—and similar remedies, those men who are inclining toward either extreme. But let us finally be physicians. Just as a flame is extinguished in two commonly violent ways—either by being blown about by winds or, on the contrary, by being stifled by ashes—so we dissipate the spirit quickly through the venereal effect, or we stifle it slowly with Saturnian weight, and often we express it by compressing it, and likewise resolve it. The spirit, indeed, frequently flying to the outermost parts, renders the innermost parts either empty or alien to life. But when forced to the innermost parts, it renders the rest of the surrounding limbs less suitable for life. Since, therefore, both old age and Venus bring burdens to our interior parts, and Saturn to our exterior parts—Venus indeed especially, since from any of her movements the body is easily weakenedis shaken and sags. This happens especially to Saturnian associated with the planet Saturn, linked to melancholy and contemplation types when their physical and mental strength is undermined by any office of contemplation, care, or labor. Although anyone born for contemplation or for lust is generally strongest by nature in their respective calling, nature often joins power with pleasure and ease. Therefore, let each person know himself, and be his own moderator and physician. Let those who intend to engage in intercourse frequently consult others. I, however, have advised those who intend to exercise their intellect in the previous book. Finally, they ought to use all diets and remedies by which the limbs, spirit, senses, intellect, and memory may be strengthened. They should repeat their cogitations at intervals, and not expect even the slightest labor from contemplation. This applies especially when they first begin to turn gray, although there are some who do not produce gray hairs through a weakness of nature while still young, but rather through sickness, some preceding ailment, or even the resemblance of their parents, from whom they were generated when those parents were already graying.

2.17.1:
*The medicine of the elderly, and again concerning habitation and diet*
The rule of the Chaldeans referring to ancient Babylonian sages is perhaps to be approved for recovering youth: to purge away the foreign humors imbibed by the body by degrees, both the interior ones with competent medicines and the exterior ones through frictionand baths and the provocation of sweat, and in the meantime, to fill the body little by little with wholesome and nutritious foods. There are some who promise to lead out all old and putrid humors entirely with certain trochisci lozenges or medicinal tablets made from viper or prepared hellebore. Once these are purged, and the most wholesome humor is recreated with healthy foods, they promise to restore youth. Those who are more cautious feed hens with hellebore, and then feed the human being with those hens. I believe that such a cure, being dangerous, should be attempted in youth rather than in old age, lest they happen to experience that youth promised by Medea the mythological sorceress who rejuvenated her father-in-law to Pelias the king whom Medea tricked into being boiled alive. For Hippocrates the father of Greek medicine asserts that young men who take exquisite purging medicines age quickly. But where diet does not suffice, you may use a clyster, or manna, or especially washed aloes safely. If your belly is rather restricted, use manna with chicken broth for the virtue of the myrobalans. If not, you will preserve yourself as a youth even in old age by this: Take one ounce of washed aloes, two drachms of emblic myrobalans an Indian fruit used in medicine, the same amount of chebulic myrobalans, two of purple roses, and the same amount of mastic; make pills with mallow and wine-fig, when the moon is happilypositioned and enjoys the favorable aspect of Jupiter, especially if it or Jupiter itself possesses the fixed houses. For these things contribute greatly to the longevity of life. You may also usefully combine rhubarb here with aloes, namely, half a part of aloes and half of rhubarb, and whenever it is necessary, take one pill in the morning, up to three or five, and drink a little wine. When you fear phlegm more, you may also conveniently take a third part of agaric a medicinal mushroom in these pills, together with two parts of aloes, omitting the rhubarb. But I have found that first composition of pills to be the safest for many years at any age. Make a concoction of this kind at the same hour: take one ounce of each of emblic, belleric, Indian, and chebulic myrobalans; two of cinnamon; one of leopard’s bane doronicum and purple roses; two of red sandalwood; one drachm of saffron; and a third of a drachm of musk and the same amount of amber. After this, pour in white sugar with rose waterboil it, make boluses, and soften them. We have experienced that taking these four hours before a meal is useful for strengthening vitality, and for illuminating and firming the spirit. It will be especially beneficial if you drink a little wine on top of it. It will also be useful to frequently sprinkle heated bread with wine and rose water, and season it with a little cinnamon and an abundance of sugar. Frequently mix these two things with almond milk and a little bread. For such mixtures recall the nature of Jupiter. Beyond all the things we have explained or at least indicated in the previous sections, all city-dwellers must carefully avoid all these things: cold of any kind, cold after heat or heat after cold, night mists, winds blowing from a marsh or bursting through a narrow space, places where the air is moved too violently or not moved at all, any habitation that is too humid, stench, mold, and torpor. These things apply most diligently to the followers of Mercury the god associated with intellect and merchants, and most diligently of all to the elderly, who, after they have lightly rubbed their whole body in the morning, should sootheit against the discomforts of the air and labor with warm oil or some slightly bitter wine, into which they have previously infused myrrh, rose, and myrtle. They should frequently carry sage in their mouths, as it is most friendly to the nerves and teeth. And when they are forced to return to liquid foods, like infants, due to a defect of the teeth, let them take the softest things. They should fortify milk with moderate wine. They should use fire only as a medicine, as much as the necessity of expelling cold and exciting innate heat demands; otherwise, it is like a predator that would dry up the natural moisture. They should follow the sun as long as it delights them, as a form of nourishment, avoiding distillation catarrh or excess fluid buildup and similarly declining from heat. They should choose easy movements, which are quite necessary for exciting heat. But they should hate the labors of the body, and even more those of the mind; and likewise long thirst, and the middle, and staying awake.

2.18.1:
*On the nourishment of the spirit, and the preservation of life through scents*
We read that in certain hot regions, which are fragrant everywhere with many odors, many people of slender body and weak stomach live almost on the scent alonenourished by odors. Perhaps this is because the very nature of the place, by turning almost all the juices of herbs, fruits, and produce into odors, also resolves the humors of the human body into spirit there. Since, therefore, both odor and spirit are a certain kind of vapor, and like is nourished by like, it is not surprising that both the spirit and the spiritual person receive the greatest amount of nourishment from odors. Indeed, nourishment of whatever kind it may be—whether through odors or fomentations— is especially necessary for the elderly and the frail, so that we might somehow compensate for a deficiency of more solid and abundant food. Some, however, are accustomed to doubt whether the spirit is nourished by odors. I, for my part, believe that it is perhaps nourished by them only in such a way that, unless foods that are thick are finally reduced through digestion into vapors, the spirit itself—which we have said is a vapor—would receive no nourishment from them. Thus, an odor full of life suddenly recreates the spirit, which other things can barely restore even in the end. We call the vapor into which cooked food is finally converted an “odor,” since an odor is everywhere a certain kind of vapor: just as it is maintained here.
2.18.2: The vapor drawn inward from food, unless it pleases the spirit with some scent, hardly provides any nourishment to the spirit. For this reason, we greatly approve of our Avicenna Persian physician and philosopher, who says that the body is nourished by sweetness, but the spirit by a certain (to use his words) “aromaticity.” Since the thickness of the body cannot coalesce except through thickness, such as is found in sweetness. The thinness of the spirit, however, can be restored by nothing other than a certain smoke and vapor, in which the aromatic quality itself thrives. We call the aromatic quality something fragrant, sharp, and in a way, styptic. Furthermore, since the liver provides nourishment to the body through the blood, it is greatly increased by sweetness. The heart, however, because it both creates spirit and generates nourishment for the spirit, rightly desires aromatics. It is beneficial, however, for aromatics to be nourished by sweetness for the sake of the heart, that is, to be seasoned; and for sweet things to be mixed with aromatics for the liver, while avoiding excessive sweetness. What more is there to say? Galen Ancient Greek physician himself, following Hippocrates Ancient Greek physician, thinks that the spirit is nourished not only by odor, but by air. By air, I say, not simple air, but rather one that is suitably mixed.
2.18.3: If we are to place our trust in these men, we shall judge that there is no choice of foods, nor of any other thing, more necessary for life than that of air accommodated to us. For air, being most easily and always affected by the qualities of both lower things and celestial bodies, and surrounded by an immense (if I may say so) amplitude, and penetrating us everywhere with perpetual motion, miraculously reduces us to its own quality: especially the spirit, particularly the vital spirit thriving in the heart, into whose inner chambers it blows both continuously and suddenly; thus affecting the spirit immediately as it is itself affected. And through the vital spirit, which is like the material and origin of the animal spirit, it affects the animal spirit as well. The quality of this is of the greatest importance to those gifted people who labor much with this kind of spirit. Therefore, the choice of pure and luminous air, odors, and music concerns no one more than them. For these three are judged to be the primary fomentations of the animal spirit. But air is chosen as the most important thing for life. For those born in the eighth month in Egypt North African country live for a long time, andsome in the temperate regions of Greece Southern European country live very healthily through the benefit of the air, which Aristotle Greek philosopher relates and Avicenna confirms. But truly, just as the body, being composed of various things, must be nourished by various (although not at the same table) foods, so the spirit, being similarly composed, must be delighted and fostered by a certain variety of air that is always chosen. It must also be refreshed daily by a similar variety of chosen odors. For air and odor seem to be, as it were, a certain kind of spirit. Now, indeed, Alexander Alexander of Aphrodisias, Greek commentator and the Peripatetics followers of Aristotle, along with Galen, conclude that the vital and animal spirits are nourished by both odor and air because each is mixed and conformable, and that each inhaled substance penetrates into the heart, where it is cooked and tempered for life, and diffused through all channels: where each, once cooked, again nourishes the spirit (as they say), especially the animal spirit. They also say that inhaled air is useful not only by cooling the heat but also by nourishing it. For even very cold animals breathe. They add that thicker air is meant for the natural spirit as if it were more corporeal…
2.18.4: …and that the subtle, pure, and luminous air is meant for the vital spirit, and especially for the animal spirit. Nor should it seem surprising that a spirit so thin is nourished by thin things; since many small fish are nourished by the clearest water, and basil lives, grows, flowers, and smells sweet in similar water. I pass over the nutrients, that is, the elements, by which some claim the chameleon a lizard known for color-changing and the salamander a mythical creature associated with fire are nourished. Let us return to our own matters. It certainly matters a great deal what kind of air we breathe, and what kind of odors we inhale. For our spirit becomes like them. The soul sustains us through life only to the extent that the spirit maintains the harmony that binds it to the soul. Indeed, the spirit in us lives first and foremost, and, as it were, it lives alone. Does it not happen that, due to some sudden accident or emotion, life, sensation, and motion suddenly desert the limbs, as the spirit has retreated to the inner chambers of the heart? And often they return immediately to the limbs through friction and odors as the spirit returns there, as if life resides in the volatile spirit itself rather than in the humors or the limbs. Otherwise, because of… so that the thick tenacity of these things might allow life to approach the limbs and depart from them more slowly. Whoever, therefore, desires to prolong life in the body, cultivate the spirit first of all. Increase it with nutrients that increase the blood, specifically those that are temperate and clear. Foster it always with choice air, nourish it daily with sweet odors, and delight it with dreams and songs. But meanwhile, avoid odors that are too hot, flee from those that are too cold, and grasp at those that are temperate. Temper the cold with the hot, and the dry with the moist. Know, indeed, that every odor, because it is the most subtle part of a body, has some degree of heat. Seek odors rather from things that nourish themselves: from aromatic pears, peaches, and similar fruits. Even more so from fresh, warm bread, and most especially from roasted meats, rather than from wine. And just as a taste that pleases wonderfully is very often the cause or occasion of quick nourishment for the body, so believe that an odor acts in the same way toward the spirit. I wish to remind you again that Democritus, in order to comply with his friends, kept his spirit alive for four days just by smelling warm bread; and he could have kept his spirit even longer, had it pleased him. There are those who say he did this with the scent of honey. I, if he indeed used honey, believe he infused honey dissolved in wine onto the warm bread. For the scent of honey is not to be spurned. Honey exists as the flower of flowers, and it nourishes no little by its very sweetness, and for a long time preserves things whole from putrefactio decay by its own quality. Therefore, if one knows how to use this for food in such a way that it does not clog the passages with excessive sweetness, nor stir up bile with a certain heat, they will surely possess a support for a longer life. Use this condiment, at the very least, with cold and moist things.
