But to recall you to odors: whenever you fear excessive suffocation and compression of the spirits, which frequent sorrow and lethargy portend, embrace surrounding odors. However, when you fear the flight of exhaling spirits, accept odors rather as infused into nutrients. accept them. And if you take in any odors besides from the outside, apply them as a shield only to your left ribs. Do you not see how suddenly the womb itself rushes upward or downward at the presence of odors? How swiftly the spirit flies to the mouth and nostrils, enticed by the bait of a sweet scent? Where, therefore, the spirit is perceived to be either scant or very fugitive, which cowardice and bodily weakness often declare, or which occurs for many small reasons, do not so much cast odors from the outside as inject them within to entice, or rather to feed and retain it. Above all, choose the scent of wine. For an odor exhaling from nature nourishes the spirit greatly, both by nourishing the body most abundantly and swiftly, and by affecting the senses with pleasure. Such wine is, above all others, warm, moist, fragrant, and clear. I would say that Saccharum sugar is the same, if it would take on a scent. Cynnamomum cinnamon is also similar, and fragrant anisum anise and sweet maratrum fennel, if they add a certain greater sweetness to their sharpness. But what nature has not made temperate, fashion for yourselves.
2.18.5: From these, whenever you fear the distraction of the spirits, apply those that are hotter, sharper, and most subtle, which can restrain the flight of the spirit and steady it for a while, such as saffron, cloves, cinnamon, toasted bread, rose water, and rose vinegar, rose, myrtle, violet, sandalwood, coriander, quince, apple, and citrus. I dread camphor, however, when one must act against shriveling. But I always favor fresh mint, which is healthful for the mind and safest for the spirit. Finally, remember that all things contrary to poison are very healthful for life, not only by taste but also by smell, especially thriacam treacle/antidote. We have explained these in the book against the pestilence, and we shall relate them also in the following book. Among them, however, so that nothing may escape you, we count wine. For just as hemlock is a poison to man, so is wine to hemlock, not when drunk at the same time, but shortly thereafter. And lest I entice you here only with odors,
2.18.6: I order an electuary to be composed for you, to be tasted daily in the morning, pleasant to both smell and taste, and very healthful for life. Take three ounces of chebulic myrobalans, one of emblic, one of Indian, and one of belleric; a half-ounce of leopard’s bane two ounces of cinnamon, one drachm of saffron, a third of a drachm of ambergris, and the same amount of musk. Mix them diligently. Add as much rose sugar as satisfies the taste, as much red sandalwood as is enough for the color, and likewise as much honey of emblic or chebulic as is appropriate for the consistency of the electuary; add as many almond leaves as there are ounces mentioned above. When, however, a complex composition is too difficult, we have tested this simple one to be the best: namely, of chebulic myrobalans, sweet fennel, and sugar dissolved in rose water. When taken both on an empty stomach and after dinner, you will find that preserved myrobalans are better; but if dry, they should at least be soaked in oil for a full day. prolonged. Instead of mixing them, infuse them in sweet almonds or cow’s butter. Avicenna Persian physician and philosopher confirms for us a preparation of emblic and Indian myrobalans dried medicinal fruits with the honey of anacards and cooked butter. Likewise, he suggests chebulic myrobalans with ginger and iron filings, preferably with vinegar. Petrus Aponensis Peter of Abano, medieval philosopher and physician also approves a composition of saffron, mace, and castoreum, taken in equal parts and mixed with wine. He affirms that life is accustomed to being prolonged even in those who are almost dying. Finally, Haly Haly Abbas, Persian physician, an excellent astrologer and doctor, asserts that the use of triphera a complex medicinal electuary and similar things makes life longer. Indeed, in every triphera, the myrobalan is the foundation, but they temper this with certain subtle and mild substances, especially where the myrobalan is drier, so that it may penetrate without obstructing the passages or excessively drying or constricting the bowels. Furthermore, we use wine most conveniently, provided it is moderate, so that it does not dilute the mixture. However, I believe the composition of Peter which I just mentioned, if indeed it is useful, is more useful by smell than by consumption.

2.19.1:
*The Medicine of the Magi for the Elderly*
The Magi ancient Persian priestly caste or wise men, observers of the stars, came to Christ, the leader of life, with the star as their guide, offering a precious treasure of life: gold, frankincense, and myrrh. They dedicated three gifts to the Lord of the stars for the three lords of the planets. Gold, indeed, for the temperament of Jupiter the most temperate of all. Frankincense, moreover, for the Sun, burning with its specifically Phoebean heat and fragrance. Finally, myrrh, which strengthens and preserves the body, for Saturn, the firmest of all the planets. Come here, therefore, all you old men to the wise Magi, bearing gifts that will also prolong your life, with which they are said to have once honored the author of life. Come, old men, I say, who endure old age heavily. Come, furthermore, all of you whom the fear of approaching old age disturbs. Accept, I pray, these vital gifts with cheerfulness. Take two parts of frankincense, and one part of… myrrh, and half a drachm of gold leaf. Pound the three together, combine them, and form them into pills with a certain pure wine. Prepare this at an opportune time, when Diana the Moon enjoys a favorable aspect of Phoebus the Sun or Jupiter. Take a small portion of such a treasure with a little drink of pure wine, unless perhaps the summer is hot; then it is better to drink rose water. If, however, any of you fears the heat at any time, he should add chebulic or emblic myrobalan in an amount equal to the weight of the frankincense, myrrh, and gold combined. This will undoubtedly protect the natural humors from putrefaction, and will drive off the resolution of moisture for a longer time. This will cherish, confirm, strengthen, and nourish the three spirits within you: the natural, the vital, and the animal. This will again invigorate the senses, sharpen the intellect, and preserve the memory.
2.19.2: It will again invigorate the senses, sharpen the intellect, and preserve the memory.

2.20.1:
*On Avoiding the Dangers Imminent from every Seventh Year of Life*
Since astronomers have distributed the individual hours of the day to the planets in order, and similarly the seven days of the week, and have assigned the offices of the planets by months even within the very fetus, why should we not arrange the same throughout the years? Just as Saturn the outermost planet ruled the infant hiding in the womb during the first month, and the Moon the innermost planet during the last, so let us lead the newborn with the order now reversed: the first year of his life ruled by the Moon, the second (if you wish) by Mercury, the third by Venus, the fourth by the Sun, the fifth by Mars, the sixth by Jupiter, and the seventh by Saturn… and from there the order is repeated similarly throughout life. Therefore, in every seventh year of life, a very great change occurs in the body, and it is consequently most dangerous, since Saturn is commonly a stranger to us, and the governance returns immediately from him, the highest of the planets, to the Moon, the lowest. The Greek astronomers call these years climacteric critical or dangerous years; we call them scalar or gradary or decretory. Perhaps, indeed, the planets rule the very movement of the humor or nature in diseases by the same order through the days. Whence every seventh day is also called judiciary for the same reason. The fourth is also critical, since it holds the middle place in the seven. Therefore, if you desire to prolong life to old age, uninterrupted by such steps, whenever you approach every seventh year, consult an astrologer diligentlyfrom which a dangerous crisis threatens you, learn it thoroughly. Then, either consult a physician or summon prudence and temperance. Indeed, Ptolemy himself confesses that the threats of the stars can be warded off by these remedies. He even adds that the promises of the stars can be increased, just as a farmer increases the virtue of the soil. Petrus Aponensis proves with many arguments, and by the testimony of Aristotle, Galen, and Haly, that the natural end of life is not determined to a hair’s breadth from the beginning, but can be moved further or nearer. He asserts this from both the stars and from the material, and concludes, with these authors and reasons, that even a natural death can be deferred by both the mechanisms of astrology and the defenses of physicians. Therefore, neither do we rashlylabor at these precepts. Do not let it be tiresome to inquire of physicians what your diet should be by nature, and of astrologers which star favors your life; and when this star is well-disposed, and the Moon is favorable to it, compose what you have learned to be beneficial. Nor should you be ashamed to listen to those who seem to have attained a prosperous old age not so much by fortune as by virtue. Furthermore, Ptolemy and other professors of astronomy promise a prosperous and long life through certain images crafted from specific stones and metals under a certain star. Indeed, we are composing a commentary on Plotinus regarding these images in part, and for the most part regarding the rest of celestial favor; we think this book should be subjoined to this work hereafter, just as we wish this to be written after the book we composed concerning the healing of lite dispute/sicknessthe health of the learned. But as for the celestial favor I was just speaking of for a long youth, now, as much as it is permitted to speak like a poet, and as much as it is permitted for a physician to act, we shall seek it from Phoebus and Bacchus. The youth of Phoebus and Bacchus is eternal, For unshorn hair becomes both gods. Phoebus and Bacchus are always inseparable brothers; both are almost the same. Phoebus is indeed the soul of that sphere, while the sphere is Bacchus. Moreover, Phoebus is the entire circuit of the sphere itself, while Bacchus is the entire circle flaming within this circuit. Indeed, Phoebus is the life-giving light in this flaming globe, whereas Bacchus exists therein as the heat that is salutary because of the light. Therefore, they are always brothers and companions, almost always one and the same. But what is this? If the Sun in spring is indeed Phoebus…
2.20.2: …at his own turn exciting the song of birds, and in turn tempering the seasons with his lyre: in autumn, however, the same Sun exists as Bacchus, the author of wine. Father Liber, who loves the hills, brings us three things for preserving youth: first these sunny hills, and on these hills, especially the most sweet wine, and in wine, perpetual security. Phoebus, the brother of Bacchus, bestows three things with equal kindness: first, divine light; by the fomentation of this light, sweetly scented herbs; and in the shadow of this light, the lyre and eternal song. If these things are weighed especially, then with these threads, Clotho would no longer be a Fate who cuts the long threads of life for us. Almost all poets sing of three Fates, and we, not being poets, also sing of three. Indeed, prudence in every diet begins a long life for us…
2.20.3: …prudence also in enduring cares produces a long life; but negligence in enjoying the heavens shortens life. Pythagoras celebrates three temperances above all: we also celebrate three at present: keep temperance in passions, keep temperance in every diet, and keep temperance of the air. For by this providence, with God aspiring, you will push far away the intemperance of the humors, which is the cause of premature old age and untimely death. That author of life will aspire, if you desire a long life only on the condition that you may live longer with the human race, and most of all that you may live for Him by whom the whole world lives while aspiring.

3.0.1: MARSILIO FICINO OF FLORENCE An epistolary preface to the third book, On Obtaining Life from the Heavens, addressed to the most serene King of Pannonia.
3.0.2: The ancient philosophers, most fortunate King of all, having most diligently examined the powers of the heavens and the natures of the lower world, and judging that a man is wise in vain if he is not wise for himself, appear to have rightly directed all their research primarily toward obtaining life for themselves from the heavens. They judged, as I believe, that both the elements and the things composed of them would be known in vain, and that the motions and influences of the heavens would be observed too rashly, unless these things, once known and joined together with them, should one day contribute to their own life and happiness. Such contemplation proved useful to them, it seems, first of all for the present life. For Pythagoras, Democritus, and Apollonius of Tyana, and whoever devoted themselves to this goal, obtained prosperous health and long life through the use of the things they had come to know. Furthermore, it contributed to the future life, both by spreading glory among posterity and by enjoying it in eternity before God. Indeed, from the marvelous order of the whole world, they finally knew its ruler, and they loved the known One above all. But for you, glory throughout all future ages, magnanimous [king]integrity, magnificence, and perpetual victory promise. Divine clemency also promises a life blessed in eternity with God for your distinguished piety and justice. Finally, the lucky stars have decreed for you a prosperous life among mortals, long in years as far as I have been permitted to conjecture from certain signs. But that they should perform what they promise with the firmest faith, and increase it with a fuller abundance, your own diligence and the care of physicians and astrologers can undoubtedly achieve. Indeed, the most learned astrologers and physicians admit that this can be done through knowledge and prudence. Since, therefore, I had recently composed a commentary among the books of Plotinus a thirdcentury Neoplatonist philosopher dedicated to the great Lorenzo de’ Medici, on the book of Plotinus that treats the drawing of favor from the heavens, I have now decided to select it from among the other things counted in our commentaries, with the approval of Lorenzo himself, and to dedicate it especially to your majesty. I truly hope that while I look to your life and prosperity, I shall meanwhile be looking to the life and splendor of our age and of the human race. And so that these works of ours might more effectively benefit royal health and prosperity, I have thought they should be sent through Valori. I beg you, therefore, most clement King, to embrace this Valori of ours. For your nature, virtue, and authority are so powerful that even Valori himself cannot avail without you. July 10, 1489. Florence.
3.0.3: AN EXHORTATION OF MARSILIO FICINO TO THE READER OF THE FOLLOWING BOOK.
3.0.4: Greetings, ingenious guest. Greetings again, whoever you are, thirsting for health, you who are heading toward our threshold. See, I beg you, eager guest, how hospitable I am. It was surely the duty of the person entering to bid health immediately to the host: I, however, anticipating [your] health, have bidden you greeting first. I have willingly welcomed you, the entrant, still unknown. To you who lingers with me, I will give the promised health, if God shall aspire. You have therefore found a guest-house that is friendly to all and now full of love for you. If by chance you carry with you anything contrary to love, if you possess any hatred, I beg you to put it aside before you touch these vital medicines. For love and the pleasure of your parents gave you life: hatred and grief, in turn, take it away. To the person whom hateful grief torments, no place is left anywhere for vital medicine. Therefore, from now on I address you no longer as a guest, but as a friend. The workshop of your Marsilio is somewhat larger than just these boundaries you see here. For it is not defined by this following book alone, but also by the two preceding ones. Indeed, it is a certain medicine to help life with all its strength, so that your life may be strong and long. And everywhere it strives to be helped by the aid of physicians and from the heavens. Truly, this workshop of ours offers various antidotes, drugs, poultices, ointments, and remedies according to the different talents and natures of men.
3.0.5: If any of these should perhaps please you less, then indeed dismiss those, but do not on that account reject the rest. Finally, if you do not approve of astronomical images—which are otherwise used for the health of mortals, and which I recount rather than approve—dismiss these, with my permission and even my advice if you wish. Do not, however, neglect the medicines confirmed by a certain heavenly aid, unless by chance you neglect life itself. For I have long since learned through frequent experience that there is as much difference between medicines of this kind and others made without astrological selection as there is between wine and water; so that even an infant born in Florence in the month of March, in the eighth month from conception, with Saturn retrograde ascending, half-alive, seems to have been restored to life by us—or rather by God—so much so that he has now almost completed his third year in good health. And now, if I were to tell more of this kind, I would be speaking the truth. I would not do so in a boastful manner, which is completely alien to a philosopher, but rather in an exhortative one.
3.0.6: We have spoken to you enough, partly reconciling you, and partly exhorting you. Therefore, let us proceed to speak with Plotinus, so that we may consult for you more diligently.
3.0.7: THE BOOK OF MARSILIO FICINO OF FLORENCE On Obtaining Life from the Heavens, composed by the same author among his commentaries on Plotinus.
3.0.8: In what the virtue that attracts favor from the heavens consists, according to Plotinus: namely, in the fact that the world soul and the souls of the stars and demons are easily enticed by adapted bodily forms.

3.1.1: If these two things alone were in the world—on one side, intellect, and on the other, body—but without a soul: then neither would the intellect be drawn to the body (for it is completely immovable and lacks the affect that is the principle of motion, as being very far removed from the body), nor would the body be drawn to the intellect, as it is ineffective and inept for motion by itself, and far removed from the intellect. But if a soul is interposed, conforming to both, an attraction will easily occur in both directions and toward both. First, the soul itself is led most easily of all, since it is the first thing that moves, and it moves of itself and spontaneously…
3.1.2: Furthermore, since it is, as I have said, the middle of all things, it contains all things in its own way within itself, being close by reason to both sides. Therefore, it is reconciled with all things, even those that are far apart from one another, for they are not far from it. For beyond the fact that it is conformable to divine things on one side and to perishable things on the other, and leans toward both by its affect, it is meanwhile entirely present everywhere. Added to this is the fact that the world soul possesses at least as many seminal reasons of things as there are ideas in the divine mind; by these reasons, it fashions as many species in matter. Hence, each individual species corresponds properly to its idea through its own seminal reason and can often easily receive something from there, since it was created from there through this reason. Therefore, if at any time it should degenerate from its own form, it can be formed again through this medium which is closest to it, and through that medium, it can be easily reformed from there, provided that you duly apply to a certain species of things, or an individual of it, many things that are scattered but conformable to the same idea. Presently, into this matter so opportunely prepared, you will draw a unique gift from the idea through, indeed, the seminal reason of the soul. For it is not the intellect itself, properly speaking, that is led, but the soul. Therefore, let no one think that certain divine beings, completely separated from matter, are drawn to specific worldly materials, but rather demons and the gifts of the animated world and living stars. Let no one, again, wonder that the soul can be, as it were, enticed by material forms.
3.1.3: For it has made such foods, suitable to itself, by which it might be enticed; and it always and willingly dwells in them. Nor in the whole living world is anything found so deformed that a soul is not present to it, or that the gift of the soul is not inherent in it. Such congruities of forms, therefore, to the reasons of the world soul, Zoroaster called divine enticements, which Synesius also confirmed to be magical lures.
3.1.4: Finally, let no one believe that absolutely all gifts are drawn from the soul to a certain species of matter at a certain time, but only, according to the opportunity, the gifts of the seed from which such a species has sprouted, and of conformable seeds. Therefore, this human being, by applying only human things, does not claim for himself the gifts of fish or birds, but human and similar ones. However, by applying those things that pertain to a certain star and demon, he undergoes the proper influx of this star and demon, just as wood prepared by sulfur is ready for a flame that is everywhere present. And this occurs not only through the rays of the star and demon themselves, but also through the world soul itself, which is everywhere present, in which the reason of any star and demon flourishes: partly indeed as seminal for generating, and partly as exemplary for knowing. For this soul, according to the ancient Platonists, built with its own reasons figures in the heavens beyond the stars, and impressed upon these stars such parts that they themselves are also certain figures, and it impressed properties upon all these. In the stars, however, figures, and parts, the propertiesare contained all the species of inferior things and their properties. He posited forty-eight universal figures: namely, twelve in the zodiac, and thirty-six outside it. Likewise, in the zodiac, thirty-six corre sponding to the number of faces. Again, there are three hundred and sixty corresponding to the number of degrees. For in every degree there are several stars, from which images are made there. Similarly, he divided the images outside the zodiac into more figures according to the number of faces and their degrees there. Finally, he established certain relations and proportions from these universal images to other universal images, which themselves also exist there. Such figures have their own continuity from the rays of their stars cast into one another by a certain peculiar property. From these highly ordered forms, the forms of inferior things depend, being ordered from there. But even those celestial ones, as if disconnected among themselves, proceed from the reasons of the soul conjoined to one another, and in a certain way, mutable from the stable ones. But these, insofar as they do not comprehend themselves, are referred to the forms in a mind, whether animal or more eminent, which comprehend themselves, which, as multiples, are reduced to the most simple one and to the good, just as celestial figures are to the pole. But let us return to the soul. When, therefore, the soul generates the special forms and powers of inferior things, it effects them through proper reasons, under the support of the stars and celestial forms,
3.1.5: …support. It exhibits the singular gifts of individuals, which are often as wonderful in some as they are wont to be in species, similarly through seminal reasons, not so much under the support of celestial forms and figures as by the position of the stars and the habit of the motions and aspects of the planets, both among themselves and toward the stars more sublime than the planets. Our soul, indeed, beyond the proper powers of our members, brings forth the power of life common to us everywhere. But it does so especially through the heart, as the source closest to the soul’s fire. Similarly, the world soul, flourishing everywhere, unfolds the power of common life here and there, especially through the Sun. Whence some place the soul, both in us and in the world, as a whole in every member, but especially in the heart and in the Sun. Always, however, remember that just as the power of our soul is applied to our members through the spirit, so the power of the world soul is expanded through all things via the quinta essentia fifth essence/quintessence, which flourishes everywhere like a spirit within the world-body, under the world soul; and especially is this power infused into those things that have drawn the most of such a spirit. This fifth essence can be assumed by us more and more inwardly, if one knows how to separate it, mixed as it is with other elements, or at least frequently to use those things that abound in it, especially the purer ones, such as choice wine, sugar, balsam, gold, precious stones, myrobalans, and things that smell very sweetly and those that shine.
3.1.6: Especially those which, in a subtle substance, have a quality that is warm, moist, and clear. Such, besides wine, is the whitest sugar, especially if you add to it gold, and the scent of cinnamon and roses. Furthermore, just as foods duly assumed into us do not live by themselves, but are reduced by our spirit to the form of our life, so too our bodies, duly accommodated to the world-body and spirit—namely, through worldly things and through our own spirit—draw as much as possible from the worldly life. If you wish the food to seize, above all others, the form of your brain, or liver, or stomach, take a similar food as much as you can; that is, the brain, liver, and stomach of animals not far removed from human nature. If you desire your body and spirit to receive power from some member of the world—namely, from the Sun—seek those things that are, before others, solar among metals and stones, but more so among plants. But even more so among animals, especially among humans. For those things most similar to you undoubtedly confer the most. These things are both to be applied externally and to be assumed internally according to one’s strength, especially on the day and in the hour of the Sun, and with the Sun reigning in the figure of the heavens. Solar things are all those stones and flowers that are named heliotropes, because they turn to the Sun. Likewise gold and orpiment, golden colors, chrysolite, carbuncle, myrrh, frankincense, musk, amber, balsam, yellow honey, aromatic reed, crocus saffron, spikenard, cinnamon, aloe wood, and other aromatics. The ram, the goshawk, the rooster, the swan, the lion, the catharis, the crocodile, and men who are fair, curly-haired, often bald, and magnanimous; these things can be adapted partly as food, partly as ointments and fumigations, and partly for use. These things should be felt and thought of frequently, and above all, loved. And a great deal of light is to be sought. If you doubt that the stomach is lacking in the warmth of the liver, draw the faculty of the liver to the stomach, both by friction and by warm poultices, using things that agree with the liver, such as chicory, endive, spodium, eupatorium, liverwort, and livers. Similarly, so that your body is not deprived of Jupiter, move your body on the day, in the hour, and under the reign of Jupiter, and use in the meantime Jovial things: silver, hyacinth, topaz, coral, crystal, beryl, spodium, sapphire, and green and airy colors; wine, white sugar, honey, and thoughts and affections that are very Jovial, that is, constant, equitable, religious, and law-abiding. And among men, associate with those who are of such a kind, who are sanguine, beautiful, and venerable. But remember that gold, wine, mint, saffron, cinnamon, and leopard’s bane doronicum a medicinal herb must be added to those first cooling things. Truly, Jovial animals are the lamb, the peacock, the eagle, and the bull. But modesty does not permit me to show how the virtue of Venus is attracted by turtledoves, pigeons, wagtails, and the rest.

3.2.1:
*On the harmony of the world, and on the nature of man according to the stars. How an attraction is made from each star*
No one should doubt that we, and all things that are around us, can claim heavenly things for ourselves through certain preparations. For these things were made from the heavens and are incessantly governed by them, and from there, they were primarily prepared for those things. And what is greatest, the world as an animal is more one in itself than any other animal, if indeed it is the most perfect animal. Therefore, just as in us the quality and movement of any member, especially a principal one, pertains to the others, so the acts of the principal members in the world move all things, and inferior members easily take from the supreme ones, which are ready to give of their own accord. For the more powerful a cause is, the more prompt it is to act, and therefore the more inclined it is to give. A slight preparation, therefore, applied to us in addition, is sufficient for receiving the gifts of the heavens, provided that each person accommodates himself especially to that [star] to which he is especially subject. But before the property of any one of us, we ought to consider the property of the human species. The Arab astrologers have agreed that this is solar. I conjecture that this is true from the erect and beautiful stature of man, the subtle humors, the clarity of the spirit, the perspicacity of the imagination, and the desire for truth and glory.
3.2.2: I add, furthermore, a Mercurial property to this, because of the strenuous movement of a versatile wit. And since the human race is born naked, unarmed, and needy of all things, it procures all these things for itself through its own industry, which is a property of Mercury. I add also a Jovial one, because of the tempered complexion of the body and the laws. And since we receive life in the second month, when Jupiter dominates, and we are born in the ninth, when he receives dominion again. Therefore, the human species will be able to claim even greater gifts from these three above all others, if it will accommodate itself to them more and more each day through solar, Mercurial, and Jovial things. But what of the others? Saturn does not easily signify the common quality and lot of the human race, but rather a man segregated from others, divine or brute, blessed or pressed by extreme misery. Mars, the Moon, and Venus represent affections and acts equally common to man and other living things. Let us, therefore, return to the Sun, Jupiter, and Mercury. We have mentioned some solar and Jovial things, but I do not know how we passed over the Mercurial ones. They are of this kind: tin, silver, especially quicksilver, silver marcasite, agate stone, porphyritic glass, and those things that mix yellow with green, emerald and lac: sagacious animals that are at once ingenious and strenuous, such as monkeys and dogs: eloquent, acute, and versatile men, with an oblong face and hands that are not fleshy.
3.2.3: They are to be sought and exercised when they pertain to a certain planet, with that planet dominating (as we have said) in its day and hour, if possible. Also, when it is in its own house, or exaltation, or at least in its triplicity, term, and angle of the sky, direct and outside of combustion, and more often oriental if it is superior to the Sun: likewise in the apogee and aspected by the Moon. But if anyone asks for a benefit from the Moon herself, and from Venus, he will have to observe similar times. From Venus indeed through her animals which we have mentioned, and through cornelian, sapphire, and lapis lazuli, yellow and red brass, coral, all beautiful and varied or green colors and flowers, and harmonies, sweet odors, and flavors. From the Moon through white, moist, and green things, through silver, crystal, pearls, and silver marcasite. But since Saturn dominates standing and perseverance, and Mars dominates the efficacy of motion, we are sometimes forced to ask for patronage from them as well, with times observed similarly. From the former, through certain materials that are in a way earthy, dark, and leaden, and dark jasper, the magnet, chamomile, and chalcedony, and in part through gold and golden marcasite. From Mars, through fiery, red things, red brass, all sulfurous things, iron, and bloodstone. Nor should you doubt that Saturn has something in gold. For because of its weight, it is thought to have it. Furthermore, gold is similar to the Sun, so it is in all metals just as the Sun is in all the planets and stars. Now, if anyone has convinced himself that Saturn and Mars are by nature harmful, which I, for one, would never believe, yet one must use these as physicians sometimes use poisons, which Ptolemy proves in the Centiloquium. It will be profitable, therefore, to use the power of Saturn cautiously at times, just as physicians use things that bind and contain, and even those that stupefy, such as opium and mandrake; and [the power] of Mars, just as they use euphorbia and hellebore. The Pythagorean Brahman Magi seem to have been the most cautious in this matter, for when they feared the tyranny of Saturn due to their diligent study of philosophy, they clothed themselves in white garments, used Jovial or solar sounds and songs daily, and lived for the most part under the open sky. But everywhere remember that through the affection and study of the mind, and through the quality of the spirit itself, we are most easily and suddenly exposed to the planets that signify the same affection and such study and quality. Therefore, we are often subjected to Saturn by reason of human affairs, by leisure, solitude, firmness, by theology and more secret philosophy, superstition, magic, agriculture, and by grief. We are subjected to others by civil and ambitious business, by natural philosophy, and by common…
3.2.4: MAR. F. ON LIFE FROM THE HEAVENS through civil religion and through laws, to Jupiter; through anger and strife, to Mars; through the study of eloquence, songs, truth, glory, and skill, to the Sun and Mercury. To Venus through joy, music, and festivities. To the Moon through a diet similar to plants. But hold this distinction in mind among these: the exercise of the intellect that is more public and extensive pertains to the Sun; that which is private and committed to craftsmanship pertains more to Mercury. Furthermore, music that is grave belongs to Jupiter and the Sun; that which is light belongs to Venus; and that which is intermediate belongs to Mercury. The reason for the fixed stars is similar. This is, indeed, the common rule for the human species. The proper rule for each individual, however, would be to explore which star promised what good to whom in their birth chart, and to seek favor from that star rather than another. And from each, one should not expect just any gift—nor that which belongs to others—but what is proper to it, unless perhaps you derive many common things from the Sun, as if it were the common leader of the celestial bodies, and similarly from Jupiter, and likewise all worldly things from the soul and the spiritus mundi world-spirit. That this is animated, just as any animal is, and much more effectively, is proven not only by Platonic arguments but also by the testimonies of the Arab astrologers. They also prove that through a certain application of our spirit to the world-spirit, made through physical art and affection, celestial goods are transmitted to our soul and body. Hence, through our spirit indeed
3.2.5: COMPARISON BOOK III. the medium within us, and then strengthened by the world-spirit; then from there through the rays of the stars acting favorably upon our spirit, which is similar in nature to the rays, and then adapting itself to the celestial things.

3.3.1:
*That between the soul of the world and its body, its spirit is manifest, in whose power are the four elements: And that we can draw this in through our own spirit*
Indeed, the worldly body, as far as it appears from motion and generation, is everywhere alive, which the philosophers of the Indians prove from the fact that it everywhere generates living things from itself. Therefore, it lives everywhere through the soul present to itself and entirely accommodated to it. Thus, between the tangible and partially perishable body of the world and its soul itself, whose nature differs too much from such a body, there is everywhere a spirit, just as there is between the soul and the body in us: provided that life is always communicated everywhere by the soul to the thicker body. For such a spirit is necessarily required as a medium by which the divine soul may both be present to the thicker body and thoroughly bestow life upon the same. However, every body easily sensible to you, as if accommodated to your senses, is thicker and degenerates far from the most divine soul. There is need, therefore, for the assistance of a more excellent body, as if not
3.3.2: MAR. F. ON LIFE FROM THE HEAVENS a body. Therefore, we know that all living things, as much plants as animals, live and generate through a certain spirit similar to this; and among the elements (which is most spiritual), it generates most quickly and is perpetually moved as if it were living. But you will ask in the meantime, if the elements and living creatures generate something similar to themselves by their own spirit, why do stones and metals not generate, which are intermediate between the elements and living creatures? Because, obviously, the spirit in them is restrained by thicker matter. If this is ever duly separated and, once separated, preserved, it will be able to generate something similar to itself as a generative virtue: provided it is applied to some matter of the same kind, such a spirit as the diligent natural philosophers, extracting it from gold by a certain sublimation toward fire, will apply to any of the metals and make gold. The Arab astrologers call such a spirit, duly extracted from gold or another substance and preserved, the Elixer elixir. But let us return to the world-spirit, through which the world generates all things, since all things also generate through their own spirit, which we can call both heaven and the quinta essentia fifth essence. It is nearly the same in the body of the world as our own spirit is in ours. With this first exception: that the soul of the world does not draw this from the four elements as if they were its humors, as we do ours; rather, it creates this directly (to speak in the Platonic or Plotinian manner) from its own generative virtue, as if swelling, and simultaneously with it the stars, and immediately through it brings forth those things which
3.3.3: COMPARISON BOOK III. the four elements, as if all things were in the power of that spirit. It is itself a most subtle body, as if not a body and as if already a soul: likewise, as if not a soul and as if already a body. In its power there is a minimum of earthy nature, more of water, and likewise more of air. Again, there is a great deal of fiery and stellar nature. The quantities of the stars and elements themselves have proceeded according to the measures of these grades. It thrives everywhere, the proximate author and motion of all generation in all things, regarding which it is said: > The spirit nourishes from within. It is by its own nature entirely luminous, warm, humid, and life-giving, having obtained such gifts from the higher gifts of the soul. That Apollonius of Tyana had drawn this in greatly was testified to by the Indian Hiarchas, saying: “No one should wonder, O Apollonius, that you have attained the science of divination, since you carry so much of the aether in your soul.”

3.4.1:
*That our spirit draws in the spirit of the world through the rays of the Sun and Jupiter, and to what extent it becomes solar and Jovial*
You will therefore strive to insinuate this into yourself above all. For by this means you will derive certain natural benefits, both of the worldly body, of the soul, and even of the stars and demons. For it is the medium between the thick body of the world and the soul. And in it
3.4.2: MAR. F. ON LIFE FROM THE HEAVENS are the stars and demons, and through it. Whether the body of the world and worldly things are directly from the soul of the world (as pleases Plotinus and Porphyry), or the worldly body—just as the soul is directly from God, as pleases us and perhaps the Pythagorean Timaeus—the world entirely lives and breathes, and it is permitted for us to draw in its spirit. It is drawn in, however, properly by man through his own spirit, which is by its own nature conformable to it. Especially if it is made even more akin by art, that is, if it becomes most celestial. It becomes celestial if it is purged of filth and entirely of those things that adhere to it which are dissimilar to heaven. These impurities, indeed, often infect the spirit not only if they are within the viscera, but also if they are in the mind, in the skin, in the garments, in the dwelling, and in the air. It will finally become celestial if, to the circular motion of the mind and body, it also makes itself circular: if to the more frequent sight and contemplation of light, it also becomes more refined: if things similar to heaven are applied to it with the same common diligence by which Avicenna treats the spirit in his book De viribus cordis On the Powers of the Heart. And we endeavor to treat it in our book De curanda literatorum valetudine On Preserving the Health of Scholars. Where first the vapors that obscure it are segregated by such purging medicines. Second, it is illuminated by shining things. Third, it is cultivated in such a way that it is both refined and strengthened at the same time. Finally, it will become most celestial, as the present reason dictates, if the rays and influences of the Sun are applied to it most of all [?inter]
3.4.3: The world lives and breathes. of the one dominating the celestial things. And thus, from this spirit, as if through an intermediary within us, celestial goods will first flow into our own body and mind, having been implanted in it: celestial goods, I say, of every kind. For all things are contained within the Sun. The Sun, moreover, will contribute properly to the creation of a solar spirit when it is in Aries or Leo, with the Moon looking upon it, especially in Leo. There, it so invigorates our spirit that it fortifies it against the repelling of the poison of the Epidemia plague, which appears clearly in Babylonia and Egypt, and in regions looking toward Leo, where the Sun, entering Leo, settles the plague for the very reason we have stated. Therefore, prepare solar items carefully here and there. Then begin to use solar things, yet with that caution by which you diligently avoid desiccation during the heat. The solar spirit, however, will not easily escape unless it is very abundant. For magnitude pertains greatly to the Sun. You will make it most abundant, both by diligently fostering the heart with cordial things internally and externally, and also by a diet that is composed of subtle, yet highly and easily and healthfully nourishing, foods. Frequent and gentle movement, opportune rest, air that is thin and serene and removed from both heat and frost, and especially a joyful mind, are also helpful. Again, it will not be Solar unless it is hot, subtle, and clear. You will make it subtle and clear if you avoid sad, thick, and dark things. Use bright and joyful things internally and externally.
3.4.4: You will take in light day and night. You will expel filth, as well as idleness and sloth. Above all, you will avoid shadows. However, in leading the spirit toward the heat natural to the Sun, take care that you do not lead it to the third degree of heat and dryness. For the heat of the Sun itself does not naturally dry out; otherwise, the Sun would not be the lord of life and generation and the author of growth. It happens to dry out, however, by its rays being enclosed in the concave vessels of dry matter. Therefore, you will apply to the spirit a moisture subtle to heat, such as is Solar, and especially Jovian, and you will preserve it in the spirit through the use of things of this kind, if you intend to make it solar, lest otherwise you happen to lead it toward a Martian quality rather than a solar one. Indeed, they say that Mars is similar to the Sun in few, and these quite manifest, and by no means excellent things, and is meanwhile hostile. We know, however, that Jupiter is very similar to the Sun in many and excellent gifts, even if they are more occult, and that it is most friendly. Hence, even Ptolemy, when he disputes about consonance, says that Jupiter most perfectly harmonizes with the Sun above the others, and Venus with the Moon. And all astrologers attribute universal beneficence to the Sun similarly to Jupiter, although the Sun acts more effectively, and Jupiter acts under the power of the Sun. In both, heat thrives and overcomes moisture. But in Jupiter it overcomes moderately, in the Sun it overcomes excellently: in both, beneficially. Since, therefore, they harmonize so much, you will easily be able to make the spirit Solar just as much as Jovian, and solar and Jovian things… you will be able to mix them together properly. Especially if you compose both of these together and apply them to the spirit when Jupiter looks upon the Sun with a trine or sextile aspect, or at least when the Moon proceeds from the aspect of one to look upon the other, and especially when it proceeds from the aspect of the Sun toward a conjunction with Jupiter. Separately, however, you will make it specifically Solar or Jovian when you have observed the Moon’s aspect toward the Sun or toward Jupiter. Even so, once you have attained the nature of the one, you will easily attain the nature of the other.
3.4.5: Understand, however, a sextile aspect to be when two planets are distant from each other by the space of two signs. A trine, when it differs by an interval of four signs. We measure the conjunction or the aspect of the Moon to others as twelve degrees before and as many after.

3.5.1:
*That the three Graces are Jupiter, the Sun, and Venus, and that Jupiter is the middle of the twin Graces, and most suited to us*
You will indeed find the compositions and Jovian cures, as soon as the Solar ones, in our book On Long Life and in our book On the Care of Scholars. Where we have also mixed in most of the Venusian ones. For we also fear desiccation in scholars, to which Venus resists. And this same Venus is most friendly to Jupiter, just as Jupiter is to the Sun.
3.5.2: As if the three Graces were in concord among themselves and joined together. From these three Graces of the heavens, and from the stars of the same kind, astrologers hope for and diligently seek graces, and they think they are transmitted and cared for through Mercury and the Moon as if through messengers; easily, however, and commonly through the Moon. Indeed, they think the Moon is more fortunate when joined with Jupiter or Venus than if it has looked upon them through a sextile or trine. Nevertheless, if it is also received by them while looking through a trine, they almost consider it to be joined. Similarly, if it has been perceived by the Sun and at the same time received. But if we wish to run through all the powers and effects of these three, and similar stars, one by one, we would embark on a long task, difficult to seek out, and most difficult to observe. If we betake ourselves properly to Venus, we do not easily have the Sun; if to the Sun properly, not easily Venus. Therefore, in order to embrace all three graces in one, we will finally flee to Jupiter, which is medium in nature and effect between the Sun and Venus, very tempered in quality, and which, in its own way, delivers whatever is hoped for from Venus or the Sun, more magnificently and honestly than Venus, and more temperately than the Sun, and in all things most congruent with human nature. We will therefore use the power of Jupiter when both it and the Moon have dignity, both natural and accidental, and are together, or look upon each other happily. If, at some time, that cannot be done at all, you may mix Solar things into one with Venusian ones, and you will thus make a Jovian thing composed of both, namely when the Moon goes from a conjunction of Venus to the sextile aspect of the Sun, or conversely. Remember, however, in composing things that foster and corroborate the heart and spirit, that the Moon contributes most of all if, along with these gifts, it also happens to run through airy signs, especially through Aquarius, which is thought to be most airy. Or if it is in its own domicile, or its exaltation, or the house of Jupiter or the Sun. And wherever it may be, if it holds a mansion from those twenty-eight that is suitable both for itself and for the work.

3.6.1:
*Concerning the natural, vital, and animal virtues, and which of the planets accommodate or hinder individual ones, and that most of all through aspects*
The principal discipline, however, is to correctly understand which spirit, which force, and which thing these planets signify primarily. Therefore, the Moon and Venus signify the natural and genital force and spirit, and those things which augment it. Jupiter signifies the same, but more effectively, along with the liver and stomach, and it has no small part in the heart and spirit and vital virtue, insofar as it agrees by its own nature with the Sun, indeed even by itself. Otherwise, the heart would not properly receive the vital spirit in the month of Jupiter. Hence, Jupiter…
3.6.2: The Greeks call it vita life, and the means by which there is life. Astrologers also testify that it has power over the animal spirit, saying that Jupiter contributes to finding philosophy and truth, as well as religion. And Plato, where he says that philosophers proceed from Jupiter. This is what Homer also indicated in the opinion of the ancients, saying: Such is the mind in men, as the father of men and gods brings it day by day. Indeed, he never names any deity in this way except Jupiter. The Sun signifies the vital spirit and the heart above all, and it has no small—nay, quite a significant—influence on the head, because of sensation and motion, of which it is the master; nor does it desert the natural force. Mercury signifies the brain and the instruments of the senses, and therefore the animal spirit. Consequently, the safest path will be to do nothing without the benefit of the Moon, since it commonly, frequently, and easily transmits celestial things to the lower world; they call it a second Sun, creating the four seasons of the year every month. For in its first quarter, the Peripatetics think it is hot and moist. In the second, hot and dry. In the third, cold and dry. In the fourth, cold and moist. And its light is undoubtedly the light of the Sun; it rules humors and generation, and measures all changes of the fetus in the womb by its own revolutions, and as often as it is joined to the Sun, it receives from it a vivifying force, which it infuses into the humor, and in that same place [receives] from Mercury the force that mixes the humors. Which force Mercury brings with its own curiosity, transformation into all things, and multiple gyrations. There, too, it receives the force from Venus, which leads to forms suitable for generation. It is worth remembering that the daily course of the Moon is divided into four quarters. In the first, it ascends from the East to the mid-heaven, and meanwhile increases the humor and the natural spirit. In the second, it moves from the mid-heaven to the setting, and brings about the opposite in us. The third goes from the setting underneath the mid-heaven, and again increases that spirit and humor. The fourth falls from there toward the rising, and decreases them in turn. This appears most clearly on the shores of the ocean, where the sea advances and recedes more obviously according to this course, and in the same order [is the] vigor in the sick. It is also probable that the Sun, through its own same quarters, increases or decreases the natural heat and the vital spirit; and the animal [spirit] as well, insofar as it has Mercury as a companion. Having known these things, the physician will be able to observe more opportune times for refreshing the humor, natural heat, and any spirit. But now, enough about the Moon. Nor is it fitting to dismiss Jupiter, in whose month we have indeed received life, and in another, we have been born more commonly and more happily. And he who is between the Sun and Venus, likewise between the Sun and the Moon in quality and effect, and therefore embraces everything. Indeed, we consider it impious and dangerous to pass over the Sun himself, the lord of heaven, unless perhaps someone says that he who has Jupiter already has the Sun in Jupiter, tempered there most effectively for men.
3.6.3: Certainly, not only Iamblichus and Julian, but everyone affirms that all the virtues of the celestial bodies are in the Sun. And Proclus says that at the aspect of the Sun, all the virtues of all celestial things are gathered and collected into one. No one will deny that Jupiter is a certain Sun tempered for us. You would not ignore the Moon when it is tempered toward Venus either. For it helps much toward a strong and prosperous life. Since Venus fertilizes a person and makes them joyful, you will observe this [the Moon]. Although, if you properly mix the Moon—being similar to Venus, equal in humor, and hardly less hot—with Jupiter or the Sun, you have almost arrived at Venus. What then? So that you may walk the safest and most convenient path of all at the same time, observe the Moon when it looks at the Sun and conjoins with Jupiter, or at least looks at both Jupiter and the Sun at once, or certainly when, after the aspect of the Sun, it soon proceeds to a conjunction or aspect of Jupiter. And at that very time, compose [remedies] in turn, or apply to yourself Solar and Jovian things along with Venusian ones. But if necessity or business urges you to take refuge in one of the great ones, flee to Jupiter himself or rather to the Moon together with Jupiter. For no star fosters and corroborates the natural forces in us, and indeed all forces, more than Jupiter. None, again, promises more prosperous things and more of them. And it is auspicious to receive him everywhere. To receive the Sun, however, is perhaps not safe everywhere. For he [Jupiter] always helps, while the latter [the Sun] often seems to do harm. Venus, however, is as if weak. Therefore, he alone, as the one who helps, has been called the father. Ptolemy confirms this, where he says: “Medicine hardly moves nature except when the Moon conjoins with Jupiter.” To such an extent does he believe that the entire nature of the universal body is corroborated from that source. I have even experienced that the Moon joined with Venus hardly moves medicine. Although, when we fear phlegm greatly, we observe the Moon primarily toward the Sun; when we fear bile and such dryness, [we observe it] toward Venus; yet the direction of the Moon toward Jupiter contributes in some way to all these things, and especially to expelling black bile, as well as to restoring and firming the common complexion of men. For just as licorice and oil of roses heat things that are colder and cool things that are hotter—and wine similarly: which, moreover, moistens dry things and dries more humid ones—so Jupiter is congruous to human heat, like wine, oil of roses, chamomile, and licorice. Therefore, when you hear Albumasar saying: “There is no life for the living apart from God, except through the Sun and the Moon,” understand it as it pertains to the influx common to all. However, the influx most appropriate and suitable to man is from Jupiter. There are in the nature of the body the forces of attracting, retaining, cooking, and expelling. Jupiter himself helps all these. Most of all, indeed, with the virtue of cooking or digesting, and of generating and nourishing, and simultaneously of increasing, because of his airy and abundant humor, and his ample heat, which moderately dominates the humor. Certainly, through the rays of Jupiter, which are always diffused everywhere, the light of the Sun itself is tempered most for the health of men: with the rays of Venus meanwhile constantly contributing to the same, and the Moon transferring it similarly. The rays of Venus and the Moon, being as it were more humid, need some tempering agent, just as the rays of the Sun, being as it were hotter, demand the tempering of something more humid. But the rays of Jupiter require no tempering. For what else is Jupiter but a certain Sun tempered from the beginning for the health of human affairs especially? What else, again, but the Moon and Venus, yet made hotter and more potent? Therefore, Astrologers begin a fertile, serene, and healthy year from Jupiter, and hope for remedies from him for impending diseases. And Empedocles, when he attributes proper gifts to each of the Planets, calls Jupiter alone the prince of generation, imitating Orpheus. Apart from Jupiter, they teach that the Moon is to be carefully observed in all works, as a suitable medium between celestial and earthly things. Therefore, let the Moon be in a degree, position, and aspect appropriate to the desired work. Let it not be in the ecliptic, nor under the rays of the Sun by twelve degrees on either side, unless perhaps it is in the same [sign]. minute with the Sun. Most, however, desire all the Planets to be strong when they are in unity with the Sun. They measure this unity by thirty-two minutes, such that sixteen are counted on one side, and sixteen on the other. Let the Moon not be hindered by Saturn or Mars, nor should it descend into southern latitude when it exits the twelve degrees mentioned. Let it not be opposite the Sun, nor diminished by light, nor slow in its course, which is when it does not complete twelve degrees in a single day. Let it not be in the via combusta burnt path from the twenty-eighth degree of Libra to the third of Scorpio, nor in the eighth [house], nor in the Ascendant, nor in the boundaries of Mars or Saturn. Some, however, do not want the Moon in the sixth, twelfth, ninth, or fourth [houses]. They approve of it in the other regions of the sky. Where you cannot encompass all these things, expect at least Jupiter, or
3.6.4: Venus in the Ascendant or the tenth [house]; for thus they assist the detriments of the Moon. Nor would it be irrelevant to remember that as much as the Moon is increased in light, to that extent not only is our humor increased, but also our spirit and power, and these are dilated toward the circumference: especially in its second quarter. When it is diminished, however, the opposite occurs, especially in the last quarter. Its first aspect to the Sun is superior to the second. This [first aspect] is superior to the first sextile. This [first sextile] is superior to the second. The Moon is filled with heat insofar as it is filled with light. Therefore, some seem to observe not so much how the Moon views the Sun (for it always views it), but rather that it possesses the most light.
3.6.5: It should view Jupiter or Venus in the meantime by a trine or sextile aspect. Consequently, fiery [signs] aid the attractive power: earthy ones, the retentive: airy ones, the digestive: and watery ones, the expulsive. If you wish to aid all these within yourself, you will strengthen the attractive power most through fiery things when the Moon is established in fiery signs or stations and views Jupiter, namely Aries, Leo, or Sagittarius. [You will strengthen] the retentive through earthy things, especially when it looks toward the same [Jupiter] while placed in earthy signs or stations: Taurus, Virgo, or Capricorn. [You will strengthen] the digestive and generative through airy ones, namely Gemini, Libra, or Aquarius, as often as it looks up to or approaches Jupiter under airy [signs]. [You will strengthen] the expulsive through the watery: Cancer, Pisces, or Scorpio, when it is positioned under watery [signs] and is illuminated by the rays of Jupiter. You will achieve your wishes most in all these things if Jupiter occupies the same or similar, or at least not entirely dissimilar, signs or mansions. If you are about to purge the bowels with solid medicines, choose Pisces: for liquid ones, Scorpio: but for intermediate ones, Cancer. If you are to purge through the lower parts, [choose] Pisces and Scorpio. Through the upper parts, Cancer. You will avoid the aspect of Saturn or Mars toward the Moon. For the former vexes the stomach, and the latter dissolves the intestines. You will avoid Capricorn and Taurus; for they bring nausea. You know that a member is not to be irritated when the Moon occupies the sign presiding over that member (for it moves the humors), but rather it is to be cherished. But these [things] concerning the natural virtue and spirit dominating primarily in the liver, which are divided into the four offices we have narrated, let these things suffice. But what do we advise regarding the vital virtue and spirit flourishing in the heart? That has been almost sufficiently signified. For these are aided primarily through things that are fiery and at the same time, in a certain way, airy, when the Moon looks up to Jupiter in similar mansions or houses, especially if it embraces Jupiter and the Sun. You can also confirm the animal virtue, which dominates in the head through sense and motion, primarily through airy things, with fiery ones joined, when the Moon looks up to Jupiter in similar mansions or seats; especially if it embraces Jupiter and almost [embraces] Mercury. Here, however, I warn you not to think that Mercury is watery or earthy (which I myself once suspected; otherwise, it would not contribute to motions and the quickness of wit), but know that it is in some way airy. For also because of the same cause, it is so mobile, so easily changeable, and contributes so much to talent, especially when established in Aquarius, which is highly airy. Indeed, the humor in it is tempered, and the heat is slight. Placed under the Sun, it is said to dry. When made further from the Sun, however, it is thought to moisten. In that place [near the Sun], it indeed heats much from the nature of the Sun. Here [further away], it heats very little and moistens more by its own nature. Perhaps it does not yield to Venus in heat, and it surpasses the Moon, but in humor, it yields to both. Haly proves that Mercury mixes the qualities of the celestial [bodies].
3.6.6: Because it is very easily transformed, both into the quality of the boundary which it approaches and into the nature of the star which it views. I therefore think this [planet] is transformed so easily because it has neither the excellent power that Jupiter possesses, nor an exceeding quality, such as most celestial [bodies] possess, by which it might resist alteration. Finally, it is probable that Mercury, the constant attendant of the Sun, possesses many of its powers, and therefore one may hope that certain solar things can be obtained from Mercury. Sometimes, however, they relate that Mercury imitates Mars and the Sun in certain duties, and bestows those things that pertain to the Moon. Therefore, remember these things when acting. Nor should you ever neglect the boundaries. For they say that the Planets do opposite things in different boundaries, as if they were bright or dark. Finally, when you fear Mars, oppose Venus: where you fear Saturn, apply Jupiter. And take care that you exert yourself in a perpetual motion as much as your strength allows, provided you avoid exhaustion, so that you may oppose the proper motion of Mercury to external motions that are about to be harmful, and imitate the celestial act as much as your strength allows. If you can perform spaces of motion that are wider, you will thus imitate the heavens more, and you will attain more of the powers of the celestial bodies diffused everywhere.

3.7.1:
*How members are cherished in us through the comparison of the Moon to the signs and to the fixed stars*
You will be able to cherish the whole body as we have said, but the head most especially if you observe the Planets when they are in Aries, or each one in its own primary domicile. The chest [is to be cherished] if they are in Leo. The stomach and liver if they are in Cancer and Sagittarius, or at least in Virgo. And you will have received those things which properly seek the member. It is also expedient to know which members each Planet possesses in any given sign. You can also consult properly for each individual according to the distinction of age through the four ages of the Moon. For from the new moon until the first quarter, it is young. Then until the full moon, it is young and virile. Hence, until the second quarter, it is simultaneously virile and aged. Then until the conjunction, it is aged. You will therefore happily apply the age of the Moon to the age of the body being treated if you then receive its aspect toward any of the three Graces. This aspect of the Moon truly bestows graceful things always and quickly. Nor, however, are lasting or great things easily [granted], unless, besides the intuition of the Moon, the Graces themselves also view one another now, or are about to view one another almost, either the three themselves, or two. Above all, the fixed signs provide lasting [effects]: namely Leo, Aquarius, Taurus, Scorpio. If by chance you cannot at present direct the Moon to gracious Planets, choose fixed stars having the nature of the Graces, that is, of Jupiter, or Venus, or the Sun, and choose the Moon directed toward them. It is safer, however, that the Moon in the meantime approaches Jupiter or Venus. For if the fixed stars view [us] alone, they exceed the human proportion, that is, [they exceed] the proportion of one man too much. they truly have a more moderate [relationship] with cities.

3.8.1:
*On the virtues and use of the fixed stars*
Astrologers report that certain greater stars discovered by Mercury possess very great authority. Such is the navel of Andromeda at the 22nd degree of Aries, [which is] Mercurial and Venusian. Likewise, at the 18th degree of Taurus is the head of Algol, possessing the nature of Saturn and Jupiter. They hold that diamond and mugwort are subject to it, and that it provides boldness and victory. At the 22nd degree of the same [sign] are the Pleiades, a lunar and Martial star. They subject crystal, the herb diacedon, and fennel seed to it. They think it contributes to sharpening the vision. However, what some say about it being useful for summoning demons, I judge to be a fabrication. At the first or third degree of Gemini is Aldeboran, [which is] Martial and Venusian. At the 13th degree of the same is the Goat, [which is] Jovian and Saturnian. They subject sapphire, horehound, mint, mugwort, and mandrake to it. They believe it helps toward dignity and the favor of princes, unless perhaps opinion deceives them. They wish for ruby and spurge and woodbine to be subject to it, to increase riches and glory. At the sixth or seventh degree of Cancer is the Greater Dog, [which is] Venusian; it presides over beryl, savin, mugwort, and dragonwort. It provides grace: likewise, at the 17th of the same is the Lesser Dog, [which is] Mercurial and Martial. They wish for agate, the herb succory, and pennyroyal to be subject to it: And grace to bestow grace. At the 21st degree of Leo is the Heart of the Lion, a royal star [that is] Jovian and Martial. They think the stone garnet, celandine, and mastic are subject to it, [and that it helps] to repress melancholy and to make one temperate and graceful. At the 19th degree of Virgo is the Tail of the Greater Bear, [which is] Venusian and Lunar. They think its stone is the magnet, and its herb chicory and mugwort, [and that it] protects from robbers and poisons. At the 7th degree of Libra is the right wing of the Crow. Likewise, at the 12th or perhaps 13th of the same is the left wing, [which is] Saturnian and Martial simultaneously. They say its herbs are patience dock and henbane, which, together with the tongue of a frog, increase boldness. At the 15th or 16th of the same is Spica, [which is] Venusian and Mercurial. Let an emerald, sage, trefoil, lungwort, mugwort, and mandrake follow it. May it increase riches and victory, and deliver one from anguish. Finally, at the 17th or 18th of the same is Alchameth. They subject jasper and plantain to it, [and] they hope it will firm the blood and expel all fevers. At the 4th degree of Scorpio is Elpheia, [which is] Venusian and Martial. According to another calculation, in the 5th degree of the same is [the star] Cornea, perhaps the same one, presiding over topaz, rosemary, trefoil, and ivy; they think it increases grace, chastity, and glory. At the 3rd degree of Sagittarius is the Heart of the Scorpion, [which is] Martial and Jovian, presiding over sardonyx, amethyst, long birthwort, and saffron. They think it creates good color, renders the mind joyful and wise, and repels demons. In Capricorn at the 7th degree is the Falling Vulture following this are chrysolite, savory, and fumitory. The star is Mercurial and Venusian, [and] temperate. It is beneficial in the ascendant and mid-heaven. But as for what they say, that it brings the authority for incantations, I value it at nothing. At the 16th degree of Aquarius is the Tail of Capricorn, [which is] Saturnian and Mercurial. Following it are chalcedony, marjoram, calamint, mugwort, and mandrake. They believe it provides grace in lawsuits, increases riches, and renders a man and his house safe. At the 3rd degree of Pisces is the Shoulder of the Horse, [which is] Jovian and Martial. The philosopher Thebit teaches that in order to capture the virtue of any star mentioned, one should take its stone and its herb, and make a ring of gold or silver in which you set the stone, placing the herb underneath, and wear it so that it touches you. You will accomplish this, however, when the Moon approaches the star, or looks upon it with a trine or sextile aspect, and the star is passing through the mid-heaven or the ascendant. I, however, would compose the things pertaining to such stars in the form of a medicine rather than a ring, to be applied internally or externally, with the opportunity of the aforementioned time being observed, of course. Even though the ancients highly valued rings. For Damis and Philostratus narrate that Hiarchas, the chief of the Indian sages, made seven rings in a similar manner, called by the names of the seven stars, and gave them to Apollonius of Tyana. Who then wore them singly on separate days, distinguishing them according to the names of the days: and he said.
3.8.2: [he said] that Hiarchas told Apollonius that his grandfather, a philosopher, lived for one hundred and thirty years, perhaps relying on such a heavenly gift. Which Apollonius then used, and even in his hundredth year, as they say, he appeared as a young man. Finally, if rings of this kind have any virtue from on high, I think it pertains not so much to the soul or the dense body as to the spirit, as the ring is gradually heated and affected by it, so that the spirit may be made firmer or clearer, more vehement or milder, more severe or more joyful. These affections, indeed, pass entirely into the body and in some way into the sensitive soul, which mostly indulges the body. But that they promise that rings will be useful against demons or enemies, or for the favor of princes, is either a fabrication or derived from the fact that they make the spirit fearless and firm, or even gentle, and lovable and graceful in its compliance. Now, if I were to say that celestial things contribute anything beyond bodily health to talent, art, or fortune, I would not disagree with our Thomas Aquinas, who in the third book of his Against the Gentiles proves that something is imprinted upon our body by celestial bodies, by the gift of which we are often disposed to choose what is better, even if we do not know the reason and the end. In which matter he calls them well-fortuned and (with the consent of Aristotle) well-born. He also adds that by celestial virtue some become effective in certain effects of the arts
3.8.3: () just as a soldier is happy in winning, a farmer in planting, and a physician in healing. But since herbs and stones have certain wonderful powers from the heavens beyond their elementary nature, so too [do] men [have them] in some arts. For me, however, it will be sufficient if celestial things, in whatever way, as if by medicines (whether internal or external), contribute to prosperous health, provided that while meanwhile seeking the health of the body, we do not suffer any loss of the health of the soul. Let us attempt nothing at all that is prohibited by holy religion. Furthermore, in completing any work, let us hope for and seek the fruit of the work primarily from Him who created both celestial things and those contained in the heavens, and endowed them with virtue, and always moves and preserves them.

3.9.1:
*On the dignities of the Planets in the signs, to be observed for the use of medicines*
The house of Saturn is Aquarius and Capricorn: Exaltation, Libra. The house of Jupiter is Sagittarius and Pisces: Exaltation or kingdom, Cancer. The domicile of Mars is Scorpio and Aries: Exaltation, Capricorn. The seat of the Sun is indeed Leo: Kingdom, Aries. The habitation of Venus is Taurus and Libra: Exaltation, Pisces. The abode of Mercury is Virgo and Gemini: Kingdom, Virgo. The house of the Moon is Cancer: Exaltation, Taurus. Saturn and
3.9.2: Jupiter has a triplicity in fiery and airy signs. The Sun in fiery signs only; Mercury in airy ones only. Mars, Venus, and the Moon in watery and earthy ones. Any planet, except the Sun and the Moon, possesses certain limits of its own in any sign, which we also call termini terms or boundaries. Therefore, in Aries, Jupiter holds the first six terms there: Venus the six following, Mercury the eight subsequent ones, Mars five in succession, and Saturn the last five.
3.9.3: In Taurus, following in a similar order, Venus has eight limits: Mercury six, Jupiter eight, Saturn five, and finally Mars three. In Gemini, Mercury six, Jupiter six, Venus five, Mars seven, and Saturn six.
3.9.4: In Cancer, Mars seven, Venus six, Mercury the same amount, Jupiter seven, and Saturn four. In Leo, Jupiter six, Venus five, Saturn seven, Mercury six, and Mars the same amount. In Virgo, Mercury seven, Venus ten, Jupiter four, Mars seven, and Saturn two. In Libra, Saturn six, Mercury eight, Jupiter seven, Venus the same amount, and Mars two. In Scorpio, Mars seven, Venus four, Mercury eight, Jupiter five, and Saturn six. In Sagittarius, Jupiter twelve, Venus five, Mercury four, Saturn five, and Mars four. In Capricorn, Mercury seven, Jupiter seven, Venus eight, Saturn four, and Mars the same amount. In Aquarius, Mercury seven, Venus six, Jupiter seven, Mars five, and Saturn the same amount. In Pisces,
3.9.5: Venus twelve, Jupiter four, Mercury three, Mars nine, and finally Saturn two. The Sun and Moon, however, have their limits in another way. For the Sun indeed has six signs for its limits: Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, and Capricorn. The Moon, however, has the remaining ones: Aquarius, Pisces, Aries, Taurus, Gemini, and Cancer. Therefore, we consider the Sun and the Moon to have that same authority and effect in these signs that the other planets have in their own limits. Beyond the limits, the planets have “faces” in their signs, which the Greeks call Decans ten-degree segments of a sign, occupying ten degrees of a sign. In Aries, the first face is of Mars, the second of the Sun, which follows Mars in the heavens. By the order of the Chaldeans, the third is of Venus, which succeeds the Sun in the heavens. In Taurus, the first face is of Mercury, following Venus. The second is of the Moon, which succeeds Mercury, and the third is of Saturn. For one must return to him, the number of the planets having now been completed. In Gemini, the first is of Jupiter, which is to say it follows Saturn: the second of Mars, the third of the Sun in the same order, and similarly for the rest.

3.10.1:
*How we ought to use the Planets in medicines*
We have mentioned, however, what dignities the planets have in the signs, so that whenever we are about to make or compose things that pertain to any planet, we know how to place it in its dignities, especially when when it has authority in our revolution and genesis, so that even Saturn and Mars, though otherwise to be depressed, should be elevated if they are the significators of our nativity. We shall have made it especially worth the effort from this commemoration if, whenever we are about to use the benefit of the Moon, Venus, and Jupiter in preparing medicines, we take care that they are not in the limits of Saturn or Mars, unless perhaps where we are compelled, either to restrain dissolution and repress heat through Saturn, or to warm the coldest things and arouse the torpid through Mars; otherwise, we shall choose the limits of Jupiter and Venus. We shall also accept the limits of Mercury, which will be profitable primarily for Mercurial men. Nor should it be hidden from us that highly Mercurial men, such as those who excel in talent, craft, and eloquence, are not insignificantly Solar. For Mercury is always full of Apollo. But so that anyone may understand how we describe the figures in the heavens into the houses:
3.10.2: The sign that rises from the east we call the first house of life. That which succeeds the rising is the second; and the third thereafter, and others similarly; so that the seventh house is the sign that, now descending in the west, is opposed to the ascendant. The eighth succeeds this. The ninth, however, falls from the mid-heaven, which makes the tenth house. The eleventh succeeds this. But the twelfth falls from the ascendant. Therefore, in order for the planets to be powerful, they must be held in the angles of either the east, or the west, or the mid-heaven on either side.
3.10.3: Especially in the ascending angle, or the tenth, which occupies the mid-heaven above the head, or at least in the regions that immediately follow the angles. Although they think the Sun enjoys the ninth, which falls from the mid-heaven, and the Moon even the third, which also falls. Astrologers wish two rules between these to be held in mind. One, indeed, for the sake of the sick person, and the other for the sake of the physician.
