Indeed, where the seventh house of the sick person is made unfortunate by Saturn or Mars, or its lord is unhappy, separate the physician from the sick person, if you believe Ptolemy.
3.10.4: Furthermore, when about to choose a physician, they order one to avoid the Saturnian and Martial, and to seek one in whose nativity the sixth house has been, in whatever way, made fortunate by the aspect of the Sun, or by Venus or Jupiter. We say a sign or planet is made unfortunate by Saturn or Mars unless they are their own domiciles or kingdoms, when, namely, they are either there or look upon that place by opposition or square. We call the aspect an opposition between those that differ by the longest interval. A square, however, is where one is distant from the other by a fourth part of the heavens, that is, by the space of three signs. Saturn and Mars, however, harm other planets less by conjunction, opposition, or square when they receive them as guests in their own domicile, kingdom, or limit. Just as happy planets are more beneficial when, beyond the sextile or trine aspect and conjunction, they also receive them as we have said. Planets, however, fear the conjunction of the Sun, but they enjoy the aspect, namely, trine or sextile. trine, namely, or sextile. Therefore, it is necessary to remember that Aries presides over the head and face, Taurus over the neck, Gemini over the arms and shoulders, Cancer over the chest, lungs, stomach, and forearms; Leo over the heart, stomach, liver, back, and the rear ribs; Virgo over the intestines and the bottom of the stomach; Libra over the kidneys, thighs, and buttocks; Scorpio over the genitals, vulva, and womb; Sagittarius over the thighs and under-groin; Capricorn over the knees, Aquarius over the shins and legs, and Pisces over the feet. Remembering this order, you will avoid touching a member with iron, fire, or cupping glasses when the Moon is running under its sign. For then the Moon increases the humors in the member. Their affluence both prevents consolidation and burdens the strength of the member. You will observe, however, at that time, to cherish the member with certain friendly remedies, either applied externally or internally, opportunely and happily. It is also useful to know which sign was ascending at the time of your birth. For besides Aries, this also signifies your head, and in this, the Moon looks upon your head. Furthermore, when the Moon enters Aries, you may opportunely attempt baths and washings. When it is in Cancer, happily bleed, [and] take medicine, especially in the form of an electuary. When it is in Leo, do not provoke vomiting. When it is in Libra, it is suitable for enemas. In Scorpio, do not attempt baths. There are those who neither prohibit nor command giving laxative medicine. In Capricorn, [give] medicine. for it is harmful to take it. Similarly in Aquarius. In Pisces, however, it is beneficial. Which members each of the planets has in any given sign—while necessary to know—is a long story to tell. Nor, indeed, regarding the purgation of the bowels, should Ptolemy’s precept escape us:
3.10.5: We approve of receiving purgative medicine when the Moon is in Cancer, Pisces, [or] Scorpio: especially if the ruler of the sign ascending at that time is applying itself to a planet running under the earth. But if the ruler of the ascendant is joined in the meantime above the head with a planet holding the midheaven, nausea and vomiting will be immediately incited. Finally, let us conclude with Galen, that Astrology is necessary for the physician, who, in debating critical days, says that the opinion of the Egyptians is certain, that is, that the Moon signifies the condition of the sick and the healthy from day to day, so much so that if the rays of Jupiter and Venus are mixed with the Moon, both are well-affected: but if those of Saturn or Mars, it fares in the opposite way. But having wandered further, let us finally return to the spirit and life and the Graces.

3.11.1:
*By what means our spirit may draw much from the spirit and life of the world: And which planets create and recreate the spirit. And what things pertain to each planet*
These things all tend toward this: that our spirit, properly prepared and purged through natural means, may receive much from the spirit of worldly life itself, through the rays of the stars received at an opportune time. The life of the world, indeed, is implanted in all things, [and] is evidently propagated into herbs and trees, as if they were the hairs and locks of its own body. Furthermore, it swells in stones and metals, like teeth and bones. It also sprouts in living shells, adhering to earth and stones. For these do not live so much by their own proper life as by the common life of the whole. This common life, indeed, thrives even more upon the earth in more subtle bodies, as they are closer to the soul. Through its inward vigor, water, air, [and] fire possess their own living [qualities], and are moved. This life cherishes and agitates the air and fire even more than the earth and water with perpetual motion. And finally, it vegetates the celestial bodies—as if they were the head, or heart, or eyes of the world—to the greatest degree. Whence, through the stars, as if they were eyes, it diffuses its rays everywhere, not only visible ones but also visual ones. With these, in the manner of the Ostrich, as we have said elsewhere, it looks upon the lower things, and fosters them by seeing, and even by touching them in this way, it generates, forms, and moves them in every way. Therefore, you will receive the motion of worldly life from the motion of glistening water, of serene air, and of moderately distant fire, and of the heavens, if you yourself also move gently and almost similarly, performing certain turns to the best of your ability—avoiding dizziness —surveying the celestial [bodies] with your eyes, and revolving them in your mind. Likewise, through a certain frequent use of plants and similarly living things, you can draw much from the spirit of the world: especially if you are nourished and fostered while they are still living and fresh, and as it were, still clinging to mother earth.
3.11.2: You should spend your time as frequently as possible among plants that are pleasantly fragrant, or at least not smelling bad. For all herbs, flowers, trees, [and] fruits have a fragrance, even if you often notice it less. By this odor, as if by a breath and spirit of worldly life, they recreate and vegetate you on all sides. I say that they easily refresh your body as well—since your spirit is most similar to odors of this kind—and they benefit the soul wonderfully through the spirit, which is the medium between the body and the soul. Among these, you will spend the longest time during the day out in the open air, as far as it can be done safely or conveniently, in high, serene, and temperate regions. For thus the rays of the Sun and the stars touch you more readily and purely from all sides, and fill your spirit with the spirit of the world, which gleams more abundantly through those rays. Moreover, the natural motion of the air itself, which is perpetual in a circle—though on account of its gentleness and long-standing habit it is scarcely perceived by anyone—freely licks and penetrates you as you walk or dwell out in the open during the day in spacious and elevated places, and it wonderfully provides the motion and vigor of the world to your spirit. I said, indeed, “during the day.” For we have found that the night air is hostile to spirits. It will be beneficial to use the daylight, especially if, by walking a great deal in the open, you avoid, first of all, excessive intemperance of the air. Then, you should move yourself in it more frequently when, besides the temperance and its serenity, the position of the stars is most healthy for humans. Likewise, if you choose places more fragrant than others, through which you change your location daily, you yourself are also moved, as it were, continuously and gently. I have always advised changing location, though with discretion, since the goods of the celestial [bodies] and of the whole of nature are distributed among us in different things and places, all of which should ultimately be enjoyed. I pass over the fact that variety prevents boredom— which is hostile to the spirits and proper to Saturn.
3.11.3: It brings pleasure, through which (if I may say so) Venus herself, the friend of pleasure, comes into the spirit: and what is her duty, having entered it, she immediately propagates. In sum, if one considers paradise and the use of the Tree of Life in Moses; likewise the similar diet proposed by Plato in the Phaedo a dialogue on the soul, and what Pliny says about peoples who live by odor, one will understand that what we say is true.
3.11.4: But let us descend to the nature of the spirit. The quality of the spirit is undoubtedly Jovial, at whose time it is infused into us. It is also Solar: for Jupiter infuses this, in so far as it tempers the huge power of the Sun within itself. It is also Jovial for another reason: because it is hot and moist, and abounds in heat rather than moisture, and is born from the blood, and is called a certain sanguine vapor. Again, because it is fervent and is extremely subtle and shining, and arises from the heart, it is undoubtedly judged to be Solar. It also possesses a certain Venusian virtue within itself. For it flows and overflows entirely with Venusian matter, it is transferred, propagates offspring, dilates itself to the pleasure of any sense, and flees from pain. In sum, the spirit, insofar as it conduces to the body for life, motion, and propagation, is considered Jovial, Venusian, [and] Solar. Insofar as it ministers to the mind for sense and imagination, it is judged to be Solar and Mercurial, and it is Mercurial everywhere. Since it is so mobile and so easily convertible and formable, the healthy spirit generally does not have much of Saturn, Mars, or the Moon. Otherwise, from the former it would often be stupid; from the middle one, furious; from the latter, dull in some way. For this reason, Lunar [spirits], being as it were thicker and at the same time more moist, are quite alien to the subtle and volatile nature of the spirit. Those which are Saturnine, or excessively Martial, are like poisons, naturally hostile to the spirit. The former on account of extreme cold and dryness; the latter, however, on account of dryness and consuming heat. Therefore, the spirit’s nature is considered to be Jovial and Solar above all, then Mercurial and in a certain way Venusian.
3.11.5: But for the primary distinction: the natural spirit is dedicated properly to Jupiter, the vital spirit to the Sun, and the animal spirit to Mercury. When, therefore, the situation demands that you aid any of these three spirits, you will not easily be able to help the little client by its patron, if that patron is unfortunate or weak. It is most difficult to help the animal spirit while Mercury is in an unfortunate position. is an affection. It holds such authority over the animal spirit that it is said to be able, with its own caduceus, to both lull the mind to sleep and awaken it. That is to say, by its particular aspect, it can wonderfully dull or sharpen the intellect, weaken or strengthen it, and disturb or soothe it. Therefore, as often as you study to cultivate some spirit, you will observe not only that its patron is fortunate and powerful, but you will also choose the Moon appropriately directed toward it. For the substance of the spirit is not created nor properly recreated at any time by the influx of Saturn alone, but it is always recalled from external things to internal ones, and often from the lowest to the highest. Hence, it leads to the contemplation of more secret and higher things. Nevertheless, the power of Mars and Saturn can, though rarely, benefit the spirit like medicine, whether by heating it when there is need—thereby exciting and dilating it—or conversely, by restraining it when it is too volatile. Yet the nature of the spirit is created and recreated most effectively by those things which are in agreement with those four planets. Truly, if you lean toward any Solar things strongly and without selection, you will sharpen the spirit, and eventually dry it out and dissolve it. If you lean similarly toward Venusian things, you will liquefy it little by little, or dull it. If you rely only upon Mercurial things, you will achieve very little from that. Therefore, it will be worth the effort to use Jovial things as much as possible, and to mix the others in moderately, and to use more frequently those things which are either equally common to all these, or proper to Jupiter. For these also are in a certain way common to all.
3.11.6: Commonly, those things belong to all these which possess a substance that is neither too fiery, nor entirely earthy, nor simply aqueous, nor of a most sharp or most obtuse quality, but rather moderate, smooth to the touch, and in a way soft, or at least not hard or rough; likewise, in taste, in a certain way sweet; in smell, fragrant; in sight, pleasing; in hearing, soothing and delightful; in thought, joyful. Therefore, a certain sweetness of flavor and grace is common to all these. If the sweetness is as if aqueous and at the same time oily, it pertains more to Venus the planet Venus. If it is as if insipid, or somewhat austere, it pertains rather to Mercury the planet Mercury. And these do not benefit the spirit much, yet they are sometimes necessary to blunt its excessive sharpness. If the sweetness is manifest and subtle, and has a little of a sharp, styptic flavor, it is judged to be properly Jovial pertaining to Jupiter. To this corresponds the substance of the sweet almond, pine nuts, hazelnuts, pistachios, starch, licorice, raisins, egg yolk, the meat of chickens, pheasants, peacocks, partridges, and the like. Likewise, the roots of been a type of aromatic root and elecampane. Again, odoriferous, clear wine that is somewhat sweet and styptic, and the whitest sugar. To Jupiter the planet Jupiter also belongs manna, if only it is strengthened by the infused virtue of myrobalan. Otherwise, it pertains no less to Venus than to Jupiter. This is, indeed, the substance and sweetness of Jupiter, which certainly contributes before all else to creating and recreating the spirit. Those things are truly Jovial, as we have said in the book On Long Life, which preserve youth and are healthy for the elderly. But if the sweetness is very little, and has much of a sharp and styptic quality, or even a bit of bitterness, it is considered to be Solar pertaining to the Sun. There is a similar logic and distinction regarding odors. For these are the siblings of flavors. There is also a similar one regarding colors. Indeed, aqueous, white, and green colors, somewhat saffron-colored, similar to the colors of violets, roses, and lilies, as well as odors of this kind, refer to Venus, the Moon, and Mercury. But sapphire colors, which are also called airy, likewise fuller purples, and gold mixed with silver, and those that are perpetually green, refer to Jupiter. Burning saffron, golden, pure, and clearer purple colors belong to the Sun. Any colors, if they are vivid or at least silken, are more stellar. They are also powerful in metals, stones, and glass on account of their celestial resemblance. But to return to Jupiter, its flavor and odor is such as that in a golden peach, a similar pear, or an orange, and in a lighter Malvasia wine and light Vernaccia. It is like that in fresh ginger, or cinnamon, or sweet fennel, or leopard’s bane, if these are tasted while candied with plenty of sugar. For these four, and fresh nutmeg, if they are alone, are rather Solar; also the clove and musk are Solar, but by smell, not by taste or sight. Amber is mostly Solar and Jovial.
3.11.7: Saffron is in all things Solar, although its color and odor are dedicated to all the Graces among astrologers. However, the flavor belongs properly to the Sun. Finally, all odoriferous and aromatic things, insofar as they provide a pleasing scent, pertain to Jupiter, Venus, and Mercury just as they do to the Sun; although among these, the sharper ones pertain more to the Sun, and the blunter ones rather to Venus and Mercury. Those that are properly tempered pertain to Jupiter by smell, taste, hearing, sight, and touch. Even sounds and pleasant, soothing songs look to all the Graces and Mercury; but threatening or mournful ones prefer Mars and Saturn. Nor should you wonder that we attribute much to colors, odors, and voices. For flavors indeed pertain especially to the natural spirit, odors rather to the vital and animal spirit; colors, shapes, and voices to the animal spirit. Also, the movement of the mind, whether joyful, sad, or constant, vehemently agitates the spirit into its own likeness. First the animal spirit, through this the vital, and through this, furthermore, the natural. Finally, every spirit, because it is by nature somewhat fiery, airy, entirely lucid, and mobile, is similar to lights. Therefore, it is moved and formed suddenly in either direction through colors, airy voices, and the odors and movements of the mind. And as the spirit itself turns out, it in turn makes the affection of the mind and the quality of the body in a certain way similar to it. Finally, when it is first exposed opportunely to the Graces through those things which are proper to the Graces, as it was naturally in agreement with them, it immediately receives wondrous gifts of the Graces through their rays, which are at once flourishing everywhere and kin to the spirit itself.

3.12.1:
*That natural and also artificial things have hidden virtues from the stars, through which they expose our spirit to those same stars*
When we say the spirit is exposed to the Graces through those things which are of the Graces, we believe it is accommodated not only through qualities that are seen, heard, smelled, and tasted, but also through those that are touched.
3.12.2: Remember, therefore, that heat is in the first degree of Jupiter: in the second of the Sun with Jupiter: in the third of Mars with the Sun: in the fourth of Mars. Cold is in the first degree of Venus: in the second of the Moon: in the third of the Moon with Saturn: in the fourth of Saturn. Moisture is in the first of Mercury with Jupiter: in the second of Venus with the Moon: in the third of the Moon with Venus: in the fourth of the Moon, when it is joined to Venus and Mercury. Dryness is in the first of Jupiter: in the second of Mercury with the Sun: in the third of the Sun with Mars: in the fourth of Mars with Saturn. In summary, from the qualities of the planets, which Ptolemy describes in the Quadripartitum, we conclude that the harmony gathered from all of them inclines toward heat and moisture. For the immense heat of Mars and the Sun, and the tempered heat of Jupiter, overcomes the coldness of Saturn and the meager coldness of Venus and the Moon, in such a way that heat there exceeds cold.
3.12.3: Furthermore, the moisture of the Moon and Venus—which is very great, close to us, and tempered by Jupiter—surpasses the dryness of Saturn and Mars, and the tempered dryness of the Sun. Heat and moisture, therefore, dominate over cold and dryness; similarly, heat dominates over moisture. Just as in a healthy human body, the complexion coalesces—tending toward heat and moisture, with heat reigning moderately—from the heat and dryness of the heart, the heat and moisture of the liver, and the cold and moisture of the brain. For the heat of the heart and liver overcomes the coldness of the brain. Likewise, the moisture of the liver and brain exceeds the dryness of the heart. I would not want it to be overlooked by us that a harmony exists among all the fixed stars, common to them just as we said of the planets. For astrologers consider them similar to these. Why this? So that you remember our spirit and body can be accommodated to the heavens—and claim the celestial for themselves—through a certain temperament tending toward heat and moisture, whether constant by nature or sought through art. Nor do we say that our spirit is prepared for the heavens only through the qualities of things known to the senses, but also, and much more, through certain properties divinely implanted in things, hidden from our senses, and finally, barely known to reason. For since such properties and their effects cannot consist of elemental virtue, it follows that they proceed uniquely from the life and spirit of the world through the rays of the stars themselves.
3.12.4: They therefore affect the spirit greatly and immediately through these, and it is vehemently exposed to celestial influences. For this reason, the smaragdus emerald, hyacinthus jacinth, saphyrus sapphire, topazius topaz, rubinus ruby, and the horn of a unicornis unicorn, but especially the stone called by the Arabs the bezaar bezoar stone, are endowed with hidden properties of the Graces. For this reason, not only when taken internally, but also if they touch the flesh and are warmed there, they reveal their virtue and infuse a celestial power into the spirits, by which they defend themselves against the plague and poisons. The fact that these and similar things do such a thing by celestial virtue is proven by the fact that even when taken in small weight, they have no small momentum in acting. This is rarely granted to elemental quality—that is, to fire, which is highly celestial. For material virtue requires much material to act effectively. Formal virtue, however, is very powerful even when the material is at its minimum.
3.12.5: With a similar virtue, the Phoebea Paeonia Solar peony—touching the flesh—arms the spirits against the falling sickness by a vapor infused into them from within. Similarly, corallus coral and chalcedonius chalcedony [act] against the illusions of black bile, primarily through the virtue of Jupiter and Venus, and others similarly. By a certain property of this kind, myrobalani myrobalan fruit preserve youth, sharpen the senses, and benefit talent and memory, because of Jupiter, the primary temperer of Saturn, and Mercury, the friend of the senses. Some, perhaps, will think that this tree existed in Paradise to prolong life.
3.12.6: [Men] consecrate the Achates agate stone to Mercury. Hence, natural philosophers agree that it is effective for eloquence and vision, and against poisons. Serapio writes that one who carries a hyacinth, or a seal made from one, is safe from lightning, and this virtue of it is very widely proclaimed; if it has this, we believe it holds it from Jupiter. The Aetites eagle stone has [a virtue] from Lucina—that is, from Venus and the Moon—such that when moved to the womb, it brings about birth quickly and very easily. Rasis, confirmed by Serapio, says he has frequently experienced this. Perhaps the Dictamus dittany of Crete has from Phoebus—who pierced Python—that it both resists poisonous things and draws iron from a wound. By the virtue of the Sun, ginger infused into food wards off fainting. Sentiana sedates the rabies of a dog and puts snakes to flight. Berbena verbena is said to provide prophecy, joy, expiations, and vision. Rue and zedoary act as an antidote against poisons. Frankincense supports vital and animal spirit against dullness, forgetfulness, and fear. Sage and mint, through the virtue of Jupiter—the former puts paralysis to flight, the latter strengthens the mind through its scent. By the same virtue, Pentaphyllon cinquefoil resists poisons; one leaf of it taken in wine twice a day cures a daily fever, three [leaves] a tertian fever, and four a quartan fever. Ancient priests used this herb in purifications because of its purity. Agnus castus chaste tree, by the power of Saturn, halts the motions of Venus. Iaspis jasper [halts] blood. Miraculous effects usually appear where elemental property serves occult property.
3.12.7: …as in the myrobalan, to strengthen the spirit and body. Not only does that celestial virtue act, but also a strongly styptic one; nor does the aromatic virtue do little, which wonderfully prevents putrefaction and dissolution, and strengthens the spirit. Now, truly, that saffron seeks the heart, dilates the spirit, and provokes laughter—not only does the hidden virtue of the Sun bring this about miraculously, but the very nature of saffron—subtle, expansive, aromatic, and bright—also contributes to the same. What I say about simples, I wish to be understood as said similarly of compounds. Come, tell me, how does theriac help us against poison? It does not draw out the poison. It constricts the bowels, and does not immediately change the nature of the poison. For this is not so weak and mutable; rather, it strengthens the vital spirit—which is very thin and mutable—suddenly through a certain proportion conformed to it, until the spirit itself, now strong as an agent, together with the theriac as an instrument, partly overcomes the poison, partly changes it, and partly wards it off from the heart. But by what proportion or virtue does theriac effect this? By a Jovian and Phoebean [proportion], which it seems to have claimed for itself from the mixture of many things confused together according to a certain proportion. There is a triple virtue in it: this very celestial one I was just speaking of; another celestial property previously in the herbs and aromatics from which it is rightly composed when selected, which supplies the previously mentioned virtue toward the same end. Furthermore, there is another virtue in mostparts of it, elemental rather than celestial. Yet [it is] such that it conducts itself toward moving the spirit—I speak of the styptic and aromatic quality. The former strengthens the spirit, the latter warms it. Therefore, theriac has obtained a miraculous power against hastening old age and poison, with three virtues in it conspiring equally toward the same end. One of these is indeed celestial, acquired through artificial mixture. Another is celestial again, but naturally implanted in its parts. The other is purely elemental. But that which I spoke of first, acquired from the heavens, would be much more admirable if it were composed not only through Jovian and Solar proportion and from things of that kind, but if the opportune time for this were also chosen by observing the heavens. For just as the body relates to place and time, so motion and action relate to time. Therefore, just as certain bodies and their forms grow and are preserved in certain places and times, so too do certain proper actions obtain their efficacy from certain proper times. Socrates signifies this in the Alcibiades, and Proclus explains it. Pythagoras, observing this, called the very good and perfection of things “opportune time.” For the first principle is the measure of all things for Pythagoras and Plato, such that it has distributed different places and times to different bodies and actions. Hence, just as certain things are properly [found] nowhere but here, nor at any other time than then… properly and happily grow, coalesce, and are preserved: so also does a material action, movement, or event of such a kind obtain its efficacy and perfected result only when the harmony of the heavens is consonant with the same from all sides. Indeed, this harmony is considered to have such power that it often bestows a miraculous virtue not only upon the labors of farmers and the arts of physicians— concocted through herbs and aromatics—but also upon images that are made from metals and stones by astrologers. But images now require their own proper chapter. As for choosing hours for actions and works, this is highly confirmed by Ptolemy, where he says in the Centiloquy: “He who chooses what is better seems in no way to differ from him who has this by nature.” In these words, he seems to confirm the power of both the heavens and our own will and choice. Albertus Magnus also says in the Speculum: “The liberty of the will is not curtailed by the choosing of a praiseworthy hour; rather, to ignore the choice of an hour in the inception of great matters is a precipitation of the will, not liberty.”

3.13.1:
*On the virtue of images according to the ancients, and of medicines acquired from the heavens*
Ptolemy says in the Centiloquy that “the effigies of inferior things are subject to celestial appearances,” and that the ancient sages were accustomed to fashion certain images at those times. when the planets entered the heavens in similar aspects, as if they were the archetypes of inferior things. Haly confirms this, saying: “A useful image of a serpent can be made when the Moon is in conjunction with or favorably aspecting the celestial serpent.” Similarly, an effigy of a scorpion is effective when the Moon enters the sign of the Scorpion and this sign holds one of the four angles. He says this was done in Egypt in his own time, and that he was present when the figure of incense was pressed from a seal of a scorpion made in a bezoar a stone found in the digestive tract of animals, believed to be an antidote to poison stone. It was given as a drink to one whom a real scorpion had stung, and he was immediately cured. The physician Hahamed affirms that this can be done usefully, with Serapion confirming it. Furthermore, Haly narrates that a wise man known to him in that place made images through similar industry that would move, such as we read were made—I do not know how—by Archytas. Hermes Trismegistus says that the Egyptians were accustomed to make such things from specific materials of the world and were wont to insert into them, at opportune times, the souls of demons, and even the soul of his grandfather Mercury. Likewise, he says that the spirits of a certain Phoebus, and of Isis and Osiris, descended into statues in this way, which would be of benefit or even harm to men. Similar to this is the story that Prometheus snatched life and celestial light for his clay figure. Furthermore, the Magi, followers of Zoroaster, used a certain golden ball marked with celestial characters to evoke a spirit from Hecate. To this, a sapphire was also inserted, and it was turned by a whip made of bull’s hide, and in the meantime while they chanted spells. But I willingly omit the chants. For the Platonist Psellus rejects and mocks them. The Hebrews also, having been nurtured in Egypt, learned to build the golden calf, as astrologers of that time think, to curry the favor of Venus and the Moon against the influence of the Scorpion and Mars, which was hostile to the Jews. Porphyry also, in his letter to Anebo, testifies that images are effective, and adds that aerial demons were accustomed to be insinuated immediately into certain vapors exhaled from their proper fumigations. Iamblichus confirms that in materials which are naturally in agreement with the higher powers, and which have been duly and opportunely collected and prepared, one can receive not only celestial forces, but also demonic and divine ones. Proclus and Synesius say exactly the same. Indeed, the miraculous works for health that can be performed by physicians skilled in astrology through things composed of many elements—that is, powders, liquids, ointments, and electuaries—seem to possess a more probable and better-known rationale than images: first, because powders, liquids, ointments, and electuaries, when opportunely prepared, receive celestial influences more easily and quickly than the harder materials from which images are usually made; second, because they are either taken internally having already been affected by the heavens, and are transformed into us, or at least when applied externally they adhere more, and finally penetrate; third, because images are constructed from only one or very few materials. The latter, however, from can be concocted from very many, as one wishes. If the hundred gifts of the Sun or Jupiter were dispersed through a hundred plants, animals, and similar things, you could compose these hundred items that you have gathered and create them into one form, in which you might seem to possess the Sun and Jupiter almost entirely. You know, indeed, that the lower nature cannot capture all the powers of the higher nature in one single thing, and therefore those powers are dispersed among many natures here with us, and can be collected more conveniently through the works of physicians and similar things than through images. Consequently, images made of wood perhaps have little power. For wood is perhaps too hard to easily capture a celestial influx, and if it does receive it, it is less tenacious in retaining it. Once it is torn from the bowels of mother earth, it soon loses almost all the vigor of mundane life, and easily transforms into another quality. Stones and metals, however, even if they seem harder to receive a celestial gift, retain it longer if they have received it, as Iamblichus confirms. By their very hardness, they retain for the longest time the traces and gifts of mundane life after they have been uprooted, which they once possessed while clinging to the earth. For this reason, if for no other, they are judged to be suitable materials for capturing and holding celestial things. It is also probable, as I said in the previous book, that such precious things cannot be forged under the earth without a great effort of the heavens, and that the virtue once impressed upon them by that effort endures within them.
3.13.2: For in cooking and compressing these things, the heavens have labored for a very long time. But since you cannot easily compose many things of this kind, you are forced to diligently seek out which metal is in the order of a certain star most primarily, or which stone is the highest in that order, so that even in one thing, the supreme of the whole genus and order, you may grasp the rest according to your strength and, in such a receptacle, borrow celestial things consonant with it. For example, in the Solar order, under a Phoebian man, the hawk or the rooster holds the highest place among animals; balsam or laurel among plants; gold among metals; the carbuncle or pantaura among stones; and heated air among the elements. For fire itself is considered to be Martial. However, what we have said about increasing the influx of the Sun, Jupiter, or Venus, we understand by general reasoning, but not for one in whose natal chart any of these appears as a “slayer”.

3.14.1:
*On the orders of things depending upon the stars, such as Solar things and the like. And how the spirit becomes solar*
I have said elsewhere that from each star above (to speak Platonically), a series of things proper to it depends all the way down to the extremities. Under the heart of the Scorpion itself, after such demons, humans, and the animal scorpion, we can also place the herb Asterion star-like, which is star-like in shape, shining at night, which
3.14.2: Physicians report that roses possess this quality, and they possess a miraculous power against diseases of the genitals. Under the serpent or the celestial Serpent-bearer, they place Saturn, and in a certain way, Jupiter. Afterward, they place the demons, who often put on the forms of serpents. Furthermore, they place similar humans, serpents, living creatures, the serpent-herb, and the Draconites dragon-stone stone born from the head of a dragon. Likewise, they use the common name Serpent-stone. And beyond these, the things I shall mention in what follows. Under the Solar star, that is, Sirius, they place the Sun first, then also the Phoebian demons, whom Proclus testifies have sometimes encountered men in the form of lions or roosters. Soon after, they place men who are very similar, and Solar beasts. Thence [they place] Phoebian plants, similarly metals and small stones, and vapor and burning air. By a similar reason, they believe that the fabric of things descends gradually from any star of the firmament through some planet under its property. Therefore, if (as I was saying) you grasp all Solar things opportunely through any degree of that order—namely such men, or something of such a man: likewise brutes, plants, metals, small stones, and the things that pertain to these—you will absorb the virtue of the Sun everywhere, and in a certain way, the natural faculty of the Solar demons. And consider it said in a similar way regarding others. Solar men, indeed, are those whom I mentioned before, and those who are born when Leo is rising, and when the Sun is either holding or gazing upon it, and those who are born similarly under Aries.
3.14.3: The blood of those who are healthy is also Solar from their left side.
3.14.4: The Phoebian creatures are the crocodile, the hawk, the lion, the rooster, the swan, and the raven. Nor does the lion fear the rooster for any other reason, except that the rooster is superior to the lion in the Phoebian order. For the same reason, Proclus says the Apollonian demon, who sometimes appeared in the figure of a lion, vanished immediately upon the presentation of a rooster.
3.14.5: But especially in these animals, the heart is Solar. I also believe that the sea-calf is subject to the heart of the celestial lion, and for this very reason, the leather of it, which a man wears naked when girded by a brooch made from the bone of the same, relieves pain in the kidneys. For astrologers are accustomed to use the influxes of that star against pain of this kind. Perhaps for the same reason, it is said that this skin protects us from lightning. Among plants, the palm is Phoebian, and especially the laurel, by whose virtue it repels poisonous things and lightning. The ash tree also wards off poisonous things from afar with a similar faculty. That the lotus is Phoebian is testified by its round leaves and fruits, and the opening of its leaves during the day, but their closing at night. That the peony is Phoebian is indicated not only by its virtue but also by its name. To the same category pertain flowers and herbs that are restricted when the Sun departs, are immediately opened when it returns, and continuously turn toward the Sun. Furthermore, there is gold and the Elitis eaglestone stone, which imitates the Sun with golden rays. Likewise, there is the stone that is called the eye of the Sun, having the figure of a pupil from which light shines forth. Again, the carbuncle glowing at night, or the Pantaura a mythical stone said to attract others, which contains within itself the powers of all stones. such as gold among metals, and the Sun among the stars. In short, many things indicated by us above, from which, if it is currently permitted, you may prepare an electuary or ointment under the empire of the Sun from that blood, and the hearts of those animals, and the leaves and flowers of the aforementioned trees: Likewise from flowers and herbs, and gold leaf, as well as the powders of small stones you will be able to do this, by adding saffron, balsam, aromatic reed, frankincense, musk, amber, aloe wood, ginger, mastic, spikenard, cinnamon, leopard’s bane, citrus peel, zedoary, nutmeg, mace, and cloves with yellow honey or oil of balsam, mastic, laurel, or nard, to foment the heart, stomach, and head, either internally or externally, so that the Solar spirit may emerge from them. From all these, I say, or at least from most of them, one must compose something while the Sun is dominant. You should also begin to use this under the same dominion, provided that you also wear, inhabit, look at, hear, smell, imagine, think of, and desire Solar things. Likewise, imitate the dignity and gifts of the life of the Sun. Associate with Solar men and plants, and touch the laurel assiduously. However, it will be safer for health to mix Jovial and Venusian things with the Solar. Venusian moisture is especially the moderator of Solar heat, such as water and the juice of roses and violets. But I have composed medicines of this kind in the book On Curing the Learned, then partly in the book On Long Life, and I have described those composed by others, and have even tempered some myself.
3.14.6: Likewise, we have spoken in the book Against the Plague about what kind of herbs, under the Sun and Jupiter, have wondrous powers against epidemics and poison, among which is the Perforata St. John’s wort, which is called fugadæmon demon-chaser. It is believed to ward off the harmful vapors of evil demons from us by no other faculty than that of celestial graces. And if any other herb or small stone, such as coral, seems to accomplish the same thing. The Lunar herb, handed down from Mercury, with blue and round leaves, producing one leaf daily as the Moon waxes and dropping one as it wanes, promises lunar years to the user. But let us now return to images with another kind of beginning.

3.15.1:
*On the virtue of images according to the ancients and [the virtue of] medicines. And how medicines are much more powerful than images*
If you have obtained the small stones which we described a little earlier as Phoebian, there will be no need to imprint images upon them. You will therefore hang them around your neck, enclosed in gold and on threads of saffron-colored silk, when the Sun is running through Aries or Leo, and is rising or holding the middle of the sky, and is gazing upon the Moon. Proclus, however, relates that stones in the lunar series are much more powerful. First, indeed, is the Selinitim moonstone, which not only imitates the Moon in figure but also in motion, and revolves with the Moon. If by chance you find this, and it is encircled in silver, and you hang it around your neck on a silver thread when the Moon is entering Cancer or Tau- rus, and holding the angles that are suitable for it, it will render your spirit from then on, finally, Lunar. This is provided that the Lunar stone itself, having been warmed by you, assiduously inserts its own virtue into your spirits. He mentions another stone, by the name of Helioselinon sun-moon stone, which naturally possesses the image of the Sun and the Moon joined to the Sun. Therefore, whoever brings this, enclosed in gilded silver, to their neck on similar threads, when the Moon in its own domicile or that of the Sun is conjoined with the Sun in the same minute, and holds its own angles, will carry back a Solar and at the same time a Lunar spirit, or at least such a one as emerges when the Moon is conjoined with the Sun through the center. Here, indeed, you see the scattered gifts of Phoebus, like the limbs of Osiris, being gathered by his sister Phoebe, like Isis. But I wish we could easily find a Solar or Lunar stone somewhere, so very powerful in its order, just as we have the magnet and iron under the series of the northern pole. They say that Apollonius of Tyana certainly found a Solar stone among the Indians, namely the stone called Pantaura, shining like fire, born four paces under the earth, in which there is so much spirit that it swells, and often the earth is split where a stone of this kind is conceived: thus it draws other stones to itself, just as the magnet draws iron. But this Herculean stone ravishes us even more vehemently to contemplate it at present. We see in the mariners’ compass the needle balanced to indicate the pole, affected at the extremity by the mag- to be moved by the magnet toward the Bear, moving specifically because the magnet draws it there. Since the power of the Bear also prevails in this stone, and from here it is transferred into the iron, and draws both toward the Bear. Moreover, such a virtue is both infused from the beginning and is continuously invigorated by the rays of the Bear. Perhaps Amber relates in this way to the other pole and to chaff. But tell me in the meantime, why does the magnet draw iron everywhere? It is not because it is similar; otherwise, a magnet would draw a magnet much more, and iron would draw iron. It is not because it is superior in the order of bodies; in fact, metal is superior to a small stone. What is it, then? Both are indeed contained within the order following the Bear. But the magnet holds the higher degree in that very property of the Bear, while iron holds the lower. Now, in the same context of things, what is higher indeed draws what is lower, and turns it toward itself, or agitates it in any other way, or affects it with a previously infused virtue. The lower, in turn, is turned by the same infusion toward the higher, or is otherwise agitated, or is thoroughly affected. Thus, in the series of the Sun, the lower man admires the higher. In the Jovian order, he venerates. In the Martial, he fears. In the Venetian, the lower is seized by the higher with the ardor of love, and deserts himself. In the Mercurial, the former always learns, or is persuaded by the latter. In the Lunar, the motion of the former more often begins from the latter. In the Saturnian, peace. But when I was rejoicing that I had explored these things thus far, and while still a youth I was thinking of engraving the figure of the celestial Bear upon a magnet as best I could, at the time when the Moon might look upon it more favorably. and then to hang it from my neck with an iron thread. I hoped, indeed, that I would finally be master of the virtue of that star. But when I had explored it for a long time, I eventually found the influences of that star to be for the most part Saturnian and Martial. I learned from the Platonists that evil demons are for the most part Northern, which the astronomers of the Hebrews also confess, placing harmful and Martial demons in the North, but propitious and Jovian ones in the South. I learned from the theologians and from Iamblichus a Neoplatonist philosopher that makers of images are often occupied and deceived by evil demons. I indeed saw a small stone brought to Florence from India, dug up there from the head of a dragon, round in the shape of a coin, naturally marked with many points in order like stars, which, when washed with vinegar, was moved briefly in a straight line, nay, obliquely, and soon it was carried in a circle until it exhaled the vapor of the vinegar. I truly thought that such a stone possessed the nature of a celestial dragon and, as it were, its figure, and also received its motion, insofar as through the spirit of the vinegar or stronger wine, it was rendered more familiar to that dragon or firmament. Therefore, whoever wore this and often washed it with vinegar might perhaps receive some power of that dragon, which with twin coils implicates the Greater Bear on one side, and the Lesser on the other. And near Scorpio, the Serpentarius the Serpent Bearer constellation stands, like a man encircled by a serpent, holding the head of the serpent in his right hand and the tail in his left, with knees as if bent, and head slightly tilted back. I have read, indeed, that the Magi advised the King of the Persians to imprint this image onto a Hæmatite bloodstone, which he should enclose in a gold ring, yet in such a way that he should insert the root of the serpent-herb between the stone and the gold. For he who wears this ring will be safe against poison and poisonous diseases, specifically if you make it when the Moon is looking at the Serpent-bearer. Peter of Abano a medieval physician and philosopher confirmed this image. But I, if that ring has this power, believe it to be claimed not so much through the figure as through such materials, and by being composed in this way and at such a time through celestial aid. Remember that stones growing in animals and not suffering from it, such as in the dragon, the rooster, the swallow, and others, are almost as effective as stones growing in the earth, and are referred to the same stars to which these animals belong. Hence the Alectorius stone from a cock’s gizzard, extracted from the gizzard of an old rooster, prevails with Solar power; Dioscorides ancient Greek physician says it has often been found that he who carries this stone in his mouth fights undefeated. He says the same of the Chelidonium swallow-stone, extracted from a swallow, which is red and cures the melancholic and renders one lovable and suitable. This, indeed, it has from Jupiter, through those things which we have mentioned, namely that things everywhere below the Moon are stellar. That very Platonic statement is strongly confirmed: that this machine of the world is so connected with itself that celestial things are present on earth with a terrestrial condition, and in turn, terrestrial things are present in heaven with a celestial dignity, and in the hidden life of the world and in its mind, the queen of the world, celestial things are present, yet with a vital intellect. at the same time as their property and excellence. Through these, moreover, some confirm also that magic principle: that celestial things can be drawn in some way to men at opportune times through inferior things that are consonant with the superior ones, and even that super-celestial things can be reconciled to us through celestial ones, or perhaps entirely insinuated. But as for this last point, let them see to it. It seems sufficiently probable (as we have said) that such a thing can be done by a certain art that duly and opportunely gathers many things into one. This is because of the reasons we assigned above, and because when many such things are gathered, ground up, mixed, and cooked together by a physician and an astrologer under a certain star, while they gradually undergo a new form by the very reason of their cooking and fermentation, they acquire this same form through a certain celestial fomentation, with the rays then acting within, and therefore, it is celestial. However, when a metal or a stone is engraved in a moment, it does not seem to receive a new quality, but a figure. Nor does that motion proceed through the due degrees of digestion, which natural alteration and generation are accustomed to observe. But since the celestial nature, as a rule of the lower nature, is accustomed to proceed with a certain natural tenor, and to aspire to those that are so proceeding, many rightfully doubt that such images have any celestial virtue. I, too, often doubt this, and unless all of antiquity and all astrologers thought they had a wondrous power, I would deny it. I would indeed deny it not entirely. For I suppose (unless someone has persuaded me otherwise) that they have some virtue for prosperous health at least, especially by reason of the selected material: although I judge that a much greater power resides in medicines and ointments composed with celestial favor. But I will declare in what follows what I meant when I was just speaking of the “reason of the selected material.” I will shortly bring forward, in order, those things that can be alleged for images from the opinion of the Magi or astrologers for the sake of interpreting Plotinus, if I first warn you here not to think that I approve of the use of images, but that I am narrating it. For I use medicines tempered to the heavens, not images, and I advise others daily in the same way. But if you concede that God has inserted wondrous virtues into things below the Moon, concede that even more wondrous ones are in the celestial bodies. Furthermore, if you judge it permissible for a man to use inferior things for prosperous health, judge that it is permissible to use superior things as well, and to temper the inferior things to the norm of the superior ones, just as they were tempered by God from the beginning through the art of physicians.

3.16.1:
*On the power of the heavens. On the powers of the rays, from where images are thought to derive their force*
The immense size, virtue, and motion of the celestial bodies mean that all rays of all the stars penetrate the mass of the earth, which is as a point to the heaven, in a moment and most easily, right to the center, which all astronomers…
3.16.2: [The Pythagoreans and Platonists] agree with me. And there, as it pleases the Pythagoreans and Platonists, they are strongest: both because they touch the center from every side, and because they are all collected into a narrow space. Their vehemence is such that the dry matter of the earth there, being far removed from moisture, is utterly ignited, and being ignited, is thinned and scattered through the passages on all sides, and breathes out fires just as it does sulfur. But they think this fire is very murky, and is like a certain conflagration devoid of light, just as in the sky there exists light devoid of conflagration: however, fire between the celestial and the infernal joins light with heat. Furthermore, they think the fire blowing from the center is Vestal fire: since they believed Vesta to be the life and divinity of the earth. Therefore, the ancients built the temple of Vesta in the centers of cities, and placed the perpetual fire in the middle. But lest we wander further, let us now conclude that, if the rays of the stars penetrate the whole earth in a moment, it cannot be easily denied that metal and stone, when they are engraved with images, are suddenly penetrated, and that wondrous gifts, or at least some kind of gifts, are impressed upon them. Since even in the depths of the earth they generate most precious things. But who would deny that rays penetrate through these things? Since air and its quality, and sound, which is less effective, pass through solids suddenly, and affect them with a certain quality of their own. Now indeed, if hardness were to resist rays penetrating light, it would pass through air much faster than water, and through this much faster than glass, and likewise through glass faster than crystal. light. But since it is clearly evident that at the same moment it pierces through all solids and liquids, hardness in no way resists the rays. And for this reason, they will say it must not be denied that metals receive the rays and influences of the celestial bodies, and also preserve them for a time destined for them by heaven. They preserve, I say, a certain virtue created from the contact of concurring rays. What indeed if harder matter, by the very fact that it seems to resist a superior cause, exposes itself more to the blows? Thus a sword cuts wood under wool without cutting the wool. Thus that lightning ray sometimes dissolves metal within a leather pouch without harming the leather. But since the celestial nature is incomparably more excellent than this fire of ours, it must not be thought that the duty of the celestial ray is merely such a work as we clearly see of the fiery ray, namely to illuminate, heat, dry, penetrate, thin, and dissolve, which are most known to our senses, but rather that it has many more and more wondrous powers and effects: otherwise, both inferior matter and falling sense would be completely equal to the divinity of the heavens. But who does not know the occult virtues of things, which are called “special” by physicians, are not produced by elemental nature, but by the celestial? Therefore they can (as they say) impress occult and miserable powers beyond those known upon images, just as they insert them into other things. For they are not inanimate, like the rays of a lamp, but alive and sensitive, as if shining forth through the eyes of living bodies, and they carry with them wondrous gifts from the imaginations and minds of the celestial bodies.
3.16.3: They also act with most violent force from the strong affection of the celestial bodies, and the most rapid motion of their bodies, and specifically and most of all upon the spirit, which is very similar to celestial rays. Furthermore, they act upon even the hardest bodies. For all these things are very weak in comparison to the heaven. Moreover, in various stars there are also various powers, and therefore various powers in their rays among themselves. Furthermore, different virtues arise when the blows of the rays fall in different ways. Finally, in the mutual meetings of rays, in different ways, and here or there, and then or at other times, different powers suddenly arise from the effects, much more and faster than in other different mixtures of elements and elemental qualities: and even much faster than in tones and numbers among a musician playing in different ways. If you consider these things diligently, perhaps you will not doubt, they will say, that powers are suddenly impressed upon images by a certain casting of rays, and different powers from a different casting. Is it then so fast? I pass over fascinations made by a certain sudden intuition, and most sharp loves ignited immediately by the rays of the eyes, which themselves are also certain fascinations, which we prove in the book On Love. I pass over how quickly a red eye infects the onlooker, and a menstruating woman the one who looks at a mirror. Are not certain families among the Illyrians and Triballians said to have killed people by their gaze when angry? And are not certain women in Scythia accustomed to doing the same? And the Catoblepas and royal serpents kill men by the casting of rays from their eyes. and royal serpents kill men by the casting of rays from their eyes. The marine torpedo also suddenly stupefies by touch, even from a distance through a rod. Furthermore, the little fish called the echinus is said to stop a large ship by touch alone. Moreover, spiders in Apulia, by some even occult blow, change the spirit and mind with sudden stupor. What does a rabid dog do, or even when the bite is not apparent? What does the broom, and then what does the arbutus? Do they not stir up poison and rabies with the slightest touch? Will you therefore deny that celestial bodies, with the rays of their own eyes, with which ours are associated, perform wondrous things as soon as they touch? Now indeed, a pregnant woman, by a touch, immediately marks the limb of the child to be born with a sign of the desired object. Will you doubt that rays touching in different ways produce different results? Since you yourself, when gathering the herb hellebore, whether you pull the leaf downward or upward, by this sudden touch, are the cause for the hellebore to draw out humors downward or upward? Do not celestial influences, from the beginning of the generation of each thing, bestow wondrous gifts through the concoction of matter and perfect digestion, not so much by time as by a moment? Do not countless serpents and similar living creatures jump out from the sands in a moment when the face of the sky is favorable? So great is the power of the sky in prepared materials, so great is the speed. Finally, if fire has this, that it does in the briefest time what others do in a long time, especially because it is most similar to the sky: who would doubt that the heaven accomplishes great things in almost a moment, even in less prepared matter, just as a larger flame is accustomed to? things in almost a moment, even in less prepared matter, just as a larger flame is accustomed to? Why then do you doubt, they ask, that the heaven acts in almost the same way in constructing an image? You will say, I suppose, as I was also saying, that the natural degrees of alteration are absent here. This defect indeed diminishes the celestial gift, yet it does not seem to remove it entirely. For the natural philosophers do not wish for an image to be fashioned from just any metal or stone, but from a specific one. In which, indeed, the celestial nature has already naturally initiated, and as it were already finished, the virtue for this very thing that is desired, as it has flame in sulfur. Which virtue it finally perfects when this matter is vehemently agitated through art under a similar celestial influence, and when agitated, it becomes warm. Therefore, art awakens the virtue initiated there, and while it reduces it to a figure similar to some celestial figure of its own, it then exposes it completely to its own idea, which, being thus exposed, the heaven perfects with the power with which it had begun. Exhibiting flame to sulfur, so a certain power for grabbing straw, given from heaven to amber, often weak in a certain way, becomes stronger suddenly through friction and heating. Serapio writes that a similar virtue is given to the stone Albugedi, similar to a hyacinth. But it does not pull straw until the hair is rubbed with this stone. Thus also that Jovian stone Bezaar, that is, liberating from death, which we described in the book Against the Plague, received power from the beginning against poison from Jupiter, but not to such an extent… so strong that it can transfer the same to other matters to be exercised. Indeed, when at first it has received the shape of that celestial Scorpion under its influence, it is thought to suddenly carry back a perfect power against scorpions, which it has the capacity to communicate to Mastic or frankincense. The same logic must be held concerning the hyacinth, topaz, emerald, and others, so that the construction of images has efficacy nowhere else than where the matter agrees with the star both in nature and in the effect that the craftsman desires to receive from it.
3.16.4: Furthermore, this matter must be, as it were, already such from the beginning as you aim to render it through the shape. Therefore, they advise against using any materials for images except those very ones which are known to you to possess almost the power you desire. They order, therefore, that the powers of stones and metals be investigated most diligently, and in the meantime, remember that among stones, the Carbuncle shines in darkness, and the Pantaura is especially subject to the Sun, the Sapphire to Jupiter, the Emerald to Venus, and others to Mercury and the Moon. Moreover, that metals, besides gold and silver, have hardly any power for these things. And that the safer reasoning in these matters will be if you refer pure gold to the Sun and to Jupiter: to the former because of its color, to the latter because of its tempered mixture. For nothing is more tempered than Jupiter and gold. Truly, pure silver to the Moon, but gold mixed with silver to Jupiter as well as Venus. Furthermore, the image will be more effective if the power in its material is consistent with its own special power naturally implanted, and if this is, moreover, added to another special power to be captured from the heavens through a shape. Finally, you will learn from this, as they say, that inferior shapes and forms are conformed to celestial ones, just as Perseus, by cutting off the head of Medusa, was accustomed to portend the future beheading of some, and many similar things; and they do not doubt that the Moon and other planets move certain members in us under certain signs.

3.17.1:
*What power shapes have in the heaven and under the heaven*
But lest you perhaps distrust shapes too much, they will instruct you to remember that in this elemental region under the Moon, the elemental quality can also do a great deal, namely in a transmu tation a change of substance tending toward something elemental, such as heat, cold, moisture, and dryness. However, qualities that are less elemental or material, namely lights, that is to say colors, and likewise numbers and shapes, perhaps have less power for such things, but, as they think, are very strong for celestial gifts. For even in the heaven, lights, numbers, and shapes are the most powerful of all things, especially if there is no matter there, as most Peripatetics think. For in this way, shapes, numbers, and rays, when they are not sustained by any other matter there, seem to be as it were substantial. And since mathematical forms precede physical ones in the order of things, they claim for themselves the greatest authority in the preceding degrees of the world, that is, the celestial ones, as they are indeed more simple and less needy, so that something is achieved from them not less by number, shape, and light than by some elemental property. A sign of this authority is also found under the Moon. For qualities that are very material are common to many species of things, and when these are in some way exchanged, the species are not changed entirely.
3.17.2: However, shapes and numbers of natural parts possess a property with the species that is inseparable and peculiar, as they were destined from the heavens together with the species. Indeed, they also have the greatest connection with the ideas in the mind of the world, the queen. And since they themselves and the species of numbers are a kind of image, designated there by their own proper ideas, they naturally obtain proper powers from there. And therefore, the species of natural things are bound to certain shapes, just as movements, generations, and mutations are bound to certain numbers. But what shall I say about light? For it is the act or image of intelligence. And colors are certain lights. Therefore, when astrologers say that lights, that is to say colors, as well as shapes and numbers, can do a great deal in our matters being prepared for celestial things, you should not rashly, as they say, deny these things. You are not unaware that musical concords have a miraculous power through their numbers and proportions to settle, move, and affect the spirit, the mind, and the body. However, proportions are established from numbers. are like certain shapes, or as if made from points and lines, but in motion. Similarly, celestial shapes behave in their motion to act. For these, with their harmonic rays and motions penetrating all things, affect the spirit daily so secretly, just as a powerful piece of music is accustomed to affect it openly. You know, moreover, how easily the figure of a weeping person moves mercy in many. And how much the figure of an amiable person immediately affects and moves the eyes, the imagination, the spirit, and the humors. Nor is the celestial figure any less living and effective. Does not the kind and cheerful face of a prince in a city exhilarate everyone? And does not a fierce or sad one suddenly terrify them? What, then, do you think the faces of the celestial bodies can do against the lords of all earthly things? Indeed, since even those uniting for offspring are often accustomed to imprint on their children, who are to be born long afterwards, not only the faces that they themselves have at that time, but also those they imagine. Celestial faces, for the same reason, immediately infect materials with their marks. In which, if they seem to lie hidden for a long time, they then emerge at their own times. The faces of the heaven are, however, the celestial shapes. You can call the shapes there “faces”, which are more stable there than the others; but call the “faces” the shapes which are more changed there. You can also call the aspects of the stars among themselves, completed by daily motion, “faces,” and likewise “shapes.” For they are called hexagons, pentagons, and tetragons. Someone will say: let it be that they are, as you please, most powerful for acting… celestial shapes are most powerful for acting. But what is this to shapes made by the art of images? They will answer that they do not contend that our shapes are most powerful to act by themselves, but that they are most prepared to receive the actions and powers of celestial shapes, insofar as they are made opportunely when those are dominant, and are configured precisely to them. For that shape requires a shape. Does not one cithara resound when another is sounding? Only for this reason, if it also has a similar shape, is placed in view, and its strings are placed and tensioned in a similar way. What causes the cithara to suddenly suffer from the cithara, if not some position and a certain conformable shape? The shape of a smooth, concave, shining mirror that is congruent with the heaven, for this very reason properly receives a gift from the heavens, so that it collects the rays of Phoebus most abundantly into itself, and suddenly burns anything very solid placed in its view towards its center. Therefore, do not doubt, they will say, but that a certain matter of an image to be made, otherwise very congruent to the heaven, through a shape similar to the heaven given by art, receives a celestial gift both into itself and returns it into some neighbor or the one wearing it. Not only the shape, but also the permeable disposition, which they call Diaphanous, is something ineffective and passive by its own nature. Nevertheless, because the permeable disposition is the proper receptacle of light in the heaven, therefore, wherever under the heaven this is either natural or is prepared in some way, it suddenly… a celestial light is acquired and even preserved, where together with this there is either igneous heat, as in a flame, or something airy, watery, or simultaneously viscous, as in night-shining substances, night- glowers, carbuncles, and perhaps in a certain way in camphor. Consider for yourself what follows from this for images.

3.18.1:
*What kind of celestial figures the ancients imprinted upon images. And on the use of images*
Someone will ask which figures of the heavens they are accustomed to imprint most powerfully upon images. For there are forms there that are very conspicuous to the eyes, and depicted by many as they appear, such as Aries, Taurus, and similar figures of the zodiac, and those that are manifest outside the zodiac. There are, furthermore, very many forms there, not so much visible as imaginable, perceived—or at least devised—by the Indians, Egyptians, and Chaldeans through the faces of the signs. Such as, in the first face of Virgo, a beautiful maiden sitting, holding twin ears of grain in her hand, and nursing a boy. And the rest, just as Albumasar and several others describe. Finally, there are certain characters of the signs and planets designated by the Egyptians. Therefore, they wish for all these things to be engraved upon images. Thus, if someone expects a proper benefit from Mercury, he ought to place him in Virgo, or at least the Moon there with an aspect of Mercury. And then fashion an image out of tin or silver, in which everything is contained. the sign of Virgo, its character, and the character of Mercury. And if you are going to use the first face of Virgo, you should also add the figure which we said was observed in that first face. And similarly concerning the others. The latest authors of images, indeed, accepted their entire form as round, in the likeness of the heaven. The ancients, however, as we read in a certain college of the Arabs, preferred the figure of the cross above all others, because bodies act through their power upon a surface already spread out. And this primary surface is described by a cross. For thus, in the first place, it has length and breadth. And this is the first figure, and the most straight of all, and it contains four right angles. The effects of the celestials indeed result mostly through the straightness of rays and angles. For then the stars are greatly powerful when they hold the four angles of the heaven, namely the hinges, that is, of the east and west and of the mid-heaven on either side. Disposed in this way, they cast their rays into one another such that they constitute a cross. Therefore, the ancients said the cross was a figure, made both by the strength of the stars and the receptacle of their strength. And for this reason, it has supreme power in images, and receives the forces and spirits of the planets. This opinion, moreover, was either introduced by the Egyptians or most greatly confirmed by them. Among whose characters, the cross was one significant mark, signifying their future way of life, and they used to engrave that figure onto the chest of Serapis.
3.18.2: I, however, do not believe that the excellence of the cross among the Egyptians before Christ was so much a testimony of the gift of the stars as a foreshadowing of the virtue it was to receive from Christ. But the astrologers who were immediately after Christ, seeing that wonderful things were done by Christians through the cross, but not knowing or not wishing to attribute such things to Jesus, attributed them to the celestial bodies; although they ought to have considered that miracles are not performed at all through the cross itself without the name of Jesus. That it indeed corresponds to images, because it relates to the strength of the planets and all the stars, is perhaps probable. Yet, it does not have immense power for this reason alone. It can, however, do something when conjoined with the other things that are necessary, perhaps for the prosperous health of the body. But let us return to narrating the opinions of others, as we began.
3.18.3: The ancients used to make the image of Saturn for the length of life on a stone of Feyrizech, that is, Sapphire, in the hour of Saturn, while he was ascending and happily situated. The form was: an old man sitting on a high chair or a dragon, his head covered with a certain dark linen cloth, lifting his hands above his head, holding a sickle in his hand or fish, dressed in a dark garment. For a long and happy life, the image of Jupiter on a clear or white stone. It was a man sitting upon an eagle or a dragon, crowned, in the hour of Jupiter while he himself was happily ascending in his exaltation, dressed in a saffron garment. Against timidity, in the hour of Mars, they fashioned images in the first face of Scorpio, with Mars armed and crowned. To cure diseases, they fashioned the image of the Sun in gold in the hour of the Sun, with the first face of Leo ascending with the Sun. A king on a throne, in a saffron garment, and a raven, and the form of the Sun. For joy and strength of the body, the image of Venus as a maiden, holding apples and flowers in her hand, dressed in saffron and white, in the hour of Venus, with the first face of Libra, or Pisces, or Taurus ascending with Venus. The image of Mercury for intellect and memory, in the first face of Gemini. Also, Mercury was sculpted against fevers; a man holding cloths in his hand, in the hour of Mercury, with Mercury rising; they sculpted this in marble. Occasionally they imprinted it upon some matter to be taken by the ailing. Hence they said every kind of fever was cured. The image of the Moon ascending in the first face of Cancer for growth. The form of Mercury: a man sitting on a throne, wearing a cap and crested, with eagle-like feet, holding a rooster or fire in his left hand, winged, sometimes upon a peacock, holding a reed in his right, in various clothing. The Moon, a beautiful maiden with a horned head upon a dragon or bull, having snakes above her head and under her feet. To cure stones and pains of the genitals, and to staunch blood, an image in the hour of Saturn, with the third face of Aquarius rising with Saturn. Also, they imprinted a Lion in gold, rolling a stone in the form of the Sun with his feet, in the hour of the Sun at the first degree of the second face of Leo rising.
3.18.4: They thought this would be useful for expelling diseases. For the diseases of the kidneys, they made a similar one when the Sun occupied the mid-heaven in the heart of Leo, approved by Peter of Abano and confirmed by experience, but with this condition: that Jupiter or Venus looks upon the mid-heaven, while harmful planets fall away and are unfortunate. I received from Mengus, a distinguished physician, that such an image made with Jupiter conjoined there with the Sun had freed Ioannes Marlianus, a mathematician singular in our age, from the terror with which he was accustomed to be afflicted during thunder. Furthermore, to strengthen health and avoid enchantments, they fashioned an image out of silver in the hour of Venus, with the Moon occupying the angles and looking happily upon Venus, provided that the lord of the sixth house looks upon Venus, or Jupiter with some trine aspect or opposition. Mercury, however, must not be unfortunate. They performed these things in the last hour of the day of the Sun, so that the lord of the hour held the tenth region of the heaven. Peter of Abano says that a physician can cure an infirm person through an image. Provided that in fashioning it, he observes that the angles of the ascendant, the mid-heaven, and the descendant are fortunate, and the lord of the ascendant; and by the same reason the second, but the sixth and its lord should be unfortunate. He also says that health will be firmer and life longer than had been established from the beginning, if the image is made after the nativity has been examined, in which this is placed as fortunate: namely, the significator of his life. Also, the givers of life, both the signs and the lords, especially the ascendant and its… the lord. Likewise the mid-heaven, the place of the Sun, the part of fortune, the lord of the conjunction or the prevention made before birth. Let the harmful and unfortunate planets also fall away. He concludes that no astrologers doubt that such things contribute to producing life. It would be lengthy to tell which faces the ancients observed through various signs, and which lunar stations they considered necessary in expressing images. For in the station of the Moon from the seventeenth degree of Virgo to its end, they made images against diseases and hatreds, and for a happy journey. In the station from the beginning of Capricorn to the twelfth degree, against diseases and discords and captivity. In the station from the twelfth degree of Capricorn to the twenty-fifth degree, against languor and prison. In the station from the fourth degree of Pisces to the seventeenth degree of the same, for curing diseases, for profit, for society, and for increasing harvests. And they devised others similarly in other stations with a curiosity that was often vain. I have reviewed only those that smell not so much of the Magus as of the Physician. For I suspect that such medicine is also for the most part vain. However, for other, more legitimate preparations of medicines, I believe such lunar mansions should be chosen. And also in Aries the sixth degree, and again the nineteenth degree, 26 minutes. Likewise in Gemini the tenth degree, 51 minutes. In Cancer the nineteenth degree, 26 minutes. In Libra the sixth degree, 34 minutes. In Capricorn the nineteenth degree, 26 minutes.
3.18.5: In Aquarius the second degree, 17 minutes. In the same, the fifteenth degree, 8 minutes. Furthermore, the opinion of Haly an influential Arab astrologer is to be kept in mind: that every sign is made more vivid as long as the Sun is in it, that it dominates the others, and its effect happens more than the others, so that you may direct the Moon there to receive the gift proper to it for medicines. There, I say, that is, to the sign and the face, and especially the degree: so that if you aspire to the goods of Jupiter, you should raise or unite the Moon directed toward these, as long as the Sun illuminates such a place where the Jovian property thrives. And similarly regarding the others. It would be a curious thing to narrate, and perhaps harmful, what images and how they were fabricated to bring about happiness or to inflict calamity, whether to a certain individual, or a house, or a city, by associating or dissociating spirits among themselves. I indeed do not affirm that such things can happen. But astrologers think they can, and they teach how, in ways that I do not dare to narrate. Porphyry a Neoplatonist philosopher, when he describes the life of his master Plotinus the founder of Neoplatonism, confirms that such things can be done.
