And he tells how Olympius the Magus an Egyptian magician and astrologer attempted such things in Rome against Plotinus, while he tried to bewitch Plotinus through images or things of that kind, but the attempts were retorted upon their author because of the exalted soul of Plotinus. Albertus Magnus a medieval scholastic philosopher and scientist, a professor of astrology as well as theology, says in his Speculum Mirror, where he says he distinguishes illicit things from lawful ones, that images duly constituted by astrologers acquire virtue and effect from the celestial figure.
3.18.6: And subsequently, he narrates their miraculous effects, such as Thebith Thabit ibn Qurra, a mathe matician and astronomer, Benthorad, and Ptolemy, and the other astrologers promise. And he describes images for bringing calamity and prosperity to someone, which I omit by design. And meanwhile, he confirms that they can have an effect, although as a good man he condemns the abuse of the art, and as a legitimate theologian he detests the prayers and suffumigations which certain impious people have employed for demons by making images. Nevertheless, he does not disapprove of the figures and letters and words impressed upon images for this purpose alone, so that they may receive some gift from the celestial figure. That this indeed can be compared through images, Peter of Abano a medieval physician and philosopher has confirmed. Indeed, he even affirmed that a certain region—I know not which—was destroyed through that image which Thebith narrates was fabricated by the astrologer Phedice. However, Thomas Aquinas a leading theologian, our leader in theology, fears these things more and attributes less to images. For he thinks they acquire only as much virtue through celestial figures as is conducive to those effects which the heavens are accustomed to bring about commonly through herbs and other natural things. Not so much because such a figure is in that material, as because such a composite is already placed in a certain kind of artifice that agrees with the heaven. He says these things in the third book of his Contra Gentiles Against the Gentiles, where he mocks the characters and letters added to figures: but he does not mock the figures themselves unless they are attached to demons as signs.
3.18.7: In his book on Fate De Fato, he also says that constellations give the order of being and enduring, not only to natural things, but also to artificial ones, and therefore images are fabricated under certain constellations. But if anything miraculous happens to us through them beyond the customary effects of natural things, he casts it back upon the demons, the seducers of men, which is clearly evident in his book Contra Gentiles, but most especially in the short book On the Occult Operations of Nature, where he seems to hold even the images themselves in low esteem, however they may be made: which I also, insofar as he has ordered it, hold as nothing. Moreover, to refer certain miraculous effects of images to the falsehood of demons is not alien to the Platonists. For Iamblichus a Neoplatonist philosopher also says that those who, having put aside religion and highest holiness, trusting only in images, hope for divine gifts from them, are in this matter very often deceived by evil demons, appearing under the pretext of good spirits. Yet he does not deny that certain natural goods happen from images constructed by legitimate astrological reason. Finally, I think it safer to commit oneself to medicines than to images, and that the reasons we have assigned for the power of the heavens regarding images can have efficacy in medicines rather than in figures. For it is probable that if images have any power, they do not acquire this so much through the figure, but possess it naturally as being thus affected in their material. And if anything is newly acquired while it is being carved, it is not compared so much through the figure as through… through the heating that comes from a certain bruising. Which bruising and heating, done under a celestial harmony similar to the harmony that had formerly infused virtue into the material, excites the virtue itself and strengthens it, just as breath excites a flame, and makes manifest what was hidden before, just as the heat of a fire brings into view written letters that were previously hiding in onion juice. And letters written with the fat of a kid, entirely hidden on a stone, emerge if the stone is submerged in vinegar, and they stand out as if they were carved and raised. Indeed, just as the touch of a Scopa or Arbutus arouses a sleeping rage, so perhaps a certain bruising and heating alone produces the latent virtue in the material, provided it is done opportunely. And it is expedient to use this celestial opportunity in preparing medicines. Or if someone perhaps wishes to treat metals and stones, it is better to strike and heat them alone than to shape them. For beyond the fact that I suspect these figures are empty, we should not rashly admit even the shadow of idolatry.
3.18.8: > Likewise, one should not use stars or health-giving things to expel diseases that are very similar to them. For these often increase them: just as harmful stars sometimes diminish diseases that are unlike themselves, which indeed Ptolemy and Haly teach clearly.

3.19.1:
*Regarding the crafting of the image of the Universe*
But why do we pass over the universal itself, that is, the image of the universe itself? From which, nevertheless, they seem to hope for a benefit from the universe. Therefore, a follower of these people will sculpt, if it pleases him, a certain archetypal form of the whole world in bronze, if he is able. He should then imprint it opportunely onto a gilded silver plate. But when should he most especially imprint it? When the Sun has reached the first minute of Aries.
3.19.2: For from this point, astrologers surmise the fortune of the world for at least that year, as if from the revolution of its own nativity. Therefore, at this very birth of the world, he will imprint the figure of the whole world. But do you see how beautifully an argument regarding the world’s birth might occasionally assist us? Since it is reborn every year, do astrologers not measure in the very genesis of a man the first sign, degree, and minute in which the Sun appeared? And there they lay the foundation of the entire figure. And in every subsequent year, when the Sun first enters the same minute, they consider the man as if reborn, and from there they predict the fortune of the year. Just as, therefore, they would not be able to do this in a man unless he were, as it were, reborn, and he could not be reborn in this way unless he had once been born: so too one may conjecture that the world was once born, namely, when the Sun was placed under the first minute of Aries, since through the same position every year, a certain fors chance/fortune of the world, as if reborn, revolves. At that time, therefore, he will craft the figure of the world. He will be careful, however, not to sculpt or imprint the figure on Saturday, the day of Saturn. For on this day, God, the creator of the world, is said to have rested from the work which He had begun on the ideal day of the Sun. For just as much as the Sun is suited for generation, so much is Saturn inept. He should have finished the work on Venus, which signifies the absolute beauty of the work. But enough regarding the principles of the worldly fabric. For our own Giovanni Pico della Mirandola has recently expressed the divine mysteries of the Genesis of the world, given by Moses, in a divine manner. Therefore, to return to the plan, he also will not sculpt his own world on the day or hour of Saturn, but rather on the day or hour of the Sun. He will imprint it at the birth of the year, especially if Jupiter and Diana are approaching in a favorable state. Indeed, they will think it best to apply colors to the work in addition to the lines. There are, in truth, three universal yet singular colors of the world: green, golden, and sapphire, dedicated to the three graces of the heavens. Green indeed is similar to Venus and the Moon; that is to say, it is moist, proper to moist things and those being born, and accommodated to mothers. No one doubts that the golden color belongs to the Sun, and it is not alien to Jupiter and Venus besides. Finally, we dedicate the sapphire color most especially to Jupiter, to whom even the sapphire stone itself is said to be consecrated. Whence the lapis lazuli lazurite stone, endowed with this color, has a prerogative among physicians because of its Jovian virtue against black bile caused by Saturn, and it is born with gold, distinguished by golden marks; thus Jupiter is the companion of gold just as it is of the Sun. And the Armenian stone has a similar power, possessing a color similar in a certain way to green. They will judge it, therefore, to be expedient for capturing the gifts of the celestial graces to look upon these three colors most frequently, and to insert the sapphire color into the spheres of the world in the model which you are crafting. They will think it worthwhile to add golden stars to the spheres to mimic the heavens themselves, and to dress Vesta or Ceres, that is, the Earth, in a green garment. The follower of these people will either wear such a model himself or look upon it when set before him. Indeed, it would be useful to look at a sphere endowed with its own motions, such as Archimedes once crafted, and recently a certain Florentine of ours, by the name of Lorenzo. And not only to look at it, but also to consider it in one’s mind. Accordingly, in the very inner sanctum of his house, he will build a room fashioned into a vault and adorned with figures and colors of this kind, where he may most often be awake or sleep. And having gone out of the house, he will perceive the spectacles of individual things not with as much attention as he will the figure and colors of the universe. But let those creators of images see to those things. You, however, will fashion a more excellent image within yourself: namely, when you know that there is nothing more orderly than the heavens, nor anything more temperate to be conceived than Jupiter. You will hope to attain the benefits of the heavens and Jupiter only if you have made yourself most orderly and most temperate in your thoughts, affections, actions, and way of life.
3.19.3: …distinguished by golden marks; thus Jupiter is the companion of gold just as it is of the Sun. And the Armenian stone has a similar power, possessing a color similar in a certain way to green. They will judge it, therefore, to be expedient for capturing the gifts of the celestial graces to look upon these three colors most frequently, and to insert the sapphire color into the spheres of the world in the model which you are crafting. They will think it worthwhile to add golden stars to the spheres to mimic the heavens themselves, and to dress Vesta or Ceres, that is, the Earth, in a green garment. The follower of these people will either wear such a model himself or look upon it when set before him. Indeed, it would be useful to look at a sphere endowed with its own motions, such as Archimedes once crafted, and recently a certain Florentine of ours, by the name of Lorenzo. And not only to look at it, but also to consider it in one’s mind. Accordingly, in the very inner sanctum of his house, he will build a room fashioned into a vault and adorned with figures and colors of this kind, where he may most often be awake or sleep. And having gone out of the house, he will perceive the spectacles of individual things not with as much attention as he will the figure and colors of the universe. But let those creators of images see to those things. You, however, will fashion a more excellent image within yourself: namely, when you know that there is nothing more orderly than the heavens, nor anything more temperate to be conceived than Jupiter. You will hope to attain the benefits of the heavens and Jupiter only if you have made yourself most orderly and most temperate in your thoughts, affections, actions, and way of life.
3.19.4: And after we have fallen into a mention of celestial temperature, it will perhaps be opportune to remember that there is no excess of elementary quality in the heavens, to speak in the Peripatetic manner; otherwise, whether it were so composed, it would have been dissolved so many centuries ago, or even if it were simple, it would have lost everything else due to such great magnitude, power, and motion. But indeed, as something most moderate, it moderates all things and mixes diverse things into one. Furthermore, it has earned life through this very temperance of its own, as well as the excellence of its form, in a divine manner. For we see that composite things attain life only when the perfect mixture of qualities seems to have broken the prior contrariety, as in plants. Then, it attains a more perfect life in animals, in so far as they have in them a complexio constitution/balance of humors further removed from contrariety than in plants. In human beings, again for the same reason, it is more perfect and already, in a certain way, celestial. Since the human constitution has already approached the celestial temperature, especially in the spirit, which, beyond the subtlety of its substance and the temperance of its qualities —by which it agrees with the heavens—has also obtained celestial light. Furthermore, where this spirit is such to the highest degree, it is celestial in the highest degree, and has divinely obtained celestial life before all others. And in so far as one makes and keeps oneself as such in every way of life and law of living, to that extent does one carry back the singular gifts of the celestial bodies. When, however, we say there is no… excess of elementary quality in the heavens, we understand either that there is no such quality there, but rather virtues that are the producers of tempered qualities, or if there are any qualities there that are in some way similar, they have, as it were, an aerial temperance. And where we name certain things there as “cold” and “dry,” we accept these in the Platonic manner: that is, that what is the cause of the least heat is called “cold,” and that which shows us the least moisture is called “dry.” Thus, the astrologer Abraham says that Saturn leaves our body in a certain way cold and dry, because it brings less heat and moisture to us. For the same reason, the flesh of an ox and a hare, while hot and moist in themselves, are cold and dry to us. From this induction, take these two corollaries: First, indeed, if bodies that are more temperate live more, then the heavens, which are most temperate, must live the most. Or rather, conversely, from the fact that the heavens possess the most absolute life because they are most precisely tempered, one may conjecture that in as much as other things approach its temperance and life, to that extent do they receive a more excellent life. The second, however, is that life is a form perfect in itself, one which perfects the body, and exhibits the principle of motion. A principle, I say, that is intimate, of a motion that is both acted upon from within and facilitated outward through every part. If, therefore, this itself is life, consider it grasped by the mind that whoever has not recognized that such a form exists in the heavens, the most excellent of bodies, with a motion that is always perfect and circling, vivifying all things, and gradually those things more so which have either naturally approached closer to its likeness, or which daily expose themselves more aptly to its influxes.

3.20.1:
*How much power images are thought to have over the spiritus spirit/vital essence, and the spirit over them. And concerning the affection of the user and the operator*
We have learned that if anyone uses helleborus hellebore, a medicinal herb rightly, and bears it powerfully, it changes—through exquisite purgation and its own hidden property—the quality of the spirit and the nature of the body, as well as part of the movements of the mind, and [the person] seems almost to be reborn. Whence they recount that Medea a mythological sorceress and the Magi ancient Persian priests/wise men were accustomed to restore youth by certain herbs, which they do not so much “restore” as “preserve,” just as myrobalani dried fruits used in medicine do. Astrologers believe that propitious images have a similar power, through which they change the nature and morals of the wearer in a certain way, and restore them for the better, so that [the wearer] has already emerged as another person, or at least preserves healthy well-being for a very long time. Truly, they believe that harmful images have a power over the wearer [similar to] the potency of hellebore taken without art or measure, namely, poisonous and pestiferous. But against another person, for whose calamity they were fashioned and intended, they have the power of a bronze, concave mirror—so directed that, once the rays are collected and reflected toward the opposite side, they burn those nearby, and compel those at a distance to grow dim.
3.20.2: Hence arose the story or opinion that believes that, by the machines of astrologers and the sorceries of magi magicians, humans, beasts, and plants can be star-struck and wither away. I, however, do not quite understand that images have any power over a distant object. I do suspect, however, that they have some power over the wearer, though I do not think it is such as most people imagine; and I consider this [to be] on account of the material rather than the shape, and, as I have said, by a long interval I prefer medicines over images. Although the Arabs and Egyptians attribute so much to statues and images fashioned by astronomical and magical art that they believe the spiritus stellarum spirits of the stars are enclosed within them. By “spirits of the stars,” some understand wonderful celestial forces, while others understand even demons, the attendants of this or that star. Therefore, they believe that the spirits of the stars, whatever they may be, are introduced into statues and images, not otherwise than as demons are accustomed sometimes to occupy human bodies, and through them to speak, move, be moved, and perpetrate wonders. They believe that the spirits of the stars do similar things through images. They think that demons, the inhabitants of mundane fire, are insinuated into our bodies through igneous humors or fiery things and likewise through fiery spirits and affections of this kind. Similarly, [they believe] the spirits of the stars [are introduced] through rays opportunely received, and through suffumigations, lights, and vehement tones [introduced] into the suitable materials of images.
3.20.3: And [they believe] they can effect wonders upon the wearer or one who approaches. We think these things can indeed be done through demons, who are not so much constrained by a certain material as they are gladdened by veneration. But more on this elsewhere. The Arabs relate that when we rightly fashion images, if our spirit—through imagination and affection—is most attentive to the work, it is joined to the stars along with the spirit of the world itself, and with the rays of the stars through which the spirit of the world acts. And, being thus joined, [our spirit] is itself also a cause so that a certain spirit of some star—that is, a certain vivid virtue—is infused into the image from the spirit of the world through the rays, most especially one consentaneous to the spirit of the human operator at that time. Such a work is also aided by suffumigations accommodated to the stars, insofar as such suffumigations affect the air, the rays, the spirit of the maker, and the material of the image so precisely. For my part, I judge scents to be very similar in nature to the spirit and the air, and when they are kindled, [I judge them] also consentaneous to the rays of the stars. If they are Solares Solar/of the Sun or Iouij Jovian/of Jupiter, [they act] to affect the air and spirit vehemently so as to catch the gifts of the Sun or Jupiter —which is then dominant—opportune under the rays, and [I judge that] the spirit, thus affected and thus endowed, can, through a more vehement affection, not only act upon its own body, but also affect a nearby body—especially one that is naturally conformable but weaker—with a similar quality. I think, however, that the harder material of an image can scarcely receive the slightest thing from scents and the imagination of the operator; yet, the spirit itself is so affected by the scent that one thing is made from both. That this is evident is clear from the fact that a scent does not act further on the sense of smell after it has acted sufficiently. For the sense of smell and anything else suffers nothing from itself or from something very similar. But more on these elsewhere.
3.20.4: Therefore, I judge that the intention of the imagination has power not so much in the fashioning of images or medicines as in the applying and assuming of them: so that if anyone, while wearing an image that has been—as they say—rightly made, or while using a medicine in the same way, should vehemently desire help from it, and should believe without doubt and hope most firmly, a very large heap of aid will certainly accrue from this. For where either the virtue of the image, if there is any, penetrates the skin of the toucher once it is heated, or at least the natural virtue in its chosen material, or certainly the vigor of the medicine taken inwardly slips into the veins and marrow, bearing with it a Iouium Jovian/Jupiterlike property, the spirit of the human is transferred into a spirit of this Jovian kind by affection, that is, by love. For the power of love is to transfer. Faith and hope, which are not doubtful, fix and settle the human spirit, already thus stirred, into the Jovian spirit. If, as Hippocrates ancient Greek physician and Galenus ancient Greek physician teach, the love and faith of a sick person toward an inferior and external physician contribute greatly to health (indeed, Avicenna medieval Persian physician says this confidence effects more than medicine), how much are we to think it conducts toward celestial aid, [given that] the affection and faith toward the celestial influx is already innate in us, acting within, and penetrating the viscera?
3.20.5: Now, the love itself and the faith toward a celestial gift is often the cause of celestial assistance, and conversely, love and faith sometimes perhaps proceed from this: that the clemency of the heaven already favors us toward this very thing.

3.21.1:
*Concerning the virtue of words and song for capturing a celestial benefit. And concerning the seven degrees leading to celestial things*
Furthermore, certain words pronounced with a sharper affection are judged to have great power regarding images, [the power] to direct their effect precisely thither where the affections and words are intended. Thus, to reconcile two people with a most ardent love, they fashioned an image under the Moon conjoining with Venus in Pisces or Taurus, while meanwhile observing many things curiously regarding the stars and words, which it is not my intention to relate. For we are not teaching love-potions, but medicines. It is more probable, however, that such effects are accomplished either through Venereos dæmonas Venus-demons—who rejoice in these works and words—or simply through deceitful demons. For they say that Apollonius Theaneus a legendary philosopher and miracle-worker often caught and betrayed Lamiae monstrous, spirit-like creatures—namely, certain deceitful and Venus-like demons who simulate beautiful girls and entice handsome men, whom they [then] devour.
3.21.2: However, Origen asserts against Celsus, and Synesius and Alchindus disputing on Magia Magic, that there is a certain and great power in specific words. Likewise, Zoroaster forbids the changing of barbarous words, and Iamblichus does the same. Also, the Pythagoreans were accustomed to performing certain miracles with words, songs, and sounds in the manner of Phoebus and Orpheus. The ancient doctors of the Hebrews observed this above all others, and all poets sing that wonderful things are effected by incantations. Even that most serious man, Cato, in his work Re rustica On Agriculture, sometimes uses barbarous chants in curing the diseases of beasts. But it is better to set aside chants.
3.21.3: However, that harmony by which the young David used to deliver Saul from madness, unless the mystery should command it to be referred to divinity, perhaps someone will refer it to nature. But since, for the number of the seven planets, there are also seven degrees through which the attraction from the higher things to the lower occurs, the voice holds the middle degree and is dedicated to Apollo. The harder materials, stones, and metals hold the lowest degree and seem to refer to the Moon. Those things which are composed of herbs, tree fruits, gums, and members of animals have the second place in the ascent, and they correspond to Mercury, if we follow the order of the Chaldeans in the heavens. The third [degree] consists of the most subtle powders and their vapors selected from the aforementioned things, and odors and things pertaining simply to herbs, flowers, and ointments belonging to Venus. The fourth [degree is] words, songs, and sounds, all of which are duly dedicated to Apollo, the author of music above all others. The fifth [degree is] vehement concepts of the imagination, forms, motions, and affections, referring to the power of Mars. The sixth [degree is] the discourses of human reason and consulted deliberations pertaining to Jupiter. The seventh [degree is] the more secret and simpler intelligences, as if already separated from motion, joined to the divine, and destined for Saturn, whom the Hebrews rightfully call by the name of Sabath the Sabbath/Rest.
3.21.4: Why these things? So that you may understand that, just as from a certain composition of herbs and vapors made through art—both medical and astronomical—a certain common form results, like a certain harmony endowed with the gifts of the stars, so from tones first selected according to the norm of the stars, and then composed according to their suitability with one another, a common form is made, and in it some celestial virtue arises. It is indeed very difficult to judge which tones specifically correspond to which stars, and likewise which compositions of tones correspond specifically to which stars and aspects. But partly by our diligence, partly by a certain divine lot, we cannot attain this otherwise than as Andromachus was fatigued for a very long time in composing the theriaca antidote/treacle, and finally, after the diligence, obtained the power of the antidote by divine lot. That this indeed happened divinely, Galen and Avicenna confirm. Nay, rather, Iamblichus and Apollonius Tyaneus are witnesses that all medicine had its beginning from oracles. And therefore, they place Phoebus, the prophet, in charge of medicine.
3.21.5: We shall bring forward three rules for this, if we first admonish you not to think that we are speaking here of worshipping the stars, but rather of imitating them, and capturing them through imitation. Neither should you believe that we are dealing with gifts which the stars will give by choice, but rather by natural influx. To this indeed manifold and occult [influx], we strive to adapt ourselves through exquisite methods, just as we daily adapt ourselves to healthily receive the manifest light and heat of the Sun. But to adapt oneself to its occult and wondrous gifts is the duty of the wise man alone. But now let us arrive at the rules for adapting songs to the stars.
3.21.6: The first is to inquire what powers each star, planet, and aspect has in itself, what effects they have, what they take away, and what they bring; and to insert these into the meanings of our words: to detest what they take away and approve what they bring. The second is to consider which star dominates a specific place or person most. Then to observe what tones and songs these regions and people commonly use, so that you may apply similar ones together with the aforementioned meanings to the words which you strive to dedicate to those same stars. The third is the daily sites and aspects of the stars, and under these to explore to what kind of speeches, songs, motions, leaps, manners, and acts most men are usually incited, so that you may imitate certain such things to the best of your ability in songs, which will please a heaven similar to them and will receive a similar influx. Remember, however, that song is the most powerful imitator of all. For it imitates the intentions and affections of the mind and the words; it also represents the gestures, motions, and acts of men, as well as their manners. And it imitates and performs all things so vehemently that it suddenly provokes both the singer and the listeners to imitate or do the same things.
3.21.7: By the same power, when it imitates celestial things, it miraculously provokes our spirit toward celestial influx on the one hand, and the influx toward the spirit on the other. Now, the very matter of music is altogether purer and more similar to the heavens than the matter of medicine. For this air is indeed warm or tepid, still breathing, and in a way living, composed of its own articulations and limbs, just like an animal; it does not only carry motion and present an affection, but it also carries a meaning, as if it were a mind, so that it can be called a certain airy and in some way rational animal. Therefore, a song full of spirit and sense, if by chance it responds to this star or that, both according to its meanings and its articulations and the form resulting from those articulations, and also according to the affection of the imagination, it transmits no less virtue into the singer and from him into the nearest listener than any other composition transmits, as long as the song keeps its vigor and the spirit of the singer, especially if the singer himself is by nature phœbeus Phoebus-like/Sun-like and has a vehemently vital and, moreover, animal spirit of the heart. For just as natural virtue and spirit, when most powerful, immediately soften and melt the hardest foods and soon render the austere things sweet, and also generate a progeny outside themselves through the production of seminal spirit: so, when vital and animal virtue is most efficacious, it acts powerfully there through a certain intensification of its own spirit by means of song, both through conception and agitation into its own body, and through its effusion it immediately moves the one nearby, affecting both its own [spirit] and another’s with a certain property of the stars, which it conceived both from its own form and from the chosen opportunity of time.
3.21.8: By this reasoning, many Easterners and Southerners (especially the Indians) are said to have an admirable power in words, being for the most part Solar. I say they have a power that is not natural, but vital and animal, almost the most powerful of all, as do all those who are especially Phoebus-like in other regions. A song, however, conceived with this virtue, opportunity, and intention is almost nothing other than another spirit newly conceived in you by your spirit, having become Solar, and acting both in you and in the neighbor with Solar power. For if a vapor and a certain spirit sometimes [pass] through the rays of the eyes, or otherwise if the spirit emitted from the heart is able to bewitch, infect, or otherwise affect a neighbor, then a spirit flowing forth more abundantly and fervently, at once from the imagination and the heart, and more powerful in motion, is all the more capable of this. It is therefore not at all surprising that certain diseases of the mind and body can thus sometimes be removed or even induced, especially since a musical spirit properly touches and acts upon the spirit that resides between the body and the soul, affecting both with its own emotion. You will concede, indeed, that there is a marvelous power in an aroused and singing spirit if you grant, with the Pythagoreans and Platonists, that the spirit is a heaven, arranging all things with its movements and tones. Remember, however, that all music proceeds from Apollo. Jupiter is musical only insofar as he is in concord with Apollo. Furthermore, Venus and Mercury derive music from their proximity to Apollo. Moreover, only these four pertain to harmonic consonances; the remaining three possess only voices, not songs. Now, we attribute slow, deep, raucous, and plaintive voices to Saturn; to Mars, the opposites: swift, sharp, harsh, and threatening. To the Moon, we attribute those in between. We assign to Jupiter grave, intense, sweet, and constantly joyful consonances. Conversely, we attribute to Venus those songs that are voluptuous, with lewdness and softness. Between these, we attribute the middle ground to the Sun and Mercury. If they are venerable, simple, and intense, together with grace and sweetness, they are judged to be Apollonian.
3.21.9: If they are somewhat more relaxed, yet still energetic and manifold, they are Mercurial. You, therefore, will win over each of these four to yourself with their own songs, especially if you apply sounds appropriate to the songs, so that when you have called out by singing and playing in their manner at an opportune time, they seem to respond immediately, either like an echo or like a string on a lyre trembling whenever another, similarly tuned, is vibrated. And as Plotinus and Iamblichus suggest, this will happen to you naturally from the heavens, just as a resonance or tremor is produced from a lyre, or an echo from an opposite wall. Indeed, as often as your spirit—through a certain frequent usage of Jovial, Mercurial, or Venusian harmonies (made, naturally, when these are ruling)—sings most attentively to this very end and, having been conformed to the harmony, turns out to be Jovial, Mercurial, or Venusian, it meanwhile turns out to be Phoebean, since the power of Phoebus himself, the leader of music, thrives in every consonance. And conversely, becoming Phoebean yourself from a Phoebean song and sound, you meanwhile claim for yourself the power of Jupiter, Venus, and Mercury. And again, from the spirit thus affected within, you affect the soul and body in a similar way. Remember, however, that a speech composed aptly and opportunely, and one that is full of emotion, meaning, and vehemence, has a power similar to songs. It is not helpful to recount how much power Damis and Philostratus say certain Indian priests have in prayer, nor even by what words they affirm Apollonius summoned the shades of Achilles. We are not speaking now of gods to be worshipped, but of a certain natural power of speech, song, and words. That there is a Phoebean and medicinal power in sound, and a certain one at that, is evident from the fact that those in Apulia who have been bitten by a Phalangium a type of venomous spider all lie stupefied and half-dead until each hears their own specific sound. Then, indeed, they dance to the sound appropriately, sweat from it, and recover. And if, after ten years, they hear a similar sound, they are suddenly stirred to dance. I infer that this sound is Phoebean and Jovial based on the evidence.
3.21.10: How we may adapt ourselves to the heavens in seven ways. And to whom Saturn is malevolent and to whom he is propitious. Whom Jupiter defends against Saturn. How the heaven acts upon the spirit, the body, and the soul.

3.22.1: Since the heaven is composed by harmonic reason and moves harmonically, and brings about all things through harmonic motions and sounds, it is rightly the case that, through harmony alone, not only humans but all these inferior things are prepared, as much as they are able, to receive heavenly things. We distribute the harmony capable of higher things into seven degrees of things in the higher realms: namely, through images (as they believe) constituted harmonically; through medicines tempered by their own certain consonance; through vapors and odors fashioned with a similar harmony; through musical songs and sounds. To the order and power of these, we wish to refer bodily gestures, leaps, and dances; through concepts of the imagination and harmonious movements; through appropriate discursions of reason; through tranquil contemplations of the mind. Just as we expose the body daily to the light and heat of the Sun through its own harmony—that is, through a suitable position, habit, and posture—so we also prepare the spirit to compare itself with the hidden powers of the stars through its own similar harmony, compared by images (as they suppose) and certainly by medicines and odors composed harmonically. And finally, through the spirit thus prepared for the powers above (as we have often said), we expose the soul and body to them. The soul, I say, insofar as it is inclined by emotion toward the spirit and the body. In the soul, we now place imagination, reason, and mind. Our imagination can indeed be so disposed, composed, and conformed to Mars or the Sun, either because of the quality and movement of the spirit, or through our own choice, or even both, that it becomes an immediate and proper receptacle for the influx of Phoebus or Mars. Similarly, reason can prepare itself for Jupiter by a certain imitation, either through imagination and spirit together, or through deliberation, or both, so that it receives Jupiter and the gifts of Jupiter much more, on account of its own dignity and proximity, than the imagination or the spirit does: just as imagination and spirit, by the same reasoning, receive heavenly things much more than any inferior things and matters. Finally, the contemplative mind, insofar as it separates itself not only from those things which we sense but also from those which we commonly imagine and argue about according to human customs, and recalls itself to separated things through emotion, intention, and life, exposes itself in a certain way to Saturn. Saturn is propitious to this alone. For just as the Sun is an enemy to nocturnal animals but a friend to diurnal ones, so is Saturn to humans, whether they lead an open, vulgar life or truly flee the company of the masses.
3.22.2: Yet, he is adverse to those who do not cast off vulgar affections. For Jupiter has granted the common life, while Saturn has claimed for himself the separated and divine life. To the minds of men who are truly segregated from this world as much as they are able, he is in a way a friend, as if they were related to him. For even to the spirits inhabiting the sublime air, Saturn himself (to speak Platonically) is in place of Jupiter, just as Jupiter is a helping father to humans leading a common life. Saturn is most hostile to none so much as to those who simulate a contemplative life but do not practice it. For Saturn does not recognize these as his own, nor does Jupiter—the temperament of Saturn itself—help those who flee the common laws, customs, and interactions of men. For Jupiter has usurped these for himself (as they say) while Saturn was bound, and Saturn has usurped segregated things. Wherefore, those Lunar peoples…
3.22.3: Those whom Socrates describes in the Phaedo—inhabitants of the most eminent surface of the Earth, higher than the clouds—living soberly, content with fruits, and dedicated to the study of secret wisdom and religion, taste the happiness of Saturn and lead a life so prosperous and long-lived that they are considered not so much mortal men as immortal spirits, whom many call heroes, a golden race rejoicing in a certain Saturnian age and kingdom. I think perhaps the Arab astrologers meant this when they say that beyond the equinoctial line toward the south there are certain most subtle inhabitants, spirits who seem neither to be born nor to die, and that Saturn and the Dragon’s Tail have power there. Albumasar seems to confirm this in his book Sadar, saying that certain regions of India are subject to Saturn, and that the men there are very long-lived and depart only in extreme old age. He assigns the reason that Saturn does not harm his own housemates, but rather outsiders. Do not neglect the power of Saturn. The Arabs say he is the most powerful of all. Indeed, the planets undergo the forces of those they approach, but all approach him rather than the reverse, and the planets joined to him act according to his nature. For he himself is the head of the most expansive orbit among the planets. Every planet is indeed the head, heart, and eye of its own orbit. Saturn is also closest to the countless stars and is most similar to the Prime Mover, and he makes a long circuit. He is the highest of the planets. Hence they call him happy, the one to whom he has happily aspired. And although people generally fear him greatly as one alien to the common life of men, they still believe he can be appeased, even for the common life, if at some point he has had power and dignity in the ascendant, or if his own Jupiter has looked upon him favorably, or has received him excellently in his own boundaries. Otherwise, his influence, if received improperly—especially in dense matter—becomes like poison, just as an egg becomes poisonous through putrefaction or burning. From this arise or emerge certain people who are unclean, idle, sad, envious, and exposed to unclean spirits, whose company you should flee far away. For the poison of Saturn lies dormant elsewhere, like sulfur removed from a flame. In living bodies, however, it often flares up, and like burning sulfur, it not only consumes but also fills everything around it with harmful vapor, and infects those nearby. Jupiter arms us against his influence, which is generally foreign to men and in some way dissonant, both through his own natural quality and through his specific foods and medicines, and (as they think) also through images, as well as through habits, occupations, studies, and matters properly pertaining to him. Those who flee the harmful influence of Saturn and undergo his propitious one are not only those who take refuge in Jupiter, but also those who turn their whole mind to the divine contemplation signified by Saturn himself. For by this pact, the malignancy of fate can be avoided, as the Chaldeans, Egyptians, and Platonists think. Since they do not want celestial bodies to be vain, but rather divinely animated and furthermore governed by divine minds, they surely want not only many things pertaining to the body and spirit to proceed from there to men, but also many goods to redound in some way into the soul—not from bodies into the soul, but from souls. More than this, however, many such things flow from the superior minds to the heavens. If you wish to assign all the reasons why Moses was moved to command the leisure of the Sabbath to the Hebrews, perhaps beyond the higher and more secret allegory, you will find the day of Saturn, inept for civil and military actions, but apt for contemplations, and that on that day divine protection against dangers is to be entreated. Indeed, Abraham and Samuel, and many of the Hebrew astrologers, confess that this can be obtained against the threats of Mars and Saturn through the elevation of the mind to God, and through vows and sacrifices, confirming that Chaldean precept: if you raise a mind burning for the work of piety, you will also preserve the frail body. It is worthy of consideration that, as Iamblichus says, celestial and worldly divinities have certain powers that are superior, and others that are inferior. By the former, they bind us to fatal effects, but by the latter, they conversely release us from fate, as if they possessed keys, as Orpheus says, for opening and closing. Therefore, the divinity is much more superior to the world, redeeming us from fatal necessity. It is also very worthy of investigation that the Hebrew practice of dissipating evil things imminent from the heavens in the slaughtering of animals and in the sacrifice of our own possessions is to deflect them from us to our own. But we leave these things to be explored by our Pico. Finally, wherever we say that the gifts of the heavens descend to us, understand that the endowments of celestial bodies come into our bodies through our spirit, which is duly prepared; and that the same also flow into the spirit earlier through their rays, naturally or however exposed to them; and also that the goods of celestial souls partly leap into the same spirit through rays and from there redound into our minds, and partly reach the minds of men exposed to them from their souls or from angels. Exposed, I say, not so much by a natural pact as by the choice of free will or affection. In summary, whoever imitates the beneficence, action, and order of the heavens through vows, study, life, and habits, consider them more similar to the supernal, receiving greater endowments from there; but those who are artificially dissimilar and discordant to the celestial disposition end up miserable in secret, and finally unhappy in the open.

3.23.1:
*> In order to live and act prosperously, first know your talent, star, and Genius, and the place convenient to them; dwell there, and follow your natural profession*
Whoever is born of a sound mind and in control of himself is naturally instituted by the heavens for some honest work and way of life. Whoever therefore wishes to have the heavens propitious should first undertake this work and this kind of life, and pursue it diligently. For the heavens favor their own beginnings. You are made by nature for this very thing above all else: what you do from your tender years, what you speak, what you imagine, what you wish for, what you dream, what you imitate, what you attempt more frequently, what you accomplish more easily, in what you progress most greatly, in what you take delight above all others, and what you leave behind with reluctance. This is surely that for which the heaven and the ruler of heaven have brought you forth. Therefore, they will favor your beginnings and will aspire to your life as long as you pursue the auspices of your progenitor himself, especially if that Platonic tenet (in which all antiquity agrees) is true: that to each one who is born there is a certain spirit, a guardian of life, destined by his very star. Who also aids in this very office to which the heavens have deputed the newborn. Whoever, therefore, having examined his own talent through the arguments we have just stated, finds his natural work in this way will simultaneously have found his star and his spirit. Following the beginnings of these, he will act prosperously and live happily: otherwise you will experience adverse fortune and find the heavens hostile. Therefore, there are two kinds of unfortunate men above all others. The first are those who, professing nothing, do nothing. The second are those who undertake a profession alien to their talent and contrary to their Genius guiding spirit/ natural inclination. The former languish in idleness, while the heavens all the while incite them to action; the latter, while they pursue things alien to their celestial patrons, labor in vain, deserted by those supreme patrons. The first is confirmed by the ancient proverb: God helps the active, but is hostile to the lazy. The second is confirmed by a similar proverb: Do nothing against the will of Minerva the goddess of wisdom. I believe this is the reason why Jupiter is beseeched in the Pythagorean verses: either to relieve the human race from so many evils himself, or at least to show us which daemon guardian spirit we ought to follow as a guide. Therefore, it will be worth the effort to investigate to which region, above all, your star and your daemon have designated you to inhabit and cultivate from the beginning: for they aspire more fully there. That is indeed the place where your spirit, once having set out, is in some way refreshed; where the senses remain more lively; where the condition of the body is more robust; where most people favor you; and where your vows succeed. Therefore, test these things: choose this region: cultivate it happily. You will leave this place unhappy, clearly, unless you intend to return and pursue similar things. But in the meantime, exercise yourself with frequent movements in this region, and perform certain circles like those of the heavenly bodies. For, by movement and revolution of this kind, you will be preserved by those things that are similar to your own nature.
3.23.2: You will also remember to keep in mind what pertains usefully to habitation. Just as the countryside provides the food necessary for life to the city, but the city consumes it, so life itself is increased by frequent rural retreats—where weariness will take hold of you least—but it is worn down by both the leisure and the business of the city. As for what pertains to both habitation and profession, that advice of the oriental astrologers must not be ignored: that by a change of name, profession, clothing, diet, or place, the celestial influx is changed for us, sometimes for the better, sometimes for the worse. The daemons may also be exchanged, or we may conduct ourselves differently toward them here and elsewhere.
3.23.3: The Platonists will judge this. Astrologers, along with the Platonists, agree that the daemon who is the guardian of each person can be twofold: the first is proper to one’s birth, the second to one’s profession. And as often as the profession agrees with one’s nature, the same daemon for both—or at least a very similar one—is present with us, and our life will henceforth be more in harmony with itself and more tranquil. But if the profession disagrees with the talent, the daemon acquired through art is discordant with the natural Genius, and life becomes laborious and anxious. As for those desiring to find what kind of daemon presides over each person from birth, Porphyry investigates a rule based on the planet that is lord of the birth. Julius Firmicus says the planet that is lord of the birth is either the one that holds the most dignities there, or, according to a firmer opinion, the one whose domicile the Moon is about to enter after the sign that a man already holds at his birth. However, he does not think the daemon should be investigated by the same rule. Rather, according to the opinion of the Chaldeans, it is investigated from the Sun or the Moon—from the Sun to the Moon in a daytime birth, and from the Moon to the Sun in a nocturnal birth. When the interval between these has been calculated, you perform an equal space descending from the degree of the ascendant and observe at which term you end. For they believe the daemon belongs to the same star as that term. In summary, they are accustomed to weighing the course of life and fortune from the lord of the birth and the daemon at the same time. I have added fortune because some calculate the lot of fortune by almost the same method. The ancients desired their daemon to have descended from some angle of the heavens: from the East, the West, or the mid-heaven on either side, or at least from the eleventh or fifth station. The eleventh follows the mid-heaven above our heads and is called the good daemon, and it looks at the degree ascending from the East by a sextile aspect. The fifth follows the mid-heaven of the antipodes and is called good fortune, and it observes the ascending degree by a trine aspect. In the third place, they hoped that the daemon—if it had to come from a cadent station— at least came from the ninth or the third. For the ninth is called God, and the third, the goddess. The former looks at the ascending degree by a trine, the latter by a sextile. They dreaded the cadent twelfth and sixth. The former they called the evil daemon, the latter, evil fortune.
3.23.4: We, however, deeming it superfluous to hope for things that are past, advise that the same stations that they sought for daemons and fortune should be observed for planets and stars in order to make them accommodating for a task, so that they might be in the angles, or in the two succeeding houses we mentioned, or at least in the two cadent houses we named earlier. For it is not without reason that they say the Sun rejoices in the ninth, the Moon in the third, Jupiter in the eleventh, and Venus in the fifth. These look upon the ascending degree. But let us return to our subject. Whether, therefore, through the experience and diligence I spoke of earlier, or through this art I just recounted, we first investigate the instinct of our nature and our daemon, we will judge him unfortunate who professes no honest office. For he truly has no leader for his profession who does not undertake an honest work, and he has hardly any natural leader at all: because the office of the stars and daemons—or the angelic leaders divinely disposed for our guardianship—is always to act excellently and in a most expansive way. Furthermore, we judge him unfortunate, as we said above, who, through a profession contrary to nature, submits to a daemon different from his Genius. Remember, however, that according to the dignity of the professions, more worthy daemons—or, if you prefer, angels—are received, and even more worthy ones in public governance. It is possible, however, for an art and a course of life to be accepted that are not contrary to your Genius and talent, and not far removed, even if you have progressed toward better things.
3.23.5: Remember again to enter into the familiarity of those upon whom celestial graces breathe. You will weigh this from the goods of the soul, body, and fortune. For just as scent exhales from musk, so something of the good exhales from a good man into his neighbor, and often it remains infused. A gathering of three happy men, or two who are wonderfully redundant with one another, would be marvelous. Finally, remember to flee far from the unbridled, the shameless, the malicious, and the unhappy. For these are full of evil daemons or rays; they are malefic harmful/cursed, and like lepers and those who are pestilential, they harm not only by touch, but also by proximity and their very gaze.
3.23.6: Indeed, the very proximity of animate bodies is thought to be a contact, on account of the effective exhalation of vapors flowing outward from heat, spirit, and emotion. The familiarity of the wicked and cruel will be most pestilential, if it is true that after the vegetative life is infused into us in the second month of Jupiter, the sensitive soul, enslaved to disturbances, is subsequently infused in the third month of Mars. For thus, those who are carried by perturbation, full of Mars, infect their neighbors with a
3.23.7: Martian contagion. Conversely, frequent association and close commerce with the happy and excellent, as we have said, is accustomed to benefit us marvelously. They say that Apollonius of Tyana detected an old man at Ephesus under whose figure a daemon lay hidden, which was contaminating the whole city with plague by its mere presence. How much Socrates profited many by his mere presence, Xenophon and Plato testify.

3.24.1:
*By what reasoning the learned may recognize their own nature, and follow a regimen agreeable to their spirit*
Since I am speaking to students of literature, I want each one of you who is captivated by the love of letters to remember first that you are Mercurial, and furthermore Solar, insofar as Mercury himself is Solar. And this is a condition common to all these. But in truth, beyond the Mercurial nature, whoever excels in grace of speech, charm, dignity, and elegance should acknowledge both Apollo and Venus in himself. He who is more inclined toward laws or natural and common philosophy should not be unaware that he has Jupiter as his patron. But he who is driven deeply to investigate the most secret things with curiosity should know that he is not only Mercurial, but also Saturnian. Under the sovereignty of Saturn are all those who are diligent in any study until the very end, especially those who are negligent in other matters. Finally, if it is true, as some both physicists and astronomers teach, that the soul endowed with intellect descends into the human conception in the month of the Sun—that is, the fourth—then those who live most by the intellect and are from the beginning foremost in this way, turn out to be Solar daily. Therefore, the favor of these planets must be sought by these men. Medicine is to be prepared under their influence. One must dwell in their regions. But to Apollo, leader of the Muses, I summon you first, O learned worshippers of the Muses. Therefore, whoever among youbeloved brothers in the love of the Muses, you who are stronger in intellect by far and much longer than in body, you should certainly know that in your nativity, Phoebe provided very little matter, but infused a very great amount of the Phoebean spirit. Indeed, you also resolve the humors and nourishment in your body into spirit to a very great extent every day. Therefore, each one of you is almost entirely spirit. A certain spiritual man, I say, masked in this small earthly body, tiring this spirit more than others with a perpetual labor, so that he, more than the rest, must be constantly recreated in spirit, and furthermore, in old age—in which the spirit usually becomes thicker—must be recalled to its proper subtlety. You surely know that a thick body is nourished by four thick elements. Know, therefore, that a spiritual body is nourished by its own four subtle elements.
3.24.2: For this, wine acts as earth; the very scent of wine performs the role of water; song and sound move the air; and light represents the fiery element. Therefore, the spirit is nourished principally by these four: wine, I say, and its scent, and song, and similarly by light. But I do not know how, starting first from Apollo, we have immediately fallen into Bacchus. And with good reason, we have arrived from light to heat, from ambrosia to nectar, from the intuition of truth to the burning love of truth. Phoebus and Bacchus are certainly brothers and inseparable companions. The former brings you two things above all, namely light and the lyre. The latter likewise brings two, wine and the scent of wine, to recreate the spiritthe use of which daily makes the spirit itself Phoebean and free. Therefore, prepare yourselves to receive the light of the Sun daily in such a way that you live in the light as frequently as possible—insofar as a certain distillation and drying can be avoided—at least in the sight of the light, now from afar, now up close, now covered, now open, tempering the power of the Sun for your own vital use everywhere, and representing the Sun at night with fire, meanwhile not forgetting the zither and song. Breathe, both while waking and sleeping, the living air—the air living with light. Likewise, you must conduct yourselves toward the pure gift of Bacchus, created by the benefit of Apollo. Therefore, receive wine in the same proportion as light. Receive it abundantly, insofar as neither the distillation nor the drying of which I spoke, nor drunkenness, occurs. And besides the substance of wine taken twice daily, inhale its scent more frequently, partly by rinsing the mouth with wine when the spirit needs recreating, partly by washing the hands with the same, and partly by applying it to the nostrils and temples. We have conversed enough, brothers, and we have drunk enough. Therefore, farewell.

3.25.1:
*On astrological diligence in procreating children. In preparing feasts. In buildings and habitation and clothing, and how much it is permitted to care for such things*
But it is also pleasing to address briefly the severe guardian of religion. Come, tell me, what is it you condemn in the use of the stars, guardian? Whatever, you will say, takes away from our free will, whatever detracts from the worship of a single day. I do not only not condemn these things with you, but I even strongly loathe them. I know you even execrate, and I moreover dread, some who, when they wish God to be implored, resort to Jupiter when that vast head of the dragon is in mid-heaven; they take refuge, being as miserable as they are foolish, from the very dragon that once fell from heaven, dragging a third of the stars with it, finally to be devoured. But will you concede to choosing opportune hours for conducting contracts, marriages, conversations, journeys, and similar works? I do not see that you would easily agree to these, as I do not know what kind of fear for our free will you harbor. I, therefore—even if the great theologian Albertus Magnus allows these things, and perhaps some reason will dictate that celestial matters are thus subject to our prudence for our use, just as herbs are provided to a physician—will nevertheless rather believe you at present. And as difficult as you are now in permitting these things, I myself will just as easily dismiss them. However, you have for a long time (as I believe) permitted observations of the Moon and therefore of other stars for curing diseases and, for that reason, for preparing remedies. It has also been conceded by you, and furthermore approved, that when the Moon is waxing and increased in light, and not otherwise made unfortunate, one may sow fields with seeds and plant vines and olive trees. Why, therefore, should we not use the benefit of the Moon, Jupiter, and Phoebus for planting (to speak like a cynic) a human being? Forindeed, we always use the office of Venus for these things. But I would have spoken more correctly if I had said, “they always use it.” For Venus herself is Diana to me. What, furthermore, shall we say about our regimen? Will it not be allowed, and will it not be beneficial, under a fortunate star to make wine in autumn, and to prepare bread and feasts daily? And if we are unable to await the aspects of the stars in preparing these, it will be advantageous at least to accept those that are ascending, or otherwise angular —the Sun, Jupiter, Venus, and the Moon. For thus, everything we use, being happily affected from the heavens, will happily affect us. Thus far I see you will concede without controversy, unless perhaps you say that our life would then be nothing other than a perpetual servitude. To this, I will add that mortals would serve in vain to accumulate money and honors, to which they are perpetually enslaved, unless in the meantime they accumulate more days of life for themselves through physical diligence. Therefore, let them either serve God alone, which is indeed the most important thing, or if they are to serve anyone else, let them indulge in a healthy and long life rather than in money and vain honors. We are therefore in agreement. But will they build houses recklessly, or inhabit unlucky ones? Where a certain contagious calamity of a building infects the inhabitant so much that the poisonous vapor of a plague is preserved even for two years in the wall. Such also is that which, lurking from an epidemic in clothing, long afterward infects and destroys the unwary user. But since we have stumbled upon the mention of clothing, will you prohibit, pious father, in the making of a garmentor the first breath that should be put on, to diligently catch the breath of Venus, so that the garment, having been made, as it were, Venusian, might similarly affect the body and spirit with a certain prosperous quality? Do not physicians forbid fox furs, yet approve of lambskins? Perhaps a star affects nascent garments daily, in the same way it affects those born once from the beginning. That garments and other works of art receive a certain quality from a star, Thomas Aquinas confirms in his book De Fato On Fate. You, therefore, will affirm this. That infected garments infect the user, the itch and leprosy are witnesses. Finally, if you care for the life of the people (as I suppose), you will permit these things. And I, with your permission, shall advise what must be observed. But if you do not exactly disapprove of caring for a life of this sort, which is near death, but warn that it should be neglected, I indeed neglect it, relying on the trust of a better life, and I advise others to do the same. Farewell.

3.26.1:
*How the superior things are drawn down through the inferior things exposed to them: And how worldly gifts are drawn down through worldly materials*
But lest we stray too far from that which we set out to interpret from Plotinus from the beginning, summarize it briefly in this way. The world, from the Good itself (as Plato teaches together with Timaeus the Pythagorean), was made as perfectly as it could be made. It is therefore not only corporeal, but also a participant in life and intelligence. Wherefore, besides this bodymanifest familiarly to the senses of the world, there lies within it a certain body of spirit, exceeding the capacity of fragile sense. In the spirit, soul thrives; in the soul, intelligence shines. And just as beneath the Moon, air is not mixed with earth except through water, nor fire with water except through air, so in the universe, there is a certain bait or fuel for coupling the soul to the body, which is that very thing we call spirit.
3.26.2: The soul is also a certain fuel in the spirit and body of the world for attaining intelligence divinely, just as a certain extreme dryness in wood is prepared for penetrating oil. Oil imbibed into this is food for the fire, I mean, for heat itself. The heat itself is the vehicle of light, and if this wood is of such a nature that it shines in the presence of fire, yet is not consumed, such as we have sometimes seen. Now by this example, we shall see whether man, or some other thing beneath the Moon, through certain preparations—partly natural, partly sought by art—can opportunely receive in a certain way certain vital and perhaps even intellectual goods from above. But that which pertains to religion here, we shall discuss elsewhere, where Plotinus will bring these things into the discussion. As for what pertains to natural influences, whatever they may be coming from above, know that they can be prepared in us and in our materials through art only when nature has provided fuel for us and ours for them, and when the heavens have conspired more opportunely toward them. Does nature not, in the very fetusas the artificer of the fetus itself, when it has affected and fashioned the little body by a certain pact, by this very preparation, as if by a bait, draw spirit from the universe? And through this, as through a fuel, does it not draw in life and soul? And finally, through a certain species and disposition of the soul, is the body thus living not made worthy of the presence of the mind, which is finally granted divinely? Everywhere, therefore, nature is a magician, as Plotinus and Synesius say; namely, it is everywhere enticing certain things with certain foods, not otherwise than the center of the earth pulling heavy things, the hollow of the Moon pulling light things, heat pulling leaves, moisture pulling roots, and other things similarly. That the world is bound to itself by this very attraction, the wise men of India testify, saying that the world is an animal, everywhere male as well as female, and that it joins with itself everywhere through the mutual love of its members and thus persists; indeed, the bond of the members exists through an indwelling mind, which, infused through the limbs, stirs the whole mass and mixes itself with the great body. Hence Orpheus calls the very nature of the world and the worldly Jupiter both male and female. To such an extent is the world everywhere greedy for the mutual marriage of its parts. That the masculine sex is everywhere mixed with the feminine, the order of signs declares—from one side, the preceding is perpetually in order masculine, the following feminine; from the other side, trees and herbs, which, just as animals, have both sexes. I omit that fire to air, and water to earth, takes the place of the male to the female, so that it is not to be wondered at that worldly members and all its parts desire a mutual marriage.
3.26.3: …and the planets also conciliate this, partly indeed males, but partly females. But Mercury, in particular, is both male and female, the father of the Hermaphrodite. Agriculture, truly observing this, prepares the field and seeds for celestial gifts, and through certain grafts, propagates the life of the plant, and leads it to another and better species. The physician, physicist, and surgeon effect similar things in our body, both for fostering our own nature and for more abundantly preparing the nature of the universe. The same is also done by the philosopher skilled in natural things and the stars, whom we are accustomed to call properly a Magus Wise man/magician, inserting celestial things into earthly things through certain enticements, and indeed no otherwise than a farmer studious of grafting inserts a new shoot into an old stock. Which Ptolemy also strongly approves, affirming that such a wise man can assist the work of the stars just as a farmer assists the power of the earth. The Magus Wise man subjects earthly things to celestial things, nay, the inferior everywhere to the superior, so that their own females may everywhere be made fruitful by their own males: as iron is to be pulled by the magnet, as camphor is to be sucked up by the heating air, as crystal is to be illuminated by the Sun, as sulfur and the sublime liquid are to be ignited by a flame, as the empty eggshell is to be lifted by the dew of the Sun, or rather, as the egg itself is to be fostered by the hen. Furthermore, just as some, by fostering eggs, even without animals, reconcile life to them from the universeand often by preparing certain materials opportunely, they produce animals without eggs and visible seeds, as a scorpion from sweet basil, bees from an ox, a bird similar to a blackbird from sage: namely, by applying life from the world to certain materials at opportune times. Thus also that wise man, when he has known what materials—whether those partly initiated by nature, partly perfected by art, and if they are scattered, they are gathered—what kind of influence from the heavens they can receive, he collects them while that star is especially reigning, prepares them, applies them, and claims the celestial things for himself through them. For wherever a certain material is exposed to the heavens, just as a reflecting mirror to your face, and an opposing wall to a voice, it suddenly suffers from above—namely, from a most powerful agent, from a power and a wonderful life everywhere present—and it brings back power through the passion, not otherwise than a mirror represents an image from the face, and a wall an Echo from the voice. Plotinus himself uses these examples, when, imitating Mercury, he says that the ancient priests or Magi wise men were accustomed to receive something divine and wonderful in statues and sensible sacrifices. But he wishes, together with Trismegistus, that through these material things, divine beings completely segregated from matter are not properly received, but only worldly ones, as I said from the beginning, and as Synesius approves. Worldly ones, I say, that is, a certain life, or something vital from the soul of the world and the souls of the spheres and stars, or also a certain motion and a vital presence as if from demons, or indeed sometimes that the demons themselves of this sort are present to the materials…
3.26.4: The man himself, whom Plotinus follows, says that the demons are aerial, not celestial, much less sublime; and Mercury himself composes statues from herbs, trees, stones, and aromatics, which (as he says) possess the natural power of divinity within them. He adds songs similar to celestial ones, by which he says they are delighted, and thus are present in the statues for a longer time, and benefit or harm humans. He adds that the ancient Egyptians, who were also priests, when they could not persuade the people by arguments that there were gods—that is, certain spirits above humans—devised this magical enticement by which, attracting demons into statues, they might declare them to be divine beings. But Iamblichus condemns the Egyptians because they accepted demons not only as certain steps for investigating the higher gods, but actually worshipped them greatly. He prefers the Chaldeans, who were not occupied with demons, to the Egyptians. I say the Chaldeans, the guardians of religion: for we suspect that the Astrologers, both of the Chaldeans and of the Egyptians, attempted in a certain way to draw demons into earthen statues through celestial harmony. This is what the Hebrew astrologer Samuel seems to signify, relying on the authority of David the Astrologer, namely that the ancient makers of images created statues that pronounced future events. He relates that the harmony of the heavens was adapted to these: to melt metal into the form of a beautiful man on the day of Mercury, at the third hour—namely of Saturn— when Mercury enters Saturn in Aquarius, with the ninth region of the heavens indicating the prophecy, and it ascends— and it is the sign of the Gemini indicating prophets (as they say). Mars is burned by the Sun, and does not behold Mercury. However, the Sun looks at the place of that conjunction. Meanwhile, Venus holds some angle, is occidental and powerful. The Moon looks at the ascendant from a trine, and Saturn does likewise. These are their claims. For my part, I think first, according to the opinion of the blessed Thomas, that if they did indeed make statues speak, it was not the simple influx of the stars itself that formed the words there, but demons. Furthermore, if it should happen that they entered such statues, I do not believe these were bound there by celestial influx, but rather that they complied with their worshippers of their own volition, intending eventually to deceive them. For even if a higher nature is occasionally reconciled with a lower one, it cannot be restrained. And that disposition of the stars described a little earlier perhaps cannot concur. Although demons are not included in statues by astronomical method, yet where they have appeared present through the worship shown to them, Porphyry says they rendered oracles according to astronomical rules, and therefore frequently ambiguous ones, and deservedly so, since Iamblichus proves that true and certain prophecy does not suit evil demons, nor does it come from human arts or nature, but from divine inspiration to purified minds. But let us return now to Mercury, or rather to Plotinus. Mercury says that the priests accepted power appropriate to the nature of the world and mixed it. Plotinus, following him, thinks that the whole of it is easily accomplished by reconciling it with the soul of the world, insofar as it generates and moves the forms of natural things through certain seminal reasons divinely implanted in itself. These reasons it even calls Gods, since they are never destitute of the ideas of the supreme mind. Therefore, through such reasons, the soul of the world easily applies itself to materials which it formed from the beginning through the same, when a magus wise practitioner or priest has applied, at opportune times, the forms of things duly collected, which properly look toward this or that reason, just as a magnet toward iron, rhubarb toward bile, saffron toward the heart, Eupatorium and Spodium toward the liver, Spica and musk toward the brain. It may indeed happen sometimes that, by reasons thus applied to forms, more sublime gifts also descend, insofar as the reasons in the soul of the world are joined to the intellectual forms of that same soul, and through them to the ideas of the divine mind. This Iamblichus also approves, where he treats of sacrifices. Concerning this matter, we shall argue more opportunely elsewhere. There, it will also appear how impure the superstition of the pagan people was; on the contrary, how pure the evangelical piety has been, which we have already done to a great extent in the book on the Christian religion.

1.1: MARSILIUS FICINO’S APOLOGY, IN WHICH Medicine, Astrology, the Life of the World, and also the Magi who greeted Christ immediately upon his birth are discussed.
1.2: MARSILIUS Ficino of Florence, to his most beloved brothers in the study of truth, the three Peters— Nero, Guicciardini, and Soderin—wishes health three and four times over. Perhaps he would have spoken more correctly as a “Tripetrus” than as three Peters. For just as where there is one palm, several fingers do not make several hands, so your three bodies, friends, seem to prevent nothing from one will making one Peter. Christ, that celestial craftsman of our fatherland, created so vast a rock that this single rock was sufficient for founding the immense building of his church. I, too, have chanced upon such great rocks by a certain divine fortune that the three of you now make for my own building, which is quite arduous. Now, friends, that fortress of Pallas seems necessary to you, by which we may ward off the savage attack of impious giants far from us. For this reason, I have decided to fortify the life of my three books, which provide for public life, with your fortress constructed of three rocks first. You know, I believe, that I have composed a book on Life, divided into three booklets.
1.3: The first of which will be inscribed On Healthy Life; the second, On Long Life; the third, On Life from the Heavens. Therefore, the bait of a title so sweet will entice very many to taste it. But among such a great number, there will be many who are ignorant, I believe, and also not a few who are malicious. One, therefore, will say: “Is not Marsilius a priest?” Indeed he is. “What then do priests have to do with medicine? What, again, is their commerce with astrology?” Another likewise: “What does a Christian have to do with magic or images?” Another still, and one unworthy of life, will begrudge life to the heavens. Finally, all those thus affected will be too ungrateful for the benefit we offer them, and they will not be ashamed to be cruel against our charity, by which we provide for public life and prosperity according to the ability of our talent. This labor will therefore be common to you, but so that it may become somewhat lighter: for there are three of you against three enemies; undergo the distributed struggle. You will not refute an invective with an invective—for I know your character—but you will overcome the bitterness of another’s gall with the sweetness of your honey, which is your marvelous grace. At the beginning, most candid Nero, you will answer the first ones: that the most ancient priests were once both Physicians and Astronomers.
1.4: Which, indeed, the histories of the Chaldeans, Persians, and Egyptians testify. Furthermore, the duties of singular charity, which shine most brightly in the greatest benefit of all, pertain to no one more than to a pious priest. Indeed, the most excellent duty is, without doubt… stone, by which they might happily give birth to eggs immediately. Therefore, God himself, who through the heavens incites any animals whatsoever to medicines, certainly permits priests—not for money, I say, but for charity—to expel illnesses with medicines confirmed by the heavens..
