He does not copulate with his wife, but illuminates his wife everywhere with the rays of his sun and stars as if with eyes, and by illuminating, he makes her fertile and begets living things. Does he, therefore, while bestowing life even by looking, have no life proper to himself? And what he has given to the ostrich bird—life and a vivifying gaze—is far inferior to this very thing., and he in turn calls me his Dionysus and Liber. We are brothers, therefore. Announce to my Phoebus that the poisonous Python is now, from the swamp, emerging. I beg you, let him draw his bow. Let him shoot his arrows immediately. He will take aim at once, for I know whereof I speak, and with a single strike he will kill the entire poison. Farewell now in happiness, my most beloved brothers, worthy not only of happy health, but of happiness itself: and look after the health and happiness of my children now coming into the light, 15 September 1489, at the villa of Careggi.

1.1: THAT SECURITY AND TRANQUILITY OF MIND ARE NECESSARY for life.
1.2: Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to his most beloved brothers in the hunt for truth, Bernardo Canisiani, Giovanni Canacci, and Amerigo Corsini. Since we had instituted a certain hunt in these first words, we rightly perhaps employed dogs and runners. We have indeed aptly called philosophers “hunters,” as they are always laboring in the breathless pursuit of truth. But are they also aptly called “dogs”? Socrates says most aptly in the Respublica Republic. For those who philosophize are either legitimate or spurious. Both are dogs. The former sagaciously investigate truth itself and hold fast to it once found. The latter, however, for the sake of opinion, bark, bite, and tear. Indeed, dogs claim so much for themselves among philosophers that not only have they inserted themselves into a certain sect, but they have sometimes even formed their own sect by the name of Cynica Cynic. The Academy, moreover, has its own dogs. Therefore, I summon you here, sagacious dogs of the Academy; here I summon you, most swift runners. For there are three of you. Defend, therefore, my three children, even more tender than I fear they are, who are about to go forth among wolves. Run, I say, eagerly, for I am entrusting to you now desired business, not burdens. You know my Georgius Benignus Salviati, who long ago sagaciously attained that truth, the tracks of which you are now running about and hunting everywhere. He, like the Sun, illuminates his brothers, he himself being greater, the others lesser. Therefore, if you hear the howling of any wolves, announce it to him. That most strong George will easily put all the wolves to flight, for he once pierced a vast dragon. He will relieve me, therefore, and you at the same time, of anxiety. For one of you is accustomed, and indeed has said it quite often, that one experiences nothing more wholesome for life than to pass the time with great security. The others, however, immediately smile at the speaker. But tell me, come now, Canacci, what is this “devouring of time” of yours, so often repeated? What, in the end, do you mean? You will say: not to be, but rather to drink; not to chew or grind, but to gulp down with full throat. Since time itself is, so to speak, a liquid nature, and unstable. But this is the condition of liquids, that if you hold them in a narrow space, you suddenly lose them. For things compressed flow apart and quickly scatter. If by chance you squeeze water soaked into a sponge, you will express it and immediately disperse it. If you hold it more broadly, you will retain it; much more so with air, fire, and ether. Hence, those poets strive in vain who attempt to grasp the vast shades of the gods below with their arms. The most wide must be received quite widely. Things that are liquid and most vast must be possessed most broadly. Then, indeed, narrowness weighs heavily upon us when we reduce the soul itself and its naturally broad motion into a narrow space. Whoever weighs studies and business with precision, and always wears them away exactly in the smallest details, meanwhile miserably consumes his own life—alas, his own life. Rightly, therefore, Pythagoras seems to have taught: Beware lest you ever be confined in a narrow space, for nothing is broader than the heavens, nothing is more vital.
1.3: A very narrow earth, in turn, has the least life in the world. Finally, if we live in heaven and in time, the more broadly we absorb these things, the longer we live. Live, therefore, broadly, far from narrowness, O friends. Live joyfully. Joy created you with its heaven, which it declares with a certain smile—that is, by expansion, motion, and splendor—as if exulting. Your joy will preserve you for heaven. Therefore, live joyfully in the present every day. For anxiety about present things robs you of the present and anticipates the future. Curiosity about the future quickly carries you off into the past. Again, therefore, I beg you, and again: live joyfully. For the fates allow it, as long as you live without anxiety. But so that you may truly live without care, do not take up even this one care: that you might ever be anxiously concerned about how best to escape your worries. For this one worry, alas for miserable mortals, burns the heart with every care. Neglect, therefore, your diligence, but love negligence—and do this even negligently, as much as is allowed to you, I say, and as is fitting. I command these things to you, however, not so much as a priest, but as a physician. For without this one thing, as if it were the life of all medicines, all medicines applied to prolong life die. 16 September 1489, at the villa of Careggi.

0.1: I deemed it necessary, urged by a sense of duty to my fatherland, to compose certain counsels against the disease of the plague. However, in order that everyone might penetrate the understanding of this and exercise care, I resolved to reject all subtle and lengthy debates. It will be sufficient that whatever I am about to deliver at present, even if things cannot be said at greater length in a brief context of words, is based upon sufficient reasons and the authorities and experiences of many, both ancient and recent, especially those of our father M. Ficino, a preeminent physician who restored to their former health not a few who were infected with this plague, and it has been proven and handed down.
0.2: We implore, therefore, God the Best and Greatest, the giver of human life and the revealer of true and healthful medicines, that He might delegate to us effective remedies against the dangers of the plague, and preserve for us His vital gift of life for His own praise and glory.

1.1:
*WHAT THE PLAGUE IS, AND WHAT SORT OF THING IT IS*
THE PLAGUE is a certain poisonous vapor generated in the air, an enemy to the vital spirit: not because it opposes it on account of any elementary quality, but by a certain specific property. Just as Theriaca a medicinal treacle or antidote is friendly, not because it is hot or cold, dry or moist, but because from its entire composition a certain form results which is suited to the vital form of the spirit. Thus, that pestilential vapor is not an enemy to nature because it is hot, cold, moist, or dry, but because its proportion is, as it were, exactly contrary to the proportion in which the vital spirit consists in the heart. And just as poisons are continually born in the earth, so a poisonous vapor is frequently born in the air, yet not as potent, because it is more scattered. Nor can it be established in pure air, as long as such air is conformable to the spirit, and to fire, which from the power of its nature does not receive a mixture of another nature, whence it happens that it catches no putrefaction. Thus, pure air, by receiving no mixture, can in no way putrefy. Furthermore, a poisonous vapor of this kind is applied only to the human body in which humors are present that are apt for fever, such as…
1.2: …such as those which are disposed toward putrefaction and inflammation. For if the vital spirit is more powerful than the vapor itself, it drives it away; but if it is weaker, it flees from it, as if from its own contrary work. Wherefore it is useful to correct, purge, and strengthen the air, the humors, and finally the heart. It must be noted (so that you may understand correctly) when I say that this is a poisonous vapor, you should not believe that it is such according to its form and its whole nature, because everyone would be infected by it. But it is of such a quality that it most easily passes into the nature of poison. And it is properly made a poison when, through it, the humors in the human body putrefy to a certain degree, and simultaneously boil over. This commonly tends to happen on the third day, and sometimes sooner, especially where one abounds in superfluous humors, particularly blood and cholera yellow bile. And when it already assumes the nature of poison, it receives the quality of lime or arsenic, the effect of which is to putrefy, gnaw, and burn, both inside and out. Therefore, it is extremely necessary that we resist these three effects, especially internally, with all the industry we can muster.

2.1:
*The causes of the rise of epidemics, and which bodies are most prone to this evil*
A vapor of this kind is generated in the air, at the time of a more universal plague, from certain malignant constellations, especially from the conjunction of Mars with Saturn in human signs, and from eclipses of the luminaries.
2.2: Such is the present plague, namely in the year one thousand four hundred and seventy-nine: and such also was the year of the same thousandth, the eighth, and this harms men most. And it spreads in those places which have their horoscope or Ascendant ill-aspected on account of the aforementioned positions of the stars. In more particular plagues, however, the aforementioned poison is born from winds and the malignant vapors of ceilings and sewers, and likewise from earthquakes. But even if any cause of these is given, it still reigns most powerfully in thick air, and in marshy, foggy, and foul-smelling air. And when it extends to subtle air, it penetrates and kills more quickly: yet it reigns faster, more frequently, and for longer in thick, hot, moist, and foul-smelling air. Some doctors assert that pestilential putrefaction is present first in subtle air, but later in thicker air, but is much more durable in the thick. I do not know by what reasoning of the mind or by what foundation I should adhere to the first part, when experience shows the contrary. Furthermore, reason dictates to us that since not a pure, but only a mixed element can putrefy, the less it is mixed—as it is established that the subtle air is—the less apt it is for putrefaction. And for that reason, it does not receive it except through the constant increase of the pestilential influence of the stars. But just as thicker, mixed, and stable water is accustomed to putrefy easily…
2.3: …so, undoubtedly, thick and foggy air receives putrefaction without difficulty. Raymond gives this precept: that when a plague has been stirred up below, one must seek higher and more subtle air; but when it has arisen from above, for two months one must first flee downward to thicker, cold, moist, and pure air, where the sickness is accustomed to be rare. For the following two months, flee to the middle region of the air, and subsequently to a slightly higher one, namely dry, cold, and subtle, always fleeing the hot, moist, and foggy. Men are in such air as fish are in muddy waters. Moreover, pestilential air does to men what murky and putrid waters do to fish. But that which is poison to humans does not necessarily have to be such to other living creatures, because of the diversity of celestial signs and animal species. Hence it arises that I am completely ignorant of what to say about the opinion of those who assert that when the pestilential poison begins in the air, the birds that are always accustomed to live on high descend to the depths and inhabit the plains. But when it arises in the earth, they say that worms and serpents emerge from the depths of the earth, and birds whose habit it is to fly and live low seek the heights and approach the mountains. They add, moreover, that when the poison is ignited first in the air and later in the earth, sometimes animals flee from the heights downward, and from there seek the higher regions again. Hence it is that it is commonly said…
2.5: …creatures, or kites, yield to the pestilential air, and that places held by such kites are not subject to the pestiferous air. I have heard very often that this contagion has passed from men to pigs. Perhaps this could happen through some similarity not of spirit, but of flesh. In these days just passed, cats and dogs have carried the disease of the plague from one house to another, yet they themselves were in no way harmed by this contagion. Nor should you take any wonder from this, that sometimes a man or a beast might receive the aforementioned vapor without any harm, and yet infect others. For ignited iron consumes oakum and straw, but the iron itself is not consumed in the slightest. For this proceeds from the disposition of the subject that receives it, in which, according to Aristotle, Galen, and Avicenna, the effect of the matter most especially consists. So much so that in these recent days, a little boy of ours in the countryside stood for a whole day with an infected boy, and more than once ate food chewed in the mouth of the infected boy, yet did not take any taint of the disease from him, by which, however, others standing quite a distance away were seized. Nor should you have too much confidence in your own disposition, by thinking that you are of such health that this contagion is not to be feared by you, but observe this physical canon: That when the matter is much disposed, the agent cause, however weak, quickly produces an effect, just as a spark ignites oakum and sulfur from the aptitude of the receiver. And on the contrary: on the contrary: Whatever cause is most powerful works even upon indisposed matter, and although sulfur receives the operation of fire faster than wood, and dry wood cut into small pieces [does so] more easily than other wood. Nevertheless, a burning furnace immediately seizes wood into flame, both the thicker and the green, because the supreme power of the agent quickly disposes and informs it. And many times a pestiferous vapor of this kind becomes most powerful by the force of its own causes, nor will you be able to know when this is happening. And although at one time such a disposition is not present, it is nevertheless destined to be present at another.

3.1:
*In what manner, and what kinds of temperatures, the plague strikes most quickly from contagion*
This poisonous vapor is often so subtle that it cannot be judged by sight, and sometimes it is dissolved, but is easily regenerated thereafter, while the influence disposing it to this very thing remains, and now, even if it was small at the beginning, yet much more than sulfur when it is ignited, it expands with a faster course from place to place, and is contrary to the vital spirit of the heart, which is a vapor from subtle blood, far more than sulfur is to the nose. A vapor of this kind is ignited in bodies disposed to it only by the air, but after it is ignited in bodies, with amazing speed and ease, like sulfur, it dilates all around more than before.
3.2: MAR. FIC. ON EPIDEMICS it is ignited, especially when it has been ignited in a subtle humor and the thin air of summer, and it spreads and leaps from one body into another. And it is ignited most especially where there is a greater similarity of nature and in a body full of residues, with fetid vapors inside and out, and in foods and superfluous humors, and [in bodies] apt for inflammation and putrefaction, and where the heart has been weakened by coitus. And likewise in a body exhausted by passions of the soul, and excessively hot, or one accustomed to baths, or whose pores are too open or much obstructed. This was indeed the opinion of Galen and Avicenna.
3.3: Children and women are very apt for the plague, because their thin and soft matter is easier to transmute, and they are full of humors apt for putrefaction, and their life is beyond measure and order. For just as a hot and thick wind disturbs and confuses wine, so this pestiferous vapor infects and forces [everything] toward the heart; first the spirits, afterward the humors, which, having already putrefied, boil up. And this boiling is the fever itself, which is then scattered through the whole [body]; it boils or inflates more than other [fevers]: because the poisonous matter is so great that nature, as much as it can, immediately tries to expel this from the principal members. This vapor can indeed stain every humor, but especially blood, secondarily bile, thirdly phlegm, and fourthly melancholy. Hence it happens that those who are subject to this danger more… are those of a sanguine temperament, slightly less the choleric, thereafter the phlegmatic. And the melancholic [are subject to it] less than the rest, because the cold and dry humor is inept for inflammation and putrefaction, and mostly because they have narrow passages through which the poison must pass. For this reason, the elderly are less liable to the pestilential disease, although the plague of this year has not left even the seniors untouched. The reason for which was perhaps that, beyond other adverse aspects of the stars, Saturn retrograde was the lord of the year. It is wonderful to say that although almost the entire populace has fled from our city of Florence, nevertheless about one hundred and fifty died every day.

4.1:
*On the signs and indications of the plague*
But which signs indicate, by which it may be easily and clearly detected that a fever is pestilential, no one can show so easily, because of such a manifold diversity and deception of accidents. For the entire assembly of doctors testifies to this, especially Auenzoar and Rhazes. For the urine will sometimes be clear, because the humors will not reach the liver; a moderate fever will appear, because the poison will not be in a hot humor, and therefore it does not diffuse outwardly, thus the patient will die immediately. He will sometimes appear restored, because nature first pushed the poison from the heart in the attack; yet a little later he will be deprived of spirit, because he will not be capable of [withstanding] the second attack of the driving [force]. From which…
4.2: MAR. FIC. ON EPIDEMICS the first [force] has been exhausted by the struggle, also because the poison has been multiplied, or more changed into malignancy, or has become nearer to the heart than before. Almost all seem to move toward the better in the beginning, because then the more robust nature collects all its strength against the enemy: truly, in other less evil diseases, one is not led to such a sudden and great attempt. Furthermore, he will seem to possess the strength of virtue, because the aforementioned poison is not contrary to other members as it is to the heart from the beginning, and when it attacks the heart itself, it kills immediately. Wherefore, in these times, it is not at all convenient to delay in examining the signs of the disease, because you will be deceived, nor will nature wait for you unless you hasten by administering remedies. For this reason, therefore, when you see a fever present in these times, presuppose that it is, or could soon be, the plague, and administer the cure for a pestilential fever, and especially because as long as the poisonous influence of the air lasts, every superfluous humor is easily infected. And every infirmity, whatever it may be, will be able to easily turn into the plague, especially furious and continuous fevers. Whence it usually happens commonly that in this morbid time no sickness appears except the plague. But if other and indeed manifold sicknesses have appeared, then the plague is remitted and ceases. There are some signs of pestilential fever, namely a continuous fever without an ordered and manifest decline… with great shortness of breath and tightness of the chest, with sudden weakness of the pulse, with a heaviness of the whole body—especially of the head—delirium, anxiety, heat, thirst, and many bloodred spots in several places. With urine that is thick, turbid, and like that of beasts of burden: remember, however, that signs can be deceptive. Furthermore, note that whoever, as a child, labors under the infirmity of worms at such a time may be said to be infected with the plague, because this is matter disposed toward the plague, just as sulfur is to fire. Many physicians, ignorant of this, have been deceived in their desire to help. And beyond the cloudiness of the air and the abundance of animals generated from putrefaction, the signs of an approaching plague are principally: a multitude of worms, smallpox and measles, continuous and stubborn fevers, turbid urine, redness of the eyes, excoriations of the palate, delirium, and, in general, any fever where the humor frequently directs itself toward the heart, as this signifies that the human complexio constitution/temperament is disposed toward the plague. Know also that when a pestilential vapor endures for a long time in the air, it infects the fruits of the water and the earth; therefore, it is safer to boil the water, or to prepare what is called ferrata aqua iron-infused water, and to dilute wine with it, because wine is smoky and, according to the opinion of Avicenna and Rhazes, pure wine is not suitable in these times. Furthermore, it is appropriate to correct other things taken as food with substances of good odor, and with salty or vinegary flavors, especially when the plague
4.3: MAR. FIC. ON EPIDEMICS arises after an earthquake. It would also be of no small benefit to use things that are dry in places that are fragrant and to live in high places, and to inhabit mountains and hills.

5.1:
*Prophylactic care regarding diet and the regimen of living in a pestilential state*
During a pestilential time, one must abstain from things that are inflammatory and overly aperient, because they more easily dispose one to receive the poison. Specifically, one must guard against heat from the outside—from solar heat, or likewise the heat of fire and clothing—and from the inside, against salt, spices, and hot medicines, similarly from herbs of intense heat, and from much use of sharp things, except for onions and chicory, or radish with vinegar, because they oppose the poison. Also, avoid wine that is too smoky, and exercise after food, especially in hot weather, and avoid sweat, because it alters the humors. In infected air, it is not permitted to expose oneself much to the air, nor to excessive exercise under the open sky, because by heating the body and opening the pores, one immediately takes in much of the infected air. Also, abstain from things that cause obstruction and putrefaction, because they provide the matter for pestilential fever, such as viscous, cold, and moist things, especially when they receive some accidental or external heat. Also, avoid viscous, hot, and moist things where the moist predominates over the hot and is poorly digested; and to speak briefly, the moisture of putrefaction is the mother. And those things that are difficult to preserve outside of us are also not easily preserved within us.
5.2: Therefore, they will be able to be kept. Consequently, one must avoid fish as much as possible, although in that category, small fish are less harmful, provided they are from a clear, rocky, and running stream, fried in oil with salt, and dipped in stavesacre or vinegar, or the juice of bitter oranges with salt and a little pepper or cinnamon. One must also avoid milk and all reheated food; if you wish to use it, it should be the first among other foods and in a small quantity with a little sugar. All fruits are to be avoided, except for almonds, sour cherries, pears, apricots, peaches, quinces, hazelnuts, dried plums, sloes, medlars, and cornels, Appian apples, pomegranates, and malatesta a specific variety of apple. Do not use other fruits at all, or only rarely, or very rarely. You may, however, use for a longer time fruits and herbs that are cold, dry, and vinegary, or slightly bitter. But when using fruits that are hot and moist, such as figs, grapes, mulberries, and sweet cherries, ensure they are in small amounts and eat a bitter orange with salt immediately afterward. Furthermore, if you use cold and moist things, such as melons, soft and tender fish, or rich plums, take a little fennel and bitter orange with salt shortly afterward, drinking a little good and fragrant wine over it. You must also avoid mushrooms, moist herbs, purslane, pumpkin, and all moisture, as well as anything that is easily subject to putrefaction. You must also guard against fruits and excessively sweet things and moist herbs: I permit you lettuce mixed with mint
5.3: MAR. FIC. ON EPIDEMICS or cinnamon. You can also correct it with basil and very finely ground cloves that tend toward a certain redness and have the scent of cloves: for it is most pleasing to the heart. I also grant you pumpkin and the herb which in the Tuscan tongue is called Seluastrella salad burnet. Again, take care that you are not deceived by the opinion of Rhazes, who in very hot weather permits vegetables and cold and moist fruits, because he himself inhabited Egypt, where there is extreme dryness and where such fruits and vegetables are exquisitely ripened by nature. Be cautious, therefore, not to presume such license in regions not similar to Egypt. It should also be noted that vinegary, bitter, and sharp things are to be administered in a regimen that is equally preservative and curative, because the greatest danger threatens in heat and moisture, and in the putrefaction resulting from that in the dissolution of the spirits, and in the approach of poison to the heart. Thus, things of the aforementioned flavor resist all the aforementioned evils, because they refrigerate, desiccate, preserve, strengthen, restrict, and unite. It is worth remembering here that excessively sharp things, where there is a fear of tightness of the chest or weakness of the stomach, must be tempered with sugar, salt, almond milk, cinnamon, pepper, fennel, saffron, eggs, and a little fat. I highly recommend bread of spelt, barley, and dishes prepared from these. Also biscuits, rice, and raisins tending toward sharpness, and bread of the best grain, sufficiently baked. and with a little salt. Use capers with vinegar more often, and sometimes that kind of cheese which the Florentines call Marzellinum a type of fresh cheese. One must avoid cheese that is very fatty or salty. Nor do I recommend cabbage or legumes to you, except for lentils. Above all, I prohibit beans, nor do I recommend turnips and spinach much. I grant you parsley and parsnips. However, I prohibit rocket, dates, grape-syrup, mustard, citrons, melons, broad beans, fresh chickpeas, cucumbers, sweet and soft cherries, grapes, sweet figs, and mulberries. Do not fill yourself with too much wine, meat, and eggs, lest you multiply blood, bile, putrefaction, and inflammation. Use eggs with verjuice and vinegar and bitter oranges. Let the meats be light and dry, well cooked: chickens, small birds, castrated kids, squabs, turtle doves, and wild birds. If you use moist meats, let them be roasted, but ensure they are thoroughly filled inside with sharp and vinegary condiments, with a little pepper, cinnamon, coriander, and salt. Turbid wines are entirely harmful, especially must. Be more sparing than usual in food and drink; let the food be somewhat more substantial than the drink. Yet I do not want you to endure excessive thirst and fasting. Beware of letting your stomach become disgusted, but preserve it with a mediocrity of food and drink, with exercise and fasting, and with appropriate evacuations. Abstain from intercourse and excessive passions of the soul, unless perhaps you are entirely burdened by the abstinence from intercourse.
5.4: MAR. FIC. EPIDEMIARVM once you have understood this. Recall the saying of Avicenna Persian physician and philosopher in his third book on natural things: that the evacuation of seed through intercourse is more harmful than if forty times that amount of blood were lost. Hippocrates ancient Greek physician said that intercourse is a certain type of epileptic disease. Beware of air that is very cloudy, dense, enclosed, or humid. You must know that air which is not frequently moved and renewed, where neither wind nor sun penetrates or purges it, easily undergoes mixture and poisonous putrefaction, just like stagnant water. Remove yourself from the crowd of people, especially when you are fasting, and when heat has succeeded humidity, and humidity has succeeded heat. Also avoid air that is too hot, because it opens the pores and weakens you too much. Your dwelling should be spacious and dry, continuously receiving dry air, and in summer, fresh air from time to time. Beware, when you have become very heated, not to expose yourself immediately to cold, humid, or misty air, or to hot and humid wind, especially in infected places or when coming from an infected place. Avoid any wind blowing from the aforementioned places, unless it is very far away or has been broken by rain. However, the wind that cools, dries, and clears the air is by its nature healthy if you receive it with moderation, and it is a principal physician against poison of this kind. Take great care to avoid winds coming from pools or marshes. Flee from putrid waters containing herbs, soaked flax, and any foul odor. Be far from cabbage or any odors, or those from fetid herbs. You must also abstain from baths, midday sleep, and close, crowded company. Flee from the crowd quickly and stay far away, and return late, since the poison usually lasts for a long time and is very ready to do harm. Use dry foods, those of the best flavor, sharp and acidic, avoiding broth, fat, sweets, and viscous foods. Use subtle, clear, aromatic wines, slightly smoky but only a little, acidic, not sweet, and diluted with very subtle and clear water. In summary, at all times avoid things that generate blood in excess, or that which is watery, thick, or turbid, and likewise anything harmful to the stomach. This is the rule for food and drink. In my judgment, it is useful for everyone to have the following composition of spices sprinkled on their food: Take half an ounce of red sandalwood, three and a half drams of choice cinnamon, and half a dram of saffron. Gentilis Gentile da Foligno, a medieval physician uses these spices at all times. Take half an ounce of cinnamon, one and a half drams of manna, half a dram each of cloves and white and red behen a root used in medieval medicine, one dram of red coral, two drams of cardamom, half a dram of saffron, and sugar to the weight of everything. Likewise, some have another recipe, and it is as follows: Take two drams of pearls, half a dram of white and red coral, one scruple each of roses and spodium calcined ivory or bone, and one dram of cinnamon.
5.5: MAR. FIC. EPIDEMIARVM and one scruple of saffron. Likewise, take half an ounce of cinnamon, half a dram of cloves, two scruples of red coral, half a dram of saffron, and sugar to the weight of everything. As a first food, it is useful—unless heat is bothering you—to take figs, rue, and nuts with salt, especially in cold or humid weather. It should be noted that spices that are very hot, such as the fourth composition of those we have mentioned, should only be used in dishes that are very humid, cold, and acidic; however, we can use the others in everything. After food, prepared coriander seeds are a great help; Avicenna also claims they are beneficial on an empty stomach, and he praises them highly in such cases. When your stomach is empty, use frictions, comb your hair well, purge all superfluity, and keep your whole body clean. In the morning, prepare a moderate fire, and sometimes during the day as well, especially in humid weather.
5.6: Fumigate your house more often with good odors, and your clothes as well. Apply theriac a medicinal treacle or antidote to your nose and keep it in your mouth when it is most appropriate. In other places or times, you may use citron peel, zedoary, or a little frankincense; you can also carry the aforementioned citron fruit in your hand. Take one dram of ladanum, two drams each of white and red behen and red roses, one scruple of liquid storax, and one dram each of myrrh, mint, cloves, and sandalwood. white and red, and half a dram of camphor. Make a pomander with musk-scented rose water, and hang a piece of unicorn horn, jacinth, topaz, and emerald on your neck so that it touches your chest, and also keep one in your mouth. Avicenna said it is necessary that the jacinth and similar stones be warmed by our natural heat, which produces their virtues into action so that they may work within us. Also carry aromatic fruits in your hand to smell, especially citron, lemons, oranges, etc. Wash your mouth, face, and hands with vinegar more often, and sometimes with strong wine; do not omit the scent of mint, lemon balm, germander, rue, red violets, and myrtle. Use cold scents, but temper them with warm ones such that the cold ones predominate, especially in hot weather, because a hot scent by itself opens the pores and inflames, even if it does purge the air. Above all, take care to do this: mix equal parts of white rose vinegar and rose water with strong white wine, with a little zedoary or citron peel. Drink a little of this often, and wash your hands and face with it frequently. Carry it with you in a sponge with a piece of ash wood, and also wash your whole body with it morning and evening while it is warm. Use moderate exercise indoors when you are in infected places while your stomach is empty, and let the place for exercise be spacious. In other places, exercise outdoors, likewise on an empty stomach. Let country folk drink vinegar mixed with water instead of wine. I advise everyone to…
5.8: …not touch anything brought from infected places except with the greatest caution, nor taste anything from them unless it is cooked, cleaned, or washed. I truly do not know if I should speak of this at present, or rather pass over in silence, what some doctors are accustomed to give on an empty stomach in a drink: recently emitted urine of a boy, or lye. Let it be given as a remedy suited to country folk.

6.1:
*Preservative treatment for the epidemic. On preservative pills and powders*
The queen of all compositions, the theriac antidote handed down from heaven, is necessary for us twice a week. To recognize true theriac: it keeps its flavor in the mouth for a long time, induces a feeling of astringency in the stomach, should be four years old and no more than twelve, and it must have been previously tested on poisoned animals. Theriac, chosen according to the opinions of Galen, Avicenna, and Averroes, renders a person safe from all poison and poisonous disease. It is even admitted in pestilential fever itself. Galen said he found theriac to be more divine than all things in preserving and curing. Moses Maimonides said that a wonderful experience was had with it in the plague of Antioch. Nor do I think one should pass over in silence the model of Galen, who says: “The plague is a dragon with an airy body, which breathes poison against man, and theriac is a certain purgative…” a thing to be purged, cleansing poison and taming the dragon. Let it be taken nine hours after food, and six or seven hours before food. Whoever cannot take it, let them at least apply it to the heart, the stomach, the nose, and the pulses. Let one drachm be given more frequently to those who are older, but to others half a drachm, or one scruple. Those who are of a hot temperament should drink, in the summer time when taking theriac, a third part of a cup of rose water with a little rose vinegar. Others, indeed, of a different constitution, and at a different time, should take it with white wine mixed with water of scabious and melissa. But if theriac is not present, or if it is not suited to your nature, take Mithridatum a complex antidote against poison. On other days of the week, take pills against the disease at least four or five hours before food, specifically one or two, or more, according to one’s constitution, drinking down a little white wine with water of scabious and melissa in cold times, or rose water with rose vinegar in summer times. The older pills are these: take myrrh and crocus, one ounce of each; aloes, two ounces. But because they open, heat, and resolve the spirits too much, therefore some wash the aloes itself, and add terra sigillata sealed earth/medicinal clay or bolus armenus Armenian bole/clay according to the dose of myrrh, or add camphor to the dose of a third part of the myrrh. But bolus armenus Armenian bole is more eligible. Some compose it thus: Take six drachms of aloes, three drachms of myrrh, two scruples of citron seeds, half a drachm of tormentil.
6.2: MAR. FIC. EPIDEMIARVM one drachm of crocus, two drachms of rhubarb, one scruple of cloves, one drachm each of agaric, citron bark, and red sandalwood, two scruples of citron seeds, one and a half drachms of sorrel seeds, one and a half drachms of red coral, three drachms of bolus armenus Armenian bole, two grains of camphor; mix with syrup of citron. Avicenna and Averroes say that he who uses aloes, myrrh, and crocus will never be in danger from the plague. The aforementioned compositions temper their quality and increase their virtue. But the composition of Nicolus Nicholas of Salerno is much better, according to whom these are the true pills. Take myrrh, crocus, bolus armenus Armenian bole, amber, and red coral, one drachm of each; two drachms of emblic myrobalan; and washed aloes to the weight of all; let pills be made with fragrant white wine. I believe they would be more noble and more to the purpose if, in place of the emblic myrobalans, two drachms of terra sigillata sealed earth and three drachms of bolus armenus Armenian bole were put in; let pills be made with the acidity of citron, and let them be taken with white wine, rose water, and rose vinegar. In other matters, follow the aforementioned composition. Make sure, however, that the aloes is shiny, light, somewhat reddish, delicate, fragrant, breakable, and fatty; and when you breathe upon it, it becomes moist. Let the myrrh also be clear and the coral delicate. Without theriac and the said pills, preservation will not be well achieved. Therefore, before all others, use the two aforementioned. the aforementioned, namely theriac on two different days, and at least three pills, because by drying up humidity they preserve from putrefaction. They also strengthen the heart and tighten the passages so that the poison does not have a passage to the heart, and they drive it away from there. It seems to me that the aloes in the aforementioned pills, when times are humid and cold—likewise the constitution —should not be washed, but in other times and constitutions, to take the composition of the pills in powders is better, only when there is need for haste. It can also be taken three or four hours before supper, just as also before lunch. You may also, once in the week, or two times or more, when the pills might offend (although they are of no offense), in the winter and humid time, in place of the pills, take a dried fig with half a walnut, with a little rue and a little salt, drinking down a little rose water or rose vinegar. But if even that were to offend you, use in place of it, without taking anything else, a little toasted bread dipped in strong white wine, with a piece of orange, soaked in rose vinegar, and dipped in cinnamon. There are some who give such pills in the evening or morning, namely one for each dose. Take half a drachm of aloes wood, two scruples of tormentil, one scruple of white dittany, half a drachm of zedoary, one drachm of crocus, half a drachm of barberry, two scruples of burnt deer horn, one scruple of red sandalwood, and seed of sorrel…
6.3: MAR. FIC. EPIDEMIARVM and red coral, and bolus armenus Armenian bole, one drachm of each; two scruples of camphor; half a drachm of the gems from which the electuary of gems is made; one drachm of pearls; half a drachm of hyacinth mix with syrup of currants or of lemons. I, however, am accustomed to give pills of this kind in every season, even in the hot one.
6.4: Take zedoary, aloes wood, agrimony, crocus, round birthwort, white dittany, gentian, citron bark, and citron seed, one scruple of each; one drachm each of prepared coriander, tormentil, red sandalwood, red coral, red roses, spodium, and emblic myrobalan; two drachms of terra sigillata sealed earth; four drachms of bolus armenus Armenian bole; make pills with the acidity of citron, which you should administer with white wine, white rose vinegar, and rose water. I place much faith in this composition of ours, taking it when nothing of the pills composed with aloes is taken. Also, after the operation of the aforementioned pills, there is added to the composition itself: amber, musk, hyacinth, emerald, topaz, pearls, and unicorn horn, one scruple of each. It will be better, and also much to be praised, to drink these things with acetous wine, or white vinegar, with rose water, terra sigillata sealed earth, and bolus armenus Armenian bole, with a small portion of emerald, hyacinth, and topaz, or at least with pearls and corals. These things are much recommended by Galen and Avenzoar: others give bark… and citron seeds, and those of lemons, with wine or rose vinegar and rose water. I, indeed, am accustomed to give this simple preparation frequently, and indeed a most effective and safe one, with white wine, or rose vinegar and rose water. Take two drachms of bolus armenus Armenian bole; one drachm each of terra sigillata sealed earth and red coral; half a drachm each of citron bark, zedoary, and crocus; six ounces of rose sugar made from red roses; ten ounces of citron acidity; make an electuary. Raimundus and Arnoldus compose certain theriacal pills in three ways. First: Take three drachms of bolus armenus Armenian bole, two drachms of tormentil root, one drachm of root of the herb tunici likely a species of plantain or similar herb, sugar to the weight of all; make pills. Item: Take half a drachm of amber, one scruple of musk, six grains of camphor. Item: Take emerald, hyacinth, and topaz, in equal parts; let them be ground and washed just as Mesue washes lapis lazuli; make pills with the juice of wood sorrel. They say that stones of this kind are called by the ancients Bezoar life-saving stones, that is, liberators from death, and that they excel theriac in this, that theriac drives poison from itself, it does not draw it to itself; stones of this kind, however, do both, therefore they ought to be administered by mouth. They can also be placed upon the wound, the bite, and poisonous blisters. They also use this composition, namely of the best gold, pearls, and crushed raw silk. They also praise the electuary of diamber an aromatic composition containing ambergris, of gems, and of chere.
6.6: Mesue a medieval physician and pharmacist advises: they praise garnets, rubies, carbuncles, sapphires, emeralds, corals, kermes grains, and the stone found in the head of an asp, and likewise its horn and the horn of a unicorn. Item: a joyful electuary of Almansor a physician associated with Caliph al- Mansur with some cooling substance. Use also things that clarify the blood, such as hops, myrobalans, and fumitory. I believe that using juniper seed with myrtle seed is very useful against poison of this kind. Item: such an electuary. Take one whole citron, let it be macerated well and cooked with sugar and rose water. And where there is no citron, make it with a lemon or a whole orange. Many use vervain. I am accustomed to give the poor a little well-toasted bread, dipped in vinegar with a little rue, and sometimes with a small portion of onion. I also sometimes give a little pure wine to drink afterwards. Item: such toasted bread dipped in rose vinegar with a little cinnamon, sometimes taking an orange afterwards, and a little good wine. You will be able to administer these things, now one, now another, on those days when you do not take theriac, nor the true pills, or even on those same days after the evening. You can also use a little of this confection of ours in the evening on an empty stomach. Take four ounces each of rose sugar and diamarenati an aromatic pharmaceutical preparation; one drachm of prepared coriander and red coral; two drachms of cinnamon, but in the summer season, one drachm, half a drachm of red sandalwood and crocus, but in summer one scruple of crocus; prepare with four ounces of citron acidity; drink a little best wine or rose vinegar afterwards. You can also use it in the morning sometimes instead of the aforementioned. Raimundus said that in his time, Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars were in conjunction in the nineteenth degree of Aquarius in the year 1348, in the month of March, which conjunction indeed signified horrible things, especially severe pestilences frequently over the space of forty-five years, because it was in a human fixed sign in the house of Saturn. Among these was that pestilence of the year ‘48, where the physicians of Paris, Avignon, and Piedmont composed a new theriac they had tested themselves, and it preserved them with success. Arnoldus wrote down a prescription, which Raimundus, his student, recited in these words: Take two and a half drachms of juniper seeds; two drachms each of cloves, mace, nutmeg, zedoary, and ginger; one and a half drachms each of long and round birthwort, gentian root, tormentil, the root of the herb tunici, dittany, and elecampane; one drachm each of sage, rue, costmary seeds, mint, peony, and water mint; Roman doronicum, bay berries, sorrel seeds, citron seeds, basil, mastic, frankincense, Armenian bole, sealed earth, spodium, and bone
6.7: MAR. FIC. OF EPIDEMICS of a stag’s heart, shavings of ivory, and unicorn horn; half a drachm each of pearls, sapphire, emerald, red coral, aloes-wood, red sandalwood, hyacinth, and topaz; half a drachm each of rose sugar, borage electuary, bugloss electuary, dianenuforati a medicinal compound containing water-lily, and acidulated electuary; half a drachm each of the pulps of acid tamarind and theriac; three pounds of sugar. Make an electuary or morsels with scabious water and rose water, slightly camphorated, and with quince wine, adding forty leaves of gold. Whoever suffers from thirst outside of meals should use simple sorrel with a little cold water, or acid pomegranate wine with rose julep, or acid wine. You may also express the acidity of a citron, lemon, or orange, and drink it with water and sugar. Item: rose juice, rose sugar, diamarenati, diaprunis a plum-based electuary, and diacydonitis a quince-based electuary dissolved with strained and expressed water, drinking it with cold water. Item: roses, myrobalans, tamarind, acid cherries, dried peach plums, and ground quinces, dissolved, strained, and expressed; drink with water and sugar, putting in more sugar where there is less heat, and less sugar where there is more heat. Item: rose juice with pomegranate wine; item: oxysaccharum with fresh cold water. Quince wine is also useful for many things. It is useful to use herbs that look after the body through their own virtue, such as borage, bugloss, balm, endive, and a little mint. Item, seven
6.8: The seven principal herbs which are said to be very valuable against poison are: the first is the herb hypericum, by another name, St. John’s Wort; the second is the herb called swallow-wort; the third is elecampane; the fourth is radish; the fifth is dittany; the sixth is birthwort; the seventh is sow-thistle. To these is added by Arnoldus and Raimundus the herb tunici. Nor should agrimony, wood sorrel, chicory, horehound, hyssop, scabious, cinquefoil, capers, lemons, citruls, and oranges—which we call golden apples —be omitted, and universally everything acid, and things that possess a certain tartness. Know that vine blossoms contribute much if you are accustomed to use them in food, drink, and electuaries, and likewise scabious water, and also balm. In all these things which are administered to both the healthy and the sick, it is wonderful, because it dries out poisonous humors. And where in drying there is a need for much cooling, one should rather use waters of endive, roses, plantain, rose vinegar, or water, or the juice of wood sorrel, lemon juice, cedar, orange, chicory, pimpinella, and fumitory. But when it is appropriate to use tempered things, take borage and bugloss water; in all decoctions, put in Damascene plums, myrobalans, and tamarinds. And keep this in mind: that these four things suit all remedies well, namely white wine, white rose vinegar, and rose water, all in equal weight, with a very small quantity of crocus. Where it is necessary to act without delay
6.9: MAR. FIC. OF EPIDEMICS with a certain ease, you will administer what is appropriate in a subtle and liquid form, or by giving what we have mentioned above to be drunk afterwards. Raimundus says that if it can be deferred until the composition of the aforementioned pills is made, it is better that pills be exhibited rather than powders, both because such a composition is better fermented, which indeed, through fermentation beyond the complexion, also acquires a specific virtue against [the poison], and because by remaining in the stomach it better preserves, strengthens, comforts, and traverses the more remote parts of the body, by drinking a little of some liquid substance afterwards and abstaining from much else. Yet we do not intend for the pills to be very dry and hardened; rather, if they are such, it is fitting that they be reformed. Phlebotomy is suitable for the sanguine, namely to draw blood so that they may be preserved, if otherwise they had no flow of blood from themselves.
6.10: I understand by the sanguine those who are suitably fleshy, red in color, hairy, robust, who have large veins, and who feed on things of much nourishment. To these, I say, let blood be drawn from the right basilica vein, then after a two-month interval let a bloodletting be made again from the left basilica vein. And do not exceed the weight of a pound at one time. Let it also be done in temperate times of the year, and while the moon is in a good and fortunate aspect. Pure blood is bled at the rising of the sun, choleric at midday, melancholic at sunset, phlegmatic in the middle of the night. Raimundus therefore wishes, according to the order of Avicenna be observed according to the four species of blood enumerated above, and those four hours should be observed in extraction. These species are recognized first by their signs, then according to the four ages in which they are dominant, succeeding in the aforementioned order. And where a great abundance of blood does not appear, [the physician] should not wish for a bloodletting to be performed at all, neither for the sake of preservation nor for cure. And when you wish to extract, take care that a clyster is administered the day before, and that some non-laxative medicine is shown. Nor do I think it should be overlooked that where the blood inclines much toward other humors, it should by no means be evacuated. Remember that Galen and Avicenna, the more they exercised the art of healing, the more timid they became regarding phlebotomy, because phlebotomy draws more from the natural state and from the good, and from the spirits, than the medicine itself does; and it grants less time to discern bad blood from good. Things that are effective against worms are beneficial to infants and children, for whom danger is most imminent in these times. Administer to them in a drink, once a week, one drachm of dittany with a somewhat styptic wine, or with a wine of a decoction of wormwood and fennel flower, or semen sanctum holy seed, i.e., wormseed. Likewise, let the stomach, navel, throat, and chest be anointed with oils and bitter herbs and the like; sometimes you will also exhibit pills of rhubarb. But because a very moist and very hot complexion is dangerous in the time of plague, there is a need for refrigeration, desiccation, and frequent evacuation, which should be done with moderation according to the opportunity. Carry this small bag applied to the heart. Take two drachms of red roses, and one drachm each of red sandalwood, red coral, and spodium one-half drachm each of zedoary, aloes-wood, cinnamon, cloves, citrus peel, and saffron. Be diligent that all superfluity is purged, and take care that the belly does not remain styptic, and be slow to constrict the customary evacuations or fluxes or superfluities, hemorrhoids, scabies, natural and customary sweats, old open wounds from which humor flows without discomfort, tears, blood flowing from the nose in the usual and ordinary way, general dropsy, and the like, since these stated purgations make one more secure from the disease. I advise the governors of public affairs (according to Hippocrates’ experience) that if they arrange and order fires and fumigations from juniper, myrtle, turpentine, and incense, in the morning and evening before the doors of any halls, houses, and dwellings, the plague would be immediately expelled from that place. Laurel, sage, rosemary, and any odoriferous herbs are effective in the place of juniper. But turpentine is wonderful. Many doctors say that fire will always be useful in the time of plague, for it dissolves every vapor. Raimundus says that one should use only comforting things when thick and moist vapors appear. In hot times, they must overcome…
6.11: MAR. FIC. OF EPIDEMICS refrigeration, desiccation, and frequent evacuation, which indeed should be done with moderation according to the opportunity. Carry this small bag applied to the heart. Take two drachms of red roses, one drachm each of red sandalwood, red coral, and spodium; one-half drachm each of zedoary, aloeswood, cinnamon, cloves, citrus peel, and saffron. Be diligent that all superfluity is purged, and take care that the belly does not remain styptic, and be slow to constrict the customary evacuations or fluxes or superfluities, hemorrhoids, scabies, natural and customary sweats, old open wounds from which humor flows without discomfort, tears, blood flowing from the nose in the usual and ordinary way, general dropsy, and the like, since these stated purgations make one more secure from the disease. I advise the governors of public affairs (according to Hippocrates’ experience) that if they arrange and order fires and fumigations from juniper, myrtle, turpentine, and incense, in the morning and evening before the doors of any halls, houses, and dwellings, the plague would be immediately expelled from that place. Laurel, sage, rosemary, and any odoriferous herbs are effective in the place of juniper. But turpentine is wonderful. Many doctors say that fire will always be useful in the time of plague, for it dissolves every vapor. Raimundus says that one should use only comforting things when thick and moist vapors appear. In hot times, they must overcome… odors in coldness must overcome others; conversely, when the times are cold and moist, roses, sandalwood, myrtle, camphor, citrus peels, and pomegranates temper the hot odors, as do vinegar and slightly cooling green herbs. The Magi counseled the King of the Persians for his defense against all poison and poisonous disease, that he should have a man carved in hematite stone standing with bent knees, surrounded by a serpent, holding the head of the serpent in his right hand and the tail in his left, and that he should have this stone set and bound in a gold ring, but that the beard of a snakeweed plant should be placed under the stone in the cavity of the setting, and that he should wear this ring on his finger. Averroes praises the scent of goat urine. I warn you to use continuous remedies when you are in an infected place or near one, because contagion is frequent, and the infected air continuously harms and offends. I want you to carefully note when there is a conjunction of the Sun and Moon, and when there is an opposition, that is, when it is the full moon. Likewise, when the Moon is joined to Saturn, and more so when it is joined to Mars. Also, when it is in a square aspect with the said planets. And note (as Rasis reports) that the poison of this kind of pestilence is accustomed to be moved strongly at the rising of the Sun, at its setting, at midday, and in the middle of the night, because the Sun causes a change in the air at these four times. It reigns in Spring, more so in Summer, and most in Autumn. In
6.12: Spring, the air is hot and moist, and the dominion of blood approaches. In Summer, due to cholera, the hot air opens and penetrates much, bodies are weakened, and they are filled with corruptible things, contributing the moist matter of the air to putrefaction through heat.
6.14: …If this heat, both inside and outside, were accompanied by dryness, little harm would come, just as moist air added to the coldness of the complexion does not do much harm. But it is very dangerous where heat is mixed with moisture, either outside or inside. We have found by experience that long drought decreases the plague in a hot season, but in a cold season it excites and brings it. Finally, in autumn, the repletion of fruits is increased, as is the weakness of the body. The air is thin because it is easily susceptible to the vapors of the preceding summer, which it does not resolve due to the decrease of heat; furthermore, it is misty and variable. Often a thick and moist wind is present, heat exceeds moisture, and frequently the obstruction of the pores arrives and increases due to the coldness of the air often following the preceding heat. It should also be known that when the pores are heavily obstructed, they compress the putrescible matter inside. Conversely, when they are opened more than is proper, they suddenly take in too much poisonous air, so that sometimes (especially after sweating or intercourse) it kills in a few hours (like a sword).

7.1:
*On the method of curing according to physical reason*
In a pestilential fever, if the poison has not been purged, beware that you do not administer internally or externally things that are simply opening to the parts of the chest…
7.2: …simply opening, because they provide an entrance for the poison to the heart, and they open a way for the spirits to exhale. Instead, so that inflammation and putrefaction may be prohibited, use things that are suddenly slightly cooling and very desiccating. For they strengthen the heart and close the paths tending toward it, so that the poison does not arrive there. Also, the humor must be well purged in part, and the spirits must be refreshed more often with nourishment, and continuously administer things that are effective against the poison; this, by its own nature, seeks the heart. But if you defer until the poison has arrived there, perhaps it will be possible that the parts of the heart become greatly constricted, which, once they are constricted, it would perhaps be more harmful or dangerous to try to open again than it is profitable. Therefore, as soon as someone perceives that the head and all the members are being burdened, with a fever added at the same time, look to the signs—do not place faith in those that are lying or ambiguous—nor delay until an inflation or blister appears. But when these do emerge, as quickly as you can, immediately anoint the pulse of the temples, hands, and feet, the nostrils, the occiput, the throat, the chest, and the place around the blister and the abscess if it has appeared.
7.3: The true composition of the oil is as follows: take eight ounces of olive oil that is fifty years old, put fifty scorpions into it, and let them boil together with the oil so that they settle to the bottom. Do this in the summer, especially in the month of August. Save it and use it, for it is wonderful against poisons. But if the stomach is burdened by food…
7.5: …has occurred, vomiting must be provoked with ease, using lukewarm water, vinegar, and oil, and also with radish, even attempting the provocation with a feather; and immediately afterward, administer a clyster. And you shall renew every day a decoction of mallows and maidenhair, beet, barley, lettuce, chamomile, violet honey, red sugar, the yolk of one egg, one ounce of diasena a purgative containing senna or cassia, two drams of solutive rose juice, and a sufficient amount of common salt and violet oil. Once this is done, you shall apply to the heart an epithema a medicinal poultice made of substances that are cordials, slightly cooling by nature. Take two drams each of the waters of roses, bugloss, wood sorrel, and water lily; one dram each of lemon balm water, juice of pomegranates of medium flavor, and citric acidity; one ounce of quince juice; two drams each of white, red, and yellow sandalwood; half a dram each of spodium calcined ivory or bone, ivory shavings, lemon seeds, and sorrel seeds; six grains of grana tinctoria kermes berries; and half a dram of camphor. Let all things be ground well and heated in a clean glass vessel. Afterward, with a cloth of grain, apply it while temperate and warm to the chest, renewing it every three hours. Also, for the stomach, keep this composition in a small bag, to vivify and strengthen its spirits. Take one handful each of wormwood and mint; half a handful each of lemon balm and sorrel; one ounce of red roses; three drams each of citrus peel and rice; two drams of prepared coriander; [and] coral… red sandalwood, and one dram each of mastic, mace, and carnation leaves; half a dram of cypress nuts; compose [these] with quince juice. Likewise, administer this remedy under the armpits. Take roses, chamomile flowers, sweet clover, myrtle flowers, cypress nuts, and sandalwood, all in due quantity; let them boil in water into which a sponge or tow is dipped, which should then be squeezed out and applied while temperate and warm, and renew it quite often: for this is wonderful.

8.1:
*The use of cupping glasses and the method of curing through bloodletting*
When these things have been done and duly administered, as has been said, if a blister or sign has not yet appeared on the shins, apply two cupping glasses immediately to the buttocks, and two likewise to the hips on the posterior side. The ancients desired that after the placement of such cupping glasses, phlebotomy should be performed. And if the usual blister or sign has not appeared, it should be done from the common vein on the right side, to prohibit the poison from reaching the parts of the heart: and if such a sign or blister has indeed appeared, blood must be drawn on that same side, and this is so that the poison does not extend and dilate itself (as it is always accustomed to do) through all the veins and parts of the body. If it has appeared around the ears or neck, it should be drawn from the cephalic a vein in the arm on the side where the sign is, near the thumb of the hand. If it has appeared under the armpits, the hepatic liver vein should be evacuated…
8.2: MAR. FIC. EPIDEMIARVM in the arm of that side where the sign is. If in the groins, let phlebotomy be performed from the saphenous a vein in the leg, that is, under the ankle of the foot of the same side. Finally, in general, as often as such a sign appears from the origin of the throat up to the head, let the drawing be made from the cephalic vein on the side where the sign appears. If [the sign is] from that part down to the navel, in front or behind, let phlebotomy be performed likewise from the hepatic vein. If below the navel, the saphenous should be drawn in the manner described above. And it must be phlebotomized as quickly as possible, at least when the apostema abscess or swelling first begins to appear. You should fearlessly cause a good quantity to be extracted, unless the patient has perhaps little blood; after two ounces or so have been extracted, stop for a little while, so that it may be judged whether the blood is good or not. If it is bad, you will be able to extract more copiously; if it is good, more sparingly. In weak patients, and those not abundant in blood, the extraction of two ounces is sufficient. But do not do this at all during the time of febrile rigor. When the patient is undergoing bloodletting, he should taste or hold in his mouth a bitter orange and any kind of sorrel, applying vinegar to his nose, forehead, and the pulses of the temples; this is the common mode of phlebotomizing. Gentile da Foligno highly praises that which we are about to say, as a proven thing. If the appearing abscess has come around the shoulder blades, cupping glasses should be applied where the shoulder blades themselves are joined, but the drawing should be made from the median middle vein, which is usually called the common and black [vein]. If it has appeared in the neck or head, the cephalic should be drawn near the thumbs… of the hands. If [the sign is] under the arm or on the right side of the arm, one must phlebotomize from the pulmonary vein the vein between the middle and ring finger on the same side. If around the left arm or side, from the Salvatella vein between the little and ring finger of the right hand. If in the groins or on the left side, the drawing should be made from the paralytic vein between the knee-pit and the other nearby vein on the same side. If it appears in the right shin or foot, from the vein so called the Vena mulierum vein of women. The Spanish and Catalan doctors are accustomed, on the first day after the clyster has been performed, or at least on the second, to perform phlebotomy in two alternating turns. In robust people of good age who are full of blood, they do it on the first day in this way: First, they extract blood on the opposite side, because the humor is still in motion and has not yet become poisonous. If the abscess has appeared under the left arm, they bleed suddenly from the right hand [extracting] six or four ounces, or from the ankle of the left foot [extracting] three ounces. But after six or eight hours, with the patient refreshed and quiet, they extract from the left arm six, four, or three ounces according to the compression and the strength of the larger vein, since it shows itself more opportunely to be exposed for phlebotomy. They do the opposite where the abscess appears in the groins; first, indeed, they bleed in the arm of the same side, and second, in the foot of that same side also, from the saphenous [vein]. Truly, if the patient is not very robust, nor abundant in blood, yet possesses a natural…
8.3: MAR. FIC. EPIDEMIARVM vigor and constancy of strength, or if he is already at the end of the second or on the third day, when it is already likely that the material itself has taken its course and motion and is already infected with poison, they evacuate two or four ounces from the side of the abscess, as close to the abscess as possible. If it has appeared behind the ears, they draw from the cephalic vein of the same side. But if this cannot be easily grasped, let it be done in the median vein, with the whole body participating. But if even this is not open, let it be done in the same hand from the vein that is between the thumb and the index finger. They do the same from the middle of the second day to the following ones, but from the beginning to the middle of the second, they would perform phlebotomy from the opposite side, similarly from the first to the middle of the second. If the abscess is under the arm, it should be evacuated from the vein of the same arm, and from the common vein, or at least from the hepatic vein, or from the hand of the same [arm] below the middle finger and the one adjacent to it. If at the aforementioned time the sign itself is in the groins, you should incise the vein below the knee of the same side, or below the ankle of the same foot. If the sign tends toward the buttocks, let blood from the larger and more visible vein on the back of the foot of the same side. Their method is also such that, before the middle of the second day, they begin for the most part to extract blood on the opposite side, but after [the middle of the day], for the most part on the contrary. Let us, however, arrive at our universal canons. Because a disease of this kind is either in the blood itself, or… in humors mixed with blood: therefore, it seems to me that blood should be extracted from everyone, from the age of fourteen to sixty, as I deem it much better that the poison, which may expire through the opening of a vein, be released, rather than that the patient be greatly afflicted by the outflow of blood. Extract it a second time with an interval of six hours. For robust bodies and those highly abundant in blood, extract at most one pound; for those moderately robust and moderately full of blood, up to eight ounces; but for the weaker ones, provided they have a steady pulse, four or three ounces, or two, or at least one. However, where the dominance of cholera yellow bile prevails, the extraction should not exceed two ounces. Many command to extract until the person, who is not weak, becomes weakened. This, however, pleases me very little, since it dissolves the spirit. Where the pulse falters, nothing at all should be extracted. My greater care is that the apostema abscess/swelling should first appear, and that the hemorrhoids be subsequently provoked by friction made with rough materials, onion juice, cupping glasses, scarifications, and sanguisugæ leeches. Where blood abounds, do the same after the second venesection. Where there is a moderate amount of blood, you shall at least do this.

9.1:
*On medicines that dissolve poison and draw it outward*
Some, as soon as blood has been evacuated once at the beginning, apply an epithema a liquid application or compress. Truly, the wiser ones do this
9.2: MAR. FIC. EPIDEMIARVM at the beginning, and they renew it quite often, namely from the third hour to the third, applying it warm with a scarlet cloth. We described one above, this is the other. Take rose water, endive water, bugloss, and lemon balm, half a pound of each; two ounces of vinegar; three drachms each of sandalwood, roses, and coral; two drachms of spodium calcined ivory or bone; one scruple each of pearls, hyacinths, and sapphire; half a drachm each of white and red been a root of the Centaurea species, bone from a stag’s heart, and citrus seeds; half a scruple of musk; and one scruple each of camphor and saffron. If you detect an unusual heat in the patient, anoint the liver and the region of the kidneys with sandalwood ointment twice a day. Then, after four hours (in the accustomed manner and order), two or one drachm of the powder against the disease should be exhibited with white wine and the waters of endive and wood sorrel, along with two drachms, or at least one, of theriaca a complex herbal antidote/treacle. After this drink, assist nature toward sweating with warm cloths and fumigations. Nor would one err who administered only theriaca; however, it is more in use to give it with powders. Some add vinegar, and this does not displease me; it is also pleasing that it be administered frequently. And water of scabious and lemon balm is useful together with the theriaca, where there is not much heat. The ancient description of the powder against the disease is as follows. Take one ounce of white dittany, white coral, tormentil, Armenian bole, and gentian; half an ounce of terra sigillata sealed medicinal earth. This is more moderate. Take the beard of dittany, the beard of tormentil, agrimony, aloes wood, Armenian bole, valerian, dock, and red sandalwood, in equal parts; the beard of scabious to the weight of all; mix with the blood of a bull, dried in the sun and distilled. Another description. Take four drachms each of spodium, white dittany, gentian, tormentil, juniper berries, citrus seeds, and carline thistle; two ounces of albatrum leaves. Third description. Take one drachm each of tormentil, white dittany, burnt stag’s horn, and zedoary; two scruples each of pearls and red coral. Fourth description. Take two drachms each of tormentil, white dittany, Armenian bole, camphor, pearls, red sandalwood, burnt stag’s horn, round birthwort, and white sugar. Fifth description. Take two drachms each of tormentil and dittany; three drachms each of sorrel seed and citrus seeds; one scruple each of white ginger, cinnamon, and saffron; two and a half drachms each of Armenian bole and terra sigillata; two ounces of sugar. This powder is, as rumor has it, of great value against poison, administered both before and after. Sixth description. Take two drachms of tormentil roots; one drachm each of red sandalwood, fresh white dittany, burnt stag’s horn, pearls, Armenian bole, and round birthwort; half a drachm of camphor; two drachms of white sugar;
9.3: MAR. FIC. EPIDEMIARVM two drachms of pimpernel, myrrh, and zedoary; two drachms each of sandalwood and terra sigillata; one scruple each of citrus seeds and saffron; half a drachm each of unicorn horn and hyacinth. These powders provide vigor to the heart and aid it in expelling the poison from itself, by desiccating putrescible humors, and they restrain the pathways of the heart so that the poison does not touch it; they also frequently expel poison by way of sweat. It has been found by experience that the former description, which we called ancient, and the last of the modern ones, are far more efficient than the others. There are some who, after the provocation of vomiting (if there is need for it), having also performed an enema and anointing, first exhibit the powders and the epithema; only after its operation do they then evacuate the blood. They do this when the patient has had much blood, and perhaps they do not err in this. But where blood extraction is not possible, then due to the deficiency of blood, they exhibit medicine in place of phlebotomy, though the powder first. After the sick person has sweated or the due time for sweating has passed, one should not wait for the digestion of humor, since there is neither the delay of time nor the capacity to celebrate digestion. Indeed, when necessity looms (since that is not subject to law), the accustomed discretion of times and days is not to be observed. Nor should one put trust in any hope for the work of nature striving for evacuation, since it is irregular because of indigestion and the onslaught of the poison; indeed, oppressed nature works more than it should, if it can. Therefore, after a suitable time for sweating, you will either reduce the blood if it abounds, or if it does not abound, you will give a purgative, yet one made of things that do not disturb the stomach. For vomiting produced with violence, by dilating the pathways of the chest, causes the poison to run to the heart and pulls it toward the brain. For this reason, those who exhibit goat’s rue and such things that are vomitive and poisonous err; for nature can barely resist the poison alone. Someone might perhaps oppose us: why are physicians accustomed to induce the poisoned to vomit? I say the condition of poisons is not equal; for the others have more matter and are more suitable for expulsion through vomiting, and they are in the stomach, but this [poison] is a certain poisonous vapor and is in the parts of the chest. Let there be, therefore, no medicine that can violently produce vomiting for one who should not be damned with violence. It is, however, more approved that diversion be made through the lower parts. Let the medicine you will give be dissolved in white wine and the waters of scabious, endive, rose, plantain, bugloss, and lemon balm, in which a decoction has been made from Damascene plums, myrobalans, and tamarinds. But if the disease invades someone while their stomach is full, what must be done according to the order of the moderns? See that after anointing with oil of scorpions and theriaca, they vomit easily with warm water, vinegar, oil, and juice.
9.4: MAR. FIC. EPIDEMIARVM of radish, also attempting provocation with a long feather, then you will administer a clyster, afterwards an epithem, and some of the powders themselves. Then, at a time when the sick person is already quieter and restored, you will open a vein if they are sanguine; if not, you will administer medicine. And if, during phlebotomy, you have extracted more than four ounces of blood, refrain from medicine until twelve hours have passed since the phlebotomy. And although you have performed phlebotomy, do not place your hope in it alone, especially in a plethoric, sanguine, and robust body. Indeed, even in others from whom you have extracted little blood, medicine must still be administered at the proper time, according to the quality of their complexion and strength. Similarly, if you have given medicine first, do not be content with that; if the body is plethoric, provided the strength allows it, also command phlebotomy at the proper time and in the proper manner. And you will make this distinction, namely, in administering one and then the other, where that is possible and convenient. But where blood abounds, phlebotomy should come first and be more copious; where blood does not abound, medicine should come first, and phlebotomy should follow, though a modest one, namely for the sake of venting rather than diminishing. After the third day, no extraction of blood ought to be done, unless the quantity of blood compels you to it. As often as you administer medicine, phlebotomy, or an emetic, [you do so] to ensure that by such agitation the poison itself is not turned back from the sign inward, si signum
9.5: If a sign is apparent, ensure that in such commotion you place cupping glasses and leeches under and above the sign, and cold epithems over the heart. And before and after, you will administer through the mouth those things that defend against poison, namely theriac, Armenian bole, emeralds, hyacinths, topaz, or at least other kinds of gems, or corals with the juice of herbs against poison. When you perform a purgation, present the medicine with a little saffron in the above-mentioned decoction. The principal and safer medicine, according to the physicians of the Persians and Mesue, is one ounce of trifera persica a medicinal electuary of the Persians with two drachms of electuary Hamech, or at least half an ounce of Trifera and one or half a drachm of electuary Hamech. But to the very robust, one ounce is given with three drachms of electuary Hamech, and the Persians administer it with cold water or the juice of nightshade or endive. I have often heard of this, and I have made a successful attempt this present year. However, where Trifera and electuary Hamech are lacking, you will administer diafena a medicinal laxative in place of Trifera, and diamanna a manna-based laxative, or rose juice in place of electuary Hamech in the aforementioned manner. I have made the experiment and found this composition to be of great utility and safety. Take half an ounce each of Trifera Persica and cassia pulp, and one drachm of rhubarb, diamanna, or electuary Hamech.
