But where nature is strong and the belly is constipated, you will give two drachms of diamanna or electuary Hamech, tempered with waters of bu-
9.6: MAR. FIC. EPIDEMIARVM gloss and endive with the above-mentioned decoctions and waters. I, for my part, keep rhubarb in white wine and endive waters with a little spike for an hour, which I give in substance, mixing everything together; often I also add one ounce of manna afterwards. Pillulae de fumo terrae fumitory pills and aggregativae aggregate or compound pills also agree, in equal parts; for the robust, one drachm in total, but for others, half a drachm, drinking down white wine with waters of endive or roses and scabious. Also, the Aggregativae alone are suitable at all times, especially in less summery weather, one or half a drachm. Note that if a fever adheres to subtle and hot humors, vehement thirst, dryness of the throat, blackening of the tongue, acute headache, phrenesis inflammation of the brain or delirium, or similar horrific accidents will appear. But if it has adhered to grosser and less furious humors, the fever will appear slow, and the aforementioned accidents more remiss. Consider signs of this kind, and know that in whatever humor Trifera with agaricum agaric mushroom, used as a purgative agrees, as do the aggregativae pills, either alone or with fumitory pills. A purgative syrup, which we shall mention below, also agrees if it is in a furious matter, along with diafena and electuary Hamech or rose juice. Likewise, cassia with rhubarb, and manna with diamanna in cold decoctions. If it is in a gross, cold, and humid matter, two scruples of aggregativae pills are suitable for the robust, and one scruple of agaric pills for the weaker. For the weaker still, one ounce of diacatholicon a universal laxative with two drachms of diafenicon a laxative containing dates, or one drachm or half a drachm of trochiscated agaric agaric processed into medicinal tablets. Also, one or half a drachm of the pills against the disease mentioned above, and perhaps such pills agree in any humor. Note that agaric, well prepared and trochiscated, is singular in this case in any humor and member. Therefore, when I was more certain of its preparation, I would use it in every medicine, giving two, one, or half a drachm of its troches, according to the potency of the medicine and the complexion of the man. And where I doubted its preparation, I would steep it in oxymel scilliticum a syrup of squill, vinegar, and honey with sal gemmae rock salt, and afterwards, by straining, I would place it upon the medicine without expression. Also, it is to be noted that aggregativae pills are appropriate, and in their place, Sine quibus literally “without which,” a specific type of mild pill pills ought to be administered to the less robust. And know that it is better to give medicine than pills in this case. And if diamanna can be had, it is better than rose juice and stronger. And electuary Hamech is better than both, namely, both diamanna and rose juice. Finally, in every humor, this purgative syrup is wonderful in place of medicine, at least one ounce and at most two, with rose water and white wine. Take two drachms each of citron peel, caper root, barberry, red sandalwood, and spodium one handful each of chariophilate clove root/avens, lemon balm, bugloss, borage, and chicory; [take] one mania-
9.7: MAR. FIC. EPIDEMIARVM pulus of sorrel; one and a half handfuls of brassia likely cabbage or a wild mustard variant and liverwort; two drachms of wild endive; one handful each of the seeds of pumpkin, namely melon, watermelon, cucumber, and violets; two drachms each of thyme, epithyme, agaric, rhubarb, senna, and polypody; six drachms each of the juices of wormwood, fumitory, dwarf elder, and plantain; one drachm of chebulic myrobalans; half a drachm of citrine myrobalans; two drachms of diagridium a preparation of scammony; two pounds of white sugar; make a syrup with the vinegar of quinces. This syrup is called divine by doctors in preserving and curing, because it immediately cuts off putrescible humors, strengthens the principal members, drives the poison outward, and many experiences of it have been seen. Among other doctors, Petrus de Tussigniana and Gentilis Fulgineus commend it in a marvelous way, and it seems to me that it was made to the intention of Trifera Persica, but it is more purgative, and it pleases me greatly for persons who are not too weak and who do not have a very loose belly. It should be taken once a week by the healthy and the sick. Note that after the operation of the medicine or phlebotomy, if you have not administered medicine on the following day, one drachm of theriac is given with one ounce of rose water and a little rose vinegar. Do not fear the heat of the theriac, since such a small portion can heat very little, because elemental quality, such as heat and similar things, because they are very material, they do not work much, unless with a great deal of matter. But a specific virtue, as it is a celestial and quasi-spiritual gift, works much even with a little matter, according to Galen. Now, treacle works against poison by its specific property, and beyond this, it barely completes a degree of heat; therefore, it is far more potent for expelling poison than for heating. Likewise, a pestilential fever is much more poisonous than it is hot, but treacle should be administered with rose water, and in other matters, one must take care that they tend toward a certain coldness, as far as you are able to use this. Mithridate may also be given in place of treacle, but much more potent experiences have been seen from treacle. Therefore, Moses the Egyptian says that it was recounted to him by a certain wise physician that, while he was practicing his art in Antioch during the time of the plague, he found by the very event that all other remedies were weak, so that only those who took treacle upon his advice escaped safe and survived, while others did not. And only those who used it after the onset of the disease were freed; the others exchanged life for death. By this, it is confirmed what Galen says in his booklet On Treacle to Caesar, that it is opposed to all poisons and would be potent where others fail and are weak. However, it has this from a certain miraculous virtue. There are also those who administer urine to drink, or lye, or likewise the juice of leeks…
9.9: …with vinegar, I do not know what I should say. I advise this: do not have confidence in a purging once you have performed it, even if the sick person feels better from it. But when the patient seems to be doing better, on the third or fourth day after the purging, if there is still much superfluity of blood present, extract a little blood, and repeat the same medicinal purging. But if it does not abound to that degree, repeat at least the powders and the medicine, lest he relapse into a worse state. Some administer euphorbium with mastic and gum elemi. Take five drachms and one scruple of euphorbium, two ounces of gum elemi, one ounce and a half of mastic; for the robust, you will give one drachm by weight, and for the weak, one scruple, with waters of endive and scabious. It is indeed a dangerous medicine, nor is it appropriate except for the most robust, and only at the beginning. Some assert that gum elemi is the gum of the cedar tree. One must know that in this case, a weak medicine should not be administered —that is, one that would cause a slight operation—since nature herself, if the first medicine has not operated well, does not expect a second. Nor, however, is it proper to purge with too much force, for from this the spirits would be resolved, and this evil consists more in a certain poisonous quality than in the quantity of matter. Gentilis Fulgineus says that he had much experience with the aforementioned powder; he administered it thus from the beginning. Take half a drachm of euphorbium, one drachm of mastic; he gave one scruple of these…
9.10: …two scruples, and for those who are very plethoric, one drachm. But agaric pleases me much more, because, as Democritus, Galen, and Avicenna say, it draws some humor from all the members, and likewise has a virtue like that of treacle; it strengthens against every poison, and purges it of every poison. It primarily purges gross humors, and does not leave thin ones untouched either. It should be white, porous, round, and also easy to break, sweet, and light. It should also have moderate bitterness and stypticity, be well-ground, and mixed with a third part of rock salt, and thus be corrected with rock salt, strained honey of roses, squill oxymel, and wine infused with ginger, and thus prepared in trochics. And for the weak, it is safer that it be given mixed with other things than alone, and better in decoctions than in substance, since it frequently produces long vomiting and pains of the belly, unless it is well selected and prepared. But if it has been duly selected and prepared, it is a holy and familiar medicine according to Democritus and Mesue. For we have performed happy experiences (in the mode and order stated) with that very agaric. But regarding euphorbium, we have found that it sometimes did a very good job, but more often the opposite. Universally and in sum, be swift in evacuating and frequent, having observed the mode and order. Recreate the sick person more frequently, since otherwise the spirits are greatly resolved, and do not give only those things, whether foods or…
9.12: …medicinals, which only soften, but mix with these refrigerants, desiccants, and comforts for the heart, which also resist poison.

10.1:
*On nourishment and the regimen of the sick*
Food must be (according to Rasis and Avicenna in the fourth book of the Canon) frequent, moderate, light, boiled, and of much and moist nourishment, seasoned with acidic and cold things—that is, with endive, sorrel, vinegar, verjuice, pomegranates, oranges, lemons, sour cherries, and plums. The substance of the food should be chicken, partridge, pheasant, minced meat, consommés, distilled broths, fresh eggs; I do not forbid kid meat either. In sum, let him be nourished with liquid, moist, and nourishing things. Yet he must be nourished in such a way that nature tolerates it and fevers are not multiplied, for much more than in other cases, there is need for abundant food in this situation. Avicenna says in the fourth book of the Canon that the filling of the veins by nourishment prevents the passage of poisonous vapor of the air and humor, and that those are more frequently freed who are fearlessly aided by nourishment. Note that once a solvent clyster has been made, of which we made mention above, if there is need for other restoration, he should take something by mouth. You will perform the evacuation either with an enema or a suppository; then, at four hours, you will administer some of the nourishment about which we spoke a little above. Let the wine be white, subtle, fragrant…
10.2: …bearing, diluted with iron-infused water, or at least fresh water, in an equal part. Indeed, gilded water would be better, in which heated gold has been extinguished, or gold can also be extinguished in wine. Do not let him suffer thirst, nor his mouth be dried out, but continuously make him gargle with well-diluted white wine. Let him hold moist, slightly cold things in his mouth, let him frequently drink of the acidity of citron, and rose julep, in equal parts with pomegranate wine and water or juice of sorrel. The syrup of simple sorrel with iron-infused water is useful, and likewise the juice of citron or lemons or pressed oranges; you will give these with water and fine sugar, or perhaps better with barley water or iron-infused water. Likewise, sugared roses, or diamarenatum a confection of bitter cherries, or diaprunis a confection of plums, and diacydoniten a confection of quinces dissolved in water, strained, and expressed, or roses, sour cherries, myrobalans, tamarinds, plums, quinces, dried peaches, ground and infused in water, then strained, expressed, and presented with sugar and fresh water, are useful. White vinegar with iron-infused water and sugar is also suitable for the sick as well as the healthy. Also, oxysacchara compounded with white vinegar, the juice of acidic pomegranates, and sugar, is beneficial. The juice of pomegranates of medium flavor is also beneficial, or the juice or wine of acidic things with a little sugar, and barley water with pomegranate wine. It is good to rub gold rings in water for so long that they are worn away a little by the water. Likewise, to boil water with gold.
10.4: …good in food and drink. According to Gentilis Gentile da Foligno, a medieval physician, it is perhaps possible for gold to be reduced to a liquid form suitable for drinking in this way: Take one ounce of gold and two ounces of quicksilver. Mix them and let them remain mixed until the gold is dissolved. Then place them in an alembic with a slow fire until the quicksilver has departed from the alembic. Afterwards, take the gold from the bottom of the alembic and add forty-seven ounces of bugloss water. Place this in a well-sealed glass alembic. You shall continue the fire under it for three days and nights—I mean a wellproportioned fire. In the end, if you are skilled in the art, you will find the water minimally consumed and the gold liquefied. This is the most cordial aurum potabile potable gold, and it can be digested. Indeed, gold in other forms is of little use, because it cannot be digested at all. You will administer this twice a day on an empty stomach from these syrups: namely, of citron acidity, of lemons, of chicory, and of fumitory, half a drachm each, with one ounce of balm water and sorrel juice. Likewise, syrups of verjuice, currants, barberry rob, quinces, and pomegranates of medium flavor, along with endive and bugloss waters. Also, syrup of endive with endive water and citron acidity, with sorrel juice and the wine of acidic pomegranates; likewise, the juice of lemons, or citron, or pressed oranges to be exhibited with water and sugar. It would not displease me if, in place of water, you administered chicken broth.
10.5: …chicken broth, which is commonly called Piperata, or a partridge cooked with verjuice and endive and strained therefrom, to which is mixed something from the aforementioned juices, tempering the sorrel with sweet things, just as nature does in pomegranates of medium flavor. Also, let acidic pomegranates be seasoned well with their wine and juice alone, or even with other juices. Likewise, juice of roses, myrobalans, tamarinds, sugared roses, diamarenatum a confection of bitter cherries, diaprunis a confection of plums, and diacydoniten a confection of quinces, dissolved in water, strained, and expressed, are to be drunk with fresh water. Also, oxysacchara a mixture of vinegar and sugar with rose julep and iron-infused water. Also, juice of roses and citron acidity with pomegranate wine. Note that syrup of sorrel is useful in any syrup whatsoever. Where citron acidity is not had, squeeze lemons or oranges and temper with sugar; and where greater heat is present, give a greater quantity of sorrel: where less, a smaller. And where syrup of sorrel is not had, you will give vinegar, water, and sugar mixed together. White vinegar is better than red. Also, this excellent syrup: Take of the juice of balm, borage, and bugloss, purified, three ounces each; of rose water and white vinegar, one and a half ounces each; of citron and lemon acidity, half an ounce; of white sugar, one pound. From this, you will dispense two ounces with two and a half ounces of bugloss and sorrel water; use this as you please. And at the same time, give two trochisci medicinal lozenges of [?camphor]
10.6: MAR. FIC. EPIDEMIARVM camphor. Some of the wise, in place of syrup, give this potion: Take one pound of rose water, half a pound of fragrant white wine, and half an ounce of bolus armenus Armenian bole, an earthy clay used medicinally, perfectly pulverized and sifted. For one dose, exhibit two drachms. It is indeed a remedy both ancient and powerful. Experimenters use two things above all: namely, the juice of orange blossoms with wine in the case and after the case, and the seed of Carduus benedictus blessed thistle with wine, because these have been proven against the venom of mushrooms. The wise are also accustomed to give these: Take three ounces of scabious juice, one drachm of terra sigillata sealed earth, a medicinal clay with a little wine; likewise, two drachms of citron seeds with good wine. Also, amber and jet with wine; also, one drachm of coagula coagulants of species with wine. Coagula Coagulants are certain mucilages found in certain bladders, attached to the viscera of young goats and hares. Also, the root of palma christi castor bean with wine. These, which (as we have passed down) the wise use, remove venom from the heart. These confections are suitable for preserving and curing. Trust much in this simple, secure, and most effective composition of ours: Take two drachms of bolus armenus Armenian bole, one drachm each of terra sigillata and red coral, half a drachm each of citron rind, zedoary, and saffron, six ounces of sugared roses seasoned with red roses, and ten ounces of citron acidity. You will always give this with white wine and rose water; sometimes a little rose vinegar is to be mixed in.
10.7: …rose vinegar. From these we can also make pills, if instead of sugared roses we take half an ounce of red roses with as much citron acidity as is sufficient. Some give these compositions: Take four ounces each of sugared roses, the three sanders, and diadraganti a confection of tragacanth; ten leaves of gold; and one drachm each of pearls, hyacinths, and stag heart bone. Also, take one scruple of pearls, two drachms each of sapphire, hyacinths, and emeralds, half a drachm each of terra sigillata, the three grains, and ground raw silk; one drachm of emeralds, as much manus christi a confection of sugar and rose water as you please, and as much rose water in which gold rings or gold vessels have been rubbed as is sufficient. Also, one pound each of rose water and white sugar; half a drachm each of red and white sanders, red coral, and spodium calcined ivory or bone; one drachm of pearls; and one scruple each of hyacinths, emeralds, sapphire, and stag heart bone. All aromatics are suitable for preserving and curing, especially those that pertain to coldness and heat. And if they are not suitable for febrile heat, they are nonetheless valid against its venom, especially if they are tempered with cold things so that they incline toward some coldness, and incline more when the heat of the seasons, or of temperaments, or of acute fevers is standing. Also, note that between terra sigillata and bolus armenus this…
10.9: …is the distinction: although both are valid against venom and disease, the wise nevertheless use the earth more than the bole in other venoms, but in pestilential disease they do the opposite. All agree on this: that in other venoms, nothing is better than terra sigillata, especially exhibiting it with a little bolus armenus, juniper berries, and diluted vinegar according to the method of Galen ancient Greek physician, because it immediately constricts and closes the pectoral passages so that venom cannot pass through them, and it casts out the venom through vomiting. Likewise, for venom that is educible through laxatives, it does this when administered both after and before the case, but more securely before. Similarly, all agree that when it comes to preserving oneself from the plague and also expelling it, bolus armenus surpasses all other simples, especially when exhibited with white wine and rose water, according to the order of Galen, Serapion an ancient medical author, and Avicenna a medieval Persian physician, who say they are experienced in having been easily preserved and having had their humors healed with this during the time of the great plague. Bolus armenus is indeed red, slightly saffron-colored, delicate, and breakable. Terra sigillata, however, is slightly reddish, a little acidic and dry to the taste, somewhat viscous, yet not so tenacious that it sticks to the fingers. Note that sometimes the disease takes its beginning with an abundance of blood-stained sputum. In this case, the bole is not given, nor anything else that is a stricture of this poisonous blood. Rather, this flow is aided with pectoral substances.
10.10: Blood is to be drawn from both saphenous veins, according to the quality of the complexion. But if the sick person is very sanguine, blood is also drawn afterward from the median vein, and friction to the stomach must not be neglected while fasting. See to it that a sponge soaked in rose water, rose vinegar, and aromatic wine is held to the nose, and also frequently wash all pulse points and the face with these. Where there is suspicion of future delirium, sometimes apply rose water with rose vinegar to the forehead. And unless you fear excessive drowsiness, add a little camphora camphor. Take care that the invalid does not fall into too deep a sleep: for five or six hours during the day and night are sufficient, since excessive sleep draws the venom inward. Cupping glasses placed on the back, as well as friction and ligatures around the extremities, contribute equally to delirium and drowsiness. Likewise, a suppository made of hard soap with a little rock salt is helpful. Moderate sleep at the beginning of the disease is useful, but one should not stay awake so long that the spirits are exhausted. The room should be ventilated by frequently opening and closing it: the air is varied by this, yet it must be ventilated in such a way that the patient does not feel it and suffer any cold. Linens soaked in vinegar should be stretched along the sides of the bed. Sprinkle the walls and the floor of the room with water mixed with vinegar, and scatter and place fronds, vine shoots, reeds, willows, roses, seedlings, and leaves of gourds and any other greenery, as well as flowers and fragrant fruits, here and there and in the corners.
10.12: Prepare a fumigation from sandalwood, roses, myrtle, camphor, turpentine, frankincense, lemon peels, and the peels of pomegranates and common apples, adding a little clove and saffron. Above all, take care to change and renew the invalid’s shirt and all cloths, linens, and fumigations every six hours, along with the vessel for the fumigation. If it can be done conveniently, you will change the bedding and the room every twenty-four hours. Before one is introduced, however, the room must be thoroughly cleaned and fumigated with good scents, as is fitting. Otherwise, the clothing, bed, and dwelling will be infected with venom. Nor do I wish to pass over in silence the fact that where unusual heat appears, along with strength of the stomach and freedom from intestinal pain, Rafis Rhazes, a medieval Persian physician and Iohannitius Hunayn ibn Ishaq, a medieval medical scholar were accustomed to give cold, fresh water in large quantity once for drinking. I, however, to act more securely, would give three pounds of fresh barley water with three ounces of sugar. And perhaps I would also give half a pound of cucumber juice, well mixed with one ounce of sugar, and afterward one ounce of juice of oranges or pomegranates and one dram of sugar. A certain compatriot of ours, a robust man, as soon as this disease attacked him, immersed himself in cold water and remained there for two hours, coming out freed; however, this is a most fallacious experiment.
10.13: Perhaps it would be safer to sit in warm waters that do not reach the pectoral regions, since these parts must not be opened, nor should humors be provoked toward them. Some in this case have taken poisons, especially those of a cold nature, and perhaps also those of a hot nature, before or after theriac a complex medicinal antidote or terra sigillata sealed earth with bolus armenus Armenian bole/red clay and water mixed with vinegar, and similar things that are against venom. Among whom, a certain physician was freed. It seems to me, however, to be a very dangerous matter.

11.1:
*On Treatment through the Art of Surgery*
In this case, one must not wait until an inflammation or blister appears, but having performed a purgation or phlebotomia bloodletting, be quick and prompt to extract the venom by making a ruptorium a caustic agent to induce an opening/blister with ferment and cantharides dried blister beetles, or another of those we will describe below. Apply it to the muscle of the right arm below the inner elbow on the side where the pulse is usually felt, though not directly over the pulse. You will do the same over the ankle of the right foot, four fingers to the inside, so that a blister is formed; open it and keep it open. If the usual sign appears, and the inconvenience and shortness of time hinder the observed order, let bloodletting and purgation be performed. Having done these, or only the bloodletting, make the ruptorium and apply it to the same side at a distance of six fingers below the sign. There are those who do not rely on the variation of time, but even outside the order, they first and afterward, and simultaneously, try to cure with remedies as best they can.
11.3: The order of some moderns is such that, where nothing prevents it, the invalid is first purged with clysters, powders, bloodletting, and medicine. Afterward, however, ruptoria blistering agents should be applied as we have said (even if the sign is not appearing), and it is safer to place ruptoria and other things appropriate to this disease immediately (whether the sign appears or not). If a sign seems to appear, do it thus. If it has appeared around the ears, apply the ruptorium to the back of the neck, but on the same side where the sign is. If under the arm, the ruptorium should be placed on the muscle of that same arm, or near the pulse, but not over it. If in the groins, place it next to the ankle, that is, on the ankle of the foot of the same side. When it appears elsewhere, apply the ruptorium below the sign at a distance of six fingers, or a sixth of a foot, provided that it is not placed (however it may be) over the chest. And if it should be in the throat, namely on the anterior side, the ruptorium should be placed on the back, namely on the neck. But if it should be in the back part in the same place, it should not be applied to the front, but rather below the location of the sign, and thus you will permit the ruptorium to remain there until it has made a blister, which you should open and apply butter and cabbage leaves over; also a sponge soaked in this decoction: take camomilla chamomile, bristanica great water dock, melilotus sweet clover, and scabiosa scabious herb, one handful of each, and let them boil in half a pound of water until half is consumed. Because this draws out the venom, renew it and keep it, and use it frequently until the end of the cure.

12.1:
*Description of Simple Blistering Agents*
These ruptoria blistering agents are: swallow-wort, vitriol, verdigris, rancid nut, birthwort, arsenic, quicklime, universal antidote, dodder, lime with soap of fullers, aura, houndstongue, ferment with lye, galbanum, horsetail, euphorbium, pigeon dung, hawk dung, goose and duck dung, cress, live snails ground with their shells, a flayed and roasted frog, calamint, field mint, birthwort, radish, mistletoe, knotgrass, costus, pepper, sea sponge stone, flame-flower ground, nettle, mustard, virgin’s bower, horsemint, scabious, hemp, hempseed, cantharides blister beetles, and rock salt. Ground egg yolk with a lot of salt, greater comfrey, and scabious ground between two stones are wonderful. Said ruptoria must be applied quickly, as I had said, and perhaps equally over the appearing sign. In delicate persons, milder ones should be used, and in others, stronger ones. And it is safer that they be placed below the sign than above it, or that less strong ones be placed above, but stronger ones below.

13.1:
*Reasons, methods, and conditions for treating an aposteme*
This sign is called an apostema abscess or swelling, which, when it comes before the onset of fever, indicates that the heart is strong and capable of expelling the venom, and then the fever is…
13.2: MAR. FIC. EPIDEMIARVM is the settling of an apostema abscess or swelling. It is the opposite when it comes after the fever. For this apostema is of two generations: one is a blister, named anthrax a carbuncle or malignant boil and carbunculus carbuncle. The other is an inflation, called bubo swelling of a lymph node and glandula glandular swelling. The blister commonly exits through the emunctories, and the further it is from the principal members, the less dangerous it is. Black is the worst of all; green in the second place is a little less bad; livid in the third, and red in the fourth. And the drier it is, the worse it is. An inflation usually occurs in the emunctories, that is, the purifiers of the principal members, of which there are three: in the places behind the ears, under the arms, and in the groins. The brain sends the poison down through the emunctories behind the ears and into the neck. The heart sends it under the arms. The liver sends it to or around the groins. For this reason, an inflation is worse than a blister, since it indicates that much of the poison has run down to the principal members. And the closer the inflation is to the heart, the more dangerous it is. The treatment for both—for the blister as well as the inflation—is almost the same. Some people, when an apostema appears before the fever and far from the heart, suddenly apply ligatures between the site of the pain and the heart, and they place cold, dry things on top for the sake of repulsion. But on the specific site of the pain, they place hot, moist, dissolving things. Others, as soon as the apostema begins to appear, place suction cups on top and to the side, as we have said, and blistering agents, exhibiting this medicine immediately. cinnamon. Take of prepared black hellebore, senna, and cinnamon, half a drachm of each, and half a scruple of diagridium scammony resin; let them be infused in four ounces of pomegranate wine and one ounce of sugar. If it could stand in infusion for many hours, it would be better; afterwards, strain and squeeze it out, to be given when the apostema appears before the patient sleeps. Truly, they prepare the hellebore in this way: they cut it lengthwise into small pieces, put it into a sweet apple, and wrap the apple in oakum previously dipped in rose water, and thus they cook it under hot ashes. Once cooked, they discard the apple, re-cook the hellebore in another apple in the same way as before, and it is stored separately from the apple. To the most robust, they give the hellebore mixed with the prescribed mixtures, in the manner and order mentioned. To others, however, and those less robust, they give only the apple of the second cooking. They prepare scammony by cooking it in quinces or in a paste of barley flour made with quince wine. I do not reject the rules of these people, but we return to our own.

14.1:
*Rules and methods for applying blistering agents*
When it is not opportune to draw blood with suction cups or leeches, nor to burn the sign, one must place blistering agents from the aforementioned, and also from those compositions which I shall mention in the following, either under or above, or simultaneously on both sides. However, you provide the aforementioned if it seems the opportunity of time is present, after it has been extracted
14.2: MAR. FIC. EPIDEMIARVM blood and the sick person has rested a little, or at least after the administration of the medicine and its perfect operation. And if there is no one present who can work with his hand, give the powder; if you do not have that, exhibit the medicine. If you do not have the medicine either, apply the blistering agents without delay above and outside the sign, with moderation, as we have said, and in order. And if time presses, and nothing has yet been done, exhibit both the purgation and the blistering agents at the same time, and never cease from the administration of remedies, nor delay, hoping that you will do everything with more convenient time. Take care not to place on the sign things that are so cold and styptic astringent that they drive the poison inward. Use those things which are apt for drawing out and dissolving, such as hot things. And sometimes they must be tempered a little if you are going to continue them with cold things, so that excessive inflammation is avoided, yet not with things so cold that they constrict because of it. And do not fear the pain much, since it draws the poison to the apostema. I do not want you to tolerate excess, however, because it would add strength to the poison, and would simultaneously increase the fevers, and would exhaust nature too much. I do not want you to consolidate the site of the blistering agent by art until three months have passed; when you do this, indeed, repeat the purgation. A certain Florentine of ours lanced a blister in this spring, and because he was so liberated from this disease that he was not different from healthy men not long after he first consolidated the wound; however, after forty days had passed, he was again infected by the disease and died in the space of two days, mainly because he had restricted the wound without purgation. For you should know this: that he who dies after the seventh day, it happens more from poor care than from the nature of this disease. Know that after the poison has run down to the apostema so much that the principal members have been alleviated by it, unless you draw, rectify, and purge it very well and continuously, the internal poison of the apostema is exasperated further, and by contraction, it vents inward and kills. Therefore, continuously fortify the heart itself by constricting its paths internally and externally, evacuate the humours more often, and rectify and purge the poison of the wound. Do not hope for anything certain from those who act against the reason of health; on the contrary, do not cease from remedies because of this in the present, especially if the seventh day has not yet passed.

15.1:
*Compound blistering agents and certain strong plasters*
Blistering agents are compounded in many ways, and are strong in drawing the poison to the outside. We will narrate many, so that you may conveniently use the help of any one according to opportunity. Take figs, orris root, and crushed grains of wheat, in equal parts; this matures it quickly and breaks it. Likewise, ferment leaven/yeast with oil and salt. Likewise, pitch with raisins and honey. Likewise, sparrow dung with pork lard. Likewise, pulverized glass with turpentine. Likewise, if human dung were not abominable, it is worth much before and after the rupture by placing on top the crumb of bread dipped in boiling
15.2: MAR. FIC. EPIDEMIARVM oil. Likewise, oil cooked with ashes. Likewise, ten cantharides blister beetles, with one ounce of raisins, one and a half ounces of leaven, and one ounce each of scabious, houndstongue, greater comfrey, and antidote, incorporated with lily oil. And if you wish to make it stronger, add salt and columbine herb and rue, two drachms of each. Likewise, cress with oil and salt. Likewise, orpiment arsenic trisulphide and pepper, two drachms of each, and ten dried figs; make a plaster with as much honey as suffices. Likewise, borax, sal ammoniac, scabious, antidote, garlic, and pepper, in equal parts; make a plaster with the juice of scabious. Likewise, galbanum, white lily roots, human dung, and greater comfrey ground between two stones. Likewise, four ounces of leaven, one handful each of mustard, rue, scabious, and wormwood, one third part of white lily roots, two drachms of vitriol, ten cantharides, one ounce of galbanum, and three rancid nuts; add as much white lily oil as suffices. Let the herbs and roots be cooked in the oil, and let a plaster be made, adding the other ingredients according to art. Likewise, cantharides with soap oil. Likewise, four parts of oak ashes, which dyers use, and six parts of lime; mix, and when you use it, place the aforementioned plaster on top. But this plaster just mentioned you will make with oil of black olives, and it is stronger if the oil is boiled with the ashes. Likewise, leaven, nettles, the fat of dried meat, marsh-mallow root, and mallow, in equal parts. There are five herbs in this case that are very suitable both in all plasters and also when taken internally, since they resist poison both inside and out, and are, as it were, balanced: namely, consolida comfrey, scabious, agrimony, brictanica great water dock, and aristolochia.

16.1:
*On balanced plasters*
The aforementioned blisters and plasters are very strong, both for breaking open and for quickly extracting poison. But they should not be continued, since they would cause too much inflammation. However, one could use them more where the abscess is not of a very green, red, or black color. And also where there is not much corrosion, I will suggest some more balanced and suitable ones where there is fear of great inflammation. Take two ounces of marsh-mallow root, one head of white lilies, one and a half ounces of linseed flour; let them boil in common water, and let them be pounded with leaven and old lard, and apply it warm. Likewise, take two handfuls of bran not entirely purged of flour, and let it be cooked in vinegar. Likewise, columbine with vinegar and rose oil. Likewise, barley flour with the juice of great water dock or comfrey. Likewise, onions cooked with butter, adding casricas dried figs afterwards, and leaven with camomile oil can be sweetened (if needed due to the vehemence of the pain) by adding cooked apples or marsh-mallow and mallow, and their
16.2: MAR. FIC. EPIDEMIARVM mucilage. But if greater sweetening is needed, take onions cooked and apples cooked, namely with butter and camomile oil. Likewise, mallow, marsh-mallow root, scabious, one handful of each; let the herbs boil in common water, with which the flour is incorporated. Let the herbs be pounded, and let everything be seasoned together with one ounce of hen fat and the same amount of camomile oil, and half a drachm of saffron; it is a most delicate plaster. Likewise, scabious, columbine, chicory, greater comfrey. After these, a plaster of celery, great water dock, and bitter vetch flour is suitable with the juices of the aforementioned herbs, according to some even with theriaca treacle/antidote. Likewise, a plaster of opoponax a medicinal gum resin pounded with raisins. Likewise, asafoetida, rue, and nitre with honey. It will sometimes be good to have been anointed with treacle, with cooked onions and mallow placed on top. Some also place orange blossoms on top, and leaves pounded with lard and mallow. As for the treacle itself, some hold that nothing should be placed on top of it, since it sends the poison back inside.

17.1:
*Most balanced plasters*
When the blister is very black, and excessively burning, and inflames, corrodes, and expands very quickly, the things you administer ought to be more balanced, drying with some degree of coldness, and resolving with balanced heat, for example. Take plantain and galls cooked with vinegar, likewise lentils with mixed bread, mixed with sifted bran. Likewise, sour pomegranates of medium flavor cut into four parts and cooked in vinegar until they dissolve; let them be crushed and applied. They are suitable from the beginning of the disease until the state of decline. This other plaster is suitable before the ulceration caused by the blister. Take acacia, tragacanth, opium, pomegranate bark, one drachm of each, verdigris, white henbane; make a plaster with wine and keep it for use. When you see that ulceration has already occurred, place a somewhat drying plaster on top of it. Take esara perhaps a specific medicinal composition with wine and pomegranate pulp and similar things; take care that the parts surrounding the area do not rot; protect them with Armenian bole, rose water, rose oil, rose vinegar, and the rest. In the retreat of the inflammation, with the ulceration remaining, place a plaster made of litharge and those things which are beneficial for malignant and corrosive wounds—that is, those that cool, dry, and repel—some of which we mentioned above. But make everything balanced, and repeat as is expedient, along with internal purgations.

18.1:
*On the method of mitigating pain around the abscess itself*
The things discussed in the previous chapter are verified in very black and corrosive blisters, but in others not of such great inflammation, be more moderate and more mature in repelling. If you strive to mitigate the burning and pain coming partly from the disease, partly from the blistering agents or from the inflammation,
18.2: MAR. FIC. EPIDEMIARVM place around the affected area the crumb of warm, fresh bread, taken first from the oven, dipped in sharp wine or plantain juice. Likewise, cook the aforementioned crumb, and also lentils, in vinegar; apply and change often, and so that the plaster does not dry out, place plantain leaves on top immediately. When you remove the plaster, let the surface of the wound be washed with sharp or vinegary wine; place barley flour with honey on top. However, I understand that these things should be placed not on, but around the wound, although according to and other learned and experienced men, these things we have mentioned do not repel much, but rather they drive away heat, comfort the place of the pain, and resolve with a certain balanced heat. Treat the remaining wound afterwards with those things that pertain to poisonous and corrosive wounds.

19.1:
*On the method of cutting the rotten flesh of the abscess itself*
When the wound is deadened, take care immediately that this sad flesh falls away. Take bear’s breech, marsh-mallow root, periwinkle herb, mallow leaves, one ounce of each; let them be cooked, pounded, and mixed with unsalted pork lard and old butter; let them be left together for three days; afterwards, let them be strained and pressed, adding a little wax and mastic to the strained liquid; keep it for use. And so that the wound forms a proper crust, which you may afterwards tear away well, when you have used the said plaster, let it be anointed with butter and oil. Do not remove the crust with any violence (that would indeed cause much harm); wait until nature begins to do it by itself, which you may afterwards assist with the aforementioned things. Meanwhile, so that the poison does not corrode and run through the healthy parts of the body, it is necessary to assist in this manner. Have a large cupping glass so that (when it is applied) it encompasses the whole wound in this way: namely, that when placed on top, it touches only the healthy flesh all around, so that the wound cannot be touched by the cupping glass in any part. Therefore, apply this cupping glass so as to draw the poisonous blood from the deep, and to prevent it from turning back inside.

20.1:
*On the method of cleaning the wound*
Once the abscess has ruptured and the matter of the poison has been extracted, constricting and simultaneously cleansing agents must be administered. Take barley flour with honey and a little salt; place cabbage leaves on top. Likewise, pulverized sarcocolla a gum resin and honey in equal parts: if you want it stronger, cook the honey first, but afterwards add the sarcocolla. It is indeed a solemn composition according to and, since it cleanses every wound and every purulent sore. I likewise recommend for this purpose the plaster diaquilon a standard lead-based plaster.

21.1:
*On the method of regenerating good flesh*
When the wound has been cleaned, to regenerate good flesh, take basil leaves
21.2: MAR. FIC. ON EPIDEMICS well pulverized. Item: take yellow-wort, great centaury, five-leaf herb, and great comfrey, ana in equal parts; let it be distilled in the spring through an alembic, or make a juice from these herbs, and let them stand together until they are well mixed. Afterward, add to them a fifth part of aqua vitae brandy or distilled spirit, and keep it for use, for you will find it marvelous in regenerating flesh. Item: the beard of asphodel, that is, burdock, boiled with wine lees, is also beneficial for this. Item: a plaster made of green coriander with honey and raisins.

22.1:
*On the various methods of extracting blood from the sign. On the method of cauterizing by fire*
All the aforementioned care regarding the sign, which (as we narrated before) is done with simple and compound vesicants, would be considered more praiseworthy by the opinion of all Italian doctors if done in the manner we are about to describe, by postponing the vesicants themselves and proceeding as follows: Place cauteries at a distance from the sign, as we have already said, and at the same time place a large cupping glass over the sign. Once it is removed, touch the sign itself in various places with a razor and lancet; afterward, replace the cupping glass to draw blood, and remove it once the attraction of blood ceases. Then, apply three well-purged leeches, and once these are full and removed, cut the chicks of roosters or pigeons or doves in half, and apply them hot, one after the other. After the second one, some must be anointed… with theriac a complex medicinal antidote, then let the animal rest. Some, instead of these, pluck the feathers from the area around the rooster’s anus, and take one ounce of a somewhat dark and almost green soap, and half a scruple of opium, and after pounding them well with very finely pulverized white salt, they make a suppository for the rooster and apply the whole thing on top. Once this is done, restore the patient and afterward cauterize him gently. I do not mean with wax or boiling oil, because they clog, but with gold, or silver, or iron heated to fire; the instrument itself should have a flat, round top in the shape of a fairly large quadrant, and in the middle of this surface, there should be an edge or point in the shape of a diamond, though not too sharp. And after the burning, anoint with butter, cover the place with a cabbage leaf, and let him rest. This is much more preferable to vesicants, because it works more quickly, expels the poison more effectively, and furthermore leaves a better quality in the limb. Afterward, they use the things for placing on the wound, and around it, which we commemorated above to be administered after the vesicant, and in the same way. Some people suffering from the pestilential disease show no other sign than spots, similar to measles, disseminated across the skin of the body. These kinds should be wrapped in a warm crimson cloth and kept from the cold; two large sponges should be applied to the back with the kidneys and the chest, warmed and soaked in a decoction of melilot, chamomile, and lentils, and well squeezed, and on an empty stomach, let them be…
22.2: MAR. FIC. ON EPIDEMICS frequently changed. You shall also give in drink a decoction of dried figs, lentils, kermes grains, and saffron.

23.1:
*On the treatment according to the custom of the Spanish and Catalans*
We have spoken in the preceding sections about the treatment of this kind of disease according to the intention of the Greeks, the Latins, and also the Barbarians, and especially according to the usage of the Italians; but at present, we shall consider these medicines according to the custom of the Spaniards, and likewise the Catalans. Therefore, according to them, a clyster enema is performed immediately; afterward, if blood abounds, phlebotomy bloodletting. If not, medicine is exhibited according to the quality of the peccant humor. From the beginning, they apply an epithem a liquid topical medication; then, after some evacuation has been made, at least with a clyster, they proceed to the treatment of the aposteme abscess/swelling. According to their custom, nothing inflammatory or burning should be placed on the aposteme, because they induce spasms, ignite fevers, and make the poison more malignant, especially if the aposteme is in the emunctories glandular regions like the armpits or groin. They also say that maturatives substances that ripen sores and maceratives should not be applied at the beginning, since they cause gluing, clogging, putrefaction, and overheating, and drive the poison inward. Nor do they say that cold things should be administered, nor anything (because it dries) with a sponge, nor with a cloth because it encloses vapors inside and constricts. But it is laudable to use clean wool or tow coarse flax fiber (especially from hemp); the present decoction is most familiar, especially to those who are… naturally delicate, and even in the emunctories: Take chamomile flowers, melilot, maidenhair fern; let them boil in water, soak the wool or tow, squeeze it out with your hands, apply it lukewarm or slightly warm, and renew it every hour until it resolves or opens. Afterward, once the fifth day has passed since the opening, use maturatives and things that cleanse and regenerate. For boils, so that they may be ruptured safely, pulverized scabious is applied, either alone or with old pig lard and salt. If the boil is green or black, but is not in the emunctories, open it suddenly in various places with a lancet or razor so that the poison may quickly exit. Then wash the boil with salt water so that coagulated blood does not remain there, and apply leeches. After it has been ruptured and purged of poison, once the fifth day has passed (as above), apply maturatives, cleansers, and regenerators. Besides these (unless the patient is of a very tender age), a large cupping glass should be placed not on top of, but below the boil at a distance of six fingers. Afterward, an opening should be made with a lancet or razor, and the cupping glass should be applied again to draw the blood, specifically two or three ounces, or even more according to the state and consent of the strength. Take care, when the sign is in the emunctories, not to apply cupping glasses to the sign itself, nor to incise it, nor to disturb it too much by using cupping glasses frequently, because in this way spasms are increased, many hot humors are drawn, the poison is made worse, and many perish by doing so. But if…
23.2: MAR. FIC. ON EPIDEMICS the sign appears near the ears or in the throat, apply the cupping glass backward below the vertebrae of the neck, not on top or on the shoulder blades. If, however, it appears under the arms, apply the cupping glass below on the same side, slanting toward the back. If in the groin, apply the cupping glass to the thigh or backward below the buttocks. In any of these cases, do it thus: place the cupping glass at a distance of six fingers away from the sign (as we have said), and by scarifying, draw the blood with cupping glasses or leeches. But on top of the sign, you will place the aforementioned decoction so that it may temperately soothe and resolve it. Along with the decoction, it would be good if you could apply some poison-drawing stone, pulverized or whole, such as emerald, hyacinth, or topaz. However, according to some of these people, we may apply leeches to the sign, and sometimes even cupping glasses. Even if it is in the emunctories, nothing should be done with violence; afterward, wash with salt water. This is done when the sign is extremely swollen or of a bad color; and when the sign has been opened, after the fifth day has passed, they use maturatives. But if this very decoction performs the least amount of operation, you shall reduce it to the form of a drip or drop. When the aposteme itself is more swollen than usual, some, after the third day, forcefully incise it along the length of the limb in which the sign appears, specifically through the spaces between, avoiding veins and arteries. And if blood were to flow too much, they meet it with tow soaked in egg yolk and oil of roses. but not in egg white, because it is cold and viscous. At that time, they comfort the sick with cordials internally and externally. Truly, the wiser among these do not approve of this incision, judging it to be of the greatest danger, especially in the emunctoria glandular drainage sites/lymph nodes. But after the fifth day, if the fever is not severe and the sign is not very poisonous, black, or green, and if it also approaches rupture, with the body well purged, begin with maturatives agents that ripen an abscess after you have done what we have said, in order to ripen the apostema abscess/swelling. Take the root of marsh mallow, the root of lilies, elecampane, wild cucumber, onions, half a pound of each; of fat figs, fenugreek seed, linseed, one ounce of each; of the leaves of marsh mallow, bear’s breech, violet herb, one handful of each. Let them be boiled vigorously in water and well crushed. If this maturative is made for delicate persons, the aforementioned should be strained, boiled, crushed, and pressed. Afterward, add one pound of fresh pig lard, melted and strained, or as much as is sufficient. Some add snails, well crushed, together with the shell; for this is appropriate where the skin is very thick, such as in the groins and behind the ears. Others add leaven and coarse bread, two ounces of each, or more or less, according to the opportunity for drawing and rupturing, which is a method more suitable for blisters than for the swellings of the emunctoria. There are also other, lighter maturatives, such as wheat flour boiled together with oil and water until they reach a slight consistency.
23.3: MAR. FIC. ON EPIDEMICS or with the crumb of bran bread, and with fat figs boiled together and afterward crushed. We can add olive oil, or oil of sweet almonds, or fresh pig lard. If such lard were old and salted, this poultice would be useful for gently rupturing blisters. We can also add fresh chicken fat if a poultice is made with such fat, lard, and fresh butter, violet oil, and boiled lily roots for the delicate and infirm. These kinds of maturatives (as we said before) must be made after purging, when the fever has ceased, and after the sign is opened and purged of poison, even after the fifth day has passed. Then they use mundificatives cleansing agents, afterward regeneratives, and lastly consolidatives healing agents for the sign. If the blister is black or green and corrosive, and it is not in the emunctoria, cut it with a deep incision using a lancet or razor. Afterward, you will administer a drip with somewhat warm salt water, so that the blood (as we have said) may not coagulate; then apply a cupping glass or leeches, or the plucked-out vent of a cock. Some apply a living snail, some a living frog; however, this can be done when the sign is not in the emunctoria. Afterward, apply some simple rupturing agent, which we have provided above, or even this one: take an egg yolk with a little salt, but no stronger, because it would worsen the blister. This should be changed often. But if even this were to irritate the blister too much, use only crushed scabious, or old salted pig lard, or both together. both together. There are some very strong rupturing agents that ought not to be placed over the emunctoria, nor where a severe fever is present, and even if they are placed where the fever is not so strong, they are of very little benefit. Take raw figs and leaven. Furthermore, if this does not work, they make this stronger, while observing the manner and order narrated. Take well-crushed cantharides and a third part of pig lard; place this over the poisoned blister three or four times. Surgeons say this is often tested; when they wish to have it even stronger, they add a fourth part of fuller’s soap, which they say acts wonderfully on a malignant blister in a robust man. Also, another strong one for blisters: take half an ounce of well-pulverized glass, one ounce of wheat grains crushed or chewed by the teeth, two egg yolks, one dram of saffron, one ounce of turpentine; let them be mixed well and applied with clean tow. Others apply quicklime with soap. But because such burning and violent things frequently make the apostema and fevers more malignant, it is safer to ensure before ulceration that the material does not return inward, and that it does not become as if rabid by these sharp things, especially in weak constitutions or in those who are very choleric. Therefore, for these intentions, it is useful to apply Galen’s poultice over the entire limb. Take plantain, lentils, bran bread, in equal parts; let them be boiled in water until they reach a certain
23.4: MAR. FIC. ON EPIDEMICS solid consistency, and apply it to the place of pain and all around over a wide space. Avicenna adds galls where more subtle blood appears than the compact kind. Also, for this, a poultice of sweet pomegranates and acidic fruits boiled in vinegar and water is useful, especially where burning material appears. However, after the heat begins to cease, Avicenna’s poultice is appropriate, made of fat figs, raisins, nuts, and barley flour, boiled together to ripen and rupture. After the rupture has occurred, the wound should be cleansed with the juices of parsley, wormwood, and plantain, with honey of roses and flour, boiled with a little washed turpentine; then it is consolidated according to the order of other wounds. Indeed, an ointment made of Armenian bole and rose oil is placed around it. Some, from the beginning, because of the strong attraction, place the herb flammula (that is, crushed dodder) between the muscles of the calves or the arm, or over the shoulder blades, which, by causing ulceration of the emunctoria, draws the humors to itself and away from the principal members. This remedy is useful in robust bodies and where no fever is present, but not elsewhere or otherwise. Some perform an actual cautery upon the sign with a red-hot iron, which is more appropriate for the robust and where the fever is not severe. Raymond says that theriac and Armenian bole do not draw the poison to themselves but drive it far away; therefore, he says they should not be taken by mouth after the second or third day, when the material is already poisonous and has touched the heart itself, unless it has been well evacuated and corrected. Furthermore, he forbids them ever to be placed upon the sign, nor does he want them applied unless the sign is outside the emunctoria, and also before the third day, and in the surrounding area, not on top. The Armenian bole can be administered even after the seventh day, once the wound has been purged of poison, by anointing the surrounding area. Thus, therefore, it is appropriate in the third day before the wound has become poisonous, and it is appropriate after the seventh day, after the wound has been purged of poison. However, the surrounding area should be anointed with rose oil, rose vinegar, and rose water to defend the limb. Up to this point, we have related the opinions of the Spaniards and Catalans, along with the corrections of Arnold and Raymond, those singular physicians. The truth is, and Raymond is of this opinion, namely that the infirm should not be purged with bloodletting, medicine, or vomiting when the apostema is very full and poisonous (that is, once the second day has passed), lest the poison be turned inward by such motion. This opinion seems to require correction according to others, namely that it ought to be purged if there is need (with the stated observations) even after the second day, but in such a way that while it is being purged, you apply cupping glasses and leeches below and above the sign, and that the heart is defended internally and externally with cold cordials. And this method, too, is not entirely alien to the intention of the aforementioned Raymond.

24.1:
*On the preservation of those who stand by and care for the sick*
In addition to what has been said at the beginning for preservation (namely the theriac an antidote or counter-poison, pills, and similar things), those who attend the sick, unless they have been emptied of bloody superfluity, ought to extract a little blood from the common vein, having performed a good purging with one drachm, or at least half a drachm, of the aforementioned pills. It is useful to frequently inhale powders and medicine against the disease, as has been said in the preceding chapters, and they should remain as far as possible from the sick, especially when they are fasting. The living space should be frequently aired, and fumigations should be performed as mentioned above, never omitting turpentine. They should carry in their hands burning torches and coals well-lit and smoking with good odors, and they should wash their whole body with warm vinegar twice a day, namely morning and evening. They should change their clothes often, and renew the fumigations more frequently, especially with frankincense, turpentine, juniper, myrtle, sandalwood, roses, and camphor or rosemary, laurel, and similar things. One should hold in the hands an orange and a bundle of rue or greater celandine, and mint and lemon balm with myrtle and fresh flowerets; one should always be well-purged of all excess in custom and food. Repeat again that health-giving scent with rose water, rose vinegar, malmsey wine, zedoary, or lemon peels; above all, let them wash their hands and face with these things often. Of which also of this composition they should drink a little, and also hold to the nostrils a sponge dipped in the same mixture, tied to a staff of ash wood: since ash has such great power against poison that no poisonous animal dares to approach its shadow, nor its scent; for it would rather concede itself spontaneously to be consumed by fire than adhere closely to this tree. Let them make fires and hearths quite often throughout the whole house, especially with wood and odoriferous things. And let not him who has once been freed from this disease think that he cannot subsequently perish in this case, because in the present year this disease attacked one of our Florentines three times; who, although perfectly freed the second time, could not escape death the third. Again, in the same year in the month of September, I freed a certain little woman from the plague; she was indeed healthy, just like the others who had remained safe, but when she moved among the diseased, she was reinfected after eighteen days and perished. No one should be confident in the fact that he is stronger and healthier than others, since the poison destroys the strong just as it does the weak. Indeed, this poison offends the sanguine and robust more than the rest, because the paths of the chest are open to them, and they have a very hot heart and much hot and humid blood; therefore, the very heat of the heart pulls in much pernicious air through the open passages, and indeed pulls it in suddenly, before it can be tempered by the transition. For the heat of the blood is stirred up very quickly and
24.2: MAR. FIC. EPIDEMIARVM it is inflamed. The humidity is immediately subject to putrefaction and is converted into poison. Just as the more wine there is in a vessel, and the more potent it is, it turns into that much more, and that much more biting, vinegar, so the blood in the chest becomes potent into poison in proportion to how abundant and hot it is. Indeed, when the blood itself becomes poison, it is very easily transformed into the same state by the slightest contact with it. For parts that touch each other convert themselves into poison. Nor should you overlook this, O you who care for the patient: the closer you are to them, whether by kinship, or by the correspondence of complexion, nature, or constellation, the greater is the danger of contagion to which you are subject. This is because there is a certain readiness in the quality for transfer, so that a transformation can be fulfilled from like to like, just as fire to air, air to water, and water to earth. And when two lutes or two lyres are played in the same key, then the movement resonates, and the voice of the one passes into the other.
24.3: If you ask through what paths the poison enters, I answer that it enters through all the pores of the body, especially those that are most open. It offends more quickly when it enters through the nostrils, the mouth, and the pulses. It is much stronger if it finds paths open in hot, humid, and subtle humors. Even though it also arises from similar humors, if the influence of Mars occurs with a different and contrary mode, and with the influence of Saturn, it manifests itself more slowly. It often remains in clothing for a long time & for a long time, and through the open paths of the skin and veins near the heart, nor is anyone seen to be burdened by it, because it is a little bit, a light vapor, nor does it have such contrariety to other parts as it does to the heart itself; yet when it first becomes contiguous to the heart, it harms it manifestly, not secretly. Similarly, the poison of a mad dog, and indeed other things, reveal their harm even after a long time. Finally, I would have you know that the poison remains in persons for a period of two months. Walls, iron tools, and things constructed of wood, unless they are corrected with washings, fumigations, and fires, perhaps reserve their poisonous nature for a year or more. Woolen clothes and that type, unless they are aired, washed, and frequently fumigated, or placed by the fire, to the wind, or to the sun for three years and more, remain infected. You know indeed the musty odor of an orange in which a capsule has grown moldy, which is preserved for many years. Similarly, the odor of musk remains for a long time in the cotton where it was before. Indeed, as fire is to oil, so wool is the food of this poison, and indeed this wool nourishes the poison so that it not only preserves it but also increases and simultaneously strengthens it. One must not use the vessels of those who are infected for food or drink, nor should anything that has adhered to them be touched. You must live pleasantly, because joy comforts the vital spirit; live continuously and soberly, since sobriety and restraint are of such value that, through them alone, Socrates the philosopher kept himself unharmed in many and indeed grave pestilences (which had been at Athens).
24.4: Therefore, Aristotle and Galen say that such is the disposition in pure bodies that they almost never feel the plague, or if they are infected, they at least do not perish. Behold, I now hand to you two singular things to preserve yourself. Have an emerald prepared so that it can be drunk, so that it can be touched, held in the mouth, and suspended from the neck, the virtue of which against poisons is so great that, as witnessed by Rasi, Auenzoar, Serapio, fires and buboes fall from the body by its mere sight. I am accustomed to give the poor wild radish, a little at a time so that it does not inflame the blood, for it has such efficacy against poison that it makes a scorpion break apart at its touch: and Dioscorides says that if the hands are washed with its seed ground with vinegar, and one touches serpents, they cannot do harm. The Bezoar stone (if one could have it) is worth more than all against poisons, for although in the Persian idiom all that is called bezoar by the ancients has the property and virtue of expelling poisons. Yet according to Serapio and Rasi, the Bezoar stone is primarily called a certain stone resisting all poisons, whether hot or cold bites, or all poisonous ulcers by its virtue, and it helps whether it is taken by mouth, held in the mouth, suspended from the neck, or finally applied externally in any way. It originates in Syria, in India, and in the parts of the Orient, and is diverse, of three different colors.
24.5: For some is light-blue and dark, some light-blue, dark, and green, but another is white and somewhat light-blue, namely similar to the color of clear white wine; this is the best among the rest, light, delicate, soft, without taste, shining like light. Its dose, when it is received by mouth, is twelve grains. Rasi and Serapio testify that they often found in their own times that this most precious stone surpassed all medicines, whether simple or compound, and even compound theriacs, by its own quality in resisting poisons. Hahamed says it should be bound in a ring and an image of a scorpion inscribed on the stone when the moon is in Scorpio, regarding the Ascendant. When this is done, frankincense should be sealed with it when the moon is in the sign of Scorpio. And if afterwards you give of such pulverized frankincense in the required amount in a poisoned drink, it will be as effective against poisons as the stone itself. Abdallahamarach says that he saw this stone, which he says the son of Mamari had bought, and that he himself had given a palace in Cordoba for the solution of the stone. Serapio says that the same stone works wonders not only in men but also in certain other animals; first, that by touching the sting of a scorpion with this stone, it loses its power of stinging. Furthermore, he asserts that when ground and mixed with water and put into the mouth of a serpent, it kills it.

25.1:
*Flee quickly, far away, and return slowly*
It seemed best to reserve the declaration of the principal rules in this matter until the end of the book. Flee the company of men as much as you can, especially when you are fasting. You should always remain apart from a companion by the space of at least two cubits, and in a free, open place; and when you speak with him, remain even further apart, at least by an interval of six cubits, and under the open sky or in an airy place. Beware that the breath of the winds does not blow from him toward you. Between yourself and him, let there be the sun, fire, odors, or a wind tending toward him; for narrow places, as well as crowds of people, are very dangerous. I also remind you that morbid contagion is multiplied by the proximity of walls and the contact and continuation of houses. Above all, I advise that you flee quickly and far away from those places where the plague threatens, and return slowly. I said “quickly”— that is, as soon as the signs of an approaching plague appear. These signs are indeed when the air of that place seems to be outside its natural disposition, leaning toward hot and humid; when it appears misty, with dense clouds and dust; when winds are heavy and tepid; and also when the waters and fields smoke and smell, and likewise the fish are of bad taste and odor. When many animals born from putrefaction appear over the earth, and there is an abundance of fungi and rotting herbs, the fruits of the earth and animals are insipid and are preserved poorly; they become turbid. and alive. Many terrestrial and aerial animals depart from that place. Unusual fevers arise—latent, furious, continuous, deceptive—with anxiety of the chest, prostration of the pulse, phrenesis, turbu lence of the urine, excoriation of the palate and intestines, redness of the eyes, worms, measles, many disturbances of women, rabid anger, quarrels, dire wars, monsters of nature, and signs, either from nature or from God, that are wondrous, greatly unseen, and rare. These things which we have mentioned are the omens of an approaching plague. Therefore, flee then before you become one of the twelve thousand signed. This, in truth, can happen in two ways: either because you will have already been caught by the contagion of the infected, or because you will have already received the sad quality of the infected air, so that that air gradually becomes familiar to you, in such a way that neither your nature resists the air, nor the air resists it. But if you seek another air suddenly, the first air will depart and your nature will resist it, and from this nature comes the origin of the plague. And I also advise that you flee far away, namely, that you betake yourself to those places to which neither things, nor people, nor sounds, noises, or rumors of the infected place can reach you. And be so remote that high mountains intervene, by which the access of vapors may be prohibited, so that they cannot touch you by the breath of winds or the dilation of air. Consider the disposition and situation of the place to which you run; namely, that it may not be similar in any way to the pestilential air, such as in heat, cold, humidity, dryness, clouds, rains, or winds. Finally, be established in such a place, so that winds, clouds, and rains cannot in any way blow, dilate, or move from there toward you. Nor should it escape you that the horoscopus the Ascendant or rising sign of any infected city or castle often extends the plague to all those places that lie under it from the beginning of the city or castle, and which have some conformity with that Ascendant. Thirdly, we say that you should return slowly, because the infection remaining from the past illness, even if it is very small, is powerful enough to suddenly stain all those who began their flight even at a not-untimely hour. For those who frequent an infected place after having fled it earlier are subject to greater danger than those who always remained there, though with caution, because nature tolerates sudden and new accidents poorly. And besides this, these qualities (as we said before) remain for a very long time in walls, woodwork, clothes, any cloths, and the rest. As for the disposition of the air alone, one condition is sufficient: so that where all who are there have remained immune from this disease for three months, it can be judged that the air is by then purified. But be most cautious in the approach and contact of those things that retain poison more than the air does. The structure of furnaces in walls preserves poisonous heat longer than wood; but it is purified (as we have often said) with fires, washings, ventings, fumigations, odors, and the rest. People are generally purified in the space of fourteen days: houses, woodwork, and the rest in twenty-one. Cloths, garments, and things of this sort in the space of twenty-eight days. During these times, have separate vessels for drinking and eating, as well as any bedding, or at least, if you cannot do so for other things, have the linens purified by washings and fumigations. Horses, money, furniture, baggage, and similar things, unless you act very cautiously, are accustomed to keeping the poison for a long time; therefore, be vigilant, cautious, and prudent, and provide for all things in an orderly fashion.

1.1: The regimen of life useful at any time of the year.
1.2: It will also be very beautiful to consider the seasons of the year in the regimen of life. In winter, one must use both stronger exercise and fuller food, especially if the weather is northern. If, however, it is southern, it is proper to exercise similarly, but to remove something from the food and drink. And on the whole, throughout the humid time, make the body altogether dry; but through the cold time, make it warmer, and then eat warmer meats and vegetables, and drink wine more undiluted.
1.3: With the arrival of Spring, let one be evacuated by vomiting, another by the bowels, and another by bloodletting from an opened vein, according to everyone’s custom or promptness of mind. In Summer, rest is beneficial, as is lighter exercise and scanty food, which indeed must be chosen from a cooler kind. Then, however, it is proper to add to the drink, and to apply whatever can cool and moisten. Throughout Autumn, there is a need for greater caution, since it is uneven and disordered in every way, and introduces multiform diseases. Therefore, one must beware lest any error be made regarding cooling, and one must also abstain from venery and cold drink. Nor indeed should one trust oneself to the air, neither during the morning cold nor during the midday heat. It is harmful to be filled with fruits, not only because of satiety, but also because vicious humors are born from them, and they also excite flatulence, if indeed
1.4: The best of all fruits, figs and grapes, both produce flatulence and spoil the nourishment if they are consumed before other foods. When they are taken beforehand, however, they neither cause bloating nor corruption. When the air begins to grow cold, it is necessary to warm the body in proportion to the cold, and to do everything as one does when winter has already advanced. It would not be out of place, once the equinox has passed, to cleanse the body using one of the methods we have mentioned, so that any redundancy retained during the winter does not cause distress.
